## 1. Executive Summary

### 1.1 What Suraksha is

Suraksha (brand: Suraksha / Suraksha Guards, primary domain **surakshaguards.in**) is a private-security company that is simultaneously building the **digital infrastructure layer for Indian private security guarding**. It runs two connected businesses on one platform:

1. **Suraksha's own guarding operation (B2C + B2B services).** Suraksha deploys PSARA-licensed armed and unarmed guards, PSOs, bouncers, patrol staff and supervisors to homes, housing societies/RWAs, offices, factories, warehouses and events. Revenue is service revenue per guard per month (live anchors: unarmed from ₹18,500/month, armed officer/PSO from ₹38,000/month, plan cards at Home & Society ₹18,000 · Business ₹22,000 · Enterprise custom, all excluding 18% GST) [CONFIRMED]. This operation is itself a tenant on the platform — tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ`.
2. **Software and reach sold to the rest of the industry (B2B SaaS).** India has approximately 35,000 PSARA-verified licensed private security agencies [ASSUMPTION: A-001]. Suraksha sells them (a) discovery and credibility via the **TRINETRA** marketplace and (b) the **Agency Portal**, a full agency-operations SaaS on Starter ₹5,000 / Professional ₹10,000 / Enterprise "Contact Sales" plans [CONFIRMED].

The strategic thesis is that these two businesses are not a distraction from each other — they are the same asset used twice. Running a real guarding operation is what makes the software correct: rosters, wake-checks, replacement flows and invoice disputes are specified from lived operations, not from interviews. Selling the software is what makes the guarding operation national: Suraksha does not need a PSARA licence in every state to be present in every state, because the agencies already licensed there become supply, and the marketplace becomes the demand router. Neither half is defensible alone; together they compound — more agencies produce more verified supply, more supply wins more demand, more demand makes the SaaS indispensable.

### 1.4 Strategic thesis in five statements

| # | Statement | Consequence for the product |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | Guarding is a **proof business**, not a manpower business. Clients are not buying a person; they are buying evidence that the post was covered. | Attendance, patrol, wake-check and incident data are the product, not a feature. Every surface exposes proof. |
| T2 | The industry's operating system today is **paper, Excel and WhatsApp**. | The product must beat WhatsApp on speed and beat paper on trust, in Hindi, on a ₹7,000 Android phone. |
| T3 | **Licence geography** determines who may legally serve where. | Licence is a first-class object with state/district scope, expiry and verification state — not a PDF in a folder (§3.4). |
| T4 | The guard is the **weakest-served** participant and the highest-leverage one. | Guard identity, verified work history, on-time salary visibility and portable portfolio are strategic, not charity. |
| T5 | Trust in this market is **transferable**: verification done once can be sold many times. | Verification (agency licence, guard KYC, police verification, training) is built as a reusable platform service. |

### 1.5 How to read this document

**Requirement IDs.** Every substantive requirement carries an ID of the form `SUR-<AREA>-<nnn>` (three digits, zero-padded). Sections 1–10 use area code `PLT` (platform-wide foundation). Section 11 uses `B2C`, section 12 `B2B`, section 13 `B2G`. The full area-code table lives in the canon. Requirement IDs are stable: once assigned, an ID is never reused for a different requirement, even if the original is withdrawn (a withdrawn requirement is marked `[WITHDRAWN]` and kept in place). Business rules use `BR-nnn`, test cases `TC-<AREA>-nnn`, risks `R-nnn`, assumptions `A-nnn`, decisions `D-nnn`.

**Honesty labels.** Nothing in this document pretends to be settled when it is not. Five inline markers are used:

| Label | Meaning | What a reader should do |
|---|---|---|
| `[CONFIRMED]` | Stated by the founders or visible in the live product. | Build it. |
| `[RECOMMENDED]` | Our professional recommendation; safe to build; not yet founder-ratified. | Build it unless management objects. |
| `[ASSUMPTION: A-xxx]` | A belief the plan rests on that has not been validated. | Validate before it becomes expensive to be wrong. |
| `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-xxx]` | Management must choose; we have not chosen silently. | Blocks the affected work item until answered. |
| `[FUTURE]` | Deliberately out of current scope. | Do not build now; do not architect it away either. |

**Cross-references.** Each concept has exactly one canonical home. This part of the document owns the ecosystem map, product inventory, personas, roles, and the B2C/B2B/B2G lifecycles. It deliberately does **not** contain screen-by-screen UI (§14–§25), the permission matrix (§31), the data model (§32), or step-form workflows (§29). Where those are needed, this part cross-references them rather than restating them.

**Open items.** Every unresolved question raised in this part is tagged inline **and** repeated in the "Open items raised here" table at the end, using the `D-1xx` / `A-1xx` / `R-1xx` ranges reserved for sections 1–25. The consolidated registers live in §53–§55.

## 2. Vision

### 2.1 Positioning statement

**Suraksha is the digital infrastructure layer for Indian private security guarding.** Not a guard supplier that happens to have an app; not a software vendor that happens to know security. The infrastructure claim means three specific things:

- **Identity layer.** A guard, an agency and a licence each have one verified digital identity that other participants can rely on without re-verifying.
- **Proof layer.** Duty performed anywhere in the network produces tamper-evident, timestamped, geo-anchored evidence that a client, an agency and a regulator-facing audit can all read from the same record.
- **Transaction layer.** Demand for guarding finds licensed, verified supply, and money moves through the same rails that carry the proof — so billing is a consequence of attendance rather than an argument about it.

### 2.2 Three-year vision (through FY 2029)

| Dimension | Three-year target state |
|---|---|
| Own guarding operation | Profitable, multi-city, running entirely on the platform with zero paper registers; a reference implementation the sales team can show live. |
| Agency SaaS | The default operating software for small and mid-size PSARA agencies in the states Suraksha covers; measured in paying tenants, not signups. |
| Marketplace | The most complete public directory of verified PSARA agencies in India, with verification status that buyers actually trust. |
| Guard workforce | A guard's Suraksha profile is worth carrying between employers because it holds verified KYC, training, tenure and duty record. |
| Data | The largest structured dataset of Indian guarding operations: attendance patterns, attrition, wage benchmarks, incident taxonomy. |
| Government | Credible B2G participation: tenders tracked, bids submitted, contracts serviced with SLA evidence. |

### 2.3 Ten-year vision (through FY 2036)

| Dimension | Ten-year ambition |
|---|---|
| Category | "Suraksha-verified" is the phrase a procurement officer uses when specifying a guarding vendor, the way "ISO-certified" is used today. |
| Network | A national supply network where any client requirement in any serviceable district is matched to a licensed agency within minutes, with SLA-backed fulfilment. |
| Workforce | A guard's verified work portfolio is portable across the industry and unlocks adjacent services (training, credit, insurance, benefits) [FUTURE]. |
| Platform | An open API layer that HRMS, ERP, facility-management and insurance systems integrate with, making Suraksha the record of truth for guarding delivery. |
| Adjacency | Extension into adjacent verified-manpower categories (facility management, housekeeping, technical manpower) using the same identity/proof/transaction spine [FUTURE]. |
| Public value | Attendance, wage-timeliness and training data that materially improves conditions for the guard workforce and gives buyers real quality signal. |

### 2.4 What winning looks like

Winning is not "most downloads". Winning is four observable behaviours:

1. An RWA secretary in a tier-2 city cancels their incumbent guarding vendor because the Suraksha app proved the night guard was asleep and the incumbent could not disprove it.
2. A 40-guard agency owner stops maintaining an Excel roster within 30 days of signing, because the portal is faster than the spreadsheet, not because they were told to.
3. A guard chooses one agency over another because the first one pays through a system where he can see his attendance and payslip.
4. A procurement officer at a PSU shortlists on the basis of a Suraksha verification badge and an SLA report they can download themselves.

### 2.5 North-star and supporting metrics

| ID | Metric | Definition | Why it is the right measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| NS-1 | **Verified Guard-Shifts Delivered (VGSD) per month** | Count of shifts that produced a complete, geo-verified check-in and check-out with no unresolved exception, across all tenants. | It is the single number that rises only when real duty is really performed and really proven. It cannot be inflated by signups, page views, or listings. |
| S-1 | Proof completeness rate | VGSD ÷ total rostered shifts. | Measures whether the proof layer actually works in the field. |
| S-2 | Paying agency tenants | Tenants with an active paid subscription and ≥1 guard active in the last 30 days. | Filters out dormant signups. |
| S-3 | Tenant 90-day retention | Share of tenants still active and paying at day 90. | The only honest early signal for SaaS in this market. |
| S-4 | Client-reported post-failure rate | Client-raised incidents of absent/sleeping/unreplaced guard per 1,000 shifts. | The trust metric the whole B2C promise rests on. |
| S-5 | Salary-on-time rate | Share of payroll runs disbursed on or before the committed date, per tenant. | The guard-side loyalty driver. |
| S-6 | Time-to-fill a replacement | Median minutes from replacement trigger to a confirmed guard en route. | Operational competence, and the hardest thing for competitors to copy. |
| S-7 | Verified agency listings | Marketplace listings that passed licence verification and are unexpired. | The marketplace's only real inventory. |
| S-8 | Quote-to-contract conversion | B2B quotations accepted ÷ quotations issued. | Commercial health of the enterprise lane. |

Numeric targets per horizon are set in §51 Roadmap; this section defines the metrics, not the targets. Instrumentation contracts for each metric are owned by §42 Analytics.

## 3. Industry Context

### 3.1 The two sectors of Indian security

India's security provision splits into a government/public sector and a private sector. Suraksha operates **entirely in the private sector** [CONFIRMED]. The distinction matters to the product because the two sectors have different legal bases, different personnel types, and different relationships to the platform: government forces are never platform users, but they are the counterparty in escalation (police response to an SOS), the source of verification (police verification of guards), the regulator (MHA/PSARA), and — for B2G — the customer.

| Sector | Bodies and personnel types | Relationship to Suraksha |
|---|---|---|
| Government / public | State Police forces; Central Armed Police Forces (CRPF, CISF, BSF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles); the Armed Forces (Army, Navy, Air Force); Special Protection Group (SPG) for designated protectees; National Security Guard (NSG); state armed constabulary; Home Guards; Railway Protection Force (RPF); Forest and Excise enforcement wings. | Not users. Appear as: escalation counterparty (§24), verification source (police verification), regulator (MHA/PSARA), B2G customer (§13), and as a recruitment source — ex-servicemen and retired police are the premium supply pool for PSO and supervisory roles. |
| Private | Private Security Agencies (PSAs) and their personnel: unarmed guards, armed guards, PSOs/close protection officers, bouncers, supervisors, field officers, patrol staff, gunmen for cash-in-transit, dog handlers, control-room operators, fire-and-safety staff, women guards for frisking/female premises. | This is the entire operating field of the platform. |

CISF deserves specific mention because it is the boundary case: it provides security to designated critical installations and, under its consultancy wing, to certain private industrial units. Where a client considers CISF cover, the private lane competes on cost and flexibility, not on statutory footing. The platform makes no claim of equivalence.

### 3.2 The private-security manpower taxonomy

This taxonomy is the vocabulary of every quotation, roster and payroll line in the platform. It must exist as configurable reference data (`guard_category`) with rate cards attached, not as an enum in code.

| Category | Typical deployment context | Distinguishing requirement | Typical shift pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unarmed security guard | Housing societies, offices, retail, hospitals, schools, warehouses | PSARA-mandated training; basic literacy; uniform | 8h or 12h, day/night rotation |
| Armed security guard / gunman | Banks, ATMs, jewellery, cash-in-transit, high-value warehouses | Valid arms licence held by the agency or individual per applicable state rules; separate training and weapon custody records | 8h, usually day-weighted |
| Personal Security Officer (PSO) / close protection | Executives, political figures, HNIs, film and event personalities | Higher physical/training standard; often ex-forces or ex-police; discretion and travel readiness; frequently armed | 12h or travel-based, multi-shift teams |
| Bouncer / crowd management | Nightclubs, concerts, weddings, sports venues, political rallies | Physical standard; crowd-control training; event-day surge staffing | Event blocks of 4/6/8/12 hours |
| Supervisor (field) | Any site with ≥6 guards, or a cluster of small sites | Guard-management competence; reporting; smartphone literacy | Overlapping day shift, plus night rounds |
| Field Officer / patrol officer | Multi-site cluster within a city | Two-wheeler/vehicle mobility; night round checks across sites | Roving, including night checks |
| Night patrol staff | Gated colonies, industrial estates, construction sites | Checkpoint discipline; anti-sleep wake-check compliance | Night only |
| Women security guard | Female frisking points, hospitals, schools, malls, women's hostels, event female-search lanes | Female-only deployment requirement; safe-transport and facility considerations | Day-weighted; night only with documented safeguards |
| Dog handler (K9) | Industrial estates, event venues, VIP advance checks | Handler certification; animal welfare and boarding logistics | Site-specific |
| Fire & safety / ERT staff | Factories, malls, high-rises | Fire-safety training certificate; equipment familiarity | Shift-based |
| Control-room / CCTV operator | Corporate campuses, industrial units, command posts | Screen-monitoring discipline; incident logging literacy | 8h, three-shift |
| Housekeeping-attached manpower | Bundled facility contracts | Not security personnel; appears in the same invoice | Day-weighted |

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-PLT-013 | Guard categories must be reference data with per-category attributes: armed/unarmed, gender constraint, required certifications, minimum age/height where a client contract specifies it, default shift length, and a rate-card link. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-014 | The platform must support a deployment being priced and rostered against a category, so a replacement is validated as category-equivalent before it is accepted (see BR reference in §30). | [RECOMMENDED] |

### 3.3 PSARA / PASARA — the regulatory frame

The private security industry is regulated by **PSARA (Private Security Agencies Regulation Act)**, administered under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, with licences issued by state-level controlling authorities [CONFIRMED]. The product treats the regulation as data, never as hard-coded logic, and this document states no legal conclusions.

The operationally decisive facts for the product:

- Licences are issued at **state** level and at **district** level [CONFIRMED].
- An agency that wants to operate across four states requires **four separate state licences** — one per state [CONFIRMED]. There is no single national licence for a private security agency.
- An agency operating only within one city/district takes a district-scoped licence [CONFIRMED].
- Licences carry a validity period and are renewable; lapse has operational consequences that the platform must be able to enforce as configured restrictions (BR-002).
- Guard-side verification and training obligations sit alongside the agency licence: police verification of personnel and prescribed training are tracked per guard as documents with expiry.

### 3.4 Why licence geography is a first-class product object

Every meaningful platform behaviour depends on knowing *where an agency may lawfully operate*, and that is not a text field.

| Platform behaviour | Dependency on licence geography |
|---|---|
| Marketplace search and filtering | An agency appears for "Gujarat" only if it holds a live licence with Gujarat scope. |
| Demand routing / allocation | A booking in district X is offered only to agencies with X in scope (state licence covering X, or district licence for X). |
| Verification badge | The badge is per licence, per state — not a global company badge. An agency verified in Rajasthan is not thereby verified in Maharashtra. |
| Compliance dashboard and alerts | Expiry countdown must be per licence, so a Karnataka expiry alerts the Karnataka branch. |
| Onboarding gate | Tenant activation requires at least one live licence; expanding to a new state requires a new licence record. |
| Tender eligibility (§13) | Most government tenders require a licence valid in the tendering state, often with a validity horizon beyond contract start. |
| Business rule BR-002 | Expired licence triggers configured operational restrictions — which requires a per-geography licence record to act on. |

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-PLT-015 | A Licence entity must record: issuing authority, jurisdiction type (State \| District), jurisdiction identifiers, licence number, issue date, valid-until date, scope of services permitted, document files, verification status and verifier identity. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-PLT-016 | An agency's serviceable geography must be derived from its live licences, not entered independently; any manual override must be a logged exception with a reason and an approver. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-017 | Licence verification must be performed by a human Verification role with recorded evidence; no automated verdict may set a licence to Verified. Any future authority-side verification API is [FUTURE] and must not be assumed. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-PLT-018 | Licence expiry must generate a staged alert ladder (T-90 / T-60 / T-30 / T-15 / T-7 / T-1 / expired) to the agency's Owner, Admin and Compliance roles, and to Suraksha's Compliance role for marketplace-listed agencies. | [RECOMMENDED] |

### 3.5 How agencies actually operate today

This is the competitive baseline. The product is not replacing a rival SaaS in most accounts; it is replacing a working, cheap, human system that the owner trusts.

| Function | How it is done today | Failure mode it creates |
|---|---|---|
| Roster / duty chart | Handwritten duty chart on a register or a whiteboard; monthly Excel sheet at larger agencies | Double-booked guards; no audit of who authorised a change |
| Attendance | Paper muster at the site, signed by the guard and the client's representative; photo of the register on WhatsApp | Retrospective editing; disputes at month-end; no proof of actual presence |
| Shift communication | WhatsApp groups per site or per supervisor | No record structure, no escalation guarantee, group leaves with the employee |
| Night checks | Supervisor phone call to the site landline or guard's mobile | Unverifiable; a guard can answer and go back to sleep |
| Salary | Cash or bank transfer computed manually from the muster; advances noted in a diary | Errors, delays, disputes, no payslip, attrition |
| Client invoicing | Excel invoice built from the muster; emailed or hand-delivered | Attendance-invoice mismatch; 30–90 day disputes; delayed collection |
| Compliance | Physical file of licences and certificates; renewal remembered by the owner | Expiry surprises; scramble before inspection or tender |
| Client acquisition | Owner's personal network; references; occasional local listing | No pipeline visibility; feast-famine revenue |
| Tenders | An employee checks portals manually, irregularly | Missed deadlines; incomplete documentation; disqualification on technicalities |
| Legacy software | Some mid-size agencies run desktop attendance/payroll software, often unsupported, single-machine, no mobile | Data trapped on one PC; no field capture; no client visibility |
| Digital presence | None, or a one-page site with a phone number | Loses to any competitor a buyer can actually evaluate online |

Two consequences for product design follow directly. First, **the desktop app is not a nostalgia feature** — a meaningful share of agencies genuinely prefer installed software and intermittent connectivity, and the download channel is a credibility signal. Second, **migration is a first-class product**, not a service afterthought: the Enterprise OCR migration capability exists because an agency's real data lives in registers and spreadsheets and will never be re-keyed.

### 3.6 The economics of guarding

| Economic fact | Magnitude / character | Product consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Wage-led cost base | Guard wages plus statutory contributions dominate the cost of a contract; the remainder covers uniform, supervision, admin and margin | Payroll accuracy is existential; a payroll error is a bigger event than a UI bug |
| Thin operating margin | Competitive bidding compresses the management fee; volume, not price, is the lever | Software must pay for itself in leakage recovered (billed absentees, overtime errors), not in "productivity" |
| Working-capital squeeze | Guards are paid monthly regardless of when the client pays; client receivables commonly run 30–90 days | Receivables ageing, collection reminders and dispute resolution are core SaaS value, not accounting hygiene |
| High attrition | Guard turnover is high; replacement recruitment is continuous | Recruitment pipeline, fast onboarding and document reuse are operational necessities |
| Absenteeism and coverage risk | Every absent guard is either an uncovered post (SLA breach) or a double-shift (fatigue and overtime cost) | Replacement workflow and reliever pool management are the daily job of the product |
| Night-shift risk concentration | Sleeping-on-duty is the single most cited client complaint and the biggest contract-loss cause | Wake-check is a headline capability across B2C, B2B and the SaaS |
| Billing disputes | Month-end attendance reconciliation is the standard conflict point | Client-side monthly attendance approval before invoicing (§12) removes the dispute at source |
| Seasonality | Event security spikes around festivals, weddings and concert seasons; industrial demand is steadier | Surge staffing, temporary badge issuance and event-block pricing must be supported |

## 4. Business Problem

Twelve problem statements, grouped by whose pain it is. Each is stated as an observable failure, not as a missing feature. Impact is characterised qualitatively where we have no measured baseline — inventing precise numbers here would be dishonest [ASSUMPTION: A-101].

### 4.1 Client-side problems

| ID | Problem | Observable symptom | Impact | Addressed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P-01 | **Total opacity of delivered service.** The client pays for a post to be covered and has no way to know whether it was. | Client learns about a gap only when something goes wrong or a neighbour mentions the gate was empty. | Trust collapse; contract churn; guarding treated as a commodity because quality is invisible. | Customer App + client portal live view, attendance (§11, §15, §16); Command Center (§24) |
| P-02 | **No proof of duty.** Attendance is a paper muster the vendor controls, so there is no independent evidence. | Vendor produces a signed muster; client cannot dispute it; both sides argue from the same unverifiable page. | Month-end disputes; deductions negotiated rather than computed; relationship friction. | GPS attendance with dual timestamps (SUR-PLT-004), client monthly approval (§12) |
| P-03 | **Billing disputes at month-end.** The invoice is built from data the client never saw until it arrived. | 30–90 day payment delays; part-payments; credit notes issued after argument. | Cash-flow damage to the agency; administrative cost to the client; poisoned renewals. | Attendance-derived invoicing + client approval gate (§12, §35) |
| P-04 | **Guard sleeping, absent or substituted at night.** The highest-risk hours are the least supervised. | Night incident reveals the guard was asleep, or a different unbriefed person was on the gate. | Actual security failure; insurance and liability exposure; the single biggest cause of contract loss. | Anti-sleep wake-checks, geofenced check-in, patrol checkpoints, night escalation (§18, §24) |
| P-05 | **No SLA visibility for enterprise buyers.** Contracts specify response times, supervision frequency and coverage but nothing measures them. | The security head cannot answer "did the vendor meet SLA last quarter?" without asking the vendor. | Vendor performance managed by anecdote; renewals decided politically; no leverage. | SLA definition, measurement and reporting (§12, §42) |

### 4.2 Guard-side problems

| ID | Problem | Observable symptom | Impact | Addressed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P-06 | **Delayed and opaque salary.** The guard does not know his computed attendance, deductions or payment date until money arrives, if it arrives on time. | Guard asks the supervisor repeatedly; disputes over days worked; advances tracked in a diary. | Attrition, distress borrowing, low motivation on post, cash-flow anxiety for the lowest-paid participant. | Guard App attendance ledger, payslip view, salary status (§18); payroll engine (§20) |
| P-07 | **No portable identity or verified work portfolio.** A guard with eight years of clean service starts from zero at every new employer. | Re-verification, re-training, re-documentation on every job change; documents lost between employers. | Wage suppression, repeated onboarding cost across the industry, no reward for reliability. | Guard identity + document vault + verified work history (§17, §18) |
| P-08 | **Exploitation and unsafe conditions with no recorded channel.** Excess hours, denied reliefs, unsafe posts, deducted wages — all handled verbally. | Guard works a double shift because no reliever came; complaint goes nowhere. | Human cost; safety failure through fatigue; the industry's reputational floor. | Duty-hour records, grievance/ticket channel, SOS, fatigue-visible rostering (§18, §20, §29) |
| P-09 | **No career path or skill progression.** Guard → supervisor → field officer is informal and network-driven. | Training certificates are a compliance box, not a step to better pay. | Poor supply quality at the top of the pyramid; no reason for a good guard to stay. | Skills/training records, role progression, marketplace visibility of qualified profiles (§17) |

### 4.3 Agency-side problems

| ID | Problem | Observable symptom | Impact | Addressed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P-10 | **Manual rostering, payroll error and compliance expiry.** Duty charts on paper, salary computed by hand, licences remembered by memory. | Guard double-booked across two sites; payroll recomputed three times; a licence found expired during a tender. | Leakage on every axis at once: overtime paid twice, absentees billed wrongly, work lost on a technicality. | Agency Portal roster/attendance/payroll/compliance modules (§20); BR-001, BR-002 |
| P-11 | **No CRM, no tender visibility, no digital presence.** Growth depends entirely on the owner's phone book. | Leads forgotten; a matching state tender closes unnoticed; a buyer searching online finds nothing. | Structural growth ceiling; the agency stays the size of one person's network. | CRM + tender discovery (§20), Trinetra listing and profile (§19) |

### 4.4 Market-level problems

| ID | Problem | Observable symptom | Impact | Addressed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P-12 | **Discovery, verification, trust and fragmentation.** A buyer cannot find, compare or verify agencies; ~35,000 agencies are individually invisible; verification is repeated wastefully by every buyer. | Buyer picks whoever a broker introduced; licence is checked by looking at a photocopy; price is the only comparable. | Adverse selection — the best-run agency and the worst-run one look identical to the market. | Trinetra verified directory + verification-as-a-service + demand routing (§19, §22) |

### 4.6 Why now

| Enabler | State today | Why it makes this buildable now |
|---|---|---|
| Smartphone penetration among guards | Low-end Android is near-universal in the workforce | Field capture no longer requires the agency to issue hardware |
| Data cost | Cheap mobile data across tiers 1–3 | Continuous location and photo evidence is affordable |
| Digital payments | UPI ubiquity; Razorpay-class rails | Client payment and, prospectively, guard disbursement can be automated |
| Digital identity infrastructure | Standard KYC and verification service providers exist | Verification can be productised rather than manual-only |
| Enterprise compliance expectations | Buyers increasingly demand documented vendor compliance | Creates pull for exactly the evidence the platform produces |
| Vernacular AI | Voice and text models usable in Hindi and major Indian languages | The literacy barrier that killed earlier attempts is now addressable (§25) |

## 5. Product Goals

Goals are outcomes with measurable success criteria and a time horizon. Horizons: **H1** = first 6 months from build start, **H2** = 6–18 months, **H3** = 18–36 months. Numeric targets marked [ASSUMPTION: A-102] are planning placeholders until baselines exist.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| GOAL-01 | **Make duty provable.** Every rostered shift produces tamper-evident evidence of coverage. | Proof completeness rate (S-1) ≥ 95% of rostered shifts on Suraksha-operated sites; ≥ 85% across agency tenants. [ASSUMPTION: A-102] | H2 | Guard App, OPS, Agency Portal |
| GOAL-02 | **Let a client book a guard online, end to end, without a phone call.** | ≥ 60% of new B2C bookings complete self-serve through booking → payment → confirmation with no manual intervention. [ASSUMPTION: A-102] | H1 | Main website, Customer App |
| GOAL-03 | **Eliminate the month-end billing argument.** Invoices are generated from client-approved attendance. | ≥ 90% of B2B invoices issued against a client-approved attendance sheet; disputed invoice value < 3% of invoiced value. [ASSUMPTION: A-102] | H2 | Client portal, Agency Portal, §35 |
| GOAL-04 | **Make the night shift the safest shift to sell.** | Wake-check acknowledgement rate ≥ 97% on night posts; median wake-check escalation-to-resolution < 10 minutes. [ASSUMPTION: A-102] | H1 | Guard App, Command Center |
| GOAL-05 | **Replace a missing guard faster than the client notices.** | Median time-to-fill (S-6) < 45 minutes on urban sites during operating hours; < 90 minutes at night. [ASSUMPTION: A-102] | H2 | OPS, Agency Portal, Guard App |
| GOAL-06 | **Give every guard a payslip, an attendance ledger and a salary date he can see.** | 100% of guards on the platform can view their own attendance and payslip; salary-on-time rate (S-5) ≥ 95% for tenants using platform payroll. | H2 | Guard App, guard platform, §20 |

## 6. Non-Goals

Explicit exclusions. Each is a decision, not an oversight, and each has a rationale and a boundary statement so engineering knows exactly where the line falls.

| ID | Non-goal | Rationale | Where the line falls |
|---|---|---|---|
| NG-01 | **Not a job board or general staffing marketplace.** | Guarding supply is mediated by licensed agencies; disintermediating them destroys the SaaS business and creates liability Suraksha cannot carry. | Guards have profiles and can be discovered *by their own agency and by Suraksha*; the platform does not run open guard-to-client hiring. Cross-agency guard sourcing is [FUTURE] and would require a separate compliance design. |
| NG-02 | **Not a payroll bureau or employer of record for other agencies.** | Employment liability, statutory filing and wage disputes for another company's staff are a different business with different regulatory exposure. | The platform *computes* payroll and *generates* disbursement files/payslips for a tenant. The tenant remains the employer, the filer and the payer. Suraksha does not sign or file on a tenant's behalf. |
| NG-03 | **Not a weapons, ammunition or arms dealer, and not an arms-licence broker.** | Arms trade is a licensed activity entirely outside Suraksha's business and risk appetite. | The platform *records* armed-deployment attributes, weapon custody in the asset register, and licence documents as data. It never facilitates acquisition, transfer or sale of weapons or ammunition. |
| NG-04 | **Not a government-system integrator; no government API integration is claimed.** | No public, contracted, stable API is available to us for tender portals or PSARA licence verification, and asserting one would put a fiction in the build plan. | Tender data enters by manual or assisted ingestion (§13). Any future authorised integration is [FUTURE] / [DECISION REQUIRED: D-101] and must be contracted before it is designed. |
| NG-05 | **Not a replacement for PSARA licensing or any statutory process.** | Licensing is a state function; the platform is a record-keeper and reminder, not an authority. | The platform tracks licences, expiries and document packs, and can produce audit-ready exports. It never issues, renews, validates against an authority, or asserts legal validity. |
| NG-06 | **Not a provider of legal, tax or statutory-compliance advice.** | Advice creates professional liability and the rules vary by state and change frequently. | Compliance features present configured rules, deadlines and checklists supplied as reference data, clearly attributed and dated. No screen states what the law requires as a conclusion. |
| NG-07 | **Not a general-purpose ERP or accounting package.** | Competing with Tally/Zoho Books on ledgers is a losing, undifferentiated fight. | The platform owns operations-derived finance: invoicing from attendance, receivables, payroll computation, branch P&L views. It *exports* to accounting systems (§37) rather than replacing them. |
| NG-08 | **Not a hardware manufacturer or CCTV/alarm installer.** | Capital-intensive, service-heavy, unrelated operating model. | The platform integrates with biometric devices at the Enterprise tier and can ingest data from third-party systems; it does not sell, install or maintain hardware. |
| NG-09 | **Not a physical training institute or certification authority.** | Training delivery is a regulated, location-bound business. | Training and certification are recorded, tracked and expiry-alerted. Partner training delivery is [FUTURE]. |
| NG-10 | **Not an insurer, lender or benefits provider.** | Regulated financial activity requiring licences Suraksha does not hold. | The platform may, in future, share verified work history with licensed partners with explicit guard consent [FUTURE]. No credit or insurance product is built in-house. |
| NG-11 | **Not an emergency-response service.** | Suraksha does not dispatch police, fire or ambulance, and must never imply it does. | SOS and incident escalation route to the Command Center and to configured contacts, which may include emergency numbers dialled by a human. No screen may promise emergency response times. |
| NG-12 | **Not a facility-management or housekeeping operator at launch.** | Focus. The guarding operating spine must work first. | Bundled non-security manpower may appear as invoice lines on a contract; operational modules for those categories are [FUTURE]. |
| NG-13 | **Not building a public consumer social/review network for guards.** | Reputation systems over low-wage individuals invite abuse and legal exposure. | Client ratings attach to the *engagement and the agency*, with guard-level feedback visible only inside the employing tenant and Suraksha ops. |
| NG-14 | **Not offering white-label resale of the platform under an agency's own brand at launch.** | Support, security and brand-dilution cost before product maturity. | Agencies get profile/website management within the Professional plan (their own web presence, Suraksha-powered). Full white-label is [FUTURE] / [DECISION REQUIRED: D-102]. |
| NG-15 | **Not international at launch.** | PSARA-shaped compliance, Indian payment rails, Indian languages and Indian wage structures are deeply baked in. | Data model keeps country and currency explicit so the assumption is isolated, but no non-India requirement is in scope. |

### 7.4 Data-flow narrative: a booking from tap to invoice

The canonical end-to-end path. Step-by-step workflow form is owned by §29; this is the narrative that explains how the surfaces interlock.

1. **Demand capture.** A client configures a requirement in the Customer App or on the main website: service lane, location, guard category, count, start date, duration and shift pattern. Serviceability is checked against pincode reference data. A standard configuration returns a live price; a non-standard one routes to quotation. (Full flow: §11.)
2. **Commitment.** The client authenticates (phone-first OTP), supplies site/address details, and pays via Razorpay — or accepts a quotation issued by Suraksha sales. A Booking record is created with `status=Pending`, and a GST invoice or payment record is written to the ledger in integer paise.
3. **Fulfilment decision in OPS.** The booking lands in the OPS fulfilment queue. Suraksha decides between: (a) deploying its own guards (tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ`), or (b) routing the requirement to a licensed agency tenant whose live licence covers the district and whose available strength and category match. Licence geography (§3.4) is a hard filter in both cases.
4. **Structural setup.** A Site is created (or matched) for the client's address, with geofence and contacts. One or more Posts are defined on the Site — each Post is a guarded position needing N guards per shift. Posts generate Shifts across the contracted period; the roster assigns specific guards to specific Shifts as Assignments.
5. **Guard-side handoff.** Assigned guards receive the duty in the Guard App (and on the guard platform): site, post instructions, reporting time, supervisor contact, geofence. The client receives "guard assigned" with the guard's name, photo and ETA where applicable.
6. **Proof generation.** At the site, the guard checks in inside the geofence; the app records `device_time`, `server_received_time`, GPS coordinates and a verification photo, working offline and syncing when connectivity returns. During the shift the guard scans patrol checkpoints and acknowledges night wake-checks. Every one of these events streams to the Command Center, to the client's live view and to the agency's live operations map.
7. **Exception handling.** A missed check-in, geofence breach, missed wake-check or SOS raises an alert with a severity (P0–P3) and an escalation timer in the Command Center (§24). Replacement, if triggered, creates a new Assignment and notifies the client with the reason and the substitute guard's details.
8. **Consolidation.** Attendance accumulates per Assignment. At period end, the attendance sheet is presented for approval — client-side approval for B2B (§12), automatic for standard B2C monthly service unless disputed.
9. **Money.** The approved attendance drives invoice generation: contracted rate × approved units, adjusted for absences, replacements and overtime, plus GST. Payment is captured or reconciled; a double-sided ledger entry records every movement. On the supply side the same attendance drives payroll computation and the guard's payslip.
10. **Feedback and repetition.** The engagement closes or renews; the client rates the engagement; ratings and SLA performance feed the agency's marketplace profile and Suraksha's internal quality scoring, which in turn influences step 3 for the next booking.

### 7.5 Cross-surface dependency rules

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Single source of truth | Attendance is written only by the Guard App / guard platform / authorised manual entry in OPS or Agency Portal. No other surface may create attendance. |
| No surface-to-surface calls | Surfaces communicate through shared domain services and the event stream, never by calling each other's endpoints. |
| Client visibility is derived | The client live view renders a filtered projection of the real-time stream; it never receives raw guard location history beyond the contracted site and period (§39). |
| Tenancy boundary | An agency tenant sees only its own guards, clients, sites and money. Suraksha OPS sees across tenants only through explicitly defined administrative views, each audit-logged. |
| Degradation | If the real-time path is unavailable, attendance and duty must still be capturable offline and reconciled later; live map degradation must never block duty (§45, §49). |

| 2 | Suraksha OPS | Web (desktop-density) | Internal admin + command center | Super Admin, Founder/Management, National/State/City Operations, Command Center Operator, Finance, Compliance, Verification, Support, Sales, HR, Recruitment, Marketing, Auditor | Phase 1 | Canonical full-capability internal surface |
| 3 | Guard platform | Web (mobile-friendly) | Guard self-service | Guard, PSO, Bouncer, Supervisor (field), Specialised Personnel | Phase 2 | Fallback + records; not the primary daily tool |
| 4 | TRINETRA | Web (responsive) | Marketing + marketplace + downloads | Public, Agency Owner, Agency Admin | Phase 1 | Canonical marketplace surface |
| 5 | Agency Portal | Web (desktop-density) | Full SaaS/ERP | Agency Owner, Agency Admin, Branch Manager, Operations Manager, Field Officer, Agency HR, Recruiter, Payroll, Agency Finance, Agency Compliance, Agency Sales, Agency Viewer | Phase 2 | Canonical full-capability agency surface |
| 6 | Suraksha Customer App | Android + iOS | Native/cross-platform client app | Same as #1 | Phase 2 | Role-optimized (see §8.3) |
| 7 | Suraksha Guard App | Android-first (iOS later), offline-first | Field capture app | Guard, PSO, Bouncer, Supervisor (field) | Phase 2 (critical path) | Purpose-built; no web parity concept applies |
| 8 | Suraksha Agency App | Android + iOS | Agency companion | Agency Owner, Agency Admin, Branch Manager, Operations Manager, Field Officer | Phase 3 | Role-optimized (monitor + approve) |
| 9 | Suraksha Admin App | Android + iOS | OPS companion | Command Center Operator, Operations roles, Founder/Management, Support | Phase 3 | Role-optimized (alert + approve) |
| 10 | Agency Portal Desktop | Windows (.exe/.msi), macOS (.dmg Apple silicon + Intel), Linux (.deb/.rpm/AppImage) | Packaged Agency Portal | Same as #5 | Phase 3 | Full parity with web + desktop-native extras |

Phase definitions are indicative here and owned by §51 Roadmap. The Guard App is marked critical path because GOAL-01, GOAL-04 and the client live view all depend on it; until it ships, attendance is ops-entered and the client portal shows manually captured data.

### 8.3 Parity philosophy: why mobile apps are not shrunk desktops

The master brief asks explicitly whether desktop screens should be reproduced on mobile. The answer is **no, with one exception**, and the reasoning is per app rather than a blanket rule. Reproducing a dense operations console on a 5.5-inch screen produces a surface that is worse than the web at everything and better at nothing; the mobile advantage is *situational* — the user is standing, moving, interrupted, and reacting to a push notification.

| App | Stance | Reasoning | What is deliberately excluded |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Suraksha Customer App** | **Role-optimized, near-parity on transactions** | The consumer's whole relationship fits on a phone: book, pay, watch, complain, approve, rate. There is no dense analytical work in the client's job. So the app carries the full booking and monitoring capability, and simplifies only bulk/administrative tasks. | Bulk site import, multi-site org-chart administration, complex client-side RBAC configuration, large report building — pushed to the portal with a "continue on web" handoff. |
| **Suraksha Guard App** | **Purpose-built; parity is a meaningless concept** | The guard has no desktop. This app is not a companion to anything — it is the primary system of record for field events, designed for a low-end Android device, poor connectivity, gloves, night-time, and low literacy. | Anything not needed on post: analytics, other guards' data, financial screens beyond his own payslip, configuration. |
| **Suraksha Agency App** | **Role-optimized: monitor, approve, respond** | The agency owner's phone job is the 6 a.m. check ("is everyone on post?"), the mid-day approval, and the incident phone call. Roster construction, payroll runs and invoicing are seated, multi-hour, high-consequence tasks that belong on a large screen. | Payroll execution, invoice generation, bulk roster building, settings/RBAC administration, OCR migration, report designer. These are *viewable* on mobile, not *executable*. |
| **Suraksha Admin App** | **Role-optimized: alert, triage, approve, assign** | The internal user on mobile is on call. The app must win the first 60 seconds of an alert: see it, understand it, act or escalate. | Finance operations, verification deep-dives with document comparison, configuration, subscription management, bulk data operations. |
| **Agency Portal Desktop** | **Full parity, plus desktop-native extras** | This is the exception. The desktop app targets exactly the users who want *more* screen and *more* capability, often on the office PC that was already running legacy software. Reducing it would defeat its purpose. | Nothing removed. Adds: OS-native notifications, multi-window (live map on one monitor, attendance on another), local biometric-device integration at Enterprise tier, auto-update channel with release notes, secure local session storage honouring the same session/MFA policy. |

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-PLT-024 | Every mobile app must define its capability set by user situation (standing, interrupted, reacting) rather than by mirroring a web navigation tree; any capability excluded from an app must offer an explicit "continue on web/desktop" handoff that deep-links to the exact web screen with context preserved. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-025 | The Guard App must be usable on a low-end Android device (target: 2 GB RAM, Android 9+) with a data budget suitable for a metered prepaid plan; the target device profile and data budget must be fixed before mobile build starts. [DECISION REQUIRED: D-103] | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-026 | The desktop application must be functionally identical to the Agency Portal web app, share the same account and data, and honour the same session and MFA policies; divergence in business behaviour between desktop and web is a defect. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-PLT-027 | Every surface must degrade to read-only rather than to an error state when a dependent service (real-time, payment, AI) is unavailable, and must display which capability is degraded. | [RECOMMENDED] |

### 8.4 Surface-to-plan entitlement note

Agency-side capability is gated by subscription plan (Starter ₹5,000 / Professional ₹10,000 / Enterprise Contact Sales) [CONFIRMED]. Entitlements are enforced at the platform layer, not per client, so the web, mobile and desktop surfaces all obey the same gate. Plan feature lists are canonical in the canon and are not restated here; per-module gating is specified in §20 and enforcement in §31. Usage limits (guards, users, sites per plan) are unsettled — D-003.

## 9. Personas

Sixteen personas. Names are illustrative; the attributes are the specification. "The one feature that wins them" is a design constraint — if that feature is weak, the persona does not adopt, regardless of everything else. Personas are referenced by ID (`PER-nn`) throughout §11–§25.

### 9.1 Client-side personas

#### PER-01 · Rekha Sharma — Individual homeowner, 44, Ahmedabad

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | Independent bungalow in a semi-gated lane. Husband travels; two school-age children; elderly mother-in-law at home. Wants one night guard, 8 p.m.–6 a.m., starting this month. Has never hired a guard directly; the neighbour uses a local vendor. |
| Device & connectivity | Mid-range Android (₹15–20k), home Wi-Fi, 4G outside. Uses WhatsApp, UPI, food delivery apps daily. |
| Literacy & language | School-educated, comfortable in Gujarati and Hindi, functional English for app UI. Reads prices carefully; does not read terms. |
| Goals | Get a verified, background-checked guard quickly; know he is actually awake at 3 a.m.; pay online; be able to stop the service without a fight. |
| Frustrations | Vendors quote on the phone and change the number later; the guard "who came for the interview" is not the guard who arrives; no idea what to do if he does not show up one night. |
| Success looks like | Booked in under 10 minutes on the phone, guard's photo and name known before he arrives, a night-check notification she can ignore because it always says "acknowledged". |
| Products touched | Main website, Suraksha Customer App |
| Key screens | Service select → configure → price → checkout; guard-assigned card with photo; live status; attendance calendar; invoice; replacement request |
| The one feature that wins her | **Night wake-check with a visible acknowledgement record** — proof the guard was awake, without her having to check. |

#### PER-02 · Prakash Nair — RWA secretary, 58, Pune

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | Honorary secretary of a 210-flat society. Manages a 6-guard contract across two gates and a night patrol round. Answerable to a managing committee and to a WhatsApp group of 400 residents who complain loudly. Renews the guarding contract annually against three quotes. |
| Device & connectivity | Android phone plus a home laptop. Uses Excel for society accounts. Broadband at home. |
| Literacy & language | Retired bank officer. Fully literate, English + Marathi + Hindi. Comfortable with spreadsheets, wary of apps that hide numbers. |
| Goals | Prove to residents that the gate was manned; control per-flat cost; handle complaints with evidence; hand over clean records to the next secretary. |
| Frustrations | Residents claim the gate was empty at 2 a.m. and he cannot disprove it; the vendor's monthly bill never matches his own count of absent days; guard rotation means no one knows the residents. |
| Success looks like | A monthly attendance sheet he can put on the noticeboard, and a deduction on the invoice that he did not have to argue for. |
| Products touched | Main website, Customer App, client portal |
| Key screens | Multi-post site view; attendance calendar per gate; monthly attendance approval; invoice with absence deductions; incident log; guard roster with photos |
| The one feature that wins him | **Client-side monthly attendance approval that drives the invoice** — the argument becomes arithmetic. |

#### PER-03 · Sunita Rao — Factory administration officer, 39, Bhiwandi

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | Admin/HR officer at a 400-worker manufacturing unit. Owns the guarding contract operationally: 14 guards across main gate, material gate, weighbridge, and night patrol, plus a supervisor. Also owns canteen, transport and housekeeping vendors. Guarding is one of five headaches. |
| Device & connectivity | Office Windows desktop, company Android phone. Reliable connectivity in the office, patchy in the plant. |
| Literacy & language | Graduate; English for work, Marathi/Hindi with vendors and guards. Comfortable with ERP-style software. |

| Success looks like | Shift changeover visible in real time, visitor log searchable, and a compliance pack she can export the day an auditor asks. |
| Products touched | Client portal (web-primary), Customer App for alerts |
| Key screens | Site + post view with shift coverage; visitor log; incident register; attendance approval; document/compliance pack export |

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|

### 9.2 Guard-side personas

#### PER-07 · Ramesh Yadav — Fresh guard, 23, migrant from Gorakhpur to Gurugram

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | Six weeks into his first guarding job. Lives in a shared room with four others. Sends money home monthly. Posted at a residential tower gate on rotating shifts. Was recruited by a supervisor who knows his village. |
| Device & connectivity | ₹7,000 Android, 2 GB RAM, Android 11, cracked screen. Prepaid data pack of 1.5 GB/day but often exhausted; hostel Wi-Fi unreliable; basement/stairwell posts have no signal. Battery is the real constraint. |
| Literacy & language | Class 10, reads Hindi (Devanagari) slowly, minimal English. Understands icons and voice far better than text. Uses YouTube and WhatsApp voice notes; rarely types. |
| Goals | Mark attendance without argument; know his salary date and amount; not get scolded for something he did not do; get his ID and documents accepted once, not five times. |
| Frustrations | The register was signed by someone else and his day was marked absent; ₹500 deducted with no explanation; supervisor changes his post by phone at 9 p.m.; he has no proof of anything. |
| Success looks like | Tap once to check in, see "present" turn green, and see his month's days and pay adding up. |
| Products touched | Suraksha Guard App (primary), guard platform (rare, when the phone is broken) |
| Key screens | Today's duty card; check-in/out; attendance ledger; payslip; documents; SOS; notices |
| The one feature that wins him | **A visible attendance ledger he cannot be argued out of** — his month's work, counted in front of him. |

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | 22 years in the Army, five years as a PSO. Currently assigned to a business family: school runs, office, travel, occasional out-of-city trips. Armed deployment where applicable. Discretion is the job; being visible in an app is not natural to him. |
| Device & connectivity | Mid-range Android, always-on data, comfortable with maps and calls. Frequently in vehicles and inside private premises. |
| Literacy & language | Fluent Hindi and Punjabi, functional English. Disciplined about reporting; used to formats and logs. |
| Goals | Clear assignment briefs and route plans; a clean, discreet record of duty; recognition of his grade and rate; travel and out-of-station allowances computed correctly. |
| Frustrations | Being treated like an entry-level guard in the same app; location tracking of a principal's movements makes him uneasy; allowance claims settled two months late; nobody records the extra 4 hours he worked at a wedding. |
| Success looks like | Duty and allowances recorded exactly, privacy of the principal respected, and his profile clearly shows PSO grade and service record. |
| Products touched | Guard App (PSO mode), guard platform |
| Key screens | Assignment brief; discreet check-in; duty-hour log with overtime; allowance claim; document/skills profile; incident report |
| The one feature that wins him | **Accurate overtime and allowance capture tied to duty hours** — money he currently loses, recovered automatically. |

### 9.4 Suraksha-internal personas

| Success looks like | A prioritised queue where P0 cannot be lost, each alert carrying its full context and one-click actions, and a handover report generated automatically. |
| Products touched | OPS command center (primary), Admin App (away from desk) |
| Key screens | Live map; alert queue by severity with timers; alert detail with guard/site/contact context; call and escalation actions; incident creation; shift handover log |
| The one feature that wins him | **A severity-ordered alert queue with enforced escalation timers and a one-click action log** — the job becomes possible instead of frantic. |

#### PER-16 · Nisha Verma — Suraksha City Operations Manager, 34, Ahmedabad

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Context | Owns fulfilment and quality for Suraksha's own guarding operation in one city: ~90 guards, 40 client sites, four supervisors. Also the escalation point for the local agency partners Suraksha routes work to. Reports to State Operations. |
| Device & connectivity | Laptop + Android phone, field-mobile most afternoons. |
| Literacy & language | English + Hindi + Gujarati, MBA-level, comfortable with dashboards and P&L. |
| Goals | Fill every new booking within the promised deployment window; keep attendance above target; keep client complaints low; keep local guard supply healthy. |
| Frustrations | New bookings arrive without site detail and need three calls; guard supply is short exactly when demand spikes; partner agencies' quality varies and she cannot see inside their operation; escalations reach her after the client is already angry. |
| Success looks like | A fulfilment queue with SLA countdown, a supply view showing available guards by category and area, and partner-agency quality scores she can act on. |
| Products touched | OPS (primary), Admin App, Command Center views |
| Key screens | Fulfilment queue with deployment SLA; allocation screen (own guards vs partner agency); supply availability; city dashboard; partner performance; client escalations |
| The one feature that wins her | **An allocation screen that shows own-supply and licence-eligible partner supply side by side with quality scores** — fulfilment stops being phone-based guesswork. |

## 10. Roles

This section defines **what each role is** — its scope, ownership, daily actions, and the boundaries of its visibility and authority. It is deliberately not the permission matrix: the granular per-module, per-action grid lives in **§31 Permissions**, and entity-level field visibility lives in **§32**. Where this section says "may view", §31 says exactly which endpoint and which field.

Role names are canonical and fixed. No surface may invent a role name; custom labels are display aliases over these roles [RECOMMENDED].

### 10.1 Reading the role tables

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Scope | The data boundary: platform-wide, tenant, branch, site, self |
| Owns | What breaks if this role does not do its job |
| Daily actions | The three to five things they actually do |
| Data visibility | What they can see, and the hard boundary they cannot cross |
| Financial access | None / view / operate / approve |
| PII access | None / masked / full-with-audit |
| AI access | Which of the four AI action classes are available (Read-only · Recommendation · Approval-required · Automated) |
| Admin rights | Whether they can grant roles, change configuration, or alter another user's access |

### 10.6 Role assignment rules

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-PLT-033 | One human identity may hold multiple role grants across multiple contexts (e.g. Guard in tenant A and Individual Customer on the Suraksha side); each grant is independently scoped and independently audited. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-034 | No role may grant itself additional privilege; privilege escalation requires a distinct role with admin rights and produces an audit entry naming grantor, grantee, privilege and reason. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-035 | Segregation of duties must be enforced for money: the identity that executes a payroll run or issues a credit note may not be the identity that approves it, unless the tenant is a single-user tenant, in which case the exception is recorded on every such transaction. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-036 | Every role's default AI action class must be configurable per tenant within the platform-wide ceiling; no tenant configuration may raise a role above the ceiling defined in §41. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-PLT-037 | Client-side roles are scoped by the client organization and never by the serving agency; an agency cannot create or modify a client user's role grants. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-038 | Guard-side roles are mutually compatible (a Guard may also be a Supervisor for a cluster); role stacking must not widen data visibility beyond the union of each role's explicit scope. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-039 | Every role must have a defined behaviour when its scope becomes empty (branch closed, site archived, assignment ended): access to historical records is retained read-only for a configured retention window, then revoked. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-PLT-040 | Break-glass access (Super Admin viewing tenant data for support) must require a stated reason, be time-boxed, notify the tenant Owner, and appear in the tenant's own audit log. | [RECOMMENDED] |
