## 34. Real-Time Architecture

Real-time is what the brand promises on the public website — live GPS tracking, a 24/7 command center, night wake-checks — so this section is where over-engineering is most tempting and most expensive. The organising principle: **be genuinely real-time exactly where a human's response time is on the clock, and be honestly near-real-time everywhere else.**

### 34.1 The real-time requirement set

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-RT-001 | Every real-time surface shall display its data freshness; no surface shall present stale data as live. |
| SUR-RT-002 | SOS shall reach an operator's screen within 5 seconds of server receipt at the 95th percentile, and shall never be batched, throttled, de-duplicated or delayed by load-shedding. |
| SUR-RT-003 | The real-time path shall degrade to polling automatically when a live transport is unavailable, and the client shall show a degraded-connection indicator (SUR-CMD-009). |
| SUR-RT-004 | No real-time delivery mechanism shall be the system of record; every real-time message shall be reconstructible from the durable store. |

#### 34.1.1 The requirement table

| # | Capability | Latency target (server event → visible) | Update frequency | Fan-out per event | Truly real-time? | V1 transport |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **SOS** | ≤5 s p95, ≤10 s p99 | Rare (target <5/day/1,000 guards) | 5–30 recipients (operators on scope, shift lead, supervisor, on-call) | **Yes — hard requirement** | WebSocket to console + push + SMS + voice call trigger |
| 2 | **Command center alert queue** | ≤5 s p95 | 50–500/day at V1 | 2–8 operators | **Yes** | WebSocket |
| 3 | **Wake check due / missed** | ≤10 s | ~3 per night guard | 1 guard (push) + operators (WS) | **Yes for the miss**, scheduled for the due | Push + WebSocket |
| 4 | **Incident escalation state** | ≤5 s | Low | Ladder participants | **Yes** | WebSocket + push |
| 5 | **Guard status (on duty / late / absent / unreachable)** | ≤30 s | Per state change, a few per guard per shift | Ops watchers of that scope | Near-real-time | WebSocket delta |
| 6 | **Attendance check-in/out** | ≤30 s | 2–6 per guard per day | Supervisor + ops board | Near-real-time | WebSocket delta (batched per 5 s) |
| 7 | **Live deployment view (counts, gaps)** | ≤60 s | Continuous | All ops users on scope | Near-real-time | WebSocket delta, 15 s coalescing |
| 8 | **Guard GPS position on the map** | 30–120 s is acceptable | Adaptive 30 s–5 min per guard | Operators viewing that map region only | **Near-real-time — explicitly not real-time** | WebSocket, viewport-scoped, 10 s coalescing |
| 9 | **Patrol progress** | ≤60 s | Per checkpoint scan | Supervisor + site watchers | Near-real-time | WebSocket delta |
| 10 | **Client live view (their sites)** | ≤120 s | Low | 1–5 client users | Near-real-time | SSE or polling |
| 11 | **Notification inbox badge** | ≤10 s | Low | 1 user | Near-real-time | WebSocket or push |
| 12 | **Chat/support message** | ≤3 s | Low | 2 parties | Yes (small scale) | WebSocket |
| 13 | **Dashboard KPI cards** | 5–15 min | Low | Many | **Not real-time** | Polling / cached aggregate |
| 14 | **Analytics and reports** | Hours | Low | Many | **Not real-time** | Materialised views (§32.6) |

Honesty about #8 matters most. A guard standing at a gate does not need a 1-second position update; a 60-second update is operationally indistinguishable and costs an order of magnitude less in battery, data, ingest capacity and storage. The one exception is an active SOS or an active pursuit, where the server commands the device into a high-frequency mode (§34.3.1) for a bounded window.

### 34.2 Transport decision

#### 34.2.1 The options

| Transport | Strengths | Weaknesses | Cost at V1 scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WebSocket** | Bidirectional, low latency, one connection carries many subscriptions, efficient for the console | Stateful — needs sticky routing or a shared pub/sub; connection storms on deploy; mobile background limits; proxy/corporate-firewall issues | ~1 connection per open console/portal tab; a single node handles 10–20k connections |
| **SSE** | Simple, HTTP/2-friendly, auto-reconnect built in, works through most proxies, no upgrade handshake | Server→client only; older browsers cap connections per origin; needs a separate channel for client→server | Similar server cost, simpler ops |
| **Push (FCM/APNs)** | Reaches a backgrounded or killed app; the only option when the phone is asleep; free at our volume | Not guaranteed, not ordered, high and variable latency (seconds to minutes), payload-limited, requires a user-visible notification for high priority on some OS versions | Free; the cost is reliability |
| **Polling** | Trivial, stateless, cache-friendly, survives everything | Latency = interval; wasteful at high frequency; N clients × interval = load floor | Cheapest to build, most expensive to run at short intervals |
| **Long polling** | Works everywhere, near-WS latency | Holds a connection per client anyway, without WS efficiency | Middle |

#### 34.2.2 Decision per use case

| Use case | Client | V1 [RECOMMENDED] | Scale design |
|---|---|---|---|
| SOS to operator | Command Center console (web) | **WebSocket**, plus an unconditional push and SMS to the shift lead as independent paths | Same, plus a dedicated SOS channel isolated from all other traffic |
| SOS confirmation to guard | Guard App | HTTP response + push | Same |
| Alert queue | Console | **WebSocket** | Same, sharded by scope |
| Guard status / attendance / deployment board | Agency Portal, OPS | **WebSocket** with 5–15 s coalescing | Same |
| Map positions | Console, Agency Portal | **WebSocket, viewport- and scope-scoped**, 10 s coalescing | Add a geospatial fan-out tier |
| Client live view | Client portal / customer app | **Polling at 60 s** (SSE `[FUTURE]`) | SSE |
| Guard App inbound (new assignment, wake check, SOS ack, recall) | Guard App | **Push (FCM/APNs)**, with a foreground WebSocket only while the duty screen is open | Same; push remains primary because the app is usually backgrounded |
| Guard App outbound | Guard App | **HTTP** (batched pings, events) — never a persistent socket in the background | Same |
| Notification badge | All web clients | WebSocket if connected, else poll on focus | Same |
| Dashboard KPIs | All | **Polling on interval + on focus** | Same |
| Support chat | Web + apps | WebSocket | Same |

**The V1 design is deliberately smaller than the scale design:** one WebSocket gateway process type, one Redis pub/sub backplane, subscription topics keyed by `tenant:<id>:scope:<branch|site>` and `tenant:<id>:map:<geohash5>`, and everything else on HTTP. No message broker for client fan-out, no per-user queues, no presence system beyond "is a socket open", no client-side event sourcing.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-RT-005 | The Guard App shall not maintain a background WebSocket; inbound urgency shall arrive by push notification and outbound data shall be batched HTTP. |
| SUR-RT-006 | Every WebSocket subscription shall be authorised at subscribe time against the caller's §31 scope, re-authorised on token refresh, and terminated immediately when the underlying permission is revoked. |
| SUR-RT-007 | Every live surface shall fall back to polling within 10 seconds of a socket failure, without user action, and shall reconcile by fetching the authoritative state rather than replaying missed messages. |

#### 34.2.3 WebSocket protocol shape

Connection: `wss://rt.surakshaguards.in/v1/stream?access_token=<jwt>` (token also accepted via the first message for browsers that cannot set headers). The gateway validates the token, resolves tenant and scope, and holds the connection.

Client → server messages: `subscribe` (topic list), `unsubscribe`, `ping`, `set_viewport` (map bounds + zoom, which the gateway translates into geohash subscriptions), `ack` (for at-least-once console delivery of P0 alerts).

Server → client messages:

```json
{"type":"event","topic":"tenant:018f0a:site:018f20","seq":48211,
 "event":"attendance.checked_in","occurred_at":"2026-08-15T14:41:52Z",
 "data":{"assignment_id":"018f7a…","guard_id":"018f31…","late_minutes":0}}
{"type":"snapshot_required","topic":"tenant:018f0a:site:018f20",
 "reason":"gap_detected","last_seq_seen":48180}
{"type":"heartbeat","server_time":"2026-08-15T14:44:03Z"}
```

The `seq` per topic is the recovery mechanism: a client that detects a gap requests a fresh snapshot from the REST API rather than asking for replay. This keeps the gateway stateless and means no message needs to be durable — which is why SUR-RT-004 holds.

Heartbeat every 20 s; client reconnects with exponential backoff plus jitter (1 s → 30 s cap), and on reconnect always re-fetches the snapshot. Deploys drain connections over 60 seconds with a `reconnect_after` hint spread across clients so a deploy does not produce a thundering herd.

### 34.3 The GPS ingest pipeline

#### 34.3.1 Sampling strategy on the device

Fixed-interval sampling is the single biggest avoidable cost in this product — in battery, in mobile data (which the guard often pays for), and in storage. Sampling is adaptive and **server-steered**: every ping batch response carries `next_config` (§33.3.9 Spec T1), so policy changes without an app release.

| State | Interval | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| On duty, stationary inside geofence, battery >30% | 120 s | Nothing is changing; the useful signal is "still here" |
| On duty, stationary, battery ≤30% | 300 s | Preserve the device for the shift and for SOS |
| On duty, moving inside geofence | 60 s | Patrol movement |
| On duty, moving, outside geofence | 30 s | The interesting case: either a legitimate excursion or an unauthorised departure |
| On patrol (active patrol record) | 30 s | Route reconstruction needs density |
| Off duty | **No tracking at all** | §39 — tracking a person outside their shift is not defensible; the app stops the location service, and the OS-level indicator going dark is part of the guard's trust in the product |
| SOS active | 5 s for 15 minutes, then 15 s | Bounded high-frequency window |
| Command-triggered (`ping-now`) | Immediate single high-accuracy fix | Operator asks, device answers |
| Significant-change fallback (iOS background, doze on Android) | OS-driven | Accept what the platform gives; record the gap honestly |

Additional device rules: use the fused/platform location provider, not raw GPS, unless accuracy demands it; suppress a ping whose distance from the last one is under 10 m **and** whose age is under the interval (movement-gated dedup at source); never drop a ping that changes geofence state; always record and upload pings flagged as mock rather than hiding them.

#### 34.3.2 Batching and compression

Batches flush on whichever comes first: 10 pings, 60 seconds of buffer, a geofence transition, a network transition from offline to online, or the app entering the foreground. Batches are gzip-encoded JSON — measured at roughly 75–80% reduction on this shape, which is enough that a binary format (protobuf/CBOR) is not worth the tooling cost in V1 and is listed in the do-not-build list. Offline buffering: up to 7 days or 20,000 pings in a local store (SQLite), oldest-first eviction with a preserved sample so a long offline period still yields a usable trail; the app reports its backlog size in each batch so the server can see which devices are struggling.

#### 34.3.3 Ingest path

```
Guard App ──gzip batch──► POST /v1/tracking/pings  (validate, assign batch_id)
                              │  (returns 202 in <20 ms; no DB write here)
                              ▼
                    Redis Stream  gps.ingest  (partitioned by guard_id hash)
                              │
                    ┌─────────┴──────────┐
                    ▼                    ▼
          consumer group "writer"   consumer group "signals"
                    │                    │
        batch COPY into location     geofence eval, idle, deviation,
        (500–2000 rows/txn)          mock flags, last-position update
                    │                    │
                    ▼                    ▼
          Postgres partitioned      outbox/pub-sub → alerts, WebSocket,
              location table         guard_last_position read model
```

Why a Redis Stream rather than a full broker in V1: it is already deployed for rate limiting and caching, it gives consumer groups, acknowledgement and replay, it handles our V1 volume (~15 writes/second average, ~150/second peak) with enormous headroom, and it costs nothing extra to operate. Alternatives: Kafka (right at 10–50× this volume, wrong overhead for a pilot), SQS/managed queue (fine, adds cloud coupling and per-message cost), direct-to-database (rejected — a slow primary would then stall the guard's app). Trade-off: Redis Streams are memory-bound and less durable than Kafka; mitigated by a bounded stream length, `appendonly` persistence, and the fact that a lost ping is an acceptable loss whereas a lost check-in is not — check-ins do **not** go through this path, they are synchronous transactional writes.

#### 34.3.4 Deduplication

Three layers: the device suppresses near-duplicates; the ingest endpoint drops pings whose `(device_id, recorded_at)` is already in a 10-minute Redis set; the database has a unique index on `(device_id, recorded_at)` per partition as the final guard. Duplicate counts are returned to the client so a buggy app version is visible in telemetry rather than silently doubling storage.

#### 34.3.5 Out-of-order handling

Offline replay routinely delivers pings hours late and interleaved with live ones. Rules: pings are stored by `recorded_at`, not arrival order, so the trail is correct regardless; `guard_last_position` is updated only if the incoming ping's `recorded_at` is **newer** than the stored one (a compare-and-set), so a late batch cannot rewind the live map; derived signals (geofence enter/exit, idle, deviation) are computed only for pings less than 15 minutes old — a geofence exit discovered six hours late is stored as history and reported in the daily exception list, but it does not fire a live alert, because alerting on stale events produces operator distrust faster than anything else.

#### 34.3.6 Storage tiering

Per §32.4.4 and §32.5: daily partitions, compressed after 2 days, downsampled at 30 days, cold at 90 days, purged at 13 months. The write path uses `COPY` in batches, `FILLFACTOR=100`, and no spatial index on the raw ping table.

#### 34.3.7 Accuracy and trust handling

| Signal | Rule |
|---|---|
| `accuracy_m > 100` | Stored, but excluded from geofence *decisions*; the check-in flow asks the guard to wait for a better fix, with a 60-second timeout after which the check-in is accepted with a `low_accuracy` flag and routed to supervisor verification |
| `accuracy_m > 500` | Treated as no fix for all derived signals |
| `is_mock = true` | Stored, flagged, and a `guard.mock_location_detected` event raised at P2; three occurrences in 7 days escalate to P1 and block auto-verified attendance for that guard pending review. The guard is told the flag was raised — silent surveillance flags are both unfair and, in practice, counterproductive |
| Impossible speed | A position implying >120 km/h between consecutive on-foot pings is flagged `implausible_movement` (not rejected), because a guard in a vehicle is a legitimate case that the flag lets a human resolve |
| Device integrity failure | Recorded on the device row; attendance from a failing device requires supervisor verification (§38 owns the attestation check) |

#### 34.3.8 Derived signals

| Signal | Computation | Emitted as |
|---|---|---|
| `geofence.entered` / `geofence.exited` | State change vs the previous ping's `geofence_state`, with hysteresis: a transition must persist for 2 consecutive pings or 90 seconds to fire, which eliminates the boundary-jitter storm that otherwise dominates alert volume | Event → alert per §24 rules |
| `guard.idle` | No movement beyond 15 m for longer than the post's configured idle threshold (default 45 min day, 20 min night for patrol posts) | P3 informational, P2 at night |
| `guard.route_deviation` | For an active patrol, distance from the expected route polyline exceeds `tolerance_m` (default 75) for 3 consecutive pings | P2 |
| `guard.offline` | No ping for 3× the expected interval | P2, P1 at night or at a high-risk site (§24 sets severity) |
| `guard.left_site` | Geofence exit while on duty without an authorised reason (break, escort, patrol route leaving the fence) | P1 |
| `guard.arrived` | Geofence entry within 30 min of shift start | Informational; pre-fills the check-in screen |
| `battery.critical` | `battery_pct ≤ 10` and not charging while on duty | P2 to supervisor — a dead phone means no SOS |

Derived signals are computed in the `signals` consumer, not in the database, and are emitted through the same outbox/event path as everything else so the alerting rules in §24 see one uniform stream.

### 34.4 Event streaming, queues and background jobs

#### 34.4.1 Queue topology (V1)

| Queue / stream | Technology | Purpose | Ordering | Retry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gps.ingest` | Redis Stream, 8 partitions by `guard_id` hash | Ping ingest | Per guard | Consumer group re-delivery; 3 attempts then drop with a counter (a lost ping is acceptable) |
| `outbox.relay` | Postgres table + relay process | Reliable domain events (§32.7.5) | Per `partition_key` | 10 attempts, exponential, then dead-letter |
| `events.fanout` | Redis Pub/Sub | WebSocket fan-out | None (best effort) | None — clients recover by snapshot |
| `notifications.send` | Redis Stream, 4 partitions | Outbound push/SMS/WhatsApp/email | Per recipient | 5 attempts with provider failover (§36) |
| `webhooks.deliver` | Redis Stream, partitioned by endpoint | Outbound webhooks | Per endpoint | 8 attempts (§33.4.2) |
| `jobs.default` / `jobs.heavy` / `jobs.critical` | Redis-backed job queue | Background work; `critical` is reserved for escalation timers and SOS follow-ups and is never shared with report generation | Per job | Per-job policy |
| `dlq.*` | Redis Stream (never auto-purged) | Dead letters from every queue above | — | Manual replay from an ops screen |

Why not Kafka/RabbitMQ in V1: message volume is under 100/second sustained; Redis is already in the stack for cache and rate limits; adding a broker adds a cluster, a schema registry conversation and an on-call surface for a problem we do not yet have. The migration trigger is in §34.7. Trade-off accepted: weaker durability than Kafka, mitigated by the outbox being the durable layer for everything that matters — Redis carries *delivery*, Postgres carries *truth*.

#### 34.4.2 Event catalogue (internal)

The internal event names are the same as the webhook catalogue (§33.4.1) plus internal-only events that are never exposed externally: `guard.mock_location_detected`, `guard.offline`, `guard.idle`, `guard.left_site`, `battery.critical`, `escalation.rung_fired`, `storm.entered`, `storm.exited`, `tenant.entitlement_changed`, `user.permissions_changed`, `payroll.exception_raised`, `reconciliation.mismatch_found`, `audit.chain_broken`.

#### 34.4.3 Ordering guarantees

Per-aggregate ordering only, delivered through the `partition_key`. No global ordering. Every event carries `occurred_at` and a per-aggregate `sequence`. Consumers that need ordering (the WebSocket gateway, the analytics loader) discard events with a lower sequence than one already applied for that aggregate; consumers that do not (notifications) ignore sequence entirely. This is stated once and is not renegotiated per consumer.

#### 34.4.4 Dead-letter handling

Every queue has a DLQ. A message entering a DLQ raises a P2 alert (P1 for `jobs.critical` and `outbox.relay`), is visible in an OPS screen with the payload, the error and the attempt history, and supports single or bulk replay after a fix. DLQs are never auto-purged; a DLQ with entries older than 7 days raises a P1 because it means nobody is looking.

#### 34.4.5 Job scheduler design

A single scheduler leader (leader-elected via a Redis lock with a 30-second TTL and fencing token) enqueues due jobs; workers execute. Every job is: idempotent on `(job_key, scheduled_for)` recorded in a `job_run` table; time-boxed with a hard timeout; resumable where it processes many rows (a cursor is persisted); and monitored for both failure and *non-execution* — a job that silently stops running is the more dangerous failure, so every job has a freshness alert on its last successful completion.

#### 34.4.6 Background job inventory

| Job | Cadence | Purpose | Idempotency | Missed-run behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sched.wake_checks.materialise` | Every 5 min | Create Pending wake checks for the next 60 min from schedules, randomised within the window | Unique on (assignment, due_at slot) | Catches up; never creates a check whose window has already passed |
| `sched.wake_checks.dispatch` | Every 30 s | Send the challenge for checks due now | Unique on wake_check id | Late dispatch shortens the window; if >50% of the window is gone the check is marked `Cancelled` with reason `dispatch_delayed` rather than failing a guard for our fault |
| `sched.wake_checks.timeout` | Every 30 s | Mark unacknowledged checks Failed, raise the alert | Unique on wake_check id | Catches up |
| `sched.escalation.tick` | Every 10 s | Fire due escalation rungs (§34.5.3) | Unique on (escalation, rung) | Catches up; a delayed tick is recorded on the escalation so SLA reporting stays honest |
| `sched.shift.start_watch` | Every 5 min | Detect shifts starting soon with no assignment or no check-in | Unique on (shift, check type) | Catches up |
| `sched.attendance.autoclose` | Every 15 min | Close attendance for shifts ended + grace with no check-out | Unique on attendance id | Catches up |
| `sched.attendance.noshow` | Every 5 min | Mark no-shows past the cut-off, trigger Replacement | Unique on assignment id | Catches up |
| `sched.expiry.scan` | Daily 05:30 IST | Documents, licences, training, medical, contracts, subscriptions, insurance — transition Active→Expiring→Expired and emit reminders per `expiry_reminder_days` | Unique on (entity, reminder day) | Catches up; a missed day sends the overdue reminder once, not five times |
| `sched.invoice.generate` | Daily 01:00 IST | Contract-driven draft invoices for contracts whose `billing_day` matches | Unique on (contract, period) | Catches up |
| `sched.invoice.dunning` | Daily 09:00 IST | Reminders at due−7/due/+7/+15/+30 | Unique on (invoice, stage) | Catches up, one stage per run |
| `sched.payroll.prepare` | Monthly, tenant-configured | Create the Draft run and pre-flight exception list | Unique on (tenant, period) | Alerts if missed — never auto-runs late without notice |
| `sched.subscription.billing` | Daily 02:00 IST | SaaS subscription charges, grace and suspension | Unique on (subscription, period) | Catches up |
| `sched.roster.autogenerate` | Weekly, tenant-configured | Draft next period's roster from templates (never published automatically) | Unique on (site, period) | Catches up |
| `sched.readmodel.refresh` | 00:30/06:30/12:30/18:30 | Materialised view refresh (§32.6.3) | Naturally idempotent | Skips if a refresh is running |
| `sched.partition.maintain` | Daily 04:30 | Create future partitions, compress old ones, detach per retention | Idempotent by name | P1 if runway <7 days |
| `sched.archive.export` | Daily 05:00 | Export detached partitions to cold storage with checksum verification | Unique on partition | Retries |
| `purge.*` | Per §32.5.5 | Retention enforcement | Recorded in purge_record | Skips, alerts |
| `recon.*` | Per §32.7.6 | Reconciliation | Read-only or cache-only writes | Alerts |
| `sched.webhook.retry` | Every 30 s | Drive the webhook retry schedule | Unique on (delivery, attempt) | Catches up |
| `sched.outbox.relay` | Continuous | Publish outbox events | `SKIP LOCKED` claim | N/A |
| `sched.device.health` | Hourly | Flag devices not seen in 48 h while assigned; battery and integrity trends | Idempotent | Catches up |
| `sched.trust.recompute` | Nightly | Guard reliability score, agency trust score, response-time percentiles | Idempotent | Catches up |
| `sched.storm.evaluate` | Every 30 s | Storm-control thresholds (§34.5.4) | Idempotent | Catches up |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-RT-008 | Every scheduled job shall record a `job_run` row with start, end, outcome and rows processed, and shall have a freshness alert that fires when its last successful completion exceeds its cadence by a defined factor. |
| SUR-RT-009 | Safety-critical schedulers (wake-check dispatch and timeout, escalation tick, no-show detection) shall run on the `jobs.critical` queue with dedicated workers, and shall never share capacity with reporting, export or bulk jobs. |
| SUR-RT-010 | A wake check that the platform failed to dispatch on time shall not be recorded as a guard failure; it shall be cancelled with a system-fault reason and counted separately in reliability metrics. |

SUR-RT-010 is a small rule with a large effect: without it, our own outage degrades guards' reliability scores and, downstream, their pay and deployability.

### 34.5 The alerting path: event to command center screen

#### 34.5.1 The path

```
 Source event (SOS / wake-check timeout / geofence exit / no-show /
               patrol miss / licence expiry / client escalation)
        │
        ▼
  Outbox event (durable, in the source transaction)
        │
        ▼
  Alert evaluator  ── applies §24 severity rules + site risk band + client tier
        │            ── applies de-duplication (never to P0) and correlation
        ▼
  alert row created (status Pending, ack_target_seconds snapshotted)
        │
        ├──► Redis pub/sub  ──►  WebSocket gateway  ──►  operator consoles
        │                                                (scope-filtered)
        ├──► notifications.send  ──►  push / SMS / WhatsApp / voice
        │
        └──► escalation created (policy + version pinned), next_fire_at set
                    │
                    ▼
             sched.escalation.tick (every 10 s)
```

End-to-end budget for a P0: source write ≤200 ms, outbox relay ≤500 ms, evaluator ≤300 ms, pub/sub + gateway ≤200 ms, browser render ≤300 ms — approximately 1.5 seconds typical against a 5-second p95 target, leaving genuine headroom rather than a design that only just meets the number.

#### 34.5.2 Console delivery reliability

P0 and P1 alerts use acknowledged delivery over the WebSocket: the gateway expects a client `ack` within 3 seconds and, failing that, re-sends, then marks the console session unhealthy and routes the alert to another operator on scope while raising an "operator console unresponsive" signal. The console also polls `/v1/alerts?status=open` every 20 seconds as a belt-and-braces reconciliation — the poll is cheap and it means a silent socket failure can never hide an alert. This redundancy is deliberate and is not "over-engineering": it is the one place where a missed message has a human consequence.

#### 34.5.3 The escalation timer mechanism

§24 owns escalation *policy* (which rungs, who is on them, what the intervals are). This section owns the *mechanism*.

| Aspect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Storage | The escalation row holds `current_rung` and `next_fire_at`; the ladder is pinned by `policy_id` + `policy_version` at creation, so editing a ladder never alters escalations in flight |
| Firing | `sched.escalation.tick` runs every 10 s and claims due rows with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED WHERE next_fire_at <= now() AND status='Active' LIMIT 200`, ordered by `next_fire_at` |
| Why polling, not timers | In-process timers die with the process and are invisible to operations. A durable row plus a 10-second poll is simple, survives restarts and deploys, is observable, and 10-second granularity is well inside every escalation interval in the policy (the shortest is 60 s) |
| Firing an rung | In one transaction: write `escalation_rung_event`, set `current_rung = current_rung + 1`, set the next `next_fire_at` from the pinned policy, emit the notification events. Idempotent on `(escalation_id, rung_index)` |
| Pause vs cancel | Dispatch grace and operator actions **extend** `next_fire_at` (recorded as a decision with actor and reason) — they never cancel the escalation (per §24) |
| Acknowledgement | Acknowledging an alert pauses the current rung's timer; resolving completes the escalation with `completion_reason` |
| Ladder exhaustion | When the final rung has fired and nothing is acknowledged, the escalation stays `In Progress`, re-notifies the final rung on the configured repeat interval, and raises a distinct "escalation exhausted" P0 that cannot be de-duplicated |
| Clock discipline | Everything uses server time; a tick that runs late records `fired_late_by_ms` on the rung event so SLA reporting distinguishes our lateness from a human's |
| Observability | Metrics: escalations open by rung, tick lag p95, rungs fired per hour, exhausted count. Tick lag over 30 s is P1 |

#### 34.5.4 Storm control

§24 owns the policy for suppression; the mechanism: a rolling 60-second counter per (tenant, alert_type, site) and a global counter. Thresholds (configurable, defaults: 20 alerts of one type at one site per minute, or 200 alerts tenant-wide per minute) open a `storm_window`, during which non-P0 alerts of the storming type are **aggregated** into a single rolling summary alert with a count and a member list rather than being created individually. P0 alerts are never affected (SUR-CMD-021), and the storm window itself is logged with actor, scope, reason and duration.

The mechanism's honest failure mode: a genuine mass-incident (a fire at a large site producing 40 real alerts) looks like a storm. This is handled by making the aggregated alert P1 by construction, by never suppressing SOS, and by requiring an operator to explicitly review the member list before closing an aggregate — the aggregate cannot be resolved with a single click.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-RT-011 | P0 alerts shall bypass de-duplication, correlation, storm aggregation and rate limiting at every layer, and this shall be asserted by an automated test. |
| SUR-RT-012 | The console shall maintain an independent 20-second reconciliation poll of open alerts in addition to the live stream, and shall visibly badge any alert discovered by the poll rather than the stream. |
| SUR-RT-013 | Escalation timers shall be durable database state driven by a polling scheduler; in-memory timers shall not be used for any safety-relevant deadline. |

### 34.6 Geospatial capability

#### 34.6.1 Database/service choice

**[RECOMMENDED] PostGIS in the same Postgres instance.** Why: the geospatial workload is small and highly structured — point-in-polygon against a handful of known fences, distance sorting over a few thousand candidate guards, and city/state filtering. PostGIS does all of that in the same transaction as the operational data, with no extra service, no data synchronisation and no consistency question. Alternatives: a dedicated geospatial service (Tile38, Redis GEO) gives faster moving-object queries but adds a second source of truth for position — and we already keep the hot answer in `guard_last_position`, which is the cheap part of what Tile38 would provide; a managed geospatial API (Google/Mapbox geofencing) moves per-evaluation cost to a vendor and sends location data off-platform, which is the wrong trade for the most sensitive data we hold. Cost: zero incremental. Scaling: geofence evaluation does not scale with fence count because of §34.6.2. Lock-in: none. Security: keeping location evaluation in-house avoids exporting guard positions to a third party — a material privacy advantage (§39).

#### 34.6.2 Geofence evaluation and its cost

The naive design — for each incoming ping, search all fences — is O(pings × fences) and is what makes geofencing expensive. We do not do it. A ping arrives with an `assignment_id`; the assignment resolves to one site and at most a handful of fences (site attendance fence, post fence, patrol fence, restricted zones), all of which are held in an in-memory cache in the signals consumer, keyed by site and refreshed on `site.geofence_changed`. Evaluation is therefore 1–5 point-in-polygon or distance checks per ping, in-process, with no database round trip: at V1 volume (~15 pings/second average) that is arithmetically negligible, and it stays negligible at 10× the volume.

Circle fences use a haversine distance comparison (cheaper than a polygon test); polygon fences use a bounding-box pre-check then a ray-cast. Hysteresis (§34.3.8) is applied before any event is emitted. The only case that requires a real spatial query is "which guards are near this point", which runs against the small `guard_last_position` table with a GiST index.

#### 34.6.3 Map tiles and provider

| Consideration | Position |
|---|---|
| Requirement | Street-level maps for India with reliable coverage of small roads and industrial areas; markers, clustering, polylines, polygon drawing; reverse geocoding for addresses; the console must render 200–500 markers smoothly |
| Options | **Google Maps** — best India coverage and geocoding, highest cost, strong lock-in, per-load pricing that scales with console usage. **Mapbox** — good styling and vector performance, weaker Indian small-road data in places, moderate cost. **MapMyIndia/Mappls** — strongest Indian addressing and a domestic vendor, less familiar tooling, worth evaluating specifically for reverse geocoding. **OpenStreetMap self-hosted tiles** — no per-view cost, full control, real operational work to run and update |
| V1 [RECOMMENDED] | A **map abstraction layer** in the frontend with one provider behind it (start with Google for coverage), plus aggressive caching of reverse-geocoding results (§32.1.9) since that is the metered call that scales with ping volume. Never reverse-geocode a ping on ingest — only on demand, for display. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-247]` on the provider, driven by a coverage test on 20 real client sites and a cost model at projected console usage |
| Cost control | Tile loads are the console's cost driver: cache aggressively, avoid re-initialising maps on tab switch, cluster markers, and never auto-refresh a map that no one is looking at (the console pauses map updates when the tab is hidden) |
| Lock-in | Contained by the abstraction layer; the switching cost is a frontend adapter plus a geocode cache re-fill, not a rewrite |

#### 34.6.4 Offline maps

The Guard App does **not** need offline maps in V1. What a guard needs offline is: their assignment details, the checkpoint list, the site address and gate instructions, an SOS button and an event buffer — none of which require a map. A static site image (a pre-rendered map thumbnail cached with the assignment) covers the "where is this gate" need at a fraction of the complexity. Full offline vector maps are on the do-not-build list. Supervisors doing multi-site visits are the plausible future case, and that is `[FUTURE]`.

### 34.7 Scale evolution

#### 34.7.1 V1 (pilot/city) topology

```
   Clients (web ×5, mobile ×4, desktop)
        │ HTTPS
        ▼
   CDN ──► Load balancer / WAF
        │
        ├──► API app servers (2–4 instances, modular monolith, stateless)
        ├──► WebSocket gateway (2 instances, sticky by connection)
        └──► Worker pool (2 instances: default / heavy / critical queues)
                 │
   ┌─────────────┼────────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────┐
   ▼             ▼                ▼              ▼                ▼
 Postgres     Postgres        Redis          Object          Providers
 primary      replica       (cache, rate     storage      (Razorpay, FCM,
 (+PostGIS,   (analytics,   limits, streams,  (S3-like)     SMS, WhatsApp,
  partitions)  reports)      pub/sub, locks)                 Zoho, maps)
```

One region (India), one availability zone plus a standby, one database, one Redis, one deployment pipeline. This is a deliberately small topology and it will comfortably run the pilot's 8,000 guards.

#### 34.7.2 Pan-India topology (target, not V1)

| Change | Trigger metric |
|---|---|
| Split GPS ingest into its own service and its own database | Ping rate >1,500/s sustained, or ingest lag p95 >10 s |
| Replace Redis Streams with Kafka (or a managed equivalent) | >2,000 events/s sustained, or a need for >7-day replay, or more than 6 independent consumer groups |
| Extract the real-time gateway to its own autoscaling tier with a dedicated pub/sub backplane | >20,000 concurrent sockets, or gateway CPU >60% sustained |
| Read replicas per region; primary stays single-region | Read latency p95 >300 ms from a distant region, and >30% of reads originating there |
| Build the columnar analytics warehouse | Triggers in §32.6.5 |
| Cell/pod topology (Model D, §32.1.1.5) | >500 tenants, or a single incident affecting >20% of tenants twice in a quarter |
| Database-per-tenant for the largest Enterprise tenants | Triggers in §32.1.1.4 |
| Multi-region active-passive with a documented RPO/RTO | Contractual DR requirement, or a regulator/enterprise buyer requiring it (§49 owns the DR design) |
| Separate audit-log and notification storage from the OLTP instance | Either table exceeding 30% of database size, or vacuum pressure affecting OLTP latency |
| Dedicated SOS path (separate compute, separate database connection pool, separate provider account) | Any single incident in which SOS latency exceeded target because of unrelated load — one occurrence is enough |

#### 34.7.3 Do not build this in V1

Explicitly out of scope, with the reason:

| Not building | Why |
|---|---|
| Kafka or any dedicated message broker | Redis Streams cover 100× our volume; a broker is an on-call surface without a problem |
| Microservices | Canon §4 settles this: modular monolith. Service extraction is justified by load or team boundaries, and we have neither yet |
| Event sourcing / CQRS as an architecture | The outbox plus a few read models gives the benefits we actually need without the reconstruction cost |
| A separate time-series database (ClickHouse/Influx) | Partitioned+compressed Postgres handles Year-2 volume |
| Second-by-second GPS tracking | No operational value; ruins battery and trust; §34.1 explains |
| Offline vector maps in the Guard App | §34.6.4 |
| Binary wire protocol for pings (protobuf/CBOR) | Gzip JSON already gives ~78%; the remaining gain is not worth the tooling |
| WebRTC / live video from the Guard App | Bandwidth in the field cannot support it; recorded evidence upload covers the need |
| Multi-region active-active | Enormous consistency cost for a single-country product |
| Client-side prediction/interpolation of guard movement on the map | Draws lines that did not happen; §33.3.9 makes gaps explicit instead |
| GraphQL | §33.1.1 |
| A custom rules engine for alerting | §24's rules are a configuration table; a DSL is a project of its own |
| Per-tenant databases as the default | §32.1.1.2 |
| Real-time streaming analytics (Flink/Spark) | Nightly batch plus a few incremental read models answers every V1 question |
| Face recognition on every check-in | Optional per post; universal biometric matching is an Enterprise-tier integration and a privacy commitment we should not make platform-wide (§39) |
| An in-house map tile server | Provider abstraction is cheaper until tile cost becomes visible |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-RT-014 | Each scale change in §34.7.2 shall be justified by its named trigger metric being observed and sustained for at least 7 days; no scale change shall be made on anticipation alone. |
| SUR-RT-015 | The items in §34.7.3 shall not be built in V1; a proposal to build one shall include the trigger metric that has been met and a written note of what will be removed to pay for it. |

| D-245 | Should the Enterprise API be metered and priced separately, or bundled into the Enterprise plan? | Affects rate-limit design, quota tracking and the commercial model | Bundled with a generous default quota; meter usage from day one so pricing can follow evidence | §52, §33.1.7 |
| D-246 | Do we support client-supplied webhook mTLS for Enterprise integrators? | Some enterprise security teams require it; it is real work to operate certificate rotation | HMAC signing only in V1; mTLS on request as an Enterprise engagement | §38, §33.4 |
| D-247 | Which map provider for V1 — Google, Mapbox or Mappls? | Coverage quality in tier-2/3 Indian cities directly affects geofence usability; cost scales with console usage | Run a coverage test on 20 real sites plus a cost model, then decide; keep the abstraction layer regardless | Cost, UX, §34.6 |
| D-248 | Should client-facing live tracking be offered at all in V1, and if so at what granularity? | It is a strong sales feature and a serious privacy commitment | Site-level presence and event feed, not individual live position, unless the contract and the guards' consent both cover it | §12, §15, §39 |
| A-240 | V1 scale is ~30 tenants, 8,000 guards, 900 sites; Year 2 ~400 tenants, 120,000 guards | All volumetrics, index and partition sizing derive from this | Validate against the pilot's actual signups at month 3 and re-run the sizing | §32.4, §50, infrastructure cost |
| A-241 | 13 months of location retention is operationally sufficient for dispute resolution | Determines storage cost and privacy exposure | Review after the first 3 client disputes involving location evidence | §39, cost |
| A-242 | Guard age band 18–65 is the right configurable default | Affects validation defaults on guard creation | Confirm with Compliance; keep it configuration, never code | §30, §40 |
| A-243 | Enterprise integrators will accept generated clients from an OpenAPI spec rather than hand-written SDKs | Determines whether SDK maintenance enters the roadmap | Revisit at 10 integrating Enterprise tenants | §33.5.3, roadmap |
| A-244 | Adaptive GPS sampling (30 s–5 min) is operationally acceptable to clients who were sold "live tracking" | If clients expect second-level tracking, expectations must be reset in sales material rather than met in engineering | State the actual update cadence in the client-facing product copy | §12, §14, §34.1 |
| R-240 | A cross-tenant data leak through a missing tenant predicate | Existential for a multi-tenant B2B platform serving competitors | Three independent layers (query predicate, RLS, composite FKs) plus a CI test that enumerates tables and policies | Catastrophic: trust, contracts, regulatory |
| R-241 | GPS ingest volume grows faster than projected and degrades the OLTP primary | The live deployment board and check-in path share the database | Ingest is already off the request path and queue-buffered; the extraction trigger is defined in §34.7.2 | Availability of core operations |
| R-242 | A partition-creation job failure causes a write outage on `location` or `audit_log` | Silent until it is sudden | 30-day runway, P1 alert below 7 days (SUR-DAT-027) | Field operations halt |
| R-243 | Reconciliation finds a ledger imbalance that cannot be explained | Financial trust with agencies and clients | Ledger is append-only with balanced-transaction enforcement; imbalance is P0 and quarantined, never auto-corrected | Financial integrity, BR-003 |
| R-244 | An Enterprise API key is leaked and used to exfiltrate guard PII | Key holders are outside our security perimeter | Scoped keys, per-key rate limits, IP allow-lists, usage anomaly alerts, one-click revoke, no bulk PII endpoints in the Enterprise subset | Privacy breach, §38, §39 |
| R-245 | A webhook consumer's duplicate handling is wrong and doubles an agency's accounting entries | Damages trust in the integration and is hard to detect from our side | At-least-once documented prominently, stable event ids, a delivery log the agency can inspect, a sandbox that fires duplicates on demand | Integration trust, support load |
| R-246 | The WebSocket gateway fails silently and operators stop receiving alerts without noticing | A missed P0 is the worst outcome in the product | Acknowledged delivery for P0/P1, independent 20-second reconciliation poll, visible freshness indicator, alert on gateway health | Life-safety, brand promise |
| R-247 | Push notification latency (FCM/APNs) makes wake-check dispatch unreliable on some devices | Wake checks are a headline feature; unfair failures damage guard trust | Measure dispatch-to-delivery per device platform; SUR-RT-010 protects guards from our latency; SMS fallback for repeated push failure | Product credibility, guard fairness |
| R-248 | Map provider cost grows non-linearly with console usage | An operational surprise in month 6 | Abstraction layer, geocode caching, paused updates on hidden tabs, monthly cost review against console session count | Unit economics |



## 35. Financial Architecture

This section is the canonical home for how money is represented, moved, recorded, reconciled and reported across every Suraksha product. Every other section that mentions an amount, an invoice, a payout or a settlement refers here. Booking and quotation lifecycles live in §11 and §12; contract lifecycle lives in §12; entity field definitions live in §32; endpoints live in §33; business rules live in §30. This section owns the ledger, the money state machines, and the controls.

The financial subsystem is the part of the platform that is hardest to fix after launch. A wrong pixel is a ticket; a wrong ledger is a restatement, a client dispute, an unpaid guard and a regulatory problem at once. Accordingly this section is written to be conservative: append-only records, integer arithmetic, explicit idempotency, and no operation that changes a posted number in place.

### 35.1 Financial principles

These nine principles are binding on every module that touches money. A module that cannot satisfy them does not ship.

#### 35.1.1 Integer paise everywhere

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-001 | All monetary values shall be stored and transported as signed 64-bit integers denominated in the minor unit of the currency (paise for INR). Floating-point types shall never be used for money in any layer — database column, API payload, calculation engine, export file or report. |
| SUR-FIN-002 | Every money field shall be accompanied by an ISO-4217 `currency_code` and an integer `minor_unit_scale` (2 for INR), so that a future currency with a different scale does not require a data migration of existing rows. |
| SUR-FIN-003 | API request and response bodies shall carry money as an object `{ "amount_minor": 8732000, "currency": "INR" }`, never as a formatted string or a decimal number. Formatting to "₹87,320.00" is a presentation-layer concern only. |
| SUR-FIN-004 | Percentage-based computations (tax, commission, proration, interest) shall be performed in integer arithmetic using a numerator/denominator pair or a basis-point integer, with the rounding rule applied exactly once at the defined rounding point (§35.1.6). |
| SUR-FIN-005 | Any import of external financial data (gateway settlement file, bank statement, accounting export round-trip) shall parse decimals into minor units with explicit scale validation and shall reject, not round, a value with more precision than the declared scale. |

Rationale, stated once: `18500.00 * 0.18` in IEEE-754 double arithmetic does not reliably produce `3330.00`. At 10,000 invoices a month a systematic one-paisa drift is a reconciliation break every day. Integers remove the entire failure class.

#### 35.1.2 Double-entry ledger

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-006 | Every financial movement shall be recorded as a **Ledger Transaction** containing two or more **Ledger Entry** lines, where the sum of debit amounts equals the sum of credit amounts, in the same currency, exactly, in integer minor units. |
| SUR-FIN-007 | The balance constraint shall be enforced at write time inside the same database transaction that inserts the lines, not by a later batch job. A transaction that does not balance shall fail the write. |
| SUR-FIN-008 | No process shall ever compute a balance by mutating a stored running total as its source of truth. Balances shall be derived from ledger entries; materialised balance rows may exist as a performance cache, must carry `as_of_entry_id`, and must be verifiable by full recomputation. |
| SUR-FIN-009 | Operational documents (Invoice, Payment, Payslip, Settlement, Refund, Credit Note) shall be **projections over** ledger transactions, linked by `ledger_transaction_id`. The document is what a human reads; the ledger is what the platform believes. |
| SUR-FIN-010 | Every ledger transaction shall carry `tenant_id`. Cross-tenant transactions (Suraksha ↔ Agency settlement) shall be recorded as two mirrored transactions — one in each tenant's book — linked by a shared `settlement_reference`, never as a single transaction spanning tenants. |

#### 35.1.3 Immutability of posted transactions (BR-003)

BR-003 states that completed financial transactions can never be silently modified. The architecture implements it structurally, not by policy.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-011 | Ledger entries shall be append-only. The application shall hold no `UPDATE` or `DELETE` statement against the ledger entry table; the database role used by the application shall lack those privileges on that table. |
| SUR-FIN-012 | A posted transaction shall be corrected only by posting a **reversal transaction** that mirrors every original line with opposite signs, carrying `reverses_transaction_id`, a mandatory `reason_code`, a free-text reason, and the acting user; followed, where applicable, by a fresh correct transaction carrying `replaces_transaction_id`. |
| SUR-FIN-013 | Reversal shall require a reason from a controlled vocabulary (`data_entry_error`, `duplicate_posting`, `client_dispute_upheld`, `gateway_reversal`, `attendance_restatement`, `rate_correction`, `regulatory_correction`, `other_with_narrative`). `other_with_narrative` shall require ≥ 40 characters of narrative. |
| SUR-FIN-014 | Documents in a posted state (Issued invoice, Approved payroll run, Settled settlement, Captured payment) shall be immutable. Editing shall be offered in the UI only as "Reverse and re-issue", which creates a new document with a new number and a visible link to the reversed one. |
| SUR-FIN-015 | Every ledger transaction shall store an integrity hash over its canonical serialisation, chained to the previous transaction hash within the tenant (`prev_hash`), so that any retrospective tampering at the storage layer is detectable by re-walking the chain. |
| SUR-FIN-016 | The reversal history of any document shall be visible to any user who can view the document, not hidden behind an admin screen. A client viewing a reversed invoice shall see that it was reversed, when, and by which replacement document. |

#### 35.1.4 Idempotency on every money-moving operation

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-017 | Every API operation that can create, capture, refund or post money shall require an `Idempotency-Key` header supplied by the caller. Requests without one shall be rejected with 400. |
| SUR-FIN-018 | The platform shall persist an idempotency record keyed by `(tenant_id, endpoint, idempotency_key)` holding the request fingerprint (hash of the canonical body), the resulting HTTP status, the response body and the `ledger_transaction_id`. Retention: 90 days minimum. |
| SUR-FIN-019 | A repeat request with the same key and the same fingerprint shall return the stored response verbatim without re-executing. A repeat with the same key and a **different** fingerprint shall return 409 `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` and shall be logged as a P2 finance exception. |
| SUR-FIN-020 | Internal money-moving jobs (payroll disbursement, settlement release, recurring billing, dunning charge) shall derive a deterministic idempotency key from their business identity — e.g. `payroll_run:{run_id}:disburse`, `billing:{subscription_id}:{period_start}` — so that a re-run of the job is a no-op rather than a double charge. |
| SUR-FIN-021 | Every inbound webhook shall be deduplicated on the provider's event id in an `inbound_webhook_event` table with a unique constraint; duplicate deliveries shall be acknowledged with 200 and discarded without side effects (§35.3.10). |
| SUR-FIN-022 | Idempotency shall be enforced at the ledger layer as a backstop: a unique constraint on `(tenant_id, source_type, source_id, posting_purpose)` shall prevent the same business event from producing two postings even if an upper layer misbehaves. |

#### 35.1.5 Immutability of money-relevant inputs

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-023 | Rates, tax rates, commission percentages and statutory parameters shall be stored as **versioned effective-dated records**. A computation shall record which version it used (`rate_card_version_id`, `tax_profile_version_id`, `statutory_config_version_id`). |
| SUR-FIN-024 | Changing a rate shall never retroactively alter a posted computation. Recomputation of a past period shall require an explicit restatement action that reverses and re-posts, with reason and approval. |
| SUR-FIN-025 | Attendance data that has been consumed by an approved invoice or an approved payroll run shall be locked for that period. Later attendance corrections shall be applied as adjustments in the next open period, or by an authorised restatement, never by silent mutation (see §35.4.2 and §35.6.9). |

#### 35.1.6 Currency and rounding rules

| Rule | Definition |
|---|---|
| Currency | INR only in V1. The schema is currency-aware; multi-currency behaviour (FX rates, revaluation) is `[FUTURE]`. |
| Rounding mode | Half-up away from zero, applied to the minor unit (paise). |
| Tax rounding point | Tax is computed **per invoice line** on the line's taxable value, rounded to paise per line, then summed. The invoice total is the sum of rounded lines; the platform shall not recompute tax on the invoice total. |
| Proration rounding | Prorated amounts are computed as `floor(base * used_units / total_units)` for credits and `ceil(...)` for charges is **not** used; both use half-up, and the residual paise (difference between the sum of prorated parts and the base) is assigned to the **last** prorated line so the parts always sum to the whole. |
| Percentage representation | All percentages stored as integer basis points (18% = 1800 bp). |
| Display | Amounts display as `₹1,23,456.78` using the Indian digit grouping in all Indian-locale surfaces; exports use plain `123456.78` with a period decimal separator. |
| Negative amounts | Credit notes, reversals and refunds are represented by sign on the ledger line, never by a separate "negative document type" convention that the reader must infer. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-026 | The rounding rules above shall be implemented in one shared library used by billing, payroll, settlement, subscription and reporting. No module shall implement its own rounding. |
| SUR-FIN-027 | Where a rounding residual arises (proration splits, allocation of a payment across lines, distribution of a discount), the residual shall be assigned deterministically to a single designated line, and the allocation algorithm shall be documented in the payload as `allocation_method`. |
| SUR-FIN-028 | Every computed amount shall be reproducible: given the same versioned inputs, re-running the calculation shall produce an identical integer. Calculation engines shall be pure functions over persisted inputs, with no dependence on wall-clock time other than an explicit `as_of` parameter. |

#### 35.1.7 Separation of billing from payments

The single most common design error in this domain is conflating "what is owed" with "what moved". Suraksha separates them absolutely.

| Concern | Object | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Billing | Invoice, Credit Note, Debit Note, Subscription Charge | What does this party owe, for what, under which contract, with which tax treatment? |
| Payment | Payment, Refund, Payout, Settlement, Wallet movement | What money actually moved, on which rail, with which external reference, and did it clear? |
| Application | Payment Allocation | Which received money is applied against which billed obligation, and in what order? |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-029 | Invoices and payments shall be independent objects joined by explicit allocation rows. A payment may be allocated across many invoices; an invoice may be settled by many payments, a wallet debit, a credit note and an advance simultaneously. |
| SUR-FIN-030 | An invoice shall never carry a "paid" boolean as its source of truth. Its settlement status shall be derived from allocations: `Pending` (nothing allocated), `In Progress` (partially allocated), `Completed` (fully allocated), plus `Cancelled` and `Archived`. |
| SUR-FIN-031 | Default allocation order shall be configurable per tenant with the platform default: oldest invoice first, within an invoice — tax-inclusive line order, with an explicit manual override available to Finance that is recorded in the audit log. |
| SUR-FIN-032 | Unallocated received money shall sit as a liability (Customer Advances or Wallet), never as revenue, and shall appear on an "unapplied receipts" exception queue after a configurable ageing threshold (default 7 days). |

### 35.2 Chart of accounts and the ledger model

#### 35.2.1 Account types and normal balances

| Type | Normal balance | Increases with | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asset | Debit | Debit | Bank, Gateway Receivable, Accounts Receivable, Advances paid |
| Liability | Credit | Credit | Customer Advances, Wallet Liability, Salary Payable, GST Output Payable |
| Equity | Credit | Credit | Retained earnings (not transacted by the platform) |
| Income | Credit | Credit | Guarding Revenue, SaaS Revenue, Commission Income, Penalty Recovery |
| Expense | Debit | Debit | Wages, Agency Fulfilment Cost, Gateway Fees, SMS Cost |
| Contra | Opposite of parent | — | Sales Returns / SLA Credits (contra-income) |

| SUR-FIN-033 | Application code shall reference accounts only by role key. A tenant may remap a role key to a different account code; the mapping shall be versioned and a change shall require Agency Finance (or Suraksha Finance for HQ) approval. |

#### 35.2.3 Ledger entry structure

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ledger_transaction_id` | UUID | Groups the lines |
| `tenant_id` | UUID | Mandatory on every line |
| `branch_id` | UUID nullable | Second scoping axis for branch P&L |
| `posted_at` | timestamptz | Server clock; immutable |
| `effective_date` | date | Accounting date; may differ from `posted_at` (e.g. a 30-Jun invoice posted on 2-Jul) |
| `accounting_period_id` | FK | Resolved at post time; blocked if the period is closed |
| `source_type` | enum | `invoice`, `payment`, `refund`, `credit_note`, `payroll_run`, `settlement`, `wallet`, `subscription`, `adjustment`, `reconciliation` |
| `source_id` | UUID | The originating document |
| `posting_purpose` | enum | `issue`, `capture`, `settle`, `accrue`, `reverse`, `fee`, `tax`, `hold`, `release` |
| `line_no` | int | Ordinal within the transaction |
| `account_role` | string | Resolved to `account_id` at post time; both stored |
| `direction` | enum | `debit` \| `credit` |
| `amount_minor` | bigint | Always positive; sign carried by `direction` |
| `currency` | char(3) | `INR` |
| `party_type` / `party_id` | enum / UUID | `client`, `agency`, `guard`, `vendor`, `internal` — enables sub-ledger balances |
| `memo` | text | Human-readable line narrative |
| `reverses_transaction_id` | UUID nullable | Set on reversal transactions |
| `idempotency_key` | string | Carried from the originating request |
| `prev_hash` / `entry_hash` | bytea | Tenant-scoped hash chain |
| `created_by` | UUID | User or `system:{job_name}` |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-FIN-036 | Sub-ledger balances (per client, per agency, per guard) shall be derivable by filtering ledger entries on `party_type`/`party_id` and shall reconcile exactly to the control account balance. A daily job shall assert this equality and raise a P1 exception on any difference. |
| SUR-FIN-037 | Accounting periods shall be explicit records with states `Open`, `In Progress` (soft close), `Completed` (hard close). Posting to a `Completed` period shall be rejected; an authorised reopening shall be a logged, approval-gated event. |
| SUR-FIN-038 | Every ledger transaction shall be retrievable via the API with all lines, its source document, its reversal chain and its hash, so that an Auditor role can walk any number end-to-end without database access. |

#### 35.2.4 Worked double-entry examples

All amounts shown in rupees with the paise integer in parentheses. Every example balances; the balance check is shown.

**(1) Client prepayment — ₹50,000 advance received by UPI via the gateway**

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1100 Payment Gateway Clearing | ₹50,000.00 (5,000,000) | |
| 2 | 2200 Customer Advances | | ₹50,000.00 (5,000,000) |

Balance: 5,000,000 = 5,000,000. No revenue is recognised: the client has paid for nothing yet.

**(1b) Gateway settles to bank next day, fee ₹1,000 + tax ₹180**

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1010 Bank — Operating | ₹48,820.00 (4,882,000) | |
| 2 | 6300 Payment Gateway Fees | ₹1,000.00 (100,000) | |
| 3 | 1400 Tax Input Credit | ₹180.00 (18,000) | |
| 4 | 1100 Payment Gateway Clearing | | ₹50,000.00 (5,000,000) |

Balance: 4,882,000 + 100,000 + 18,000 = 5,000,000 ✓

**(2) Monthly guarding invoice — 4 unarmed guards at ₹18,500, tax at 1800 bp**

Taxable value ₹74,000.00 (7,400,000); tax ₹13,320.00 (1,332,000); total ₹87,320.00 (8,732,000).

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1200 Accounts Receivable — Trade | ₹87,320.00 (8,732,000) | |
| 2 | 4100 Guarding Services Revenue | | ₹74,000.00 (7,400,000) |
| 3 | 2300 Tax Output Payable | | ₹13,320.00 (1,332,000) |

Balance: 8,732,000 = 7,400,000 + 1,332,000 ✓

**(2b) Applying the earlier advance against this invoice**

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2200 Customer Advances | ₹50,000.00 (5,000,000) | |
| 2 | 1200 Accounts Receivable — Trade | | ₹50,000.00 (5,000,000) |

Open receivable after application: 8,732,000 − 5,000,000 = **3,732,000** (₹37,320.00).

**(3) Partial payment — client pays ₹20,000 by netbanking**

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1100 Payment Gateway Clearing | ₹20,000.00 (2,000,000) | |
| 2 | 1200 Accounts Receivable — Trade | | ₹20,000.00 (2,000,000) |

Open receivable: 3,732,000 − 2,000,000 = **1,732,000** (₹17,320.00). Invoice settlement status = `In Progress`.

**(4) Refund with cancellation charge — booking of ₹10,000 + ₹1,800 tax paid; cancelled inside the 25% window**

Cancellation charge = 25% of taxable value = ₹2,500.00 (250,000) plus tax ₹450.00 (45,000). Refund = ₹11,800.00 − ₹2,950.00 = ₹8,850.00.

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2200 Customer Advances | ₹11,800.00 (1,180,000) | |
| 2 | 4300 Cancellation & No-show Charges | | ₹2,500.00 (250,000) |
| 3 | 2300 Tax Output Payable | | ₹450.00 (45,000) |
| 4 | 1100 Payment Gateway Clearing | | ₹8,850.00 (885,000) |

Balance: 1,180,000 = 250,000 + 45,000 + 885,000 ✓. A tax invoice is issued for the cancellation charge; the refund leg carries the gateway refund reference.

**(5) Credit note — SLA credit of ₹4,000 taxable value against an issued invoice**

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4900 SLA Credits & Service Adjustments | ₹4,000.00 (400,000) | |
| 2 | 2300 Tax Output Payable | ₹720.00 (72,000) | |
| 3 | 1200 Accounts Receivable — Trade | | ₹4,720.00 (472,000) |

Balance: 400,000 + 72,000 = 472,000 ✓. The original invoice is untouched (SUR-FIN-014); the credit note is a separate numbered document linked to it.

**(6) Agency settlement — partner agency fulfilled work billed to the client at ₹1,00,000 taxable value; commission 12%**

Step A — accrue the fulfilment cost on client acceptance of the period's attendance:

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5100 Cost of Service — Agency Fulfilment | ₹88,000.00 (8,800,000) | |
| 2 | 2400 Agency Settlement Payable | | ₹88,000.00 (8,800,000) |

Commission of ₹12,000 is never "paid then received" — it is the difference between client revenue (4100, ₹1,00,000) and fulfilment cost (5100, ₹88,000). Where the commercial model requires an explicit commission invoice to the agency, `REV_COMMISSION` is credited instead and the full ₹1,00,000 accrues to 2400; the choice is a per-contract configuration.

Step B — settlement statement deductions (penalty ₹2,000, advance recovery ₹3,000, configured withholding 200 bp of ₹88,000 = ₹1,760):

| Line | Account | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
