## 37. Integration Architecture

Suraksha depends on external services for maps, money, messaging, identity, verification and analytics. Every one of them is a source of cost, of privacy exposure, of downtime the platform does not control, and of lock-in. This section defines how integrations are built so that any one of them can fail, be replaced, or be configured differently per tenant without a rewrite.

Two honesty statements govern this entire section, per canon §0:

1. **No API is invented here.** Where a public, reliable API is uncertain or does not exist — notably PSARA licence verification and government tender portals — this section says so and specifies a manual or assisted design instead.
2. **Every named vendor is a recommendation, not a commitment.** Named alternatives are given for each so that a procurement decision is a configuration choice rather than a re-architecture.

### 37.1 The integration framework

#### 37.1.1 Adapter pattern

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-001 | Every external dependency shall be accessed through a **capability interface** defined by Suraksha (e.g. `PaymentGateway`, `SmsSender`, `DocumentOcr`, `MapProvider`), with one adapter per vendor implementing it. No vendor SDK type shall appear in domain code, request/response models or the database. |
| SUR-INT-002 | Capability interfaces shall be defined by what Suraksha needs, not by what a vendor offers. A vendor feature that does not fit the interface is either promoted into the interface deliberately, or not used. |
| SUR-INT-003 | Each adapter shall normalise errors into a shared taxonomy: `transient`, `rate_limited`, `auth_failed`, `invalid_request`, `not_supported`, `provider_policy_block`, `permanent_failure`, and shall retain the vendor's raw error code and message for support. |
| SUR-INT-004 | Every adapter shall implement: `health()`, `capabilities()` (what this vendor supports of the interface), and full request/response logging with PII redaction per §39. |
| SUR-INT-005 | Provider selection shall be resolvable per tenant, per region and per use case through a routing configuration, so that (for example) one agency's SMS goes through aggregator A and another's through aggregator B, without code changes. |
| SUR-INT-006 | Every integration shall be independently disableable. Disabling an integration shall degrade the dependent feature with an explicit user-facing message, never produce a blank screen or a silent no-op. |

#### 37.1.2 Credential storage

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-007 | Integration credentials shall be stored in a managed secrets store (cloud KMS-backed secret manager or HashiCorp Vault), never in environment files committed to source control, never in the application database in plaintext, and never in tenant-visible configuration screens after first entry. |
| SUR-INT-008 | Tenant-supplied credentials (an agency's own SMS account, their own accounting keys) shall be encrypted with a per-tenant data key wrapped by a master key, shall be write-only in the UI (enter, replace, delete — never read back), and shall show only a masked fingerprint. |
| SUR-INT-009 | Credentials shall carry rotation metadata (created, last rotated, expiry where applicable) with alerts at 30/7/1 days before expiry, and a rotation runbook per provider. |
| SUR-INT-010 | Access to decrypt an integration credential shall be limited to the specific service that needs it, shall be logged, and shall trigger a security alert on any access outside the expected service identity. |
| SUR-INT-011 | Webhook endpoints shall verify provider signatures using a shared secret or public key stored the same way, and shall reject unsigned or invalidly signed payloads (SUR-FIN-074 applies to payment webhooks specifically). |

#### 37.1.3 Per-tenant integration configuration

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-012 | Each integration shall have a per-tenant configuration record: `enabled`, `mode` (`platform_account` \| `tenant_account`), credentials reference, feature flags, rate limits, cost cap, sandbox/production flag, and an owner contact. |
| SUR-INT-013 | `platform_account` mode (Suraksha's own vendor account serving all tenants) shall be the default for Starter and Professional plans; `tenant_account` mode (the agency's own vendor account) shall be available where the plan permits, and is a common Enterprise requirement. |
| SUR-INT-014 | Integration configuration changes shall be audited with before/after (credentials masked), and shall require the tenant's admin-level permission plus, for money-moving integrations, a second approver. |

#### 37.1.4 Sandbox vs production

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-015 | Every integration shall support three modes: `mock` (deterministic local fake used in automated tests and local development), `sandbox` (the vendor's test environment), and `production`. Mode shall be explicit per environment and per tenant, never inferred from a hostname. |
| SUR-INT-016 | Non-production environments shall be physically incapable of reaching production provider credentials, enforced by separate secret stores and network policy — not by a configuration flag alone. |
| SUR-INT-017 | The UI shall display a persistent, unmissable banner whenever a tenant is operating any integration in sandbox mode, especially payments, since a sandbox payment that looks successful is a serious operational trap. |
| SUR-INT-018 | A `mock` adapter shall exist for every capability and shall be complete enough that the entire platform can run end-to-end with zero external dependencies, which is a precondition for reliable CI. |

#### 37.1.5 Health checks, circuit breakers and observability

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-019 | Each integration shall be probed on a schedule appropriate to its criticality (payments and SMS every 60 s, OCR and analytics every 5 min) using a non-mutating operation, and the result shall feed an integration health dashboard with per-provider status, latency percentiles and error rate. |
| SUR-INT-020 | A circuit breaker per provider per capability shall open on a configured error rate or latency threshold, shall hold open for a cool-down, and shall half-open with limited probe traffic. Breaker state changes shall alert and shall be visible to operations. |
| SUR-INT-021 | Where a fallback provider exists, breaker opening shall automatically route to it; where none exists, the dependent feature shall degrade per its defined fallback (§37.2) and users shall be told what is unavailable and what to do instead. |
| SUR-INT-022 | All external calls shall carry a timeout (default 5 s for interactive paths, 30 s for batch), a retry budget, and a correlation id propagated to the provider where supported, so a slow provider can never exhaust the application's connection pool. |
| SUR-INT-023 | Integration cost shall be metered per call per tenant where the provider charges per call, and shall be reported alongside notification cost (§36.6) in the per-tenant margin view. |
| SUR-INT-024 | Every integration shall have a documented runbook: what it does, who owns it, what breaks if it is down, how to switch providers, how to rotate credentials, and the vendor's support escalation path. |

### 37.2 Integration catalogue

Each integration below is specified on the eight required dimensions. "Data shared" is deliberately precise about personal data, because these are the exact flows a privacy assessment (§39) must review.

#### 37.2.1 Maps and geocoding

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Address autocomplete and geocoding for sites and bookings, map rendering in portals and apps, geofence definition, route/ETA for replacement dispatch and field officer visits, distance calculation for travel allowance |
| Data shared | Address text typed by the user; latitude/longitude of sites; **for routing**: origin/destination coordinates. No guard name, no client name, no identifier is sent to the map provider. Live guard positions are **not** sent to a map SDK's backend beyond what tile rendering requires. |
| Pattern | Client-side SDK for rendering and autocomplete (with session tokens); server-side REST for geocoding, distance matrix and reverse geocoding, cached |
| Security | API keys restricted by application/bundle id and by HTTP referrer; separate keys per platform; server keys IP-restricted; quotas set below the billing alarm threshold; keys rotated on schedule |
| Failure fallback | Geocoding failure → manual coordinate entry with a map pin, or store the address unresolved and retry in the background. Map tile failure → static map image fallback, then a coordinates-and-address text view. Geofence evaluation is **server-side and provider-independent** (point-in-polygon on stored geometry) so attendance never depends on a map vendor. |
| Cost | Per-request pricing for autocomplete/geocode/directions; tile loads billed per session or per load. Dominant drivers: autocomplete keystrokes and map loads in the Guard App. Levers: session tokens, aggressive geocode caching (an address resolves once, forever), static maps for non-interactive views, debounced autocomplete |
| Lock-in risk | **Medium.** Stored geometry (WKT/GeoJSON) is portable; SDK-specific UI code is not. Place ids are provider-specific and must be treated as a cache key, never as a primary key |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Google Maps Platform as primary (best Indian address coverage and autocomplete quality). Alternatives: MapmyIndia/Mappls (strong Indian data, often cheaper, good for a second source), Mapbox (good rendering economics), OpenStreetMap with a self-hosted tile server plus Nominatim/Photon (lowest marginal cost, weaker Indian address quality) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-025 | Geofence evaluation, distance-from-post calculation and attendance geo-validation shall be computed server-side from stored geometry using a spatial library, with no runtime dependency on a map vendor. |
| SUR-INT-026 | Every resolved address shall be stored with its components, coordinates, resolution source and confidence, so that a later provider change does not require re-resolving the estate. |

#### 37.2.2 GPS and location tracking

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Live guard location during shifts, attendance geo-validation, patrol checkpoint proximity, SOS location, route history for incident reconstruction, field officer movement |
| Data shared | This is **not a third-party integration** — location is collected by Suraksha's own apps from the device OS and sent to Suraksha's ingest path (§34). No location data leaves the platform to a vendor. Third parties involved: the device OS location provider and, optionally, a mobile device management or telematics vendor for issued devices `[FUTURE]` |
| Pattern | Device-side collection with adaptive sampling (higher frequency on duty, on patrol, during SOS; low or none off duty), batched upload with offline queue, WebSocket/ingest endpoint per §34 |
| Security | Location collected only during scheduled duty windows plus explicit SOS; transmitted over TLS; stored encrypted; access strictly permission-gated; clients see a guard's location only for guards deployed at their own sites and only during shift hours |
| Failure fallback | No connectivity → local queue on the device with the offline-first design (canon §4), uploaded on reconnect with both `device_time` and `server_received_time`. GPS unavailable indoors → last known position with accuracy radius, network-based location, and a visible accuracy indicator; attendance falls back to the configured alternative (supervisor confirmation, QR/NFC checkpoint, biometric device) |
| Cost | Mobile data cost borne by the device; server cost is ingest and storage — the largest storage line in the platform. Levers: adaptive sampling, downsampling of historical tracks per the retention rule (D-144), compression |
| Lock-in risk | **None** — first-party |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` First-party collection, with the platform's own geofence engine. Do not adopt a third-party location-tracking SaaS: it would place the most sensitive data Suraksha holds in a vendor's hands with no compensating benefit |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-027 | Location collection shall be bounded by duty windows and SOS. Continuous off-duty tracking shall not be implemented, shall not be configurable on, and shall be stated plainly to guards in the app's privacy notice (see §39). |
| SUR-INT-028 | Any future telematics or MDM integration shall be treated as a new integration with its own privacy assessment; it shall not be added under an existing configuration. |

#### 37.2.3 Payment gateway

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Collect client payments (UPI, cards, netbanking, wallets), recurring mandates, refunds, payment links; per canon §4 Razorpay is settled for client payments |
| Data shared | Payer name, email, phone, amount, order id, invoice reference, and the customer's own payment instrument data entered **directly into the provider's SDK/hosted page**. Suraksha's servers never receive full card numbers, CVV, UPI PINs or netbanking credentials |
| Pattern | Server-created order → provider SDK/checkout on the client → webhook + server-side verify + reconciliation sweeper (the three-path design in §35.3.10) → daily settlement file ingest |
| Security | Webhook signature verification mandatory; no card data touches Suraksha systems (scope-minimising by design); tokenised card-on-file only via the provider's tokenisation; keys in the secrets store; separate keys per environment; refund and payout permissions on separate credentials where the provider supports it |
| Failure fallback | Checkout unavailable → offer alternative instruments, then a payment link retried later, then manual bank transfer with UTR capture and reconciliation via `SUSPENSE_IN`. Webhook outage → sweeper and settlement file (SUR-FIN-071/072) mean no payment is lost. Provider-wide outage → secondary gateway if configured, otherwise bank transfer with manual reconciliation |
| Cost | Percentage MDR per transaction varying by instrument (UPI typically lowest, cards highest), plus platform fees on payouts/mandates. Levers: instrument steering (present UPI first), mandate-based collection to reduce failed-retry volume, negotiating rates at volume |
| Lock-in risk | **Medium-high.** Stored provider payment ids, tokens and mandates are non-portable; mandates in particular usually cannot be migrated and must be re-collected from customers. This is the single most painful migration in the stack |
| Recommendation | `[CONFIRMED]` Razorpay primary per canon §4. `[RECOMMENDED]` design the `PaymentGateway` interface to admit a second provider from day one. Alternatives: Cashfree, PayU, PhonePe Payment Gateway, Stripe (weaker for Indian domestic instruments). Payout rail for salaries/settlements remains D-142 |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-029 | The platform shall store only provider references (payment id, order id, token id, mandate id) and the last four digits / masked VPA for display. No PAN, CVV, PIN or full bank credential shall ever be stored or logged. |
| SUR-INT-030 | Mandate migration risk shall be documented in the vendor exit plan (§37.6): switching gateways requires re-collecting mandates from every auto-pay customer, and the platform shall support running two gateways concurrently during such a migration. |

#### 37.2.4 SMS

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | OTP, P0/P1 safety failover, payment and payroll confirmations, dunning, reminders to users without the app (§36.3.2) |
| Data shared | Recipient mobile number and the rendered message body, which by template design contains the minimum personal data (first name, a reference number, an amount where the event requires it) |
| Pattern | Server-side REST to the aggregator; DLT-registered templates; delivery-receipt webhooks ingested into the delivery ledger |
| Security | API credentials in the secrets store; sender id and template id validated before dispatch; message bodies containing PII redacted in application logs; delivery receipts authenticated |
| Failure fallback | Primary aggregator degraded → automatic failover to the secondary (SUR-NTF-036). Both down → push and in-app continue; P0 escalates to voice call and to human contact through the Command Center |
| Cost | §36.6. The largest controllable communication line; OTP is usually the biggest component |
| Lock-in risk | **Low.** Templates must be re-registered on a new aggregator's DLT link, which takes days, but no data is trapped. Keep the DLT entity registration in Suraksha's own name, not the aggregator's |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Two aggregators from the outset. Candidates: MSG91, Kaleyra, Gupshup, Twilio (higher cost, strong reliability and tooling), Airtel IQ / Jio (operator-direct). Choose one high-tooling and one cost-optimised, and route by priority |

#### 37.2.5 WhatsApp

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Rich client-facing updates, guard profile sharing, invoice and report links, support conversations — where opted in and where policy and template approval permit (§36.3.3) |
| Data shared | Recipient WhatsApp number, template variables (name, booking reference, amount, link), media where attached. Message content transits Meta's infrastructure |
| Pattern | Business Solution Provider or the cloud API; pre-approved templates for business-initiated messages; 24-hour session window for free-form replies; inbound webhook into the support system |
| Security | BSP credentials in the secrets store; opt-in evidence stored; media links signed and expiring; no sensitive document delivered as an attachment — always a link requiring authentication |
| Failure fallback | Template unapproved, opt-in absent, session window closed, or provider degraded → automatic fallback to SMS or push per the event chain (SUR-NTF-040). WhatsApp is never the sole path for P0/P1 |
| Cost | §36.6; conversation- or message-based and historically volatile. Model with a wide band and a per-tenant cap |
| Lock-in risk | **Medium.** The phone number and its verified business identity are portable between BSPs but the migration involves downtime and re-approval of templates; template libraries must be re-submitted |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` A BSP with good Indian support and a migration-friendly contract — candidates: Gupshup, Interakt, AiSensy, Twilio, Infobip, or Meta Cloud API direct. `[ASSUMPTION: A-271]` that Suraksha's use cases fit approved utility/service template categories; if a category is rejected, the affected events fall back permanently to SMS/push |

#### 37.2.6 Email

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Transactional documents (invoices, statements, payslips, reports), formal notices, dunning letters, staff and agency communication (§36.3.4) |
| Data shared | Recipient email address, name, rendered body, and attachments which may contain substantial personal and financial data (payslips, invoices, attendance annexures) |
| Pattern | SMTP/API to the provider; separate subdomains per purpose; bounce and complaint webhooks ingested; suppression list maintained platform-side, not only at the provider |
| Security | SPF/DKIM/DMARC per §36.3.4; TLS enforced on transport; attachments containing sensitive data password-protected or replaced by authenticated links per tenant policy; DKIM keys rotated annually |
| Failure fallback | Provider outage → secondary provider adapter (same domain, pre-configured SPF include and DKIM selector so failover does not require a DNS change under pressure); persistent failure → in-app + push notification that the document is available in the portal |
| Cost | Low and effectively fixed; the real cost is deliverability management effort |
| Lock-in risk | **Low**, provided the sending domain is Suraksha's own and DNS is Suraksha-controlled. Templates are portable; suppression lists must be exported and re-imported |
| Recommendation | `[CONFIRMED]` Zoho per canon §4. `[RECOMMENDED]` a second provider pre-configured for failover: Amazon SES (cheapest at volume), SendGrid, Postmark (best transactional deliverability tooling), Mailgun |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-031 | DNS for the sending domain shall remain under Suraksha's control, with SPF include and DKIM selectors pre-provisioned for the secondary provider, so that failover is a configuration change rather than a DNS propagation wait. |

#### 37.2.7 Push notification

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Primary notification channel for all four apps and the web portals (§36.3.1) |
| Data shared | Device token, notification title/body/payload. Payload carries identifiers and minimal text; sensitive content is classified `requires_unlock` (SUR-NTF-030) |
| Pattern | Server → FCM (Android, Web) and APNs (iOS) via a single abstraction; token registration and invalidation lifecycle; delivery feedback ingested where available |
| Security | Service account keys / APNs auth keys in the secrets store, rotated per schedule; tokens treated as personal data and deleted on logout and account deletion; payloads contain no credentials and no full financial detail |
| Failure fallback | Per-priority failover chain (§36.4.2). Token invalid → invalidate and fail over immediately for P0/P1 |
| Cost | Effectively zero at the provider; cost is engineering and the SMS spend that push failure creates |
| Lock-in risk | **Low-medium.** FCM is effectively mandatory for Android; APNs for iOS. The abstraction protects against a change in the aggregation layer, not against the platform providers themselves, which cannot be replaced |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` FCM + APNs directly, with Suraksha's own abstraction rather than a third-party push aggregator; aggregators add cost and a failure point for a problem the platform already solves |

#### 37.2.8 KYC and identity verification

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Verify identity of guards at onboarding, agency owners at marketplace onboarding, and clients where the service or payment value requires it; verify bank accounts before payouts |
| Data shared | **Highest-sensitivity flow in the platform.** Name, date of birth, address, identity document number and image, face photo for match, bank account number and IFSC for penny-drop. Shared only with the verification provider, only for the specific check, only with recorded consent |
| Pattern | Server-initiated check via the provider's API with an explicit consent artefact captured first; asynchronous result via callback or poll; result stored as a **verification outcome record**, not as a copy of the provider's raw response where that response contains more data than needed |
| Security | Consent captured with timestamp, purpose text version, and the user's affirmative action, and stored; document images encrypted at rest with restricted access and a short retention for the raw image versus a long retention for the outcome; identifier numbers stored encrypted and masked in the UI; access to unmask is permissioned and audited; strict prohibition on using verification data for any secondary purpose |
| Failure fallback | Provider unavailable or a check inconclusive → **manual verification workflow**: document upload, human review by the Verification role with a four-eyes check for high-risk cases, outcome recorded with the reviewer's identity. The platform must function with the automated path entirely disabled, because it will be, in some states and for some document types |
| Cost | Per-check pricing, typically the largest per-guard onboarding cost after background verification. Levers: check only what the risk requires, cache outcomes with an expiry, avoid re-checking on re-engagement within the validity window |
| Lock-in risk | **Low-medium.** Outcomes are stored in Suraksha's own schema; only the check-invocation code is vendor-specific. Do not store vendor-proprietary risk scores as if they were platform truth |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` A regulated Indian KYC aggregator for document verification and bank penny-drop — candidates: Signzy, IDfy, HyperVerge, Digio, Karza/Perfios. `[ASSUMPTION: A-141 applies]` for penny-drop availability. Any identity-verification method whose availability depends on regulatory permission for the entity type shall be treated as `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-273]` and shall never be assumed available in the design |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-032 | The platform shall store the **minimum viable outcome** of any identity check (verified yes/no, method, date, masked reference, expiry) plus the evidence required for audit, and shall not retain full raw provider payloads beyond the configured evidence-retention window. |
| SUR-INT-033 | No identity verification result shall automatically reject a guard. A failed or inconclusive check shall route to human review, because document-name mismatches and address variations are routine in this workforce and an automated rejection is an employment harm. |
| SUR-INT-034 | Consent for each verification purpose shall be separately captured and revocable; revocation shall stop future checks and shall be recorded, without retroactively deleting audit evidence of checks already performed under valid consent. |

#### 37.2.9 Background verification and police verification

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Criminal record check, address verification, previous-employment check and reference check for guards, plus tracking of police verification where the deployment or client requires it |
| Data shared | Full name, parentage, date of birth, current and permanent address, identity document reference, photograph, previous employer details, consent artefact |
| Pattern | Case-based: the platform creates a verification case, submits it to the vendor (API where offered, portal/SFTP batch where not), tracks status, ingests the report, stores the outcome and the report document. Police verification is typically a **physical, jurisdiction-specific process** — the platform tracks it as a workflow with document evidence, it does not "call an API" |
| Security | Consent mandatory and recorded before initiation; reports stored encrypted with tightly restricted access (Recruitment and Verification roles only); adverse findings visible to a minimal set of roles and never to clients or other guards; a documented process for the guard to see and contest a finding |
| Failure fallback | No vendor coverage in a district, or vendor delay → manual process: physical police verification application tracked as a task with document upload, supervisor address visit with geotagged evidence, and reference calls logged. Deployment eligibility rules configured per client may allow provisional deployment pending verification, with an explicit configured rule and an expiry |
| Cost | The highest per-guard onboarding cost; varies widely by check depth and district. Levers: tiered check depth by role (armed/PSO deeper than unarmed), reuse of a valid recent check, batch submission |
| Lock-in risk | **Low.** Case data and reports are stored in Suraksha's schema |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` One national BGV vendor plus the manual path always available. Candidates: AuthBridge, IDfy, First Advantage, SpringVerify, HireRight India. `[ASSUMPTION: A-143 applies]`. **Honest statement:** there is no reliable, uniform, national public API for police verification status; the platform's design is a tracked manual workflow, and any vendor claiming otherwise should be validated in a pilot before it is designed into the critical path |

#### 37.2.10 OCR and document extraction

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Extract fields from uploaded identity documents, licences, certificates and legacy registers; the Enterprise plan's OCR-based legacy data migration (canon §1.4); extraction of tender documents (§37.2.14) |
| Data shared | The document image or PDF, which frequently contains full personal data. For legacy migration this may be an entire agency's historic guard register |
| Pattern | Asynchronous job: upload → queue → OCR → field extraction against a document-type template → **confidence-scored proposal** → human confirmation → commit. Never direct-to-database |
| Security | Documents processed in a region-appropriate endpoint with data-residency configured where the provider offers it; provider contracts must prohibit training on customer data; extraction results and source documents stored under the same access controls as the entity they belong to; extraction jobs isolated per tenant |
| Failure fallback | Low confidence or provider failure → manual data entry with the document displayed side by side. Bulk migration failure → chunked re-processing with a per-record status, never an all-or-nothing batch |
| Cost | Per-page pricing; the legacy-migration use case can be a large one-off. Levers: pre-processing (deskew, crop, downscale) to improve first-pass accuracy, template-based extraction for known document types, batching |
| Lock-in risk | **Low.** Extraction output lands in Suraksha's schema; the adapter is thin |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` A general document-AI service as primary with a self-hosted OSS fallback: Google Document AI or AWS Textract as primary; Azure Document Intelligence as an alternative; Tesseract/PaddleOCR self-hosted for cost-sensitive bulk work and for cases where a document may not leave Suraksha's infrastructure. Indian-document-specialised vendors (IDfy, Signzy) may outperform generic OCR on identity documents and are worth a bake-off |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-035 | No OCR-extracted value shall be committed to a record without human confirmation where the field is identity-bearing, financial or compliance-relevant. Confidence thresholds shall be configurable per field, and low-confidence fields shall be visually flagged for the reviewer. |
| SUR-INT-036 | Bulk legacy migration shall produce a reconciliation report (records read, extracted, confirmed, rejected, requiring review) and shall be reversible as a batch before final commit. |

#### 37.2.11 Biometric devices

Covered in depth in §37.4.

#### 37.2.12 Accounting systems

Covered in depth in §37.5.

#### 37.2.13 Government sources — PSARA licence verification

**Honest statement, per canon §0 and A-142:** there is no known reliable, uniform, publicly documented national API for verifying a PSARA licence. Licensing is administered at state and district level; states publish licence information inconsistently — some as searchable portals, some as periodic PDF lists, some not at all. Any design that assumes an API here would be fiction.

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Establish that an agency's PSARA licence is genuine, current, and covers the geography in which it is operating or bidding (canon §1: licence geography is a first-class object) |
| Data shared | With a human verifier or a state portal: the licence number, agency legal name and jurisdiction as printed on the document. No platform data is transmitted to any government system automatically |
| Pattern | **Manual/assisted verification workflow**, designed as the primary path: (1) agency uploads the licence document and enters number, issuing authority, state/district, issue and expiry dates and covered geography; (2) OCR pre-fills these fields as a proposal (§37.2.10); (3) the Verification role checks the document against the issuing authority's published source where one exists, records the source consulted, the date, and a screenshot/PDF as evidence; (4) outcome recorded as `Verified` with an evidence trail, or `Rejected` with a reason, or `Pending` with a follow-up; (5) re-verification scheduled before expiry (event DOC-06) |
| Security | Verification evidence stored immutably with the verifier's identity; the licence document itself access-restricted; no scraping of a government portal in a way that violates its terms — where a portal exists, the design is an operator opening it, not an automated crawler |
| Failure fallback | The manual path **is** the design; there is nothing to fall back from. Where a state later publishes a documented API or bulk dataset, an adapter may be added as an **accelerator** that pre-fills the verifier's screen — it shall never replace the human decision |
| Cost | Human time per verification (estimate 10–20 minutes per agency), which is a staffing plan input for the Verification team, not a vendor line item |
| Lock-in risk | **None** |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Design and staff the manual/assisted workflow as the permanent primary path. Treat any commercial "PSARA verification API" claim as unvalidated until piloted against known-good and known-bad licences. Maintain a per-state registry of *how* to verify (portal URL, contact office, published list location, or "no public source") as platform reference data, because that knowledge is the actual asset |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-037 | Licence verification shall record: the source consulted, the evidence captured, the verifier, the timestamp, and the confidence classification (`primary_source_confirmed`, `document_only`, `unverifiable_source`). A licence verified on document alone shall be visibly distinguishable from one confirmed against an issuing authority's source. |
| SUR-INT-038 | The platform shall maintain a per-state, per-district verification-method registry as editable reference data, so the Verification team's accumulated knowledge is institutional, not personal. |
| SUR-INT-039 | Licence expiry shall drive BR-002 restrictions automatically; the platform shall never rely on a manual reminder to notice an expired licence. |

#### 37.2.14 Government sources — tender discovery

**Honest statement, per canon §0 and A-145:** government tender portals in India (central and state e-procurement systems) do not offer a uniform, reliable, publicly documented API for third-party tender discovery. Some publish RSS or downloadable lists; terms of use frequently restrict automated access; formats change without notice. The Professional plan's "government tender discovery" (canon §1.4) must therefore be designed as a curated data pipeline with human input, not as an API integration.

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Surface security-services tenders relevant to an agency's licence geography, capability and size; track bid deadlines, documents, EMD requirements and outcomes |
| Data shared | Outbound: nothing automatic. Inbound: publicly published tender notices, which are not personal data |
| Pattern | Three sources, in order of preference: (1) **licensed commercial aggregator feed** where procured — a documented API/feed under contract; (2) **manual curation** — a Suraksha research function enters tenders into a structured catalogue, assisted by OCR/LLM extraction of uploaded tender PDFs into structured fields for human confirmation; (3) **agency self-entry** — an agency records a tender it found itself and uses the platform for bid workflow, documents and deadlines. Matching to agencies is a platform-side rules engine over the structured catalogue (geography vs licence coverage, category, value band, eligibility criteria) |
| Security | Only publicly published information stored; documents stored per normal controls; no credential-based access to any government portal is performed by the platform on an agency's behalf |
| Failure fallback | No aggregator → manual curation carries the feature, at reduced volume and with a stated coverage disclaimer. The platform shall state clearly to agencies what its coverage is and is not; over-claiming coverage here is a churn driver |
| Cost | Either an aggregator subscription (fixed) or curation staff time (variable with coverage ambition). This is a direct input into the Professional plan's margin |
| Lock-in risk | **Low** for the catalogue (Suraksha's own schema); **medium** commercial dependency on an aggregator if the feature's value rests on it |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Build the structured tender catalogue, matching engine and bid workflow first — these are the durable value. Treat the source as pluggable: aggregator feed, curated entry, or self-entry, all writing the same catalogue. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-274]` whether to procure a commercial aggregator for V1, since it materially changes the Professional plan's promise. **Do not scrape portals whose terms prohibit it** |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-040 | The tender catalogue shall record `source_type` (`aggregator` \| `curated` \| `self_entered`) and `source_reference` on every record, and the UI shall show agencies where each tender came from and when it was last verified. |
| SUR-INT-041 | The platform shall display an explicit coverage statement on the tender module ("we cover X states / Y categories; this is not an exhaustive list of all published tenders") rather than implying completeness. |

#### 37.2.15 Cloud storage and CDN

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Store attendance photos, patrol evidence, incident media, SOS audio/photo, identity and licence documents, invoices and payslips, report exports, app binaries for the desktop app downloads (canon §1.3) |
| Data shared | The objects themselves, many of which are personal or sensitive; object keys must not encode personal data |
| Pattern | Direct-to-storage upload from clients using short-lived pre-signed URLs (the application server never proxies large media); server-side metadata record created first; download via short-lived signed URLs or an authenticated proxy for the most sensitive classes; CDN in front of public/static assets only |
| Security | Server-side encryption with customer-managed keys for sensitive buckets; bucket-level public access blocked by policy; object keys are opaque UUIDs; signed URLs expire in minutes; lifecycle rules implementing the retention policy (§39); versioning and object-lock/WORM for financial documents and audit evidence; access logged |
| Failure fallback | Upload failure → client retries with the offline queue (Guard App); persistent failure → local retention on device with a visible pending-sync indicator and an alert to the supervisor if evidence remains unsynced beyond a threshold. Storage region outage → cross-region replication for the critical classes (§49) |
| Cost | Storage (dominated by attendance photos and GPS history), egress (dominated by report and media downloads), request costs. Levers: image compression and resizing at capture, tiered storage (hot 90 days → infrequent → archive), retention enforcement, CDN caching, thumbnail generation so full-size images are fetched rarely |
| Lock-in risk | **Medium.** Object data is portable but egress cost makes a large migration expensive; keep the storage adapter thin and avoid provider-specific features (e.g. proprietary event notification semantics) in domain logic |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` The primary cloud provider's object storage with an Indian region (AWS S3 Mumbai, or Azure Blob / GCS equivalent) plus its CDN, with a storage adapter that also supports S3-compatible alternatives (Wasabi, Backblaze B2, DigitalOcean Spaces) for archive tiers |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-042 | Financial documents (issued invoices, approved payslips, settlement statements) and audit evidence shall be stored with object versioning and a write-once retention lock for their configured retention period, so that immutability (SUR-FIN-163) is enforced by storage, not only by application code. |
| SUR-INT-043 | Media capture on the Guard App shall be compressed and resized on device before upload, with the original discarded after successful upload, since bandwidth in the field is the binding constraint. |

#### 37.2.16 Analytics and product telemetry

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Product analytics (funnels, feature adoption, drop-off), crash and error reporting, performance monitoring, marketing attribution on the public website |
| Data shared | Pseudonymous user id, tenant id, role, event names and properties, device/app/OS version, coarse geography. **Prohibited from being sent:** names, phone numbers, email addresses, addresses, identity document numbers, salary or payment amounts, guard location coordinates, client names, incident content |
| Pattern | Client and server SDKs feeding a single event taxonomy (§42); server-side event forwarding preferred over direct client-to-vendor calls for anything sensitive; consent-gated web analytics on the public site |
| Security | A **PII allow-list** enforced in the analytics wrapper: properties not on the allow-list are dropped before dispatch, and a CI check fails the build if a disallowed property name is used; crash reports scrubbed of user content; separate projects per environment |
| Failure fallback | Analytics failure shall never affect application behaviour: all calls are fire-and-forget with a bounded local buffer and a hard timeout. If the vendor is down, events are dropped after the buffer fills — analytics is not a system of record |
| Cost | Typically per monthly tracked user or per event volume; can grow quietly. Levers: event taxonomy discipline (no high-cardinality property explosions), sampling of high-volume telemetry, self-hosted alternatives |
| Lock-in risk | **Low-medium.** Historical analytics data is hard to migrate, but analytics is not operational truth; the operational data warehouse (§42) is the durable asset and is Suraksha's own |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Split the concerns: product analytics via PostHog (self-hostable, avoids sending behavioural data to a third party — significant for enterprise sales) or Mixpanel/Amplitude; crash/error reporting via Sentry (self-hostable); performance/APM via the observability stack in §48. Marketing/web analytics via a consent-gated tool (Google Analytics 4 or a privacy-preserving alternative such as Plausible/Matomo) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-044 | The analytics allow-list shall be enforced at the wrapper and verified in CI. A property whose name matches PII patterns (`phone`, `email`, `name`, `address`, `aadhaar`, `pan`, `account`, `salary`, `lat`, `lng`) shall fail the build unless explicitly exempted with a review. |
| SUR-INT-045 | Operational and financial reporting (§35.10, §42) shall be served from Suraksha's own data warehouse, never from a third-party analytics vendor, so that a vendor change or outage cannot affect the numbers the business runs on. |

#### 37.2.17 CRM

| Dimension | Specification |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Two distinct needs: (a) Suraksha's own sales pipeline for B2B/B2G clients and for agency SaaS subscriptions; (b) the **CRM module inside the Agency Portal** on the Professional plan (canon §1.4), which is a first-party feature, not an integration |
| Data shared | For (a), if an external CRM is used: lead and contact details (name, company, phone, email), opportunity value and stage, activity history. This is client personal data leaving the platform and requires the same controls as any other export |
| Pattern | For (a): bidirectional sync — leads created on the website flow to the CRM; deal stage changes flow back to the platform to drive onboarding. Implemented as an outbound event stream plus a scheduled pull, with a mapping configuration; **never** a shared database. For (b): first-party, no integration |
| Security | Field-level mapping explicitly listing what is synced; sync excludes operational, financial and guard data; API credentials in the secrets store; a documented deletion propagation path so that erasure requests reach the CRM |
| Failure fallback | CRM outage → leads queue in the platform and sync on recovery; the platform's own lead record is authoritative so no lead is lost. Feature-level fallback: the platform's own lead list is sufficient to work from |
| Cost | Per-seat subscription; grows with the sales team. Levers: keep the platform's own pipeline sufficient for early-stage, adopt an external CRM only when the sales motion demands it |
| Lock-in risk | **Low-medium**; CRM data exports are standard, but embedded workflows and automations are not portable |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Start with the platform's own lead/opportunity records; adopt Zoho CRM as the external system when needed (consistent with Zoho mail per canon §4, single vendor relationship, Indian pricing). Alternatives: HubSpot, Freshsales, Salesforce (heaviest, only if enterprise sales demands it). The Agency Portal CRM module shall remain first-party and shall not be a resold third-party product |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-046 | Where an external CRM is used, the platform shall remain the system of record for leads and shall be able to operate fully with the CRM disconnected. Sync shall be one mapped, audited pipeline, and erasure requests shall propagate to the CRM with confirmation recorded. |

### 37.3 The Enterprise custom-integration model

The Enterprise plan promises "custom integrations", "biometric integrations" and "enterprise API" (canon §1.4). Without a defined model this becomes unbounded bespoke engineering charged as a subscription — the fastest way to destroy SaaS margin.

#### 37.3.1 The four tiers

| Tier | What it is | Delivery | Commercial |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 — Configuration | An existing adapter configured for the tenant (their own SMS account, their own accounting export format, their own biometric device model already supported) | Support/onboarding task, hours | Included in Enterprise onboarding |
| T2 — Mapping | Field mappings, export layout templates, custom report definitions, webhook subscriptions, SSO/SAML setup | Solution engineering, days | Included up to a defined allowance, then billed |
| T3 — Connector | A new adapter for a system Suraksha does not yet support, built to an existing capability interface (a new accounting system, a new biometric vendor, a new payment rail) | Engineering project, weeks | Quoted one-off build fee + ongoing maintenance fee; becomes a platform asset available to others |
| T4 — Bespoke | Integration that requires new capability interfaces or client-specific business logic (a client's proprietary ERP, a specific government system, an on-premise legacy application) | Engineering project with a statement of work, weeks to months | Quoted project; explicit support and change-management terms; strong preference to generalise into T3 |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-047 | Every custom integration shall be classified into a tier at the point of sale, and the classification shall determine the price, the delivery path and the support terms. Enterprise contracts shall state the included allowance explicitly rather than promising "custom integrations" open-endedly. |
| SUR-INT-048 | T3 connectors shall be built to the shared capability interface and shall become part of the platform catalogue, available to other tenants. Suraksha shall not maintain private per-customer forks. |
| SUR-INT-049 | T4 bespoke work shall carry a defined support model (who fixes it when it breaks, what the response time is, what happens when the third party changes their API without notice) and an annual maintenance fee; unmaintained bespoke integrations shall be sunset with notice rather than silently rotting. |
| SUR-INT-050 | Every custom integration shall have an owner at Suraksha, a runbook (SUR-INT-024), automated health checks, and a named contact at the customer, recorded in the integration registry. |

#### 37.3.2 The Enterprise API

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-051 | The Enterprise API shall be the same public API described in §33, exposed to the tenant with scoped API keys or OAuth client credentials, rate limits per plan, and a sandbox tenant with realistic seed data. |
| SUR-INT-052 | Outbound **webhooks** shall be offered as a first-class enterprise capability: subscription per event type, signed payloads, at-least-once delivery with exponential backoff, a delivery log the customer can inspect, and a replay function. Customers integrating by polling shall be actively discouraged. |
| SUR-INT-053 | API and webhook contracts shall be versioned with a published deprecation policy (minimum 6 months notice, migration guide, both versions live during the window) — the absence of such a policy is the most common reason enterprise integrations become unmaintainable. |
| SUR-INT-054 | Enterprise integration usage shall be metered (calls, webhook deliveries, data volume) and reported to both the customer and Suraksha, so support cost is visible against contract value. |

### 37.4 Biometric device integration

Biometric attendance is a routine expectation in Indian guarding, particularly at industrial and corporate sites, and is an explicit Enterprise capability. It is also the most privacy-sensitive integration in the platform, so the stance is stated before the mechanics.

#### 37.4.1 Privacy stance on biometric templates

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-055 | **Suraksha's default position is that raw biometric images and biometric templates are not stored on Suraksha's cloud infrastructure.** Templates live on the device or on an on-premise controller under the client's or agency's control; Suraksha receives and stores only the **attendance event** (which enrolled identifier, which device, which timestamp, which verification result and score). |
| SUR-INT-056 | Where a deployment model genuinely requires cloud template storage (multi-site roaming guards with device-independent verification), it shall be an explicit, per-tenant, contractually documented opt-in with: separate encryption keys, a separate storage location, access limited to the matching service, no export capability, a defined retention and deletion process, and a documented privacy assessment (§39). It shall never be the default and shall never be enabled by a support action alone. |
| SUR-INT-057 | Biometric data shall never be shared with any third party, never used for any purpose other than attendance verification and duplicate-enrolment prevention, never used to train any model, and never included in any export, backup extract or analytics event. |
| SUR-INT-058 | Enrolment shall require explicit, informed, separately-recorded consent from the guard in a language they read, with a plain-language explanation of what is stored, where, for how long, and how to withdraw. A **non-biometric alternative attendance method shall always be available** (QR/NFC checkpoint, supervisor-verified photo attendance, OTP) so that consent is genuine and not coerced by the absence of an alternative. |
| SUR-INT-059 | On a guard's separation, or on withdrawal of consent, biometric enrolment shall be deleted from every device and controller within a defined SLA (default 7 days), with deletion confirmed and recorded per device. Attendance history, which contains no biometric data, is retained per the normal retention rule. |
| SUR-INT-060 | Face-matching for attendance (liveness + match against the enrolment photo) shall be treated with the same rules as fingerprint templates; the enrolment photo is biometric data, not "just a photo". |

#### 37.4.2 Device types

| Type | Typical use | Connectivity | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fingerprint terminal (wall-mounted) | Fixed sites, gate offices | Ethernet/Wi-Fi to a local network; some models push events over TCP or expose a local HTTP/SDK | The most common device class in Indian sites |
| Face recognition terminal | Sites preferring contactless; higher-value sites | As above | Higher cost; better throughput; liveness quality varies enormously by model |
| Palm/iris terminal | Rare, specific industrial clients | As above | Support only on demand as a T3 connector |
| Handheld/mobile biometric (Bluetooth fingerprint reader paired to the Guard App) | Roaming posts, temporary sites, event deployments | Bluetooth to the phone, then normal app sync | Useful where no fixed infrastructure exists |
| In-app face verification (phone camera) | Default where no hardware exists | App → platform | Liveness and match performed per SUR-INT-060 rules; the enrolment reference is treated as biometric data |
| Client's existing access-control system | Enterprise sites with an installed base | Usually a local database or an export file; occasionally an API | Integration is typically read-only event import, tier T3/T4 |

#### 37.4.3 On-premise connectivity via the desktop app

The Agency Portal desktop application (canon §1.3) is the bridge between devices on a client's local network and Suraksha's cloud. Devices generally cannot reach the internet, and should not.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-061 | The desktop app shall include an optional **device agent** that discovers and connects to configured biometric devices on the local network, polls or receives their event streams, buffers events locally, and uploads normalised attendance events to the platform over an authenticated outbound-only TLS connection. No inbound connection to the client's network shall ever be required. |
| SUR-INT-062 | The agent shall upload only attendance events (device id, enrolled user identifier, timestamp from the device, verification method, verification score, direction in/out) plus device health. It shall not upload templates or images, consistent with SUR-INT-055. |
| SUR-INT-063 | The agent shall buffer locally for a configurable period (default 7 days) so a network outage does not lose attendance, and shall reconcile on reconnect with idempotent event ids so a replay does not create duplicates. |
| SUR-INT-064 | Device clock drift shall be detected by comparing device event time against the agent's NTP-synced clock; drift beyond a threshold shall raise an alert and shall be recorded on every affected event, consistent with the canon's dual-timestamp rule (`device_time` + `server_received_time`). |
| SUR-INT-065 | Enrolment mapping (device user id ↔ Suraksha guard id) shall be explicit, auditable and one-to-one per device; an unmapped device user id shall raise an exception rather than silently creating attendance for an unknown person — a classic ghost-attendance vector. |
| SUR-INT-066 | The agent shall report device health (online/offline, last event, firmware version, storage, tamper flag where reported) with alerts on offline beyond a threshold, since a silent device means silent attendance loss. |
| SUR-INT-067 | Where no desktop machine is available on site, a small dedicated gateway appliance running the same agent shall be an alternative deployment, and a file-drop path (device export file placed in a watched folder or SFTP) shall exist as the lowest-common-denominator fallback for devices with no live protocol. |

#### 37.4.4 Vendors and the integration reality

| Aspect | Statement |
|---|---|
| Common vendors | ESSL, Realtime, Matrix, Mantra, Secureye, Hikvision, ZKTeco. Many Indian-market devices are ZKTeco-derived and expose a broadly similar SDK/protocol family |
| API reality | Documentation quality varies from good SDKs to undocumented TCP protocols. Some vendors provide a Windows-only SDK. Some devices offer a local HTTP push. Some only export CSV. **Do not assume a clean API for any given model.** |
| Consequence for design | Support a small set of device models properly (a certified device list), and provide the file-drop fallback for everything else. Publish the certified list so that clients buy compatible hardware rather than discovering incompatibility after installation |
| Recommendation | `[RECOMMENDED]` Certify 2–3 models across fingerprint and face at launch (one ZKTeco-family fingerprint terminal, one face terminal, one Bluetooth handheld), publish the list, and treat every additional model as a T3 connector with a quoted build |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-068 | The platform shall publish a certified device list with tested firmware versions, and shall warn during setup when a device reports an untested model or firmware. |
| SUR-INT-069 | Biometric attendance shall never be the only attendance path at a site. If the device fails, the Guard App path (GPS + photo) shall take over automatically with the switch recorded on the attendance record, so that a hardware failure never becomes a payroll dispute. |

### 37.5 Accounting export

Agencies and Suraksha's own finance function run accounting in an external system. The platform's job is to produce clean, reconcilable data — not to become the accounting system.

#### 37.5.1 Stance

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-070 | The platform shall be the system of record for operational and billing data, and shall **export** to accounting systems. Bidirectional sync with an accounting system shall not be built in V1: two systems that both believe they own the ledger is a reconciliation problem with no good ending. |
| SUR-INT-071 | Exports shall be generated from ledger entries (§35.2), not from documents, so that what the accounting system receives always reconciles to what the platform believes. |
| SUR-INT-072 | Every export shall be a **batch with an identity**: batch id, period, document count, control totals (total debits, total credits, invoice count, tax totals), generation timestamp and user. Re-exporting the same period shall produce the same batch or an explicitly marked re-export, never silent duplicates. |

#### 37.5.2 Export formats

| Target | Format | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| Tally-style | XML in the Tally-compatible voucher structure (Sales, Receipt, Journal, Payment, Credit Note vouchers) with ledger names mapped per tenant | Sales vouchers from issued invoices; receipts from payments; journals from payroll and settlement accruals |
| Zoho Books-style | CSV per entity (invoices, invoice line items, customers, payments, credit notes, journals, bills) matching the importer's column expectations, plus an API adapter where the tenant provides credentials | As above |
| QuickBooks-style | IIF or CSV per entity, or API via the tenant's connected account | As above |
| Generic | CSV: `ledger_entries.csv`, `documents.csv`, `parties.csv`, `tax_summary.csv` with a documented schema, plus JSON for full fidelity | Everything, for any system |
| Bank/audit | Payout register, settlement register, tax registers (§35.10) | Read-only reports |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-073 | A **ledger mapping** screen shall let the tenant map each Suraksha account role key to their accounting system's ledger/account name, with validation that every role key used in the period is mapped before an export can run. An unmapped account shall block the export with a precise message, not export to a default bucket. |
| SUR-INT-074 | Party mapping (Suraksha client/agency/guard ↔ accounting-system ledger or contact) shall be maintained with an auto-match proposal on name and tax registration, confirmed by a human, and stored so subsequent exports are automatic. |
| SUR-INT-075 | Exports shall support incremental mode (only entries since the last successful batch) and full-period mode, and shall record which entries have been exported in which batch, so an entry is never exported twice without it being visible. |
| SUR-INT-076 | Export files shall be downloadable and, where the tenant configures it, delivered to an SFTP location or pushed via the accounting system's API. API push shall be idempotent on the batch id. |
| SUR-INT-077 | A reconciliation report shall accompany every export: control totals, entries included, entries excluded and why, and any mapping substitutions applied. |
| SUR-INT-078 | Where a tenant's accounting system requires a document numbering convention different from the platform's, the export shall carry both numbers, and the platform's number shall remain the primary reference in all platform surfaces. |

### 37.6 Vendor risk and exit plans

| Vendor category | Risk if it fails or exits | Blast radius | Exit plan | Time to exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Payment gateway | Cannot collect money; mandates lost | B2C and B2B collection, subscriptions | Second gateway adapter pre-built and dormant; bank transfer + manual reconciliation as the immediate stopgap; mandates must be re-collected from customers — plan a 60–90 day dual-running migration | High effort |
| SMS aggregator | OTP and P0 failover degraded | Auth, safety escalation, dunning | Second aggregator live at all times with traffic split; DLT entity registration held in Suraksha's name | Days |
| WhatsApp BSP | Rich client messaging lost | Convenience channel only, by design | Fall back to SMS/push automatically; migrate the number to another BSP with template re-approval | Weeks |
| Email provider | Documents undelivered | Invoices, statements, payslips | Secondary provider pre-configured in DNS; portal remains the authoritative copy | Hours |
| Push (FCM/APNs) | Primary notification channel lost | All notification | No true alternative; mitigate with SMS failover and in-app; this is an accepted platform dependency | N/A |
| Map provider | Address entry and map views degraded | Onboarding UX, dispatch | Geofencing is first-party; switch to Mappls/Mapbox/OSM; re-resolve addresses lazily from stored components | Weeks |
| KYC provider | Automated verification stops | Guard and agency onboarding speed | Manual verification workflow already exists as the designed fallback; capacity is the constraint | Days (with staffing) |
| BGV provider | Background checks stop | Onboarding of new guards | Manual/physical process already designed; second vendor procurable | Weeks |
| OCR provider | Extraction assist stops | Migration and document entry speed | Manual entry; self-hosted OSS OCR as a lower-quality fallback | Days |
| Biometric device vendor | A device model becomes unsupported | Attendance at affected sites | Guard App attendance takes over automatically (SUR-INT-069); certified-list rotation | Immediate degradation, weeks to replace hardware |
| Cloud storage / cloud provider | Media and documents unavailable | Everything | Cross-region replication for critical classes; storage adapter avoids proprietary features; a full cloud exit is a multi-quarter programme and is a known accepted risk | Very high effort |
| Analytics vendor | Product insight lost | Internal only | Operational reporting is first-party (SUR-INT-045); switch vendors, accept history loss | Days |
| CRM | Sales pipeline tooling lost | Internal sales only | Platform lead records are authoritative; export and switch | Days |
| Tender aggregator (if procured) | Tender coverage drops | Professional plan value | Curated + self-entry paths keep the module functional with a stated coverage change | Immediate degradation |
| Accounting target system | Tenant changes their accounting system | Export only | Generic CSV/JSON export always available; new target is a T3 connector | Days to weeks |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-INT-079 | Every vendor in the catalogue shall have a recorded exit plan, reviewed annually, naming the fallback, the estimated effort and the data that would be lost or need re-collection. A vendor with no exit plan shall not be added to the critical path. |
| SUR-INT-080 | No single vendor shall be the sole path for: authentication, payment collection, P0 notification delivery, or attendance capture. Each of these shall have at least one independent path that works when the primary is entirely unavailable. |
| SUR-INT-081 | Vendor contracts shall be reviewed for: data ownership and export rights, a prohibition on training models on Suraksha or tenant data, data location, breach notification timelines, and termination assistance. These are integration requirements, not merely legal ones, because their absence changes what the architecture must do. |
| SUR-INT-082 | An integration registry shall be maintained in the platform listing every integration, its tier, its owner, its provider, its credentials' rotation state, its health, its monthly cost and its exit plan reference, and shall be reviewed quarterly by the CTO function. |

## 38. Security Architecture

### 38.1 Scope, stance and non-negotiables

This section is the canonical home for security controls (see canon §6). Every other section that needs a control references it by ID (`SUR-SEC-nnn`) and does not restate it. The permission matrix lives in §31 and is not reproduced here; the compliance engine and its jurisdiction rules live in §40 and are not reproduced here. What this section owns outright is the **audit system specification** (§38.12) — every other section that says "this is audited" resolves to that specification.

**Why the bar is higher here than for a typical SaaS.** Suraksha holds, in one platform: guard identity documents and government identifiers, police-verification and background-verification outcomes, client site addresses together with the security arrangements protecting them (post positions, guard counts per shift, patrol routes, checkpoint locations, shift-change times, and therefore shift gaps), live and historical GPS tracks of a low-wage workforce, incident records, and money in motion. A breach of the marketing database of a SaaS company is an embarrassment. A breach here can tell a criminal which gate at which warehouse is unmanned between 14:00 and 14:20, or hand a stalker the current coordinates of a named individual. The design must assume that the data is worth stealing for reasons that have nothing to do with fraud.

**Security principles (applied throughout, not restated per control).**

| # | Principle | What it means concretely in Suraksha |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Zero trust as far as practical | No network location grants access. Every request carries its own identity, is authorised on every call, and is scoped to a tenant on every object fetch. There is no "internal, therefore trusted" service call. |
| P2 | Deny by default | New endpoints, new fields, new report columns and new AI tools are inaccessible until explicitly granted in §31. Absence of a rule means "no". |
| P3 | Least privilege, time-bounded | Roles carry the minimum scope; elevated access is temporary, reason-coded and expiring (break-glass per §22). |
| P4 | Defence in depth | No single control is load-bearing. Tenant isolation, for example, is enforced at four layers (§38.9), each independently tested. |
| P5 | Assume breach | Detection, containment and forensic reconstruction are designed for, not bolted on. Audit logs are append-only and readable after the fact. |
| P6 | Sensitive data minimised at source | The cheapest way to protect a field is not to collect it (see §39.3). |
| P7 | Secure defaults | Every configurable security or privacy setting ships in its most restrictive usable state; loosening it is an explicit, audited act. |
| P8 | No security by obscurity | Nothing depends on an attacker not knowing a URL, an ID format, or a client-side flag. IDs are treated as public knowledge. |
| P9 | Human review for irreversible actions | Money movement, permission change, mass deletion, mass export and compliance-status change always have a human in the loop (see §26, §41). |
| P10 | Product requirements, not legal advice | Notification thresholds, retention periods and residency are **configurable policy**, reviewed by counsel per jurisdiction; they are never hard-coded (canon §0). |

**Zero-trust framing, honestly scoped.** Full zero-trust maturity (mTLS everywhere, per-request device posture attestation, continuous authorisation scoring) is not achievable at MVP for a modular monolith built by a small team. What is achievable and mandatory at MVP is the identity-centric core of it: authenticated identity on every request including internal calls, authorisation evaluated at the point of data access rather than at the edge, no implicit trust from network position, no long-lived static credentials, and full request-level audit. The remaining maturity is phased in §38.15.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SEC-001 | Every request to any Suraksha service, including service-to-service calls, shall carry a verifiable identity (user token or workload identity) and shall be authorised at the point of data access. Network origin shall never be sufficient authorisation. |
| SUR-SEC-002 | Security controls marked "MVP-mandatory" in §38.15 shall be release-blocking. A launch decision cannot waive them; only the security exception process (§38.13.4) can, and it cannot grant permanent exceptions to MVP-mandatory controls. |
| SUR-SEC-003 | Every control in this section shall have a named owner role and at least one automated test or automated check referencing its control ID. Controls with neither shall be reported monthly as unverified. |
| SUR-SEC-004 | Jurisdiction-dependent security obligations (breach notification windows, retention floors, residency) shall be implemented as configuration consumed from the compliance engine (§40), never as hard-coded constants. |

---

### 38.2 Threat model

#### 38.2.1 Assets, ranked by what a breach actually costs

| Rank | Asset | Why an attacker wants it | Worst realistic outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Site security arrangements — post positions, guards per shift, shift-change times, patrol routes and checkpoint timings | Tells you exactly when and where a site is weakest | Physical breach of a client site, planned using our data |
| A2 | Live guard location and current deployment roster | Locates a named person in real time; identifies which guard is alone | Targeted assault, kidnapping, coerced gate access |
| A3 | Guard identity documents, government identifiers, address, photograph | Identity theft; impersonation of a guard to gain site entry | Fake guard admitted to a site; mass identity fraud |
| A4 | Police-verification and background-verification records | Sensitive, defamatory if leaked, valuable for blackmail | Coercion of a guard; unlawful discrimination |
| A5 | Bank details and payroll data (guard and agency) | Direct monetisation | Salary diversion from people living on that salary |
| A6 | Client contact and contract data, rate cards | Competitive value | Competitor poaching; pricing leak |
| A7 | Incident records and CCTV/body-camera media where implemented | Reputational leverage over clients | Extortion of a client |
| A8 | Payment/settlement flows and wallet balances | Direct monetisation | Fraudulent payouts |
| A9 | Marketplace agency data (licences, coverage, pricing) | Bulk competitive scraping | Loss of marketplace differentiation |
| A10 | Platform administrative control | Everything above, plus persistence | Total compromise |

#### 38.2.2 Adversaries

| Actor | Capability | Motivation | Typical entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| TA-1 Opportunistic credential attacker | Low; automated, uses breach corpora | Any monetisable account | Credential stuffing on public login, OTP brute force |
| TA-2 Malicious or careless insider at an agency | Legitimate credentials, legitimate tenant scope | Money, revenge, moonlighting, selling rosters | Their own valid session; bulk export; screenshot |
| TA-3 Malicious insider at Suraksha | Broad scope, possibly admin | Money, coercion, exfiltration to a competitor | Privileged console, support impersonation, DB access |
| TA-4 Competitor / data broker | Moderate; scripted scraping, fake signups | Agency and pricing data from Trinetra; client leads | Public marketplace pages, fake agency account, API enumeration |
| TA-5 Criminal seeking a specific site or person | Moderate to high; motivated, may use social engineering or bribe an insider | Physical crime against a site or an individual | Phishing a Facility Manager; bribing a Supervisor; stolen guard phone |
| TA-6 Guard committing attendance fraud | Low technical, high situational | Being paid without being present | Mock GPS, shared device, photo replay, buddy punching |
| TA-7 Payment-path fraudster | Moderate | Money | Bank-detail change, fake invoice, payout tampering, webhook forgery |
| TA-8 External unauthenticated attacker | Variable, up to skilled | Anything | Exposed endpoint, dependency vulnerability, misconfigured storage |
| TA-9 Device thief | Physical access to an unlocked guard/supervisor phone | Resale, or opportunistic data | Lost or stolen handset with cached data |
| TA-10 Automated bot / scraper / spam | High volume, low sophistication | Ad fraud, lead spam, resource exhaustion | Public forms, OTP endpoints, search endpoints |

#### 38.2.3 Threat table

| Threat | Actor | Asset | Attack path | Control IDs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-01 Credential stuffing on any portal login | TA-1 | A10, A3 | Breach corpus replayed against `/login`; no MFA on client accounts | SUR-SEC-010, -011, -012, -022, -034, -081 |
| T-02 OTP brute force / enumeration | TA-1, TA-10 | A10 | Request OTP for a known mobile, iterate 6-digit space or spray many numbers | SUR-SEC-015, -016, -017, -079, -081 |
| T-03 SIM swap or SMS interception to take over a guard/client account | TA-5 | A2, A3 | Social-engineer the telco, receive the OTP, log in | SUR-SEC-019, -020, -023, -035 |
| T-04 Session token theft via stolen device | TA-9, TA-5 | A1, A2 | Unlocked phone, long-lived token, no app lock | SUR-SEC-027, -029, -104, -110, -117 |
| T-05 Insider bulk-exports the guard roster of a client | TA-2, TA-3 | A1, A3 | Legitimate role, exports "all guards" CSV, sells it | SUR-SEC-066, -093, -123, -176, D-2 and D-3 in §38.11.2 |
| T-06 Insider reads a competitor tenant's data through a shared endpoint | TA-2 | A6, A1 | Manipulates `tenant_id` in request, or a query missing a tenant filter | SUR-SEC-128 to -135 |
| T-07 IDOR on any object fetch | TA-2, TA-4 | A1–A7 | Increment or guess an object ID on a legitimate endpoint | SUR-SEC-048, -049, -050, -051 |

|---|---|
| SUR-SEC-005 | The threat model in §38.2 shall be reviewed at least every six months and on any of: a new public-facing surface, a new class of personal data, a new payment path, a new AI capability with data access, or a P0/P1 security incident. |
| SUR-SEC-006 | Every new epic shall record, in its design note, which threats in §38.2.3 it touches and which controls apply. Design review shall reject an epic that introduces a new data-exposure path without a named control. |
| SUR-SEC-007 | Threats T-05, T-06, T-07, T-10, T-11 and T-32 are designated **critical-path threats**. Their controls are MVP-mandatory and each shall have a permanently green automated test in CI (see §38.9.3, §38.15). |

#### 38.2.4 Trust boundaries

| Boundary | Between | What crosses it | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| TB-1 | Public internet and edge | Unauthenticated traffic to public pages, login, OTP, marketplace listings, webhooks | WAF, bot management, rate limits, TLS (§38.5) |
| TB-2 | Edge and application | Authenticated API requests | Token validation, role and scope resolution, tenant binding (§38.3, §38.9) |
| TB-3 | Application and data stores | Queries, object reads/writes | Least-privilege DB roles, tenant predicate enforcement, field-level encryption (§38.6) |
| TB-4 | Application and third parties | Payment, SMS/WhatsApp, maps, KYC/verification, model providers | Outbound allowlist, per-integration credentials, signed callbacks, no sensitive categories to model providers (§37, §41) |
| TB-5 | Guard device and platform | Field events, media, offline sync | Device binding, integrity signals, both-clock timestamps, server-side validation (§38.7) |
| TB-6 | Tenant and tenant | Nothing, by design | Four-layer isolation and the isolation test suite (§38.9) |
| TB-7 | Production and non-production | Nothing containing real personal data | Environment separation, data masking in lower environments (§38.10) |
