### 40.7 Audit-readiness

#### 40.7.1 The evidence pack

Three audiences ask for evidence, and they ask for different things. The platform ships three pack templates plus a custom builder.

| Pack | Requested by | Default contents | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Client Assurance Pack** | A client or their facility team, typically at contract start, at renewal, or after an incident | Agency licence status for the site's jurisdiction (status and validity dates, certificate on request per redaction profile) · deployed guard roster with per-guard compliance summary (verification state and validity dates, **not** document content) · training currency for deployed categories · insurance record summary · attendance and patrol compliance for the period · incident register for the site · SLA performance summary · supervisor visit log | PDF + XLSX annexure |
| **Procurement / Enterprise Diligence Pack** | An enterprise procurement or vendor-onboarding team | Everything in the Client Assurance Pack plus: entity and registration records · tax registration record · statutory registration records · contract templates and standard terms · policy set (privacy, security, grievance) · compliance score with formula and component breakdown · override and exception summary for the period · rule-configuration statement (§40.12) · sample registers · insurance certificates · security posture summary (§38 reference, not contents) | PDF bundle + machine-readable index (JSON) |
| **Inspection Pack** | An inspection or audit visit at a tenant or at Suraksha | Licence objects with evidence · person-level compliance records for the scope requested · statutory registers for the period · wage and contribution records for the period · filing calendar with evidence · attendance registers · training records with attestations · findings and their closure evidence · override register · the reminder trail per object · the audit log extract for the scope | PDF index + original evidence files in a structured folder tree + manifest with hashes |

#### 40.7.2 How the platform assembles a pack

| Step | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| 1. Define scope | Entity (tenant / branch / site / client / person set), period, jurisdiction, pack template |
| 2. Preview | Shows item count, total size, what is present, **what is missing**, and what will be redacted for the chosen audience. The missing list is the point: a pack that hides gaps is worthless. |
| 3. Authorise | Pack generation requires the pack permission; packs containing person-level documents require a second approval (Compliance) and record the business reason |
| 4. Assemble | Background job pulling from the evidence store and the status store as at the **generation timestamp**, with each item stamped with its status and rule version at that moment |
| 5. Redact | Redaction profile per evidence type and audience applied automatically (§39); redactions are listed in the manifest, so nothing is silently omitted |
| 6. Manifest | Machine-readable manifest: every item, its type, subject, period, status, rule version, file hash, and redaction applied; plus a completeness statement listing every requested item not included and why |
| 7. Seal | The pack is hashed and the hash recorded; a pack is immutable once generated. Re-generating produces a new pack with a new timestamp, never a mutation |
| 8. Deliver | Time-limited signed download link (default 7 days), watermarked PDFs with the recipient name, delivery recorded |
| 9. Audit | Generation, approval, download and expiry are all audited events; the download record names the recipient |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-051 | Every evidence pack shall include a completeness statement naming what was requested but not included and why (missing, out of scope, redacted, retention-expired). A pack shall never silently omit. |
| SUR-CMP-052 | Packs shall be immutable and hash-sealed; the manifest hash shall be verifiable independently of the platform. |
| SUR-CMP-053 | Person-level document content shall be included only where the pack template and the recipient's category permit it, and shall be watermarked with the recipient identity and generation timestamp. |
| SUR-CMP-054 | Pack generation shall be possible for any historical date, reproducing the status as at that date using the rule versions then in force (§40.1.4). |

#### 40.7.3 Record retention matrix

Retention values here are **configured defaults**; §39 owns the retention mechanics and data-subject handling. Values are set per jurisdiction and per record class and are effective-dated like every other rule.

| Record class | Default retention (from) | Basis of the clock | Deletion behaviour | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agency licence objects and evidence | 8 years from expiry or supersession | `valid_upto` | Archived, then evidence purged, metadata retained | Metadata (identifier, dates, status history) retained longer than the file |
| Guard KYC documents | 3 years from engagement end | Employment record close | Evidence purged; verification outcome retained | Re-engagement within the window reuses the record |
| Police verification records | 5 years from engagement end | Employment record close | Outcome retained; report document purged | Adverse-finding decisions retained with the outcome |
| Training records and attestations | 5 years from completion | `completed_on` | Certificate purged; completion fact retained | |
| Employment records | 8 years from exit | Exit date | Structured record retained; sensitive attachments purged earlier per §39 | |
| Wage and contribution records | 8 years from period end | Period end | Retained in full | Financial-adjacent; also see §35 |
| Attendance and muster registers | 5 years from period end | Period end | Retained; raw GPS traces down-sampled after 12 months (§39) | Down-sampling is a privacy control, disclosed |
| Contracts and annexures | 8 years from contract end | Contract end | Retained | |
| Invoices and tax documents | 8 years from issue | Issue date | Retained, immutable | BR-003 |
| Incident records and evidence | 7 years from closure; indefinite where litigation hold is set | Closure | Retained | Litigation hold overrides all deletion |
| Patrol, wake-check and checkpoint logs | 2 years | Event date | Aggregates retained beyond | |
| Filing calendar items and evidence | 8 years from due date | Due date | Retained | |
| Compliance findings and closure evidence | 8 years from closure | Closure | Retained | |
| Override records | Same as the underlying object | Underlying object | Retained | Never purged before the object |
| Evidence packs and manifests | 3 years from generation | Generation | Purged; manifest and audit entry retained | |
| Audit logs | 8 years, append-only | Event time | Never modified; archived to cold storage after 18 months | Canon §4 |
| AI interaction records touching compliance | Per §41.4 retention, minimum 2 years where an approval was executed | Interaction time | Redacted then purged | |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-055 | Retention periods shall be configurable per jurisdiction and record class with effective-dating; changing a retention period shall never retroactively delete records already past the new shorter period without an explicit, dual-controlled purge decision with a dry-run report. |
| SUR-CMP-056 | A litigation or investigation hold shall be settable on any entity or record set by Compliance with dual control, shall suspend all deletion for the held set, shall be visible on the affected records, and shall require an explicit release with a reason. |
| SUR-CMP-057 | Deletion of evidence files shall retain the metadata skeleton (what existed, its status history, who verified it, when it was deleted and under which retention rule) so that history remains explainable after the file is gone. |

### 40.8 Multi-jurisdiction operation

#### 40.8.1 Modelling an agency operating in four states

| Element | Model |
|---|---|
| Tenant | One `tenant_id`. Multi-state operation is never modelled as four tenants unless the agency is genuinely four legal entities — in which case each entity is its own tenant with an optional `entity_group_id` linking them for group reporting (Enterprise). |
| Jurisdiction footprint | `tenant_jurisdictions[]`: one row per (state, and optionally district) the tenant declares it operates in, with `declared_from` and `declared_to`. Declaring a footprint is what makes the jurisdiction's rules applicable. |
| Licences | One licence object per (tenant, jurisdiction) per §40.2.2. Four states = four state licence objects, minimum. |
| Branches | Branches carry a `jurisdiction_ref`. A branch cannot be created in a state absent from the footprint without a warning and an explicit confirmation, which creates the licence object in Draft. |
| Sites | Sites carry state and district, derived from address and confirmed by a human (never inferred from geocoding alone, because district boundaries and address quality both fail). |
| Guards | Guards have a home branch and a `deployable_jurisdictions[]` derived from their branch, their documents' jurisdictional scope, and any explicit extension. |
| Rules | Applicability is evaluated per jurisdiction. A guard in Gujarat is evaluated against `IN.GLOBAL.*` + `IN.GJ.*`; the same tenant's guard in Maharashtra against `IN.GLOBAL.*` + `IN.MH.*`. |
| Compliance score | Computed per jurisdiction and rolled up; the roll-up always shows the worst jurisdiction, because an average hides a blocked state. |

#### 40.8.2 District scoping

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Data | Districts are reference data with a stable code, a state parent, an official name, aliases (spelling variants and former names), and effective dates (districts get created, renamed and split). |
| Licence coverage | A licence's `districts_covered[]` is explicit. Three configured coverage modes: `all_districts_in_state`, `enumerated`, `single_district`. The mode is entered by a human from the certificate. |
| Site resolution | Site → district is resolved at site creation by address parsing plus a human confirmation step; the confirmed district is stored and is the one used for gating. Re-resolution happens only on an explicit address change, never silently. |
| District change events | If a district is split or renamed in reference data, affected licences and sites are flagged for human re-confirmation; nothing is auto-remapped. |
| Gating | The allocation gate checks: does the tenant hold a Valid licence object whose coverage includes the site's district (directly, or via `all_districts_in_state`)? If not, hard block per §40.6.1. |

#### 40.8.3 A guard deployed across a state boundary

This is the case that breaks naive models, so it is specified explicitly.

| Scenario | Handling |
|---|---|
| Guard's home branch in state A, site in state B | The gate is evaluated against the **site's** jurisdiction, always. The tenant must hold a Valid licence covering state B (and the site's district). The guard's own documents are evaluated against the union of `IN.GLOBAL.*` and `IN.B.*` rules — if state B configures an additional person-level requirement the guard does not hold, the guard is ineligible for that site while remaining eligible at home. |
| Cross-boundary allocation approval | Always requires State Operations approval (mirrors §25.15.6 cross-branch rule) and is flagged on the approval card with the jurisdictional basis: "Site is in Maharashtra; tenant licence MH-xxxx valid to 2027-03-31; guard holds all MH-required records." |
| Daily commuting deployment (site just across a boundary) | Supported as a normal cross-jurisdiction allocation; the site's jurisdiction governs. A `commute_exception` flag exists for reporting only and grants nothing. |
| Mobile duty crossing boundaries (escort, transit, PSO travel) | Modelled as a **route deployment** with an ordered jurisdiction list. The gate requires a Valid licence for **every** jurisdiction on the declared route, and the guard must satisfy every jurisdiction's person-level rules. If any is unsatisfied, the allocation is blocked with the specific jurisdiction named. Ad-hoc route changes in the field raise a P1 compliance exception rather than being silently accepted. |
| Event deployment in a state where the tenant has no licence | Hard block. The configured fallback is subcontracting to a marketplace agency holding a Valid licence for that jurisdiction (§25.15.7 step 6), with that agency's own compliance evaluated. |
| Guard relocating permanently | Branch transfer workflow re-evaluates the guard against the new jurisdiction's rules and produces a gap list before the transfer is confirmed. |
| Documents issued in one state, deployment in another | The evidence item spec may carry `jurisdiction_validity` (`national` / `issuing_state_only` / `configured_list`). Where a rule marks an item state-limited, deployment outside the issuing state requires the state's own equivalent record. This is configuration, per state, reviewed by counsel — never inferred. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-058 | Jurisdiction gating shall always be evaluated against the **site's** confirmed jurisdiction, and for route deployments against every jurisdiction on the declared route. |
| SUR-CMP-059 | Cross-jurisdiction allocations shall be visibly flagged with the licence and person-level basis on the approval card, and shall require State Operations approval. |
| SUR-CMP-060 | A route deployment whose actual path leaves the declared jurisdiction list shall raise a P1 compliance exception with the deviation recorded; the platform shall not silently permit or silently block a guard already in the field. |

#### 40.8.4 Configuration UI for adding a new jurisdiction

Screen: **Compliance → Jurisdictions → Add jurisdiction** (Suraksha Compliance; Enterprise tenants may add tenant-scoped overrides only).

| Step | Screen | Fields | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Identify | Country (fixed IN for now) · State (from reference data) · District (optional, from reference data) · Display name (localised) · Timezone · Effective from | State/district must exist in reference data; duplicate jurisdiction blocked |
| 2 | Choose a base | Start from: an existing jurisdiction's pack (clone) · the national baseline (`IN.GLOBAL`) · empty | Clone shows a diff preview |
| 3 | Object types in scope | Checklist of the §40.2.1 object types this jurisdiction will govern | At least one required |
| 4 | Rules | Per object type: the rule form (§40.1.2) — evidence list, verification method, validity basis and period, lead times, grace, consequences, severity, owner role, ladder | Expression compiler validates `applicability`; referenced roles, templates and action codes must exist |
| 5 | Registers and filings | Register templates (columns, grouping, period, format) · filing calendar obligations (periodicity, due-date expression, owner, evidence) | Due-date expressions validated against a date engine with sample output shown |
| 6 | Wage configuration | Rate table per category and skill band, effective-dated | Rates must be positive integers in paise; effective dates must not overlap |
| 7 | Counsel review | Reviewer name, type, date, reference note, status per rule or for the pack as a whole | Pack cannot be marked Reviewed with any rule Unreviewed |
| 8 | Dry run | Runs against live data for tenants declaring this jurisdiction; produces the change report | Mandatory before publish if any rule carries a blocking consequence |
| 9 | Approve & publish | Diff, change report and counsel block presented to the second approver | Requires Super Admin or Founder/Management |
| 10 | Post-publish watch | 7-day watch panel: reminders generated, blocks triggered, overrides requested, tickets raised | Rollback path always visible |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-061 | Adding a jurisdiction shall be a guided configuration task completable by a Compliance officer without engineering involvement, and shall be impossible to complete without either a recorded counsel review or an explicit "Unreviewed" acknowledgement that surfaces in the dashboard (C13). |
| SUR-CMP-062 | The platform shall not assume any government API for licence or verification lookup. Where such an interface later becomes available it shall be an optional enrichment; the manual verification path shall remain the primary path and shall never be removed. `[ASSUMPTION: A-361]` |

### 40.9 Suraksha's own compliance posture as an operator

Suraksha is two things at once: a platform operator serving tenants, and (as tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ`) a security agency running its own guarding operation. Conflating the two is a real risk, so they are separated explicitly.

| Dimension | Suraksha as operator (platform company) | Suraksha as agency (`SURAKSHA-HQ`) |
|---|---|---|
| What is tracked | Corporate registrations, tax registrations, employment records for platform staff, vendor and processor agreements, information-security posture (§38), privacy programme (§39), insurance, statutory filings for the platform company | Exactly what any tenant is tracked on: agency licences per jurisdiction, guard verification, police verification, training, employment, wage and contribution records, contracts, site records |
| Rule catalogue used | A separate `OPERATOR` object-type family plus the applicable jurisdiction packs | The same jurisdiction packs as every other tenant, with **no privileged exemptions** |
| Dashboard | An Operator Compliance view visible to Compliance, Finance, Founder/Management, Super Admin, Auditor | Appears in the tenant list like every other tenant, with the same score and the same blockers |
| Gating | Operator-level failures do not block tenant operations, except where they concern the platform's ability to process data lawfully or securely; those are handled as §38/§39 incidents | `SURAKSHA-HQ` is gated exactly like any tenant — an expired Suraksha state licence blocks Suraksha's own new allocations in that state |
| Segregation | Operator compliance records are not visible to tenants; tenant records are not visible to other tenants | `SURAKSHA-HQ` operational data is tenant data and is isolated by `tenant_id` like all other tenants |
| Conflict control | The Compliance role verifying `SURAKSHA-HQ` objects must not be the same individual who owns them; the platform enforces separation of the submitter and the verifier for `SURAKSHA-HQ` as for any tenant | Same |

**Operator-specific obligations tracked as configured records** (illustrative default set): corporate entity registration · tax registrations · statutory registrations for platform employees · data-processing agreements with each sub-processor with review dates · security certifications and their audit cycles (the canon notes the live site claims ISO 9001:2015 and government certification — those claims are tracked as evidence-backed records with expiry, and where evidence is absent the claim is flagged for removal from public content, cross-referencing P4 in canon §1.8) · insurance policies · the privacy programme's review calendar (§39) · incident-response readiness exercises (§38, §49) · accessibility conformance review of public surfaces · marketing-claims substantiation records (every public statistic on surakshaguards.in carries a substantiation record with a source and a review date — a direct control against P2–P5).

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-063 | `SURAKSHA-HQ` shall be subject to identical compliance rules, gating and dashboards as any other tenant, with no exemption path in code or configuration. |
| SUR-CMP-064 | Every public claim on Suraksha's own web properties (certifications, client counts, coverage, awards) shall have a substantiation record with a source, an owner and a review date; a claim whose record lapses shall raise a P2 finding and appear on the content owner's queue (§22.21). |
| SUR-CMP-065 | Operator compliance records shall be stored outside tenant scope and shall never be exposed through any tenant-facing API or export. |

### 40.10 Compliance events and metrics (pointer)

Compliance emits events into the shared taxonomy (§42.4) with the prefix `compliance_`: `compliance_object_created`, `compliance_evidence_uploaded`, `compliance_verification_decided`, `compliance_status_changed`, `compliance_reminder_sent`, `compliance_escalated`, `compliance_block_triggered`, `compliance_override_granted`, `compliance_override_expired`, `compliance_pack_generated`, `compliance_rule_published`, `compliance_finding_opened`, `compliance_finding_closed`. Compliance KPIs and their formulas are in §42.2.7 — they are not duplicated here.

---

### 40.11 Edge cases the compliance engine must handle

| # | Case | Required behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Certificate shows an expiry date that a human mis-keyed (e.g. 2027 typed as 2017) | Date sanity checks at entry (not in the past, not implausibly far forward, consistent with issue date); a change to `valid_upto` after verification requires re-verification |
| 2 | Renewal certificate arrives after expiry, backdated to cover the gap | Successor object records its own `valid_from`; if it covers the gap, the historical Expired period is retained in history with a "subsequently covered" annotation — it is never erased |
| 3 | Licence renewed with narrower district coverage | Diff shown at verification; sites and deployments in dropped districts flagged as a P0 exception before the successor is activated |
| 4 | Guard holds documents in two name spellings | Name-variance workflow; parent held at Pending until a canonical name decision is recorded |
| 5 | Tenant declares a jurisdiction footprint but never uploads a licence | Licence object auto-created in Draft; after a configured period (default 30 days) a P1 exception; allocations in that jurisdiction blocked from day one regardless |
| 6 | Rule change makes 4,000 guards non-compliant overnight | Dry run must have shown this; publication requires acknowledgement; consequences may be configured with a phase-in date so the block starts later than the flag |
| 7 | Evidence file corrupt or unreadable | Verification cannot proceed; item returns to Rejected with reason `unreadable`; the uploader is told exactly what to re-upload |
| 8 | Two objects claim the same licence identifier across tenants | Duplicate-identifier detection raises a P0 exception to Compliance for both tenants; neither is auto-invalidated |
| 9 | Guard exits and is rehired 8 months later | Prior records within retention are reusable; each is re-evaluated against current rules and a gap list produced; nothing is auto-accepted |
| 10 | Clock/timezone edge at midnight of expiry | Transitions computed in the jurisdiction timezone; an object expiring "today" is Valid until end of day local time; the UI shows the local expiry instant |
| 11 | Migration import of legacy records with missing dates | Imported with `source=migrated` and status Draft/Pending; never Valid. A migration completeness report lists every record needing human completion |
| 12 | Client demands an evidence pack containing guard KYC documents | Redaction profile applies; the pack shows what was redacted; releasing unredacted person documents requires the person-document permission plus a recorded business reason and is notified to Compliance |
| 13 | Object whose rule was archived (jurisdiction no longer served) | Object moves to Archived with reason `rule_withdrawn`; history and evidence retained per retention |
| 14 | Offline evidence capture (supervisor photographs a certificate in the field) | Guard/Agency App queues the upload; the object stays Pending; both `device_time` and `server_received_time` are recorded (canon §4) |
| 15 | A tenant tightens a rule then wants to loosen it back | Tenant overrides may only tighten relative to the jurisdiction rule; loosening restores the jurisdiction default and is audited, never permitted to go below it |

---

### 40.12 What this is NOT

This subsection is mandatory product content, not a disclaimer buried in a footer. It appears in the product, on the compliance dashboard footer, on the rule catalogue screen, and in every generated evidence pack.

| Statement | Where it appears |
|---|---|
| **This platform provides compliance tooling, not legal advice.** It records obligations that its operators and tenants have configured, tracks evidence against them, and applies configured consequences. It does not determine what any law requires of any person or business. | Rule catalogue header; dashboard footer; evidence pack cover page |
| **Every rule is configuration entered by a human.** Rules ship as defaults to make the product usable on day one. Defaults are a starting point, not a legal opinion, and they carry a review status. | Rule detail screen |
| **Rules require review by a qualified adviser.** Each rule's `counsel_review` block records who reviewed it, when, and with what caveats. A rule with `status = Unreviewed` is shown as unreviewed everywhere it is used, and the count of unreviewed rules is a dashboard card (C13). | Rule detail; C13; evidence pack |
| **Status is a statement about configured rules and recorded evidence, nothing more.** "Valid" means the configured evidence is present and within its recorded validity window. It is not a certification that any obligation is satisfied. | Status tooltip on every compliance chip |
| **Filing evidence is an acknowledgement recorded by the tenant.** The platform cannot observe acceptance by any authority and never claims to. | Filing calendar screen; evidence pack |
| **Verification means a named human at Suraksha checked the submitted evidence against the configured checklist.** It is not authentication of the document with any issuing authority, because no such interface is assumed to exist (SUR-CMP-062). | Verification badge tooltip; marketplace badge explainer |
| **The platform does not compute tax positions, wage entitlements, or contribution liabilities as legal determinations.** It applies configured rates and treatments and produces records. | Payroll and invoicing configuration screens |
| **Blocking is a product behaviour, not a legal outcome.** When the platform blocks an allocation because a licence object is Expired, it is applying a configured consequence chosen by the operator. | Block refusal message; override screen |
| **Responsibility for the accuracy of configured rules rests with the configuring party** — Suraksha for the seed catalogue and its own jurisdictions, the tenant for tenant-scoped tightening. | Rule editor; tenant override screen |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-CMP-066 | The "not legal advice" statement and the counsel-review status shall be rendered in-product at every point where a compliance rule or status influences a decision, not solely in terms of service. |
| SUR-CMP-067 | No product copy, notification template, AI response or export shall assert that a law requires something. Copy shall be phrased as "your configured rule requires" / "the <jurisdiction> configuration requires". This shall be enforced as a content review checkpoint on every template touching compliance (§22.20.1 review flow) and as a prohibited-phrase check in the AI output validator (§41.5). |
| SUR-CMP-068 | Evidence packs shall carry the configuration statement on the cover page, naming the rule pack versions used and the count of unreviewed rules in scope. |

## 41. AI Governance

### 41.0 Scope boundary

§25 owns **AI capability**: the ten surfaces, the intelligence layer, retrieval, the voice pipeline, model routing, the allocation engine, and the mechanisms that implement guardrails. This section owns **AI policy**: the principles those mechanisms serve, who is accountable, what is forbidden and why, what must be proved before release, how people contest AI-influenced outcomes, and how AI failures are handled as incidents.

Where §25 says "the tool declares its action class", §41 says "who decides which class, who may change it, and what evidence is required first". Capability descriptions are **not** repeated here — every surface, function and mechanism is referenced by its §25 identifier.

---

### 41.1 Governance principles

Five principles. Everything else in this section is their implementation.

| # | Principle | What it means operationally | Where it is enforced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Human accountability** | Every AI-influenced decision has exactly one named accountable human. AI is never the decision-maker of record; it is an input. Where an AI-proposed action executes, the approver owns the outcome. Where an automated action executes, the person who configured the automation owns it. | Approval records (§25.8); the Accountable Human field on every AI-influenced entity change (§41.1.1) |
| 2 | **Permission-bounded** | AI grants no authority. Any action AI can take, the requesting human could already take; any data AI can read, the requesting human could already read. AI is a faster interface to existing rights, never an expansion of them. | Policy gate before retrieval (SUR-AI-002); tool authorisation (§41.5.3) |
| 3 | **Traceability** | Every AI output is reconstructible: the inputs, the retrieved sources, the model and version, the tools called, the proposal, the human decision, the resulting change. Both directions — entity to interaction and interaction to entity. | Interaction log (SUR-AI-003, SUR-AI-021) |
| 4 | **Contestability** | Any person materially affected by an AI-influenced decision can see that AI was involved, see the basis, and contest it to a human who has the authority to change the outcome. This applies with full force to guards. | §41.6.4 contest path; §41.9 transparency |
| 5 | **Proportionate autonomy** | Autonomy is granted in inverse proportion to consequence. Reversible, low-cost, non-personal actions may be automated. Anything touching money, safety, liberty of action, employment or legal status is not. | Action-class governance (§41.2); the prohibition list (§41.1.2) |

#### 41.1.1 The accountable-human requirement

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-001 | Every entity change that an AI interaction influenced shall record an `accountable_user_id` — the approver for Approval-required actions, the configuring owner for Automated actions — and this field shall be non-null and non-system for every action class except Read-only. |
| SUR-AIG-002 | No audit record shall ever attribute a decision to "AI", "system" or "assistant" where a human was required. The permitted attribution is "<name> (<role>), acting on an AI proposal (interaction <id>)". |
| SUR-AIG-003 | Accountability shall not be delegable to a queue, a group mailbox or a shared account; approvals shall be made by identified individual users authenticated to the platform (§38). |

#### 41.1.2 The prohibition list

The canon (§1.7) fixes a list of actions AI may never autonomously execute. This section restates it as policy, adds the reason and the enforcement mechanism, and extends it where the same logic clearly applies.

| # | Prohibited autonomous action | Why | Enforcement mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Executing a payment, refund or disbursement | Irreversible movement of money; fraud surface | No tool exists (§25.7.1 row 32) |
| 2 | Changing payroll — rates, deductions, releases | Directly affects a person's income; error is felt immediately and is hard to unwind | No tool (row 29); proposals only (row 28) |
| 3 | Changing permissions, roles or entitlements | Privilege escalation is the highest-leverage attack path | No tool (row 57) |
| 4 | Deleting an account or any operational/financial record | Destroys evidence; conflicts with retention and audit | No tool (row 58); soft delete only (canon §4) |
| 5 | Terminating, blacklisting or deactivating a guard | Livelihood consequence; must be a human decision with a human reason | No tool (row 48); §41.6.3 |
| 6 | Changing a compliance status (licence, verification, training, filing) | Compliance status is evidence-backed and dual-controlled | No tool (rows 22, 24, 60); SUR-CMP-005 |
| 7 | Financial settlement, ledger adjustment, credit note | BR-003; double-sided ledger integrity | No tool (row 59) |
| 8 | Exporting sensitive data (KYC documents, salary, bank details, full contact lists) | Exfiltration surface; privacy consequence | No tool (row 58); §41.4.5 |
| 9 | Major deployment changes — cancelling a contract's deployment, mass reassignment, withdrawing guards from a site | Client and workforce consequence at scale | Approval-required with named authority (§25.15.6); bulk prohibited (§41.3.5) |
| 10 | Setting or changing alert severity, escalation state, or resolving an alert | Safety-critical determinism (§24.6) | No tool (SUR-AI-005; §25.2.5) |
| 11 | Marking attendance, acknowledging a wake check, or raising/clearing an SOS on a person's behalf | These are attestations by a human being; AI performing them destroys their meaning | No tool (§25.2.3) |
| 12 | Rejecting a job candidate | Fairness; livelihood | No tool (row 39); §41.6.2 |
| 13 | Marking training complete | Requires trainer attestation | No tool (row 42) |
| 14 | Publishing public content, pricing or a marketing claim | Brand and substantiation risk (canon §1.8 P2–P5) | Approval-required; publish rights are a separate permission (§22.21) |
| 15 | Submitting a bid or tender | Commercial and eligibility consequence | No tool (row 37) |
| 16 | Sending an external communication to a client, guard or authority | Reputation and contractual consequence | Approval-required draft only (rows 14, 18, 50) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-004 | The prohibition list shall be enforced **structurally** — by the absence of a tool implementation — and never by prompt instruction alone. A model that decides to attempt a prohibited action must find no mechanism, not merely a refusal string (mirrors SUR-AI-017). |
| SUR-AIG-005 | Adding any tool that would touch a prohibited area shall be impossible without a change to this section approved by the AI Review Board and Founder/Management (§41.10.3), and shall be blocked in CI by a tool-manifest check against the prohibition list. |
| SUR-AIG-006 | Any AI attempt to invoke a non-existent prohibited capability shall be logged as a governance event, counted, and reviewed monthly — a rising count is a signal of prompt injection or a mis-specified surface. |

### 41.2 Action-class governance

The four classes are defined in canon §1.7 and mechanised in §25.7. This subsection assigns the governance obligations of each class.

| Dimension | **Read-only** | **Recommendation** | **Approval-required** | **Automated** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qualifies when | Output is information the requester is already entitled to see; no state changes anywhere | Output is a suggestion, ranking, draft, analysis or forecast; a human must take a separate action for anything to change | A specific, parameterised state change is prepared and executes only on explicit human approval | Action is low-risk, non-financial, non-safety, non-personal, reversible in one step, and its blast radius is bounded to the requesting user's own context |
| Never qualifies when | The answer would combine data across tenants, or reveal existence of out-of-scope data | The recommendation is presented in a way that makes rejection costly or the alternative invisible | Approval would be given by someone lacking the underlying permission, or the change is on the prohibition list | The action touches money, compliance status, permissions, employment, safety, another person's record, or an external party |
| Approval authority | None; the requester's own read permission is the control | None at generation; the acting human's normal permission applies when they act | **Exactly the permission required for the underlying action** — AI adds no shortcut and no extra authority. Dual-control actions need both approvals | None at execution; the person who enabled the automation is accountable |
| Logging requirement | Interaction, scope, sources cited, latency, cost | Interaction + the full recommendation content + the ranking basis + alternatives shown | Interaction + proposal (hashed and stored in full) + risk flags shown + alternatives shown + approver identity + decision + edited parameters + execution result + link to the entity audit record | Interaction + action + parameters + reversal path + result |
| Reversibility requirement | N/A | N/A | The underlying action's own reversal rules apply; irreversible underlying actions require the higher approval tier (§41.3.4) | **Mandatory**: a one-step reversal must exist and be exposed to the user from the interaction record; an action without a reversal path cannot be Automated |
| Retention of the record | Per §41.4.6 | Per §41.4.6 | Minimum 2 years or the underlying entity's retention, whichever is longer | Per §41.4.6 |
| When AI is wrong — escalation path | User reports "this answer is wrong" from the response; routed to the AI quality queue; a wrong Read-only answer with operational consequence is a P2 AI incident | Rejection with a categorised reason is the primary signal; a pattern of rejections on one recommendation type (>configured threshold) opens a P2 review | The approver's rejection is captured; an **approved-then-wrong** case (human approved a bad proposal) is a P1 AI incident because the approval card failed to surface the decisive fact | An incorrect automated action is a **P1 AI incident by default**, auto-reverted where the reversal is safe, with the automation suspended pending review if the rate exceeds the configured threshold |
| Rate at which class may be granted | Default for all information surfaces | Default for all analytical and advisory functions | Default for all writes | **Exception, granted individually per function by the AI Review Board**, never by a developer's judgement |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-007 | Action class shall be a property of the **tool**, declared in code, reviewed at code review, and asserted in a machine-readable tool manifest that CI diffs against the approved register; an undeclared or changed class shall fail the build. |
| SUR-AIG-008 | Promotion of any function to the Automated class shall require AI Review Board approval with: the reversal path, the blast radius, the evaluation results (§41.8), a 30-day shadow-mode record, and a named owner. Demotion shall require nothing but a single owner's decision — it shall always be easy to reduce autonomy. |
| SUR-AIG-009 | Every Automated action shall be reversible in one user action from the interaction record, and the reversal shall be tested in the pre-release suite. |
| SUR-AIG-010 | An Automated function whose error rate exceeds its configured threshold over a rolling window shall be automatically demoted to Approval-required and an incident opened; restoration requires Board approval. |
| SUR-AIG-011 | Voice input shall never elevate an action's class, and no class shall be inferable from phrasing — "just do it" does not convert Approval-required into Automated (§25.5 read-back rule). |

#### 41.2.1 Class assignment governance for new functions

| Step | Gate |
|---|---|
| Proposal | Product owner submits: the function, the intended class, the data it reads, the tools it calls, the affected people, the failure modes |
| Classification review | AI Review Board assigns the class; ties resolve to the more restrictive class |
| Evaluation | The function must pass its evaluation suite (§41.8.2) before any release, at any class |
| Shadow mode | Any function proposed as Automated runs in Recommendation or shadow mode for a minimum of 30 days with its outputs logged and reviewed, before automation is enabled |
| Staged rollout | Enable for internal users → one pilot tenant → 10% → all, with the demotion trigger armed at every stage |
| Registration | The function is entered in the **AI Action Register** — the authoritative list of every AI function, its class, its owner, its evaluation reference and its last review date — which is auditable and exportable |

### 41.3 Human-in-the-loop design standards

§25.8 specifies the approval card as a component. This subsection makes its contents a **policy requirement** — an approval card missing any mandatory element is a governance defect, not a UI nit.

#### 41.3.1 Mandatory approval-card contents

| Element | Requirement | Failure if absent |
|---|---|---|
| **Proposed action** | One plain sentence naming the effect, in the approver's language, with the affected entities named (not IDs alone) | Approver cannot know what they are approving |
| **Evidence** | The two to four decisive facts with a link to each source record, each stating its freshness ("attendance as of 14:20") | Rubber-stamping |
| **Confidence** | A stated confidence or a stated basis quality, expressed in language a non-technical approver understands ("high — based on 6 prior deployments at this site" / "low — this guard is new, no site history"), never a bare percentage with no referent | False precision |
| **Alternatives** | At least two next-ranked options where alternatives exist, each selectable in one tap, plus "none of these" | Approval by absence of choice |
| **Cost / impact** | The consequence in the units the approver cares about: money, hours, SLA, headcount, client exposure, guard impact ("adds 2h overtime; guard's rest gap becomes 9h") | Hidden consequences |
| **Risk flags** | Every soft-constraint violation and unusual condition, in red, stated as a sentence | The approver misses what they would have caught |
| **One-click reject** | Reject is always present, always one action, never behind a menu, and requires only a category (free text optional) | Friction biases toward approval |
| **Edit-and-approve** | Where the underlying action supports parameter editing | The human is often right about one field |
| **Approver line** | Whether the current user may approve; if not, a route to someone who may | Dead ends produce workarounds |
| **Expiry** | Visible countdown and the stale-proposal rule (§41.3.6) | Stale approvals execute wrong actions |
| **AI disclosure** | The card is visibly an AI proposal with the interaction ID accessible | §41.9 |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-012 | The approval card shall be a single shared component; a surface rendering its own approval UI shall fail design and code review. Any element marked mandatory above shall be non-removable by configuration. |
| SUR-AIG-013 | Reject shall never be more effortful than approve. Approve and Reject shall have equal visual weight and equal interaction cost; dark patterns favouring approval are prohibited and are checked at design review (§27). |
| SUR-AIG-014 | Confidence shall never be displayed without its basis; a numeric confidence shall always be accompanied by what it is confidence *in* and what evidence produced it. |

#### 41.3.2 Who may approve

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Permission parity | The approver must hold the permission for the underlying action (§31). AI creates no approval right. |
| Dual control preserved | Where the underlying action requires two approvals (financial, permission, licence status, suspension), the AI proposal requires the same two. |
| Self-approval | Permitted only where the human could have performed the action unilaterally without AI. Where the human asked AI to prepare an action they could not perform alone, self-approval is impossible by construction. |
| Named-approver actions | Armed/PSO/close-protection assignments, Tier-1 and government client sites, critical-risk sites, cross-branch and cross-tenant assignments, working-hour overrides — all require the named authority per §25.15.6; AI cannot route around this. |
| Delegation | Approval authority may be delegated only through the platform's delegation mechanism (§31), time-bounded and audited; an AI proposal to a delegate records both the delegate and the delegator. |
| Conflict of interest | A user may not approve a proposal whose subject is themselves (their own leave, their own payroll adjustment, their own performance record); the card routes to the next authority. |

#### 41.3.3 Time limits and non-response

| Proposal type | Default expiry | On expiry | Non-response handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operational, time-critical (replacement, roster gap, allocation for a shift starting soon) | 15 minutes | Proposal voids; the underlying operational need remains and escalates through the normal operational path (§24), **not** through AI | The work does not depend on the approval arriving — the fallback is the human process |
| Operational, routine (assignment for a future shift, roster publication) | 4 hours | Voids; re-proposal on next request | Reminder at 50% of the window to the approver |
| Administrative (report definition, template, configuration draft) | 24 hours | Voids; draft retained for manual use | Reminder at 12 hours |
| Communication drafts (client notice, guard letter) | 24 hours | Voids; draft retained | The communication need escalates to the human owner |
| Compliance-related proposals (renewal task drafts, evidence checklists) | 72 hours | Voids; the compliance ladder (§40.5) continues regardless | Compliance ladders never depend on AI |
| Bulk low-risk (reminder batches) | 24 hours | Voids | — |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-015 | **Non-response shall never cause execution.** No AI proposal shall auto-approve on timeout under any configuration. Silence is refusal. |
| SUR-AIG-016 | No operational outcome shall be dependent on an AI proposal being approved; every AI-proposed path shall have a non-AI path that reaches the same operational outcome, and that path shall be the one that escalates when the proposal expires. |
| SUR-AIG-017 | An approval token shall be bound to a proposal hash; if any parameter, or any decisive underlying fact, changes between proposal and execution, the token shall be invalid and a fresh proposal required (mirrors SUR-AI-020, extended to underlying-fact drift). |

#### 41.3.4 Irreversibility escalation

| Reversibility of the underlying action | Approval requirement |
|---|---|
| Reversible in one step by the same user | Standard approval |
| Reversible but with a visible external effect (a notification already sent, a client already informed) | Standard approval, with the external effect stated on the card |
| Reversible only by a higher role or a compensating transaction | Approval by that higher role, or dual approval |
| Not reversible | Not eligible for an AI proposal at all unless the Board has explicitly approved the function, and then always with dual control and a confirmation step outside the card |

#### 41.3.5 Bulk approval policy

| Permitted | Prohibited |
|---|---|
| Homogeneous, low-risk, reversible items: renewal reminders, document-request messages, report scheduling, notification digests | Assignments and deployments · money of any kind · compliance status or evidence decisions · communications to clients · anything affecting an individual's record · anything on the prohibition list |
| Requires: the human views a sample of at least 5, confirms the total count, and sees the full list on one screen before confirming | Bulk is never a workaround for per-item approval; splitting a prohibited bulk action into a rapid sequence of single approvals with no human reading is detected by an approval-velocity check and flagged (§41.8.4) |

#### 41.3.6 Rejection as a first-class signal

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Reason categories | Wrong data · wrong recommendation · right but not now · policy/authority reason · unclear proposal · alternative preferred |
| Where it goes | Rejection reasons feed the per-surface monthly quality report and the evaluation set; a recurring category on one function opens a review |
| Never punitive | Rejection rate is a metric of the AI, never of the approver. No dashboard shall rank humans by how often they reject AI proposals, and approval rate shall never be an individual performance metric (§41.6.5) |

### 41.4 Data governance for AI

#### 41.4.1 What data may enter prompts and retrieval

The rule is simple and absolute: **the AI's data envelope is the requesting human's data envelope, intersected with the surface's purpose.** The second half matters — a Finance user's Support AI still does not retrieve payroll, because the surface's purpose does not include it.

| Requester category | May enter prompt/retrieval | Never enters |
|---|---|---|
| Anonymous website visitor | Public content, published pricing configuration, serviceability data, public FAQs | Any account data; any tenant data; any person data; the existence of any specific record |
| Individual Customer / client roles | Own bookings, contracts, sites, deployments, attendance summaries, invoices, wallet, incidents, tickets; guard first name, last initial, photo, on-duty status | Guard PII beyond the above; guard salary; internal cost/margin; internal notes; other clients' data; agency internal data |
| Guard-side roles | Own roster, attendance, payslips, documents (metadata), leave, training, incidents they reported; instructions and contacts for sites they are currently assigned to | Other guards' pay or personal data; client commercial data; site details for sites they are not assigned to; internal assessments about them that are not disclosed to them |
| Agency roles | Strictly own `tenant_id`, then branch/module scope of the user | Any other tenant's data, in any form, at any aggregation below the anonymised benchmark thresholds (§42.7) |
| Suraksha internal roles | Their §31 scope in OPS | Anything outside scope; document *content* is cited and linked, never pasted into a response |
| Auditor | Read-all within the audit scope, watermarked | Write anything |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-018 | The policy gate shall evaluate identity, tenant, role, geography, entitlement and surface purpose **before** retrieval, so a denied request never causes data to be read (mirrors SUR-AI-002). Post-retrieval filtering is prohibited as the primary control. |
| SUR-AIG-019 | Scope denial shall not disclose the existence, count or characteristics of out-of-scope data. The permitted response names the scope, not the data. |
| SUR-AIG-020 | Retrieval indexes shall be partitioned by `tenant_id`; a single index containing multiple tenants' content with filtering applied at query time is prohibited. |

#### 41.4.2 Cross-tenant prohibition

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Absolute prohibition | No prompt, no retrieval result, no cached context, no few-shot example, no fine-tuning corpus and no evaluation artefact shall contain data from more than one tenant in a single request context. |
| Shared context objects | System prompts, tool schemas, product documentation and public content are tenant-neutral by construction and are the only shared context. |
| Cross-tenant features | Marketplace search and benchmarking are the only features that legitimately span tenants; both operate on **pre-aggregated, threshold-gated, opt-in** data (§42.7) or on data the tenant published deliberately (marketplace listings), and neither passes another tenant's raw records into a model call. |
| Conversation memory | Session and long-term memory are keyed by (user, tenant); a user with access to two tenants (rare, e.g. a consultant) gets separate memory per tenant with no bleed. |
| Caching | Response and embedding caches are keyed with `tenant_id` in the key; a cache key derivable without tenancy is a build-blocking defect. |
| Testing | Production tenant data shall not be used in development or staging environments; evaluation sets use synthetic or consented, anonymised data (§41.8.1). |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-021 | Cross-tenant leakage shall be treated as a **P0 security and privacy incident** with mandatory notification per §39, regardless of whether harm is demonstrated. |
| SUR-AIG-022 | The pre-release evaluation suite shall include adversarial cross-tenant probes; a single failure blocks release (§41.8.2). |

#### 41.4.3 PII redaction before model calls

| Stage | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Classification | Every field in the retrieval schema carries a sensitivity class (public · internal · personal · sensitive-personal · financial · credential) defined in §32/§39. |
| Default handling | `sensitive-personal` (identity numbers, bank details, biometric references, health, verification report content) and `credential` classes are **never** sent to a model. They are referenced by token ("the identity document on file, verified 2026-03-04") and linked. |
| Personal data minimisation | Personal fields are sent only when the task requires them. Names and contact numbers are sent when the task is about that person; otherwise pseudonymised references are used. |
| Free-text scrubbing | Free-text fields (incident narratives, ticket bodies, notes) pass a redaction pass that masks detected identifiers before the model call, with the mapping retained server-side so the response can be rehydrated for the authorised user. |
| Document handling | Document *content* enters a model call only inside the verification/extraction workspace, for the specific extraction task, for a user holding the document permission, and never appears verbatim in a chat response (§25.2.7). |
| Output redaction | Responses pass an output redaction stage applying the requester's redaction profile; the same response text is never reused across requesters. |
| Logging | Prompts and responses are stored redacted; raw unredacted content is not persisted in AI logs. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-023 | Fields classed `sensitive-personal`, `financial-instrument` or `credential` shall be excluded from model inputs by the schema, not by prompt instruction; the exclusion shall be enforced in the retrieval layer so no surface can opt in. |
| SUR-AIG-024 | Redaction shall be evaluated as a tested capability with a measured false-negative rate, reported quarterly; a redaction miss on sensitive-personal data is a P1 AI incident. |
| SUR-AIG-025 | AI interaction logs shall store redacted prompts and responses; where an investigation requires unredacted content, access shall require dual control, a recorded reason, and shall itself be audited. |

#### 41.4.4 Training on customer data

**[RECOMMENDED] position, stated plainly: Suraksha does not train, fine-tune or otherwise improve models on tenant, client or guard data without explicit, granular, revocable opt-in — and no product capability is withheld from tenants who decline.**

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| Default | Off. No tenant data enters any training, fine-tuning, RLHF, distillation or embedding-corpus-for-model-improvement process by default. |
| Opt-in | Per-tenant, per-purpose, granted by the Agency Owner (or the client's authorised signatory), revocable at any time, with a plain-language description of what would be used and for what. Revocation stops future use; data already incorporated into a trained artefact cannot be extracted, and this limitation is stated honestly at opt-in time. |
| Never eligible, even with opt-in | Guard personal data, KYC document content, salary and payroll data, verification records, client commercial terms, incident narratives naming individuals, support conversations containing personal data, anything covered by a litigation hold. |
| Vendor terms | Every model vendor contract must contractually prohibit training on Suraksha-submitted data and must offer zero-retention or short-retention processing (§41.4.7). A vendor unwilling to commit to this is not eligible for production use. |
| What Suraksha *does* use for improvement | Aggregated, anonymised interaction telemetry (intent distributions, success/failure rates, latency, rejection categories, language performance) with no record content; synthetic data; explicitly consented and anonymised evaluation utterances (§25.4 quality measurement); and internal Suraksha-operator data for its own tenant. |
| Disclosure | The position is stated in the privacy notice (§39), in the tenant contract, in the AI settings screen, and in the procurement diligence pack (§40.7.1). |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-026 | Training on tenant, client or guard data shall require explicit per-tenant opt-in; the platform shall not ship a default-on or bundled-consent mechanism, and declining shall not degrade any feature. |
| SUR-AIG-027 | Model vendor agreements shall contractually prohibit training on submitted data and shall specify retention; the AI Review Board shall maintain the vendor register with these terms and their review dates as compliance objects (§40.9). |
| SUR-AIG-028 | Categories listed as never-eligible shall be excluded technically, not merely contractually — they are excluded from model inputs entirely by §41.4.3 and therefore cannot reach a training pipeline. |

#### 41.4.5 Export and exfiltration controls

| Control | Specification |
|---|---|
| No AI export tool for sensitive data | Per the prohibition list; AI may trigger an export the user could already perform through the normal export path, which applies its own permissions, watermarking, rate limits and audit (§38) |
| Volume ceilings | An AI-initiated read that would return more than a configured row count summarises and offers the standard export path instead of streaming the data through a model |
| Response size | Responses are bounded; a request that would enumerate a large personal-data set is refused with an explanation and the report route |
| Watermarking | AI-generated documents and exports carry the requesting user and timestamp |
| Detection | Unusual AI query patterns (broad enumeration, systematic scanning across entities, repeated boundary probing) feed the §38 detection pipeline as a distinct signal class |

#### 41.4.6 Retention of AI interactions

| Record | Default retention | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Interaction metadata (who, when, surface, model, tools, latency, cost, outcome) | 24 months | Powers §42 AI metrics |
| Redacted prompt and response text | 12 months | Extended to 24 months where an approval executed |
| Proposal payloads and approval decisions | Life of the underlying entity's retention, minimum 24 months | Part of the entity's audit trail |
| Retrieval source references | Same as the interaction | Needed to reconstruct an answer |
| Voice audio | Not retained by default; retained only with explicit consent for quality evaluation, maximum 90 days, then deleted | Transcripts follow the prompt-text rule |
| Rejection reasons and quality feedback | 24 months | Evaluation corpus |
| Evaluation artefacts | Life of the model version plus 12 months | Reproducibility |
| Incident records for AI failures | 5 years | §41.8.5 |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-029 | Deleting a user or a tenant shall remove or irreversibly anonymise their AI interaction content within the §39 timeframe, retaining only the aggregate telemetry and the audit skeleton required for accountability. |
| SUR-AIG-030 | Voice audio shall not be retained without explicit, separately-granted consent, and consent for audio retention shall never be a condition of using voice. |

#### 41.4.7 Vendor and model data-processing requirements

Every model or AI service vendor is assessed before production use, and the assessment is a compliance object (§40.9) with a review date.

| Requirement | Minimum acceptable |
|---|---|
| Training prohibition | Contractual, explicit, covering all submitted data |
| Retention | Zero-retention preferred; where retention exists, ≤30 days, stated, with a documented purpose |
| Sub-processors | Disclosed list, with notice of change and a right to object |
| Data location | Stated; where processing occurs outside India, the transfer basis is documented and disclosed in the privacy notice (§39) `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-362]` |
| Security | Assessed against §38 vendor criteria; incident notification obligation with a defined maximum notification time |
| Availability | Stated SLA; the platform must degrade safely regardless (§41.5.5) |
| Model changes | Notice of model deprecation and behaviour-changing updates; Suraksha pins model versions and re-runs evaluations before adopting a new version |
| Exit | Data deletion on termination, evidenced |
| Review | Annual reassessment; a vendor failing reassessment is removed from the router (§25.12) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-AIG-031 | Model versions shall be pinned per surface; an automatic upstream model update shall never reach production without the evaluation suite passing on the new version (§41.8.2). |
| SUR-AIG-032 | The vendor register shall record training prohibition, retention, sub-processors, data location, incident terms and review date for every AI vendor, and shall be exportable into the procurement diligence pack (§40.7.1). |
