### 45.2 Identity — SUR-EDG-022 to 025

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-022 | The same person is registered as a guard in two agencies simultaneously | Guards work for multiple agencies; agencies poach; the guard wants two incomes | Each tenant holds its own guard record — records are never merged across tenants and neither tenant can see the other's data. The platform detects the collision on the verified mobile or verified identity document and raises a `dual_employment` flag on the *new* registration's verification case. Activation requires an explicit acknowledgement by a named user in the registering tenant. Allocation then applies BR-001 across the platform: a guard cannot hold overlapping active assignments even across tenants, and the conflict is reported as "unavailable in this window" without naming the other tenant |
| SUR-EDG-023 | A client user is offboarded while holding a pending approval | Staff turnover, role change, contract handover | Offboarding (WKF-36) enumerates every pending approval, ticket and task owned by the user and blocks completion until each is reassigned to a named alternate holding the required permission, or explicitly cancelled with a reason. Nothing is auto-approved, auto-rejected or orphaned. The SLA clock on each reassigned approval continues from its original start |
| SUR-EDG-024 | A guard leaves one agency and joins another, with documents already verified elsewhere | Normal churn in the sector | Verification is per tenant. The new tenant re-verifies from its own copies; it never inherits another tenant's verification decision, and it is not shown that a prior verification exists. The guard may re-submit their own documents from their guard-platform profile, which is the guard's own record, not the agency's. The prior employment period remains in the old tenant, unreadable by the new one |
| SUR-EDG-025 | One person holds an agency role and a client role at the same site | Facility manager who also runs a small guarding contract; a client employee moonlighting | Roles are held per tenant and never blend. Each session is scoped to exactly one tenant context, chosen explicitly at login or switched deliberately. Data visible in one context is never visible in the other, including search, exports, reports and AI answers. The dual holding is flagged to Compliance for conflict-of-interest review |

#### Table B

| ID | User-visible outcome | Data / financial consequence | Notifications | Audit | Test case |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-022 | New agency sees a dual-employment flag it must acknowledge; the other agency is not told | Two payrolls in two tenants; overlap prevention stops the same hour being billed twice | Registering agency's verification queue; Suraksha Compliance | Flag raised, acknowledgement, acknowledging user, subsequent overlap blocks | TC-GRD-006, TC-AGN-004 |
| SUR-EDG-023 | Offboarding admin sees a checklist of items requiring reassignment | No approval lost; no invoice or deployment stalled without an owner | Outgoing user, incoming assignee, offboarding admin | Each item, its old and new owner, the reassigning user | TC-PLT-014, TC-OPS-006 |
| SUR-EDG-024 | Guard re-uploads once from their own profile; the new agency verifies independently | Duplicate verification effort is accepted as the cost of isolation | Guard prompted for the document set; new agency's verification queue | New tenant's verification decision only; no cross-tenant reference | TC-GRD-006, TC-PRM-001 |
| SUR-EDG-025 | User picks a context at login and sees an unambiguous context indicator throughout | None directly; conflict-of-interest review may restrict one role | User on context switch; Compliance on detection | Every context switch, and every action attributed to its tenant | TC-PRM-003, TC-PLT-011 |

### 45.3 Deployment — SUR-EDG-026 to 033

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-026 | Guard resigns mid-shift and walks off the post | Wage dispute, personal emergency, better offer, conflict with the client | Attendance closes at the recorded departure time with reason `abandoned_post`. An `UNSTAFFED_POST` record starts immediately and runs at its true duration until a replacement checks in (BR-420). Emergency replacement (WKF-18) is triggered automatically at P1. The guard's future assignments are released and become open posts. Exit processing starts, and final settlement is computed on actual attendance only |
| SUR-EDG-027 | Client cancels 2 hours before a deployment starts | Change of plan, site not ready, budget withdrawal | Cancellation is accepted but priced on the refund policy version in force at booking (BR-449), which for a same-day cancellation will typically carry a charge. The exact amount is shown before confirmation. Allocated guards are released and, where the configured policy provides a short-notice release payment, it is computed and shown to the agency. The post and shift are cancelled, not deleted |
| SUR-EDG-028 | A guard is deployed across a state boundary mid-shift | Mobile patrol routes, escort duties, sites near a border | The platform evaluates licence coverage per **site**, not per live position, so a shift at a licensed site does not become non-compliant because the guard crosses a boundary during a patrol or escort. However, if the assignment itself is to a location in an uncovered state, allocation is blocked (BR-406). A live position crossing into an uncovered state during an escort raises an informational compliance note on the assignment, and the configured jurisdiction rule for that service lane governs whether an approval is required |
| SUR-EDG-029 | A site relocates to new coordinates while a deployment is active | Client moves premises; the original pin was wrong; a temporary site becomes permanent | The geofence is versioned. A change requires a reason and takes effect from a stated timestamp; historical attendance is evaluated against the fence version in force at the event time and is never retroactively re-judged. Guards are notified of the new location before it takes effect where notice allows; if it takes effect immediately, in-flight check-ins under the old fence remain valid |
| SUR-EDG-030 | Two guards check in for a single-guard post | Roster confusion, an unreleased replacement, a guard covering for a friend | Both attendances are recorded. The second is flagged `over_strength` with the post's configured strength. Payable hours follow the configured over-strength rule — typically the assigned guard is paid and the unassigned one requires an approval to be paid — and the client is billed the contracted strength, never the actual headcount, unless the contract explicitly bills actuals |
| SUR-EDG-031 | A supervisor is scoped to a site whose contract ends mid-roster | Contract termination during a published roster | From the contract end timestamp the supervisor loses operational access to the site: no new assignments, no live tracking, no new document access. Shifts already in progress complete. Historical records remain readable to the roles that retain them per §31, and the scope change is applied within the configured session window (BR-443) |
| SUR-EDG-032 | The client demands immediate removal of a specific guard and no replacement is available | Behaviour complaint, security concern, personality clash | The removal is executed on the client's recorded request with the requesting user's identity. The post becomes an open post immediately and the `UNSTAFFED_POST` clock runs. Escalation fires to the agency operations chain and to the client contact so the coverage gap is never a surprise. The client may record a waiver of coverage for the remainder; the waiver is stored with identity and time, and the gap record still exists |
| SUR-EDG-033 | The client increases post strength mid-shift | Incident on site, VIP visit, unexpected event | Strength changes are versioned on the Post with an effective timestamp and a requesting client user. Additional guards are allocated through the normal compliance checks — no fast path bypasses BR-411 or BR-406. Billing for the additional strength follows the contract's variation clause and appears as its own invoice line with its effective period |

### 45.4 Marketplace — SUR-EDG-034 to 035

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-034 | Two agencies claim the same marketplace listing | A split partnership, a franchise and its parent, a rebrand, or an outright impersonation using a real licence number | The second claim is blocked at publication and a claim-resolution case is opened with Verification. Neither listing is silently overwritten and neither claimant is shown the other's submitted documents. The existing listing continues while the case is open, marked `claim under review` to internal roles only. Resolution requires documentary evidence and a named Verification decision; the losing claimant may appeal once with new evidence |
| SUR-EDG-035 | An agency's public rating is dominated by a single disputed review | A review from a terminated or disgruntled client; a review that breaches BR-432 | Reviews are only accepted from a client role with an `Active` or `Completed` relationship at the reviewed site (BR-432). A disputed review is flagged `under review` and is excluded from the displayed aggregate while the dispute is open, but it is never deleted. Resolution either reinstates it into the aggregate or marks it withdrawn with a reason, both visible to the agency. The aggregate always states how many reviews it is computed from |

### 45.5 Financial — SUR-EDG-036 to 040

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-036 | Payroll runs while attendance corrections are still open | Month-end pressure; a supervisor's correction arrives after the lock | A payroll run may only be created against a locked (`Completed`) attendance period (BR-422), and the period cannot lock while a manual-attendance conflict or an unresolved verification task is open. A correction arriving after lock never modifies the completed run (BR-003): it creates an adjustment carried into the next run, referencing both the correction and the original run. If the correction reduces pay below what was disbursed, the configured recovery rule applies with the guard notified before any recovery |
| SUR-EDG-037 | An invoice is issued and then the contract is backdated | Commercial renegotiation applied retroactively; a data-entry correction to the start date | Issued invoices are immutable (BR-427). A backdated contract change never re-rates an issued invoice. The delta is settled by credit note plus a fresh invoice, both referencing the original and the contract amendment. The contract carries an amendment record with its effective date, the requesting user and the approver; the original terms remain readable |
| SUR-EDG-038 | A client payment is reversed by chargeback after the agency settlement was already paid | Card dispute, fraud claim, corporate dispute | The chargeback creates compensating ledger entries; nothing is deleted (BR-003). The client invoice returns to an unpaid state with a `chargeback` marker. The already-paid settlement is **not** clawed back automatically: a settlement recovery item is created, notified to the agency with the evidence, and resolved through the dispute process with a named approver before any recovery is applied |
| SUR-EDG-039 | A tax rate changes with retrospective effect after invoices are issued | Statutory change announced with a past effective date | The platform never silently re-rates issued invoices. Each invoice line applied the rate configured as in force on its service date at issue time. A retrospective change is handled by an explicit, approved corrective run that issues credit notes and fresh invoices for the affected period, with a report listing every affected invoice and the delta before anything is executed |
| SUR-EDG-040 | A guard's bank account is closed between payslip generation and disbursement | Account dormancy, bank merger, the guard switched banks | Disbursement for that payslip fails and is held with the specific provider reason; the run is not blocked and all other payslips disburse. The payslip stays `Pending` disbursement, the guard is notified with what to update, and the corrected bank proof must be verified before the retry. The retry is idempotent on the payout reference so the guard cannot be paid twice |

### 45.6 Attendance — SUR-EDG-041 to 045

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-041 | A shift spans midnight | Standard night guarding, 22:00–06:00 | The shift is a single record with a start and end timestamp and a `roster_date` assigned by the configured attribution rule (typically the start date). Attendance, payroll, invoicing, reports and analytics all use the same attribution — the rule is defined once and referenced everywhere. Shift counts never double, and hours never split across two days unless the contract explicitly bills by calendar day, in which case the split rule is configured and applied identically in payroll and invoicing |
| SUR-EDG-042 | The attendance period is locked while a guard is still checked in on a midnight-crossing shift | Month-end lock at 00:00 while a night shift is running | The lock excludes in-progress attendance whose shift started before the boundary; those shifts complete and are attributed by the `roster_date` rule. The lock records exactly which shifts were excluded and why. A period can never lock in a way that strands an in-progress attendance without a record of it |
| SUR-EDG-043 | The geofence is redrawn while a guard is checked in | Correcting a bad polygon; the client extends the premises | Fences are versioned with effective timestamps. The in-progress attendance continues to be evaluated against the version in force at check-in; the new version governs from its effective time onward. No retroactive geofence violation is generated, and the guard is notified if the change affects where they may stand |
| SUR-EDG-044 | The guard changes the device time zone mid-shift | Travel, manual setting change, OEM auto-timezone glitch | All evaluation is in UTC internally and presented in IST. The device's reported zone is stored for diagnostics only. A zone change produces no attendance effect and no skew flag by itself; only a wall-clock divergence from server time produces a `clock_skew` flag | 
| SUR-EDG-045 | Two devices are logged in as the same guard | Old phone not signed out; a shared device at the post; credential sharing | Both sessions are permitted but the guard record is flagged `multi_device_active` with both device IDs visible to the supervisor. Attendance is deduplicated by client event ID and by shift, so a second check-in is a no-op. Repeated multi-device activity is escalated to Compliance as a possible credential-sharing pattern |

### 45.7 Data — SUR-EDG-046 to 050

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-046 | Device is factory-reset with unsynced offline data | Phone sold, stolen, reset to fix a fault, handed to another guard | Unsynced local data is unrecoverable by design — it is encrypted, app-private and excluded from cloud backup. The platform therefore minimises the window: the app syncs opportunistically on any connectivity, warns the guard whenever the pending queue exceeds the configured age or size, and notifies the supervisor when a device has been unsynced beyond the threshold. On reset, the server-side record shows a telemetry gap of exactly the unsynced window, and the supervisor is prompted to reconstruct the period through the manual-attendance path with its reason code and approver (BR-413). The loss is recorded explicitly, never papered over |
| SUR-EDG-047 | A guard exercises a data-deletion request while under an active contract | Privacy right invoked during employment | The request is recorded and acknowledged per §39. Data required for an active employment relationship, statutory retention, an open dispute or an open safety investigation is retained under the documented lawful basis, and the guard is told precisely which categories are retained and why. Categories not required are erased or de-identified within the configured window. Erasure never removes audit entries or financial records (canon §4); those are retained per policy with access restricted |
| SUR-EDG-048 | Two site records exist for the same physical address | Created by sales and by operations; a client re-onboarded; slightly different address text | Site creation runs a proximity and address-similarity check and warns at creation with the candidate match. If duplicates still exist, merging is an explicit, approved operation that re-parents assignments, attendance, incidents and invoices with a full mapping record; it is never a silent delete. Until merged, both sites function, and reports show the duplicate warning rather than silently splitting the client's numbers |
| SUR-EDG-049 | A bulk import fails part-way | Bad row in the middle of a 5,000-row file, timeout, entitlement limit reached | Imports are transactional per row with an overall run record. Every row ends in `imported`, `skipped` or `failed` with a specific reason, and the run reports all three counts. There is no partial row and no silent truncation. The user can download the failed rows as a correctable file and re-run only those; re-running is idempotent on a row key so successful rows are not duplicated |
| SUR-EDG-050 | Audit log retention boundary is reached during an open investigation | Long-running dispute or regulatory query spanning the retention period | Audit entries under a legal hold are exempt from retention disposal. A hold is applied to a defined scope (tenant, entity, date range) by an authorised role, is itself audited, and blocks disposal until released. Disposal of any audit data always produces a disposal record naming the scope, the policy and the executing process |

### 45.8 Compliance and entitlement — SUR-EDG-051 to 053

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-051 | A district's administrative boundary is redrawn or a new district is created | Routine state reorganisation in India | Geography is reference data with versions and effective dates. A boundary change creates a new version; existing licences retain the coverage they were verified for, mapped to the new codes through an explicit mapping record. Where a mapping is ambiguous, the affected sites and licences are flagged for Verification review rather than being auto-assigned. No site silently loses or gains coverage, and historical records are evaluated against the geography version in force at the time |
| SUR-EDG-052 | An agency downgrades while actively using a Professional-only module | Cost pressure, a plan trial ending, a billing failure forcing a downgrade | No data is deleted (BR-437). Before confirming, the agency is shown exact counts of what will become read-only — open recruitment candidates, CRM records, extra branches, saved advanced reports — and an export path for each. After downgrade those entities are readable and exportable but not editable, and in-flight items are neither cancelled nor completed automatically. Re-upgrading restores full editability with nothing lost |
| SUR-EDG-053 | The PSARA licence verification source is unavailable or has no public API | Government portals with no stable API; portal downtime | Licence verification falls back to the documented assisted path: document upload plus human verification by the Verification role against the issuing authority's published record, with the evidence and the verifier recorded. The platform never fabricates a verification result and never marks a licence `Verified` from an unreachable source. Verification state clearly distinguishes "verified against source" from "verified from documents" so downstream restrictions can be configured differently for each |

| SUR-EDG-053 | Agency sees which verification method was used and what it permits | Restrictions may differ by verification method per configuration | Agency and Verification queue | Method used, evidence, verifier identity, source availability at the time | TC-CMP-001, TC-TRN-002 |

### 45.9 Integration — SUR-EDG-054 to 055

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-054 | The payment gateway is down during the month-end renewal and invoicing window | Provider incident coinciding with our peak | Payment attempts fail closed with the specific provider error; nothing is optimistically marked paid. Renewals enter grace rather than restriction (BR-438), and the grace clock is extended by the recorded outage duration so no agency is penalised for our provider's failure. Invoices are still generated and dispatched; only collection is deferred. A retry campaign runs after recovery with idempotency keys so no charge is duplicated |
| SUR-EDG-055 | The maps or geocoding provider returns a wrong district for a site | Address ambiguity, provider data error, boundary imprecision | The district resolved by the provider is stored as a suggestion, not as truth. Site activation requires the district to be confirmed by an operator, and any mismatch between the typed address and the resolved district is surfaced before activation (BR-410). Licence coverage checks use the confirmed district. A later provider correction never silently changes an active site's district; it raises a review task |

#### Table B

| ID | User-visible outcome | Data / financial consequence | Notifications | Audit | Test case |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-054 | Agencies and clients see a specific "payment provider unavailable" message and an extended grace date | No restriction applied for the outage window; no duplicate charge on retry | Affected payers, Suraksha finance, on-call | Outage window, failed attempts, grace extension, retry results | TC-MON-008, TC-B2C-007, TC-API-004 |
| SUR-EDG-055 | Operator confirms the district at site creation and sees any mismatch warning | Prevents allocations under the wrong licence and the resulting compliance exposure | Operator at creation; Compliance on a later correction task | Suggested district, confirmed district, confirming user, correction tasks | TC-B2C-024, TC-CMP-005 |

### 45.10 Multi-tenancy and AI — SUR-EDG-056 to 057

#### Table A

| ID | Scenario | Why it happens | Exact system behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-056 | Two agencies merge and ask for their tenants to be combined | Acquisition, consolidation of a group's branches | Tenant merge is never an in-place operation and is never automatic. It is an approved, staged migration: a target tenant is chosen, entities are migrated with a full source-to-target mapping record, duplicate guards, clients and sites are resolved individually, and financial history is migrated as immutable records with their original tenant reference retained. Both tenants remain readable until the merge is signed off. Until sign-off, isolation between them is enforced exactly as between unrelated tenants — a pending merge grants no early visibility |
| SUR-EDG-057 | A wake check fires during a genuine emergency | The guard is dealing with an intrusion, a medical event or an SOS they just raised | While an SOS or a P0/P1 incident is open for that guard, scheduled wake checks do not escalate as missed. They are recorded as `suppressed_emergency` with the suppressing event's ID and appear in the emergency timeline so the operator can see them. Suppression is derived from an actual open safety event, never from a user-settable toggle. When the event closes, the next scheduled check resumes normally, and the suppressed checks remain visible in the compliance report labelled as suppressed rather than missed |

#### Table B

| ID | User-visible outcome | Data / financial consequence | Notifications | Audit | Test case |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-EDG-056 | Both agencies see a staged migration plan with per-entity counts and a sign-off step | Financial history preserved with original references; no settlement or invoice is rewritten | Both agency owners, Suraksha Compliance and Finance | Merge plan, every entity mapping, duplicate resolutions, sign-off | TC-PRM-001, TC-DAT-005, TC-DAT-008 |
| SUR-EDG-057 | Guard is not pestered mid-emergency; operator sees the suppressed checks in the timeline; compliance report shows them as suppressed, not missed | No wake-check penalty applied to the guard or the agency for the emergency window | Operator sees them in the SOS/incident timeline; no escalation notifications fire | Each suppressed check with the suppressing event ID, and the resumption | TC-GAP-039, TC-CMD-009 |

## 46. Non-Functional Requirements

### 46.0 What this section is, and the rule it obeys

This section is the canonical register of non-functional requirements for the whole SURAKSHA platform. Functional behaviour lives in §11–§29; the data model in §32; endpoints in §33; real-time design in §34; security controls in §38; privacy in §39; compliance in §40. This section states **how well** the system must behave, **at what scale**, **how that is measured**, and **how it is proved**. Where a requirement here restates a control that another section owns, it appears as a measurable target with a cross-reference and nothing more.

Normative IDs use `SUR-NFR-nnn`.

#### 46.0.1 The honesty rule for every number in this section

The master brief warns, correctly, against arbitrary enterprise numbers. A target like "99.99% availability" written into a PRD by a team that has never run the system is not a requirement; it is a wish that will be quietly abandoned in month four, and its abandonment teaches the team that targets are decorative. Every number below therefore carries three things:

1. **The assumption it rests on** — usually a scale assumption, a topology assumption, or a device/network assumption.
2. **The measurement definition** — a percentile with no defined measurement point is meaningless. "p95 API latency" measured at the load balancer and measured on a guard's 2G handset differ by an order of magnitude, and both are legitimate numbers about different things.
3. **A verification method** — how we will know, on a given Tuesday, whether the number holds.

Where we do not have a defensible number, this section says so and raises a decision or an assumption rather than inventing one.

#### 46.0.2 The two operating points

Every target is stated twice, for two named operating points. Anything in between is interpolated by the capacity model in §50.

| Operating point | Definition | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **MVP** | The pilot/city topology of §34.7.1: one Indian cloud region, multi-AZ, one Postgres primary + one replica, one Redis, 2–4 API instances. Scale per `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` — ~30 agency tenants, 8,000 active guards, ~900 sites. | §34.7.1, §32.4 |
| **Scale** | The Year-2 multi-state operating point per `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` — ~400 tenants, 120,000 guards, ~12,000 sites, with the extractions of §50.3 performed as their triggers fire. | §50.1 |

The pan-India stage (S4 in §50.1) is deliberately **not** given NFR targets here. Targets for an operating point 75× larger than anything we have measured would be fiction. §50 gives the capacity path and the bottleneck list for that stage; the NFR register is re-baselined when stage S3 is actually reached, and that re-baselining is itself a requirement (SUR-NFR-002).

#### 46.0.3 Verification vocabulary

Every requirement's Verification column uses one of these tokens. They map to §43–§44 (QA strategy and test cases) for the test-case detail.

| Token | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CI-GATE` | An automated check in the CI pipeline that blocks merge or release (§47.6). |
| `LOAD` | A scheduled load or soak test against a production-like environment with seeded volumetric data. |
| `SYNTH` | A continuously running synthetic probe in production (§48.6). |
| `RUM` | Real-user monitoring from production clients (web vitals, mobile timing beacons). |
| `PROM` | Continuous measurement from the production metrics pipeline (§48.3) against a recorded SLO. |
| `CHAOS` | A deliberate fault-injection exercise (dependency killed, latency injected). |
| `DRILL` | A scheduled human exercise with a recorded outcome (DR drill, continuity drill, game day). |
| `AUDIT` | Periodic manual review with retained evidence. |
| `FIELD` | Measured on real devices in real field conditions with real guards. |
| `LAB` | Measured in a controlled device/network lab on the reference device set. |

---

### 46.1 The measurement baseline

Everything in §46.2 and §46.3 depends on these baseline assumptions. They are stated once, here, and referenced rather than repeated.

| Ref | Baseline assumption | Value (MVP) | Value (Scale) | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B-1 | Registered active guards `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` | 8,000 | 120,000 | Drives GPS, attendance, notification and storage volume |
| B-2 | Fraction of registered guards on duty at the daily peak `[ASSUMPTION: A-562]` | 45% → 3,600 | 45% → 54,000 | Drives concurrency, ping rate, real-time fan-out |
| B-3 | Agency tenants `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` | 30 | 400 | Drives tenant-scoped query cost and cache cardinality |
| B-4 | Concurrent authenticated console sessions (Agency Portal + OPS + Customer Portal) at business-hours peak `[ASSUMPTION: A-562]` | ~120 | ~1,600 | Drives API concurrency and connection pool sizing |
| B-5 | Concurrent Command Center operators (Suraksha + agency command views) | 8–12 | 60–90 | Drives WebSocket fan-out and map query cost |
| B-6 | Median guard device: Android 8–11, 2–3 GB RAM, 720×1280 (§18) | — | — | All client-side budgets are set on this device, not on a test iPhone |
| B-7 | Median guard network: 4G with frequent 3G/EDGE degradation; median RTT to an Indian-region endpoint 60–110 ms `[ASSUMPTION: A-563]` | — | — | Server-side latency budgets must leave room for this |
| B-8 | Console user network: office broadband or 4G, RTT 20–60 ms to an Indian region | — | — | Console targets assume this; they are not promised on 2G |
| B-9 | Peak-to-average request ratio, driven by shift change (approx. 06:00, 14:00, 22:00 IST) `[ASSUMPTION: A-562]` | 6× | 6× | The system is sized for the shift-change spike, not the daily mean |

**The shift-change point deserves emphasis because it shapes every other number in this section.** This is not a product with a smooth diurnal curve. Roughly 60% of a day's attendance writes, geofence evaluations, notification sends and app foregrounding events occur inside three 20–30 minute windows. A system sized on daily averages will be comfortably idle for 22 hours and will fail at exactly the moment its users need it. All capacity targets below are **peak-window targets**.

#### 46.1.1 Where a percentile is measured

| Measurement point | Name used below | What it includes | What it excludes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Load balancer / API gateway | **server-side** | Application processing, database, cache, in-region provider calls | Client network, TLS handshake, DNS, client render |
| Client instrumentation beacon | **end-to-end** | Everything the user experiences, including their network and device | Nothing |
| Synthetic probe | **synthetic** | Everything from a fixed vantage point on a known network | Real-device and real-network variation |

Unless a requirement says otherwise, latency targets in §46.2 are **server-side**, because that is the part we control and can be held to. Each performance requirement additionally states an end-to-end expectation where one is meaningful, and those are expectations reported to management — not contractual promises, because we do not control a guard's tower.

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-001 | Every performance and availability target in this section shall be recorded as a machine-readable SLO definition with its measurement query, and shall be evaluated continuously rather than asserted. | 100% of §46.2/§46.3 targets have an SLO definition | Same | SLO definitions in the metrics pipeline (§48.13) | `CI-GATE` on the SLO definition file; `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-002 | The NFR register shall be re-baselined against observed production distributions at 90 days after launch and at each stage transition in §50.1; a target that has never been met and has no funded plan to be met shall be revised or removed rather than carried. | First re-baseline at day 90 | Re-baseline at each stage | Review meeting with the SLO attainment report | `AUDIT`, quarterly |
| SUR-NFR-003 | Client-perceived (end-to-end) and server-side measurements shall both be collected for every user-facing operation in §46.2, and shall never be conflated in reporting. | Both collected for all 10 operation classes | Same | RUM beacons + server histograms | `RUM`, `PROM` |

### 46.2 Performance requirements

#### 46.2.1 The operation classes

The master brief names ten operations that must carry explicit p50/p95/p99 targets. They are defined precisely here, because a target against a vague operation is unfalsifiable.

| Class | Precise definition | Primary surface |
|---|---|---|
| Page load | Navigation to a rendered, interactive console screen with its first data payload present. Measured as LCP and INP (Core Web Vitals) for web; cold and warm start separately for apps. | WEB, CPT, AGN, OPS, TRN |
| API response | Server-side duration of a single authenticated REST call, from first byte in to last byte out, excluding client network. Split into read-single, read-list, and write. | All |
| Search | Global search (§26.3) returning the first result page for a tenant-scoped query. | AGN, OPS, CPT |
| Dashboard | The full named card set of a dashboard screen (e.g. the 16 cards of §20.4) rendered with real values. | AGN, OPS, CPT |
| GPS updates | Two distinct numbers: **ingest acknowledgement** (batch POST accepted) and **visibility lag** (`recorded_at` → position visible on the live map). | GAP → CMD |
| SOS | End-to-end: guard's press → alert visible and audible on an operator console. Owned mechanically by §24.8; the *target* is here. | GAP → CMD |
| Notification | Domain event commit → provider acceptance, per priority and channel. Owned by §36.4.5; restated here as the platform-level target. | SVC |
| Reports | Two classes: interactive report render, and asynchronous report job (queued → downloadable). | AGN, OPS |
| Upload | Document or photo upload: presign call, transfer, and post-processing (virus scan, thumbnail, OCR enqueue). | All |
| AI response | Time to first useful output per interaction class. Owned by §25.11; restated here. | AI |

#### 46.2.3 The reasoning behind each target

A number without reasoning is a number nobody will defend at 3 a.m. when it is missed.

| ID | Reasoning and the assumption it rests on |
|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-010/011 | Console users are professionals working an eight-hour shift in the tool. The relevant human threshold is the ~1 second "flow" boundary and the ~2.5 second "attention held" boundary. Budget decomposition for the p95 of 2.5 s: TLS+DNS on a warm connection ≈120 ms, server TTFB ≤400 ms (SUR-NFR-013/014 plus template), CDN-served JS/CSS on a warm cache ≈300 ms, hydration and first data paint ≈700 ms, contingency ≈1 s. The Scale target degrades by ~12%, which is the honest cost of larger tenant datasets and deeper permission filtering — not zero, because pretending scale is free is how teams end up with a 6-second dashboard nobody planned. |
| SUR-NFR-012 | 2.5 s at p75 is not our invention; it is the published Core Web Vitals "good" threshold that search ranking uses. The marketing site is an SEO asset (§14) and a mostly-static CDN-served page, so the target is achievable — and if it is not met on a static page, something is badly wrong. |
| SUR-NFR-013 | 200 ms p95 server-side leaves a total perceived budget of roughly 200 + 110 (B-7 RTT) + 150 (client render) ≈ 460 ms, comfortably inside the 1 s flow threshold on a guard's 4G connection. Chosen because the dominant cost is one indexed primary-key lookup plus row-level security predicate evaluation; anything above 200 ms at this volume indicates a missing index, not a capacity problem. |
| SUR-NFR-014 | List reads carry pagination, tenant scoping, permission filtering and often a join to a read model. 400 ms p95 assumes every list query is served by one of the 25 governed indexes in §32.4 and that the CI `EXPLAIN` gate has prevented sequential scans over tables >100k rows. |
| SUR-NFR-015/016 | Writes carry a transaction, constraint evaluation (including the BR-001 exclusion constraint on overlapping assignments), an outbox insert and a commit fsync. 450 ms p95 assumes the primary is not saturated and WAL is on SSD. Check-in is given its own tighter, separately monitored SLO because it is the operation on which payroll, billing and the client's SLA all rest, and because it arrives in a 6× shift-change spike (B-9). A check-in that takes 3 seconds at 06:05 is, from the guard's point of view, a broken product. |
| SUR-NFR-017 | Assumes trigram/full-text indexed search over a tenant's own rows within the volumetrics of §32.4 — at MVP a large tenant has ~1,500 guards and ~200 sites, which is small. The Scale target loosens because a 20,000-guard tenant's search space is 13× larger and because search is the query most likely to be issued with a single-character prefix. Above the Scale point a dedicated search index becomes necessary; the trigger is in §50.4. |
| SUR-NFR-018/019 | The dashboard target is a **set** target, not a per-card one, because that is what the user experiences. 16 cards at 150 ms p95 each, issued with a concurrency of 6, gives ~450 ms of query time; the rest of the 2 s budget is transport and render. The per-card query target is the enforceable one, and it is enforced in CI against seeded volumetric data. Cards backed by aggregates must read from a read model or a materialised view, never from a live scan — that is a §32 rule, restated here as the reason the number is achievable. |
| SUR-NFR-020 | The ingest endpoint validates and enqueues; it does not write to Postgres (§34.3.3). 40 ms p95 is therefore a validation-and-Redis-append budget with generous headroom. This number matters because the Guard App is on a metered, weak connection and every millisecond of server time is a millisecond of radio-on time and battery. |
| SUR-NFR-021 | **This is the honest one.** Visibility lag as defined here excludes the device's sampling interval, which is 30–300 seconds (§34.3.1) and which dominates *actual* map freshness by two orders of magnitude. A stationary guard's dot can legitimately be 120 seconds old while the pipeline lag is 3 seconds. We therefore measure and report **both**, and the UI labels position age (SUR-UIX-004). Promising a "live map with 5-second freshness" would require a sampling policy that destroys the guard's battery and data allowance, which we have explicitly refused (§34.3.1, §39). |
| SUR-NFR-022 | Reconciles exactly with §34's P0 budget: source write ≤200 ms, outbox relay ≤500 ms, evaluator ≤300 ms, pub/sub + gateway ≤200 ms, browser render ≤300 ms ≈ 1.5 s typical against a 5 s p95. The gap between 1.5 s typical and 5 s p95 is deliberate headroom, not slack: it absorbs a garbage-collection pause, a retry, and a mobile network re-attach. The target is **identical at MVP and Scale** — this is the one number that is not permitted to degrade with growth, and §50.3 lists SOS path isolation as a first-tier extraction precisely to protect it. |
| SUR-NFR-023 | The SMS path depends on an operator network and an aggregator; 25 s p95 reflects observed Indian A2P SMS delivery behaviour `[ASSUMPTION: A-563]` and is not something we can engineer below. It is a fallback, and its number is stated honestly so that nobody designs a process assuming SMS SOS is as fast as data SOS. |
| SUR-NFR-024/025 | Restates §36.4.5. The split between provider acceptance and device receipt matters: we control the first, we can only observe the second. FCM/APNs delivery to a doze-mode Android device on a weak network is genuinely variable, which is why P0 alerts to the Guard App also ring through a high-priority channel and, for the Command Center, through a voice call rung (§24.7). |
| SUR-NFR-026/027 | The interactive threshold of 50,000 source rows is the point at which a synchronous request stops being safe under the API's 30-second gateway timeout with any margin. Beyond it, the API returns `202` and a Report Job (§33). The async targets assume a dedicated worker lane and the analytical replica, not the primary. |
| SUR-NFR-028/029/030 | Upload transfer time is bounded by the guard's uplink, not by us: 2 MB on a 3 Mbps uplink is ~5.5 s before overhead. Post-processing is asynchronous by design so a slow virus scan never blocks a guard finishing a check-in; the user-visible state is "uploaded, being checked", which is truthful (SUR-UIX-006). |
| SUR-NFR-031/032 | Restates §25.11. AI latency is dominated by the model provider, which we do not control; the design response is streaming, an acknowledgement tone at 300 ms, and a hard rule that the Command Center AI summary panel disappears rather than delays an operator (§25.11). |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-033 | No user-facing synchronous request shall exceed a 30 s server-side timeout; work that can exceed it shall return `202` with a job handle. | 100% compliance | Same | Gateway timeout config + route audit | `CI-GATE`, `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-034 | Latency targets shall be evaluated over a rolling 28-day window, per route, excluding declared maintenance windows and excluding requests rejected at the WAF as abusive. | Defined and applied | Same | SLO query definition | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-035 | A performance regression exceeding 20% on any p95 in SUR-NFR-013 to SUR-NFR-021 between two consecutive releases shall block the release. | Enforced | Enforced | Automated comparison against the previous release's load-test baseline | `CI-GATE`, `LOAD` |

#### 46.2.4 Network profile matrix — what we promise on a bad connection

The Guard App's users are frequently on 3G or EDGE at industrial sites, basements and gated perimeters. Promising uniform performance across networks is dishonest; stating the graceful behaviour per profile is not.

| Profile | Assumed throughput / RTT | Guard App promise | Console promise |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4G good | ≥5 Mbps down / 2 Mbps up, RTT ≤80 ms | All targets in §46.2.2 hold | All targets hold |
| 4G congested | 1–3 Mbps, RTT 100–250 ms | Check-in ≤4 s end-to-end; photos deferred to background upload | Console targets +40% |
| 3G | 0.3–1 Mbps, RTT 200–500 ms | Check-in ≤8 s end-to-end, text-only sync first, photos queued; SOS still ≤10 s | Console usable but not targeted; degraded banner shown |
| EDGE / 2G | <100 kbps, RTT 500–1,500 ms | Check-in accepted **offline-first** and confirmed locally; SOS attempts data then falls back to SMS within 3 s (§24.8.1) | Not supported; the console shows an explicit "connection too slow" state |
| No connectivity | — | Full offline operation per §46.14; SOS via SMS or the displayed emergency number | Read-only cached view for the desktop app; all writes blocked with an honest failure (§20.30) |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-036 | Every duty-critical Guard App flow (check-in, check-out, wake check, SOS, patrol scan, incident report) shall complete successfully on the EDGE profile in the device lab, using offline-first acceptance where necessary. | 100% of the six flows | Same | Network-shaped device lab run per release | `LAB`, `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-037 | The Guard App shall never present a blocking spinner longer than 3 seconds for a duty-critical action; it shall accept locally and reconcile. | Enforced | Enforced | Instrumented UI timing | `LAB`, `FIELD` |

These are the budgets that decide whether the product is usable on the device the guard actually owns (B-6). They are release gates, not aspirations.

| SUR-NFR-038 | Guard App download size (Android, per-ABI split) | ≤30 MB | ≤35 MB | Play Console artefact size | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-039 | Guard App installed size including caches after 30 days of use | ≤180 MB | ≤200 MB | Device lab measurement | `LAB` |
| SUR-NFR-040 | Guard App cold start on the reference low-end device to interactive home | ≤3.0 s p95 | Same | Instrumented cold start | `LAB`, `RUM` |
| SUR-NFR-041 | Guard App battery attributable to the app over an 8-hour shift `[ASSUMPTION: A-191]` | ≤4% | ≤4% | Device lab and field telemetry | `LAB`, `FIELD` |
| SUR-NFR-042 | Guard App mobile data per 12-hour shift excluding user-initiated photo/video | ≤15 MB | ≤15 MB | Client accounting counter reported in telemetry | `FIELD` |
| SUR-NFR-043 | Guard App peak resident memory on a 2 GB device | ≤180 MB | Same | Device lab | `LAB` |
| SUR-NFR-044 | Console initial JavaScript transferred (compressed) per route entry | ≤350 KB | ≤400 KB | Bundle analyser in CI | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-045 | Console total transferred bytes for a dashboard first load | ≤1.2 MB | ≤1.5 MB | Lighthouse / RUM | `CI-GATE`, `RUM` |
| SUR-NFR-046 | Desktop app cold launch to interactive (§20.30) | ≤4 s | ≤4 s | Instrumented launch timing on the reference office machine | `LAB` |
| SUR-NFR-047 | Desktop app resident memory with three windows open on an 8 GB machine | ≤900 MB | ≤1.1 GB | Lab measurement | `LAB` |
| SUR-NFR-048 | Web font payload per language (subset, per §26.10 SUR-FRQ-160) | ≤120 KB | ≤120 KB | Asset audit in CI | `CI-GATE` |

The battery and data numbers are the two that determine whether guards keep the app installed. §18 records that field workers uninstall tracking apps that visibly drain their phone, and that the guard usually pays for the data. Treating those two numbers as release gates rather than as nice-to-haves is a product decision, not an engineering nicety.

#### 46.2.6 Throughput and load targets

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-049 | Sustained API throughput at the shift-change peak with all latency targets still met | 250 req/s | 3,000 req/s | Load test against production-like environment | `LOAD`, quarterly |
| SUR-NFR-050 | Burst API throughput absorbed without error for 60 s (6× per B-9) | 600 req/s | 7,000 req/s | Load test | `LOAD` |
| SUR-NFR-051 | GPS ping ingest sustained | 60 pings/s | 900 pings/s | Load test + production metric | `LOAD`, `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-052 | GPS ping ingest burst (offline replay herd, §49.11) | 600 pings/s for 10 min | 6,000 pings/s for 10 min | Replay simulation | `LOAD`, `CHAOS` |
| SUR-NFR-053 | Concurrent WebSocket connections to the real-time gateway | 1,500 | 20,000 | Connection metric under load | `LOAD`, `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-054 | Attendance writes inside a 20-minute shift-change window | 6,000 | 90,000 | Load test of the shift-change scenario specifically | `LOAD` |
| SUR-NFR-055 | Notification fan-out for a single roster publish affecting N guards | 2,000 recipients within 60 s | 20,000 recipients within 120 s | Job duration metric | `LOAD`, `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-056 | Payroll run wall-clock time for a tenant's monthly run | 1,500 payslips in ≤10 min | 20,000 payslips in ≤45 min | Job duration metric | `LOAD`, `PROM` |

The load-test scenario set is not a generic ramp. It comprises five named scenarios that mirror how this system is actually used: *shift change*, *offline replay herd*, *large roster publish*, *month-end payroll and invoicing*, and *SOS under load* (a P0 raised while the other four run). The last one exists because the only SOS latency number that matters is the one measured while the system is busy.

### 46.3 Availability

#### 46.3.1 Availability tiers by component

The master brief asks for this explicitly, and it is right to: **the SOS path deserves a higher availability target than the marketing website, and treating them identically is the most common way a platform ends up with targets it cannot defend.**

Two clarifications before the table, because they are routinely confused:

- **Importance and achievability are different axes.** The marketing website is the least important surface and, being static and CDN-fronted, is also the *easiest* to keep up. Its target is high because it is cheap, not because it matters most. The SOS path matters most, and its target is bounded by the honest limits of a single-region topology, not by how much we care.
- **A target is a promise you will defend with money and engineering.** We do not promise four nines on a topology with one region, one primary database and a three-person on-call rotation. Claiming 99.99% (4.4 minutes/month) when a single database failover takes 5–15 minutes is arithmetic nonsense.

| Tier | Components | MVP target | Monthly budget | Scale target | Monthly budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T0 — Life safety** | SOS ingest API + retry endpoint, SOS SMS gateway, alert creation, Command Center alert delivery (console + push + voice trigger), emergency contact data read | 99.9% | 43 m | 99.95% | 21 m |
| **T1 — Operational core** | Authentication, attendance check-in/out, GPS ingest, wake checks, patrol scans, real-time gateway, guard-facing app APIs | 99.5% | 3 h 39 m | 99.9% | 43 m |
| **T2 — Business applications** | Agency Portal, OPS, Customer Portal, Trinetra authenticated area, Admin App, rostering, invoicing, CRM, marketplace | 99.5% | 3 h 39 m | 99.9% | 43 m |
| **T3 — Asynchronous and analytical** | Report generation, exports, payroll runs, analytics dashboards, AI surfaces, OCR/document processing, bulk imports | 99.0% | 7 h 18 m | 99.5% | 3 h 39 m |
| **T4 — Public marketing** | surakshaguards.in public pages, trinetra.* public marketplace browse, careers, status page | 99.9% | 43 m | 99.95% | 21 m |

**Why T0 is 99.9% and not higher at MVP.** The honest constraint chain is: a single-region topology with an automated Postgres failover has a realistic recovery time of 5–15 minutes for an instance-level failure; a bad deployment detected and rolled back takes 5–10 minutes; a cloud AZ event may take longer. Two such events in a month consume the 99.95% budget entirely. 99.9% is a target we can defend and improve; 99.99% is a target we would breach in month one and then stop measuring. **What makes the SOS path genuinely safe is not the number — it is that SOS has three independent transports (§24.8, SUR-CMD-017), one of which does not depend on our platform's data path at all, plus the manual continuity protocol in §49.12.** Availability engineering for a life-safety function is about independent paths, not about adding a nine.

**Why T4 is higher than T1.** Static content served from a CDN with an origin failover to a cached copy is genuinely near-continuously available, and it costs almost nothing to make it so. Setting its target lower than achievable would be pointless. The asymmetry is deliberate and is documented here so that nobody later "corrects" it.

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-060 | Each component shall be assigned exactly one availability tier, recorded in the service catalogue, and its tier shall drive its alerting, on-call and deployment-approval treatment. | 100% of components tiered | Same | Service catalogue with tier field | `AUDIT`, quarterly |
| SUR-NFR-061 | T0 availability shall be measured by an independent external synthetic probe (§48.6), not by internal health checks, because an internal check cannot observe the failure mode where the platform believes it is healthy. | External probe in place | Same | Synthetic SOS probe from ≥2 vantage points | `SYNTH` |
| SUR-NFR-062 | No deployment, migration, scaling action or configuration change shall be permitted to take the T0 path offline; T0 components shall be deployed with connection draining and health-gated rollout only. | Enforced | Enforced | Deployment configuration review | `CI-GATE`, `AUDIT` |

#### 46.3.2 What counts as downtime

An availability target is meaningless without a failure definition, and "the server returned an error" is too narrow — a 200 response containing a stale map is also an outage from the operator's point of view.

| Condition | Counts as downtime for the tier when… |
|---|---|
| Error rate | ≥5% of requests on the tier's critical endpoints return 5xx or time out, sustained ≥60 s |
| Latency | p95 on the tier's critical endpoints exceeds 5× its target, sustained ≥5 min |
| Correctness | The surface returns a response that is structurally valid but materially wrong (stale beyond its freshness budget, wrong tenant's data, missing a required section) — counted from detection, and always reviewed individually |
| Real-time staleness | For T0/T1: the live map or alert queue is stale by >120 s while the client believes it is live |
| Partial scope | An outage affecting a subset of tenants counts pro-rata by affected-tenant-minutes, not as a binary |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-063 | Availability shall be computed as good-minutes / total-minutes using the definitions above, per tier, per calendar month, with partial outages counted pro-rata by affected tenants. | Defined and automated | Same | SLO computation from the metrics pipeline | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-064 | Planned maintenance shall not be excluded from the T0 and T1 availability calculation. Excluding planned downtime from a life-safety number is how systems acquire scheduled blindness. | Enforced | Enforced | SLO definition excludes no windows for T0/T1 | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-065 | T3 may take declared maintenance windows (default Tuesday 02:00–04:00 IST), announced ≥72 hours ahead to affected tenants, and those minutes are excluded from T3's calculation only. | Window policy published | Same | Maintenance calendar | `AUDIT` |

#### 46.3.3 Error budgets

| Tier | MVP budget/month | Scale budget/month | Burn policy |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | 43 m | 21 m | At 25% burn in a week: written review at the next on-call handover. At 50%: no non-essential changes to T0 components until the cause is closed. At 100%: T0 change freeze except fixes; a formal review with the CTO; the tier's design (not just the bug) is re-examined. |
| T1 | 3 h 39 m | 43 m | At 50%: feature work on T1 pauses for reliability work until the budget recovers. At 100%: T1 change freeze except fixes and reliability work. |
| T2 | 3 h 39 m | 43 m | At 100%: release cadence reduced to one per week with mandatory soak, until the following month's budget is 50% intact at mid-month. |
| T3 | 7 h 18 m | 3 h 39 m | Tracked and reported; no automatic freeze — an async job being late is a degradation, not an outage, and treating it as one causes the team to stop believing the freeze policy. |
| T4 | 43 m | 21 m | Tracked; investigated but not freeze-inducing. |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-066 | Error budget consumption shall be visible on the engineering SLO dashboard (§48.12) and reported at every sprint review, whether or not anyone asks. | Visible and reported | Same | Dashboard + review agenda item | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-067 | The freeze consequences above shall be pre-agreed by management, so that the decision to freeze is arithmetic rather than a negotiation during an incident. | Agreed and documented | Same | Signed error-budget policy | `AUDIT` |

#### 46.3.4 Degradation behaviour — what happens when a dependency is down

This is the requirement that separates a system that survives a bad day from one that does not. **The default behaviour of a failing dependency must never be a blank screen or a lie.** Three principles govern every row below:

1. **Safety functions degrade last and degrade to a human**, never to nothing.
2. **Money never degrades to optimism.** A payment whose status we cannot confirm is `Pending`, never `Completed`.
3. **Staleness is always labelled.** A cached value shown as live is worse than an error, because the operator acts on it.

| Failing dependency | Immediate effect | Degraded behaviour | User-visible message | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postgres primary unreachable | All writes fail | Reads served from replica in explicit read-only mode; check-ins and SOS accepted into a durable write-ahead buffer (Redis stream + local device queue) and replayed on recovery; console shows read-only banner | "Saving is paused — we're restoring the service. Your check-in is stored and will be recorded." | Automatic failover, then buffered replay with idempotency keys (§33) |
| Postgres replica unreachable | Reports, analytics, historical map replay fail | Those queries fail over to the primary with a **reduced row cap** and a lower query timeout, so analytics cannot take the primary down; heavy exports are queued instead | "Historical reports are delayed." | Replica rebuild; queued exports drain |
| Redis unreachable | Cache, rate limits, GPS stream, pub/sub, locks affected | Cache misses fall through to the database (with a request-coalescing guard against stampede); rate limiting fails **open** for authenticated traffic and **closed** for unauthenticated; GPS ingest writes directly to a bounded local disk buffer on the API node, then to Postgres; WebSocket fan-out degrades to client polling at 30 s | Map shows "updating every 30s — reduced mode" | Redis restored; buffered pings replayed; polling reverts on the next heartbeat |
| Object storage unreachable | Uploads and document/photo reads fail | Uploads queued client-side (Guard App) or rejected with a clear retry (console); attendance **succeeds without the photo** and is flagged `photo_pending`; documents show a placeholder, never a broken image | "Photo will upload when the connection allows. Your check-in is recorded." | Queue drains; `photo_pending` reconciles; unresolved after 72 h → supervisor task |
| FCM / APNs degraded | Push not delivered | Notification router fails over per §36.4.4 to SMS for P0/P1 and to in-app only for P2/P3; SOS also triggers the voice rung immediately rather than after the push timeout | Operator console shows "push degraded — voice escalation active" | Circuit breaker half-opens; routing restored |
| SMS provider down | SMS notifications and SMS-SOS fallback fail | Secondary SMS provider takes over (§36 requires ≥2); if both are down, P0 escalation moves to voice calls and the Command Center is told explicitly that the SMS SOS path is unavailable | Internal banner: "SMS SOS path DOWN — voice escalation only" | Provider health probe recovery |
| WhatsApp BSP down | WhatsApp messages fail | Fail over to SMS for transactional categories; marketing/digest categories are held, not re-routed (re-routing a digest to SMS costs money and irritates users) | Silent for the recipient; visible internally | Queue drains within TTL, else expires |
| Razorpay unavailable | Client payments fail | Payment intents are **not** created; the portal shows an explicit "payments temporarily unavailable, your invoice is unchanged and no money has moved" state; invoices, dunning and reminders continue; no local "assume success" path exists ever | "Payments are temporarily unavailable. Nothing has been charged." | Reconciliation job pulls authoritative state on recovery (§35, §49.10) |
| Email (Zoho) down | Emails queued | Queue with TTL by category: transactional 24 h, digest 4 h, marketing dropped; invoice delivery falls back to in-portal availability plus WhatsApp/SMS notice that the invoice is ready | "Your invoice is ready in the portal." | Queue drains |
| Map tile / geocoding provider down | Map background and address lookup fail | Map renders a plain coordinate grid with site polygons and guard dots — the operational information survives without the basemap; reverse geocoding falls back to the geocode cache, then to raw coordinates | "Map imagery unavailable — positions still live." | Provider recovery; cache refills |
| AI model provider down or rate-limited | AI surfaces fail | Per §41.5.5 fail-safe: AI panels disappear rather than show stale or degraded answers; every AI-assisted flow retains its full manual path; no operational decision is blocked | "Assistant unavailable." | Circuit breaker; secondary model per §25 |
| OCR / KYC extraction provider down | Document auto-extraction stops | Documents upload and store normally; extraction is queued; verification queue shows "manual review required"; verification staff proceed manually (which is the fallback the whole verification design already assumes, A-361) | "Automatic reading unavailable — this document will be checked manually." | Queue drains |
| Identity provider (Google/Apple sign-in) down | Those login methods fail | Phone-OTP and email+password remain; the login screen hides rather than shows a broken button | "Sign in with your phone number." | Provider recovery |
| WebSocket gateway down | Live updates stop | All real-time consumers fall back to REST polling at their configured degraded interval (10 s for the Command Center alert queue, 30 s for maps, 60 s for dashboards); the alert **klaxon** for P0 is driven by the polling path too, so a gateway outage cannot silence SOS | "Reduced live mode." | Gateway restored; clients re-subscribe with a fresh snapshot (§34.2) |
| Entire platform unreachable | Everything | The §49.12 Command Center manual continuity protocol activates; the status page (hosted off-platform) is updated; SOS is received by direct phone line and SMS gateway | Status page + SMS to registered supervisors | §49 DR runbooks |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-068 | Every external dependency shall have a documented degraded mode, a circuit breaker with defined thresholds, and a user-visible message that states truth rather than a generic error. | 100% of dependencies in the table | Same | Dependency register with degraded-mode column | `AUDIT`, `CHAOS` |
| SUR-NFR-069 | Each degraded mode shall be exercised at least twice a year by deliberate fault injection in a production-like environment, and once a year in production during a declared window where safe. | 2 exercises/year | 4 exercises/year | Chaos exercise record | `CHAOS`, `DRILL` |
| SUR-NFR-070 | No degraded mode shall report success for a financial movement, a compliance status change, or an attendance record that was not durably stored. | Zero tolerance | Zero tolerance | Targeted test cases (§44) | `CI-GATE`, `CHAOS` |
| SUR-NFR-071 | A dependency failure shall never cascade into the SOS path; the SOS path shall have its own connection pool, its own rate-limit exemption (SUR-CMD-016) and its own provider credentials. | Isolated at MVP | Physically separated at Scale (§50.3) | Dependency graph review + chaos test with the main pool saturated | `CHAOS`, `AUDIT` |

### 46.4 Reliability

Availability is "is it up"; reliability is "did it do the right thing, exactly once, and not lose anything". For this product the second question matters more, because a lost check-in becomes an unpaid guard and a disputed invoice.

#### 46.4.1 Durability classes

| Class | Data | Acceptable loss | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| D0 — Absolute | Attendance events, SOS events, incidents, financial transactions, ledger entries, invoices, payroll runs, audit log, compliance decisions, documents | **Zero.** Not "very low" — zero. | Synchronous transactional write, offline-first client queue, idempotency keys, outbox, replicated storage with PITR |
| D1 — Near-absolute | Notifications, approvals, roster publications, verification outcomes | ≤0.01% (duplicates preferred over loss) | Durable queue with retry, DLQ, at-least-once delivery |
| D2 — Best effort | GPS pings, patrol route interpolation points, telemetry, analytics events, AI interaction transcripts | ≤0.1% for pings; ≤1% for telemetry | Redis Stream with bounded length; loss of an individual ping is acceptable because the trail is statistically redundant (§34.3.3) |
| D3 — Disposable | Cache entries, derived read models, session state, geocode cache, search index | 100% (rebuildable) | Rebuild from source; rebuild time is the requirement, not the data |

**The D0/D2 boundary is the most important architectural line in the platform** and it is the reason check-ins do not travel on the GPS ingest path (§34.3.3). Any change that moves a D0 item onto a D2 transport is a blocking review failure.

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-080 | Zero loss of D0 data under any single-component failure, including primary database failover, API node loss, AZ loss and client crash mid-write. | Zero in all chaos scenarios | Same | Fault injection with a seeded write stream and post-recovery reconciliation | `CHAOS`, quarterly |
| SUR-NFR-081 | Every D0 write path shall be idempotent under retry, keyed per §33.2, such that a client retrying an unacknowledged request produces exactly one record. | 100% of D0 endpoints | Same | Duplicate-submission test per endpoint | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-082 | GPS ping loss rate | ≤0.1% | ≤0.1% | Client-reported sent count vs server-accepted count, reconciled daily | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-083 | Offline event sync success within 24 hours of any connectivity | ≥99.9% of queued events | ≥99.9% | Sync reconciliation job comparing device queue receipts to server records | `PROM`, `FIELD` |
| SUR-NFR-084 | Mobile crash-free session rate (Guard App) | ≥99.5% sessions, ≥99.0% users | ≥99.7% / ≥99.3% | Crash reporting (§48.5) | `PROM`, release gate |
| SUR-NFR-085 | Console unhandled-error rate per 1,000 sessions | ≤5 | ≤3 | Error tracking | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-086 | Job success rate on first attempt, per queue | ≥99.0% | ≥99.5% | Worker metrics | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-087 | Dead-letter queue depth shall be zero at the start of each business day; any item in a DLQ shall have an owner within one business day. | Zero-at-start | Same | DLQ metric + alert OA-22 | `PROM` |

### 46.9 Maintainability

A platform of this size built by a small team fails through entropy long before it fails through load. These requirements exist to make the codebase survivable by an engineer who joins in year three.

#### 46.9.1 Code and documentation standards

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-140 | One language and one framework per tier, chosen once and recorded in an ADR; introducing a second requires an approved ADR stating the maintenance cost. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-550]` | ≤2 primary languages platform-wide | ≤3 | Repository language census | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-141 | Formatting and linting shall be automated and non-negotiable; style shall never be a review topic. | 100% enforced, blocking | Same | Formatter + linter in CI | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-142 | Module dependency direction shall be enforced mechanically: no module may import another module's internals, and no module may query another module's tables. | Zero violations | Zero | Architecture lint (dependency-cruiser class tool) | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-143 | Test coverage floors by criticality: money and ledger 90% line / 85% branch; authentication, authorisation and tenancy 90%/85%; safety path (SOS, attendance, wake check) 85%/80%; everything else 70%/60%. | Met and blocking | Same | Coverage report per module | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-144 | Coverage shall be treated as a floor and never as a goal; the authorisation matrix, tenant isolation and financial correctness suites are the real gates and are measured by scenario coverage, not line coverage. | Scenario suites defined (§44) | Same | Scenario coverage report | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-145 | Every architectural decision shall be recorded as a numbered ADR in the repository with context, options, decision and consequences; an undocumented architectural change is a review failure. | 100% of architectural changes | Same | ADR index vs change log | `AUDIT`, quarterly |
| SUR-NFR-146 | API documentation shall be generated from the source of truth (OpenAPI spec) and shall never be hand-maintained prose that can drift. | Generated, published | Same | Spec-to-implementation contract test | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-147 | Every alert shall link to a runbook, and every runbook shall be reachable when the platform is down (§49.2). | 100% coverage for P0/P1 | 100% for all | Alert-to-runbook link audit | `CI-GATE`, `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-148 | Cyclomatic complexity per function ≤15 and file length ≤600 lines, with an explicit, reviewed exemption list. | Enforced with warnings; blocking on new code | Blocking | Static analysis | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-149 | Build and test pipeline wall-clock time for a pull request | ≤15 min p95 | ≤20 min p95 | Pipeline duration metric | `PROM` |
| SUR-NFR-150 | Local development environment setup from a clean machine to a running stack with seed data | ≤30 min, one documented command | ≤30 min | Timed onboarding run each quarter | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-151 | New engineer time to first merged production change | ≤5 working days | ≤5 working days | Onboarding record | `AUDIT` |

#### 46.9.2 Technical-debt policy

Debt is not a moral failing; unmanaged debt is. The policy is deliberately simple enough that a five-person team will actually follow it.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Debt is registered, not remembered | Every knowing shortcut creates a `TECH-DEBT` item with: what was skipped, why, the risk if unaddressed, the estimated cost to fix, and an owner. A shortcut taken without an item is the only kind that is a review failure. |
| Debt has an expiry | Each item carries a review date, default one quarter. At review it is fixed, re-dated with a reason, or explicitly accepted permanently (which converts it from debt into a documented design choice). |
| Capacity is reserved, not begged for | 20% of each sprint's capacity is reserved for debt, reliability and tooling. It is spent from the top of the ranked debt register. If it is repeatedly borrowed for features, that is reported as a metric, not argued about. |
| Debt in D0 paths is not deferrable | Any debt item touching money, tenancy, authorisation, attendance or the SOS path is capped at one quarter with no re-dating. |
| Dependency freshness is debt | No production dependency more than two minor versions behind; no dependency more than one major version behind for more than two quarters; security patches per §38 SLA. |
| Dead code is deleted | Code behind a removed feature flag, an unreferenced endpoint, or an unused module is deleted within one release of becoming unused. Deleted code lives in git history, which is where it belongs. |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-152 | Technical-debt register shall exist, be ranked, and be reviewed monthly with the reserved-capacity spend reported. | Register live from month 1 | Same | Register + monthly review record | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-153 | Zero debt items older than two quarters without an explicit re-dating decision; zero D0-path items older than one quarter. | Enforced | Enforced | Register age report | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-154 | Dependency age report: no dependency more than one major version behind for >2 quarters. | ≤5 exceptions, each with an owner | ≤3 exceptions | Automated dependency report | `CI-GATE` (report), `AUDIT` (decision) |

### 46.13 Compatibility

#### 46.13.1 Browser matrix

| Browser | Supported versions | Rationale | Test depth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chrome (desktop + Android) | Last 2 stable major versions | The dominant browser on both desktop and Android in the Indian market `[ASSUMPTION: A-565]`; also the baseline for Android WebView behaviour | Full automated + manual |
| Edge (desktop) | Last 2 stable | Chromium-based; the default browser on managed Windows machines in agency and client offices | Full automated |
| Safari (macOS + iOS) | Last 2 major versions, and iOS Safari 16+ | The only engine available on iOS; client-side executives and Apple-using agency owners | Full automated + manual on the top 20 screens |
| Firefox (desktop) | Last 2 stable | Small share but disproportionately used by technically minded users and by some government office builds | Automated smoke + top 20 screens |
| Samsung Internet (Android) | Last 2 stable | Meaningful Android share in India `[ASSUMPTION: A-565]`; Chromium-based so risk is low but non-zero | Automated smoke |
| Android System WebView | 8.0+ (matches the Guard App minimum) | Any in-app web view (payments, help centre, document preview) must work here | Automated smoke on the reference device |
| **Not supported** | Internet Explorer (any), Chrome/Edge older than 2 majors, Opera Mini's extreme proxy mode | IE is end-of-life and supporting it would constrain the entire front-end toolchain. Opera Mini's proxy mode cannot run the console's JavaScript at all; the marketing site must still render usefully in it, the consoles need not. | Blocked with an explicit upgrade page, never a broken screen |

**The important honesty note.** The version shares above are assumptions taken from general market knowledge, not from our own data. `[ASSUMPTION: A-565]` The correct source of truth is our own analytics after 60 days of production traffic, at which point this matrix is revised. Building a browser matrix on a global statistic and never checking it against your own users is a standard and avoidable mistake.

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-190 | The console shall function on the supported matrix with no feature loss; an unsupported browser shall receive an explicit, branded upgrade page, never a broken layout. | 100% | Same | Cross-browser automated suite on the top 40 screens | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-191 | The browser matrix shall be revised from production analytics at day 60 and every six months after; a browser below 0.5% of sessions for two consecutive periods is dropped, and a browser above 2% is added. | Policy in force | Same | Analytics review | `AUDIT` |
| SUR-NFR-192 | The public marketing site shall render readable, navigable content with JavaScript disabled or failing, because a proportion of Indian mobile traffic runs through aggressive proxies. | Content and contact paths usable | Same | No-JS rendering test | `CI-GATE` |

| Platform | Minimum | Target | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android (Guard App) | **8.0 / API 26** | Latest stable | Matches §18's device baseline. Entry-level and second-hand handsets dominate the guard workforce, and a guard is not going to buy a phone to keep a job. API 26 is also the floor at which background execution limits, notification channels and the modern permission model exist — below it, the app's location and notification behaviour becomes unpredictable in ways we cannot support. `[ASSUMPTION: A-565]` |

| iOS (all apps) | **15.0** | Latest stable | iOS 15 runs on iPhone 6s and later, which covers effectively the whole Indian iPhone install base that is still in active use; iOS users here are clients and agency owners, not guards. |
| Android tablets | 9.0+, 8" and above | — | Supervisor and site-office use; layout targets 800×1280 and up |
| iPadOS | 15+ | — | Client and management use |

#### 46.13.4 Backward compatibility windows

This is where a system with offline clients differs fundamentally from a pure web product, and the requirement is stated precisely because getting it wrong strands guards.

| Interface | Support window | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Public REST API (`/v1`) | A major version is supported for **24 months** after its successor ships, with a published sunset date and 12 months' notice | Enterprise integrators (§33) plan on quarterly cycles; 24 months is one planning cycle plus slack |
| Guard App → server | The server shall accept payloads from any Guard App version released within the **last 12 months** `[RECOMMENDED]` | A guard's device may be offline for days, may have auto-update disabled to save data, and may be on a handset the store no longer serves the latest build to. Twelve months covers all three without becoming an unbounded compatibility tax. |
| Guard App offline payload schema | Additive-only changes for 12 months; a field may be added, never removed or repurposed, within the window | An offline queue written by an old app must be parseable by the current server, always |
| Other mobile apps → server | 6 months | These users are connected and update normally |
| Desktop app → server | 12 months, with the security version floor of §20.30 overriding | Office machines update less often; the auto-updater makes 12 months generous |
| Webhook event schema (§33) | Additive-only within a major version; consumers must tolerate unknown fields | Standard practice, stated so integrators can rely on it |

| ID | Requirement | MVP target | Scale target | Measurement method | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUR-NFR-198 | The server shall accept and correctly process check-in, SOS, patrol scan and incident payloads from every Guard App version within the compatibility window, verified by a replay corpus of recorded payloads from each released version. | 100% of in-window versions | Same | Version-replay contract test | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-199 | The compatibility window shall be enforced by a stored artefact of each released app version's payload schema; deleting an in-window schema shall fail the build. | Enforced | Same | Schema artefact registry | `CI-GATE` |
| SUR-NFR-200 | API deprecation shall be announced in-product, by email to registered integrators, and via a `Deprecation` and `Sunset` response header from the announcement date. | Enforced | Same | Header presence test + comms record | `CI-GATE`, `AUDIT` |
