## 47. DevOps

### 47.0 Scope

This section covers how SURAKSHA is built, tested, released, configured and operated: environments, infrastructure as code, cloud and region, the CI/CD pipeline with the §38 security gates wired in, branching and release, database migrations, feature flags, secrets, configuration, change management, rollback, the mobile and desktop release pipelines, cost, and the on-call model.

It does not restate security controls (§38 owns them, referenced by control ID), observability design (§48), or DR mechanics (§49). Normative IDs use `SUR-DVO-nnn`.

---

### 47.1 The team-topology assumption — and what a small founding team can actually operate

Every architectural and operational decision in this document is downstream of one number: how many engineers exist. Writing a DevOps section that assumes a platform team is the fastest way to produce a plan that is never executed.

#### 47.1.1 The assumed team

`[ASSUMPTION: A-566]` The engineering organisation at MVP is:

| Role | MVP headcount | Scale (S3) headcount | Owns |
|---|---|---|---|
| CTO / co-founder | 1 | 1 | Architecture, security accountability, final release approval, AI governance chair (§41.10) |
| Backend engineers | 2–3 | 8–10 | API, workers, data, integrations |
| Mobile engineers | 1–2 | 4–5 | Guard App (primary), other three apps |
| Frontend engineers | 1–2 | 4–6 | Consoles, marketing site, design system implementation |
| QA engineer | 0–1 (shared) | 3 | Test automation, device lab, release verification |
| Dedicated SRE / platform engineer | **0** | 2–3 | — at MVP this work is spread across the backend engineers and the CTO |
| Dedicated security engineer | **0** | 1–2 | — at MVP, security is an accountability of the CTO with an external assessor (§38) |
| Data engineer | 0 | 1–2 | — |

**Total at MVP: 5–8 engineers.** That number is the constraint that produces every "no" in the next subsection.

#### 47.1.2 What that team can and cannot operate

| Can operate | Why | Cannot operate at MVP | Why not, and the alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Managed Postgres with automated backups and failover | One control plane, provider handles patching and failover | Self-managed Postgres with hand-built HA | Patroni/repmgr is a full-time job; managed costs ~1.6× and buys back an engineer |
| Managed Redis | Same | Self-managed Redis Sentinel/Cluster | Failover semantics under partition need dedicated expertise |
| Managed container runtime (ECS/Cloud Run/App Runner class) with a small task count | Deploys are a pipeline step, not an operational discipline | **Kubernetes** | K8s is an excellent platform and a full-time operational commitment. At 2–4 API instances it adds a control plane, an upgrade treadmill, a networking model, an RBAC model and a new class of 3 a.m. failure — for zero benefit at this size. Revisit at the §50.3 extraction triggers, not before. |
| Redis Streams as the queue (§34.3.3) | Already deployed, consumer groups, replay | **Kafka / self-managed broker** | Explicitly rejected in §34.7.3; a broker is an on-call surface without a problem to solve |
| Terraform/OpenTofu with a remote state backend and a review-gated apply | Declarative, reviewable, small blast radius | A bespoke internal platform, service mesh, GitOps operators | Each is a product to maintain |
| Managed or single-node observability backend in-region | One thing to run, or none | Self-hosted Elasticsearch cluster, self-hosted SIEM | Elasticsearch operations is a specialty; §38's detection needs are met with a managed or lightweight in-region stack |
| One CI provider with hosted runners | No runner fleet to maintain | Self-hosted runner fleet | Only justified when CI cost or residency demands it; then a small, ephemeral, auto-scaled pool |
| A 3-person on-call rotation with a documented escalation path | The minimum viable rotation | A true 24/7 follow-the-sun engineering rota | Requires 6+ engineers per tier; §47.16 states the mitigations honestly |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-001 | Operational choices shall be justified against the team size that exists, not the team size that is planned. Any technology that requires a dedicated operator shall be adopted only when that operator is hired, or shall be consumed as a managed service. |
| SUR-DVO-002 | Every managed service adopted shall have a documented exit path (data export format, equivalent alternative, estimated migration effort) recorded in the service catalogue, so that "managed" does not silently become "captive". |

### 47.2 Environment topology

#### 47.2.1 The environments

| Environment | Purpose | Data | Who has access | Deploy trigger | Availability expectation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Local** | Individual development | Generated seed data only | The engineer | Manual | None |
| **CI (ephemeral)** | Per-pull-request verification | Generated seed data, torn down after the run | Pipeline only | Every push | None |
| **Preview (ephemeral)** | Per-pull-request reviewable deployment for UI/UX and product review | Generated seed data | Team + design, via identity-aware proxy | Every PR labelled `preview` | Best effort |
| **Staging** | Production-shaped integration environment; DAST target (SUR-SEC-150); load-test target | Masked or synthetic only — **never production data** (SUR-SEC-100) | Engineering + QA + product | Automatic on merge to `main` | Business hours |
| **UAT** | Acceptance by internal ops, pilot agencies and pilot clients; training environment | Synthetic tenant data plus an opt-in agency sandbox tenant containing only that agency's own deliberately entered test data | Engineering, product, ops, named external UAT users | Promoted from staging on a release candidate | Business hours, announced |
| **Production** | Live service | Real | Nobody interactively (SUR-SEC-138); automation and purpose-built admin operations only | Approved promotion (§47.11) | Per §46.3 tiers |
| **Restore-test (ephemeral)** | Automated nightly and drill restores from backup (§49.5) | Restored production backup, in an isolated account, never network-reachable from anywhere else, destroyed after verification | Pipeline; humans only during a declared drill with dual approval | Nightly + on drill | N/A |
| **DR (warm, Scale only)** | Standby in the second Indian region | Replicated production | Same rules as production | Continuous replication | Per §49.7 |

#### 47.2.2 Data rules per environment

The single rule that matters: **production personal data exists in exactly two places — production and the isolated restore-test environment.** Nowhere else, ever, including an engineer's laptop, a debugging spreadsheet, or a support screenshot.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Seed data generator | A first-class, versioned tool that produces a realistic tenant: agencies, branches, 200 guards with documents, 30 sites with geofences, 90 days of attendance, patrols, incidents, invoices and payroll. It is realistic in *shape* and *volume distribution*, and entirely synthetic in *content*. It is also the source of the volumetric fixtures the CI `EXPLAIN` gate uses (§32.4). |
| Masking pipeline | If a production-shaped dataset is ever needed in staging (for a performance investigation), it is produced by the masking pipeline of SUR-SEC-100: irreversible pseudonymisation of names, phones, emails, addresses, document numbers and bank details; coordinates jittered and re-anchored to synthetic sites; photos and documents replaced by fixtures. The masked dataset carries an expiry and is destroyed automatically. |
| Restore-test isolation | The restore-test environment has no ingress, no egress except to the backup store, no user accounts, and a maximum lifetime of 6 hours. Its purpose is verification (§49.9), not investigation. |
| UAT sandbox tenants | An external UAT participant sees only their own sandbox tenant, seeded synthetically. They may enter their own data, which is treated as production-class personal data if it contains real people, and is deleted at the end of UAT with a record. |
| No production credentials downward | Production and non-production are separate cloud accounts with separate identity boundaries (SUR-SEC-141); a credential valid in one is invalid in the other. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-003 | Four permanent environments (staging, UAT, production, plus ephemeral CI/preview) shall exist from month one; a fifth (DR warm standby) is added at the §49.7 trigger. |
| SUR-DVO-004 | Production personal data shall never exist in staging, UAT, preview, local or CI. Enforcement is by account separation, by the absence of any pipeline path from production data stores to lower environments, and by a quarterly audit. |
| SUR-DVO-005 | The seed data generator shall be maintained as product code, reviewed, and shall produce a dataset sufficient for the CI performance suite's volumetric assertions. |
| SUR-DVO-006 | Every environment shall be reproducible from IaC plus the seed generator within 4 hours by a single engineer, verified annually by rebuilding staging from scratch. |

### 47.3 Cloud provider, region and residency

#### 47.3.1 The residency stance

`[RECOMMENDED]` **Primary and all secondary storage and processing of personal data in an Indian region.** This restates SUR-PRV-090/091 as an infrastructure decision, and it constrains every choice below: the primary region, the DR region, the backup replica target, the observability backend, the error-tracking backend, the CI artefact store where artefacts could contain data, and the support tooling.

The reasoning is four-fold and none of it is a legal conclusion:
1. The platform holds data about Indian workers, Indian sites and Indian clients; the configured residency policy of the compliance engine (§40) can require in-country storage, and building elsewhere would make that configuration unimplementable.
2. Enterprise and government buyers in this sector ask the residency question in procurement, and "our data is in Singapore" costs deals in a security business.
3. Latency: an Indian region gives 20–110 ms RTT to users nationwide (B-7/B-8); a Singapore region adds 30–60 ms to every request for no benefit.
4. It removes an entire category of contractual and review work.

The cost of this stance is real and should be stated: Indian regions have a narrower managed-service catalogue than us-east-1, some services arrive late, and a few observability and security SaaS products have no Indian region at all — which is precisely why §48.1 recommends what it does. `[ASSUMPTION: A-330]` (raised in §38) covers the availability of the required managed services in-region and must be validated at architecture selection.

#### 47.3.2 Provider selection

| Provider / region pair | Strengths for this workload | Weaknesses | Cost posture | Lock-in exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AWS — ap-south-1 (Mumbai) primary, ap-south-2 (Hyderabad) DR** `[RECOMMENDED]` | Two Indian regions, so DR does not break residency. Deepest managed catalogue in-region (RDS/Aurora Postgres with PITR, ElastiCache, S3 with Object Lock, KMS with customer-managed keys, Session Manager satisfying the no-SSH stance SUR-SEC-138). Largest Indian hiring pool and partner ecosystem. | Most expensive on list price; egress pricing punishes careless architecture; the managed catalogue invites proprietary coupling | Highest list price, best discount instruments (Savings Plans, RIs) at 1–3 year commitment | Moderate — controllable by staying on Postgres/Redis/S3-API/containers |
| **Azure — Central India (Pune) primary, South India (Chennai) DR** | Two Indian regions; strong with enterprise and government buyers who already hold Microsoft agreements; good identity story | Postgres flexible-server feature parity historically trails RDS; some services India-late | Comparable to AWS, often better via existing enterprise agreements | Moderate |
| **GCP — asia-south1 (Mumbai) primary, asia-south2 (Delhi) DR** | Two Indian regions; strong networking and data tooling; Cloud Run is an excellent fit for a small team's container workload | Smaller Indian partner ecosystem; managed Postgres HA semantics differ | Often cheapest for compute at small scale | Moderate; higher if BigQuery/Spanner adopted |
| **Indian providers (E2E, CtrlS, Yotta, Jio Cloud)** | Unambiguous residency story that resonates in government procurement; materially cheaper raw compute; local support in Indian time zones | Thinner managed-service catalogue — which pushes work back onto the 5-person team the whole design is trying to protect; smaller ecosystem; fewer engineers with experience | Cheapest raw; total cost can be *higher* once self-managed database, backup and observability labour is counted | Low technical lock-in, higher operational cost |
| **Hybrid: hyperscaler for the platform, Indian provider for the DR backup copy** | Residency belt-and-braces; a second-vendor copy that survives a provider account compromise (§49.8 S6) | Two vendor relationships, two access models | Small incremental cost for object storage only | Low |

**Recommendation.** `[RECOMMENDED]` AWS ap-south-1 as primary, ap-south-2 for backup replication from day one and warm standby at the §49.7 trigger, with an immutable backup copy in a *separate cloud account* and — from Scale onward — a third copy with an independent Indian provider purely as object storage. Rationale: two in-country regions, the managed catalogue that lets 5 engineers run this, and the specific services §38 depends on (Object Lock for immutable backups, KMS with customer-managed keys and separate backup keys per SUR-SEC-102, and Session Manager so that SUR-SEC-138's no-SSH stance is implementable rather than aspirational).

**The lock-in mitigation is a design rule, not a hope:**

| Rule | What it means |
|---|---|
| Portable primitives only | Postgres (not Aurora-only features), Redis (not provider-specific data types), S3-compatible object storage, OCI containers, standard SMTP. If a feature exists only on one provider, it is used only where the alternative is materially worse and the coupling is recorded in an ADR. |
| No provider-specific code in domain modules | Cloud SDK usage is confined to adapter modules (storage, secrets, queue, mail, KMS). A provider migration touches the adapters, not the business logic. |
| IaC is portable in structure | Terraform/OpenTofu with provider-specific modules isolated behind a consistent module interface. |
| Data export is tested | The annual DR drill includes restoring the database and object storage into a *different* account, which is 80% of the work of restoring into a different provider. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-010 | All production and non-production infrastructure, backups, logs, metrics, traces, error reports and support tooling shall reside in Indian regions unless an explicit, recorded exception with a compensating control exists. |
| SUR-DVO-011 | The primary region shall be multi-AZ for the database, cache, and application tier from day one; single-AZ deployment of a stateful production component is prohibited. |
| SUR-DVO-012 | Cloud-provider-specific APIs shall be accessed only through adapter modules; a domain module importing a cloud SDK is a blocking review failure. |
| SUR-DVO-013 | An annual exit-readiness exercise shall restore the platform's data into a second account and record the elapsed time and the gaps found. |

### 47.4 Infrastructure as code

#### 47.4.1 Tooling

`[RECOMMENDED]` **Terraform (or OpenTofu) for infrastructure; the application's own migration tooling for schema; no configuration-management agent (no Ansible/Chef/Puppet) because there are no long-lived servers to configure — compute is immutable containers.**

| Option | Why / why not |
|---|---|
| **Terraform / OpenTofu** `[RECOMMENDED]` | Declarative, provider-agnostic in structure, the largest ecosystem and the largest hiring pool in India, mature policy-as-code integrations (Checkov, tfsec, Conftest/OPA). OpenTofu is the licence-safe fork; either is acceptable and the choice is recorded in an ADR. Weakness: state management is a genuine operational concern and drift is real — both addressed below. |
| Pulumi | Real programming languages, which is pleasant and also lets complexity in through the front door. Smaller Indian hiring pool. |
| Provider-native (CloudFormation / ARM / Deployment Manager) | Deepest provider integration, zero portability, and it makes the exit path in SUR-DVO-002 harder. |
| CDK | Good ergonomics, provider-coupled, and the generated artefacts are harder to review than HCL for a small team. |
| Click-ops | Rejected. Manual console changes are detected as drift within 24 hours and reverted (SUR-SEC-142). |

#### 47.4.2 Structure and practice

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Repository layout | Infrastructure lives in the monorepo under `/infra`, with `modules/` (reusable: network, database, cache, service, bucket, queue, observability) and `envs/{staging,uat,prod,dr}/` composing them. Environments differ by variables, never by copied module code. |
| State | Remote state in an encrypted, versioned, object-locked bucket with state locking; separate state file per environment; state is treated as sensitive (it can contain resource metadata) and is never in the application repository's artefacts. |
| Secrets | Never in variables files or state. Resources that need a secret reference the secret store by ARN/name; the value is injected at runtime (§47.9). A `terraform plan` output containing a secret value is a P1 incident. |
| Plan/apply flow | `plan` runs on every PR touching `/infra` and posts the diff for review; `apply` runs only from the protected branch, only through the pipeline, with a recorded human approval for production, using short-lived workload identity (SUR-SEC-152). |
| Policy as code | Checkov/tfsec plus custom OPA policies enforce SUR-SEC-136 (no public data stores, no unrestricted ingress), encryption-at-rest on every resource that supports it, mandatory tags, and a deny-list of instance types and regions. A failing policy blocks the plan. |
| Drift detection | Scheduled `plan` against production every 6 hours; any diff raises alert OA-08 and must be codified or reverted within 24 hours (SUR-SEC-142). |
| Tagging | Every resource carries `env`, `service`, `owner`, `data_classification`, `cost_center`, `tier` (the §46.3.1 availability tier). Untagged resources are reported weekly (SUR-SEC-137) and blocked at plan time for new resources. |

#### 47.4.3 What is deliberately not in IaC

| Not in IaC | Why | Compensating control |
|---|---|---|
| Domain registrar account and DNS registrar-level settings | The registrar is outside the cloud provider and is a small, rarely changed surface | Hardware-key MFA, registrar lock, two named owners, a documented change procedure, and quarterly verification of the records against a stored expected set |
| Apple Developer, Google Play and Microsoft signing accounts | Not cloud resources | Documented custody (§47.13), MFA, named owners, and an offboarding checklist |
| Payment gateway, SMS, WhatsApp and email provider account settings | Vendor consoles with no usable API for configuration | Change log kept manually with a screenshot record; settings verified quarterly against a documented baseline; API credentials themselves are in the secret store |
| The status page | Deliberately hosted off the primary infrastructure (§49.13) so it survives a total outage | Documented configuration, second owner, tested during DR drills |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-020 | 100% of cloud infrastructure shall be defined in IaC; a resource created outside IaC shall be detected within 24 hours and either codified or destroyed. |
| SUR-DVO-021 | Policy-as-code checks shall block a plan that creates a publicly accessible data store, an unencrypted store, an unrestricted ingress rule, or an untagged resource. |
| SUR-DVO-022 | The out-of-IaC surface shall be enumerated (as above), reviewed quarterly, and shall not grow without an approved exception. |

### 47.5 Source control, branching and release strategy

#### 47.5.1 Repository strategy

`[RECOMMENDED]` **A monorepo** containing API, workers, web consoles, marketing site, the four mobile apps, the desktop shell, the shared design system, shared types/contracts, infrastructure and documentation.

| Consideration | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Why | One design system consumed by ten surfaces (SUR-UIX-001); one API contract consumed by six clients; one atomic commit can change an endpoint and every caller, which is the single largest productivity gain available to a 6-person team spanning web, mobile and backend. One CI configuration, one dependency policy, one security gate set. |
| Alternatives | Polyrepo gives independent release cadence and smaller checkouts, at the cost of cross-repo version coordination — which, at this team size, means a permanent, low-grade tax of "which version of the shared package is this app on". Rejected for now. |
| Trade-offs | CI must be change-aware or build times balloon (mitigated with a task graph tool and remote caching); repository size grows (mitigated by keeping binary assets out of git); access control is coarser (mitigated by CODEOWNERS on sensitive paths). |
| Reversibility | Splitting a monorepo later is straightforward with history preservation; merging polyrepos later is not. This asymmetry is the deciding argument. |

#### 47.5.2 Branching

`[RECOMMENDED]` **Trunk-based development.** One long-lived branch (`main`), short-lived feature branches (target ≤2 days, hard limit 5), squash-merge, no release branches except a temporary hotfix branch cut from a released tag.

| Why not GitFlow | GitFlow's `develop`/`release`/`hotfix` topology exists to coordinate large teams shipping infrequent versioned releases. We are a small team shipping continuously to a service we operate. GitFlow would give us long-lived divergence, painful merges, and a false sense of stage-gating that the CI gates already provide better. |
| Why not long-lived feature branches | An offline-first mobile client and a modular monolith both punish long divergence: schema, contracts and the design system all move under a stale branch. Feature flags (§47.8) are the mechanism for incomplete work, not branches. |
| Mobile exception | Mobile release candidates are cut as a tag, not a branch, and hotfixes branch from that tag. This is the one place a release branch briefly exists, because a mobile binary in store review cannot absorb `main`'s subsequent commits. |

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Protected `main` | No direct pushes; PR required; ≥1 approval from a non-author; an additional approval from a designated security reviewer for paths listed in CODEOWNERS as sensitive (auth, authorisation, tenancy, payments, encryption, audit, AI tool surface) per SUR-SEC-151; no self-merge; linear history. |
| PR size guidance | Target ≤400 changed lines. Not a hard gate (a rename touches thousands of lines) but a reported metric, because review quality collapses above it. |
| Commit convention | Conventional Commits, enforced by a commit-lint gate, so that changelogs, release notes and the change record for §47.11 are generated rather than written. |
| CODEOWNERS | Maps every sensitive path to its required reviewer group; the file itself is a sensitive path. |
| Signed commits | Required for `main` at Scale; recommended at MVP `[RECOMMENDED]`. |

#### 47.5.3 Release strategy

| Artefact | Cadence | Versioning | Promotion |
|---|---|---|---|
| API + workers + consoles | Continuous to staging on merge; production promotion in a **daily release window** (default 11:00 IST, a time when the team is present and shift change is not) plus on-demand for fixes | `YYYY.MM.DD.N` build version; the *public API* is versioned separately and independently as `/v1` | Digest promotion of the exact staging artefact |
| Marketing site | Continuous; content changes deploy independently of application code | Same build version | Same |
| Mobile apps | Release train every 2 weeks; hotfixes out of band | SemVer `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` + monotonic build number | §47.13 |
| Desktop app | Release train every 4 weeks, aligned to the web release it embeds | SemVer | §47.14 |
| Database migrations | With the release that needs them, expand phase only; contract phase in a later release | Sequential, timestamped | §47.7 |

**Why a daily window rather than deploy-on-merge.** With no dedicated SRE, an unattended 19:00 deploy is a deploy nobody is watching. A predictable window means the engineer who wrote the change is present for the 30 minutes after it ships. As the team grows and automated verification matures, the window widens toward continuous deployment; the trigger is 30 consecutive releases with no rollback and full post-deploy automated verification.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-030 | Trunk-based development with protected `main`, mandatory non-author review, and CODEOWNERS-enforced security review on sensitive paths. |
| SUR-DVO-031 | Feature branches shall not exceed 5 days of divergence; incomplete work ships behind a flag. |
| SUR-DVO-032 | Every production release shall be traceable from the running artefact digest to the commit, the PR, the reviewers and the approver (SUR-SEC-153/154). |
| SUR-DVO-033 | Release notes shall be generated from commits and shall be published internally for every release and externally for API-affecting changes. |

### 47.6 The CI/CD pipeline

#### 47.6.1 Pipeline stages

The security gates from §38.10.3 are wired in as blocking stages, not as a separate "security scan" job that everyone learns to ignore.

| # | Stage | What runs | Blocking | Time budget | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pre-commit (local) | Format, lint, type-check, commit-lint, secret scan on staged files | Yes (local hook) | <10 s | Commit refused |
| 2 | Fast checks | Format, lint, type-check, dependency-direction lint (SUR-NFR-142), commit convention | Yes | <2 min | PR blocked |
| 3 | Unit tests | Per-module unit tests with coverage floors (SUR-NFR-143) | Yes | <5 min | PR blocked |
| 4 | Security static gates | **SAST**, **secret scanning** (full history on first run, diff after), **SCA/dependency scan**, **licence policy check** — SUR-SEC-149 | Yes | <5 min | PR blocked; Critical/High with a fix available cannot be waived without the §38.13.4 exception process |
| 5 | Integration tests | API + database + Redis + object storage (containerised), including the outbox, queue and job paths | Yes | <8 min | PR blocked |
| 6 | **Authorisation matrix suite** | Every endpoint × every role, asserting allow/deny — SUR-SEC-051 | Yes | <4 min | PR blocked |
| 7 | **Tenant isolation suite** | Cross-tenant read/write attempts on every tenant-owned entity — SUR-SEC-133 | Yes | <3 min | PR blocked. This suite has no waiver path. |
| 8 | Financial correctness suite | Ledger balance invariants, idempotency, rounding, GST arithmetic, payroll edge cases | Yes | <3 min | PR blocked |
| 9 | Migration checks | Migration lint (no unsafe lock patterns, §47.7), forward-apply on a seeded database, N-1 compatibility check (previous release's code against the new schema) | Yes | <4 min | PR blocked |
| 10 | Performance suite | `EXPLAIN` assertions on the 25 governed queries against volumetric seed data (§32.4); no sequential scan over 100k rows; p95 regression comparison vs the previous release (SUR-NFR-035) | Yes | <5 min | PR blocked |
| 11 | Accessibility | axe-core over the screen inventory; contrast token audit; 200% text-scale screenshot diff | Yes | <4 min | PR blocked on serious/critical |
| 12 | Localization | Protected-string completeness (SUR-FRQ-156), missing-key detection, pseudo-loc layout diff | Yes | <2 min | PR blocked on protected-set gaps |
| 13 | Bundle & size budgets | JS bundle budget (SUR-NFR-044), mobile artefact size (SUR-NFR-038), font payload | Yes | <2 min | PR blocked |
| 14 | Build & sign artefacts | Container image build, non-root/read-only rootfs verification (SUR-SEC-144), image vulnerability scan (SUR-SEC-145), SBOM generation, image signing (SUR-SEC-147) | Yes | <6 min | PR blocked |
| 15 | IaC checks | `terraform plan`, policy-as-code (Checkov/OPA), plan diff posted to the PR | Yes for `/infra` changes | <3 min | PR blocked |
| 16 | Preview deploy | Ephemeral environment for review | No | — | Reported |
| 17 | **Merge to `main`** | — | — | — | — |
| 18 | Deploy to staging | Digest deploy, schema migration expand phase, smoke suite, synthetic probes re-pointed | Yes | <8 min | Auto-rollback of staging; `main` marked unhealthy |
| 19 | Nightly on staging | **DAST** across authenticated flows for one role per role group (SUR-SEC-150); full E2E suite; load test (weekly); device-lab matrix run | Yes for release eligibility | Overnight | Release candidate not promotable |
| 20 | Release candidate | Tag, generate release notes, produce the change record | — | <1 min | — |
| 21 | Production approval | Recorded human approval (SUR-SEC-153); freeze check; error-budget check (§46.3.3) | Yes | Human | Promotion blocked |
| 22 | Deploy to production | Rolling deploy by digest with health gates; migrations already applied in the expand phase; connection draining for the real-time gateway (60 s, §34.2) | Yes | <10 min | Automatic rollback on health-gate failure |
| 23 | Post-deploy verification | Smoke suite against production, synthetic SOS probe forced run, error-rate and latency comparison over 15 minutes | Yes | 15 min | Automatic rollback if thresholds breached |

**Total PR feedback time budget: ≤15 minutes p95** (SUR-NFR-149), achieved by running stages 2–15 in parallel where their dependencies allow and by aggressive remote caching keyed on the monorepo task graph.

#### 47.6.2 Deployment strategy

| Stage of growth | Strategy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| MVP (2–4 API instances) | **Rolling deploy with health gates and connection draining** | At 4 instances, blue/green doubles the fleet cost for a deploy that takes 6 minutes; rolling with a 25% surge and a health gate gives most of the benefit. The real-time gateway drains connections over 60 s with a spread `reconnect_after` hint so a deploy does not produce a reconnection thundering herd (§34.2). |
| When traffic justifies (≥12 instances or ≥1,000 req/s) | **Blue/green** for the API tier | Instant rollback by traffic switch; the cost of a doubled fleet for 15 minutes becomes proportionally trivial |
| Scale | **Canary** — 5% for 15 min, 25% for 15 min, 100%, with automated analysis of error rate, p95 latency, and three domain signals (check-in success, ping ingest lag, notification acceptance) | Canary requires enough traffic for statistical significance. At MVP volume a 5% canary sees too few requests per minute for its metrics to mean anything, which is why it is not the day-one choice. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-040 | Every gate listed as blocking in §47.6.1 shall be blocking in fact; a bypass shall require a named approver, shall be recorded, and shall generate a retro-review ticket within one business day. |
| SUR-DVO-041 | The tenant isolation suite and the financial correctness suite shall have no bypass path of any kind. |
| SUR-DVO-042 | The artefact deployed to production shall be the exact artefact verified in staging, identified by digest (SUR-SEC-154); rebuilding for production is prohibited. |
| SUR-DVO-043 | Post-deploy verification shall run automatically and shall trigger automatic rollback on breach of its thresholds without requiring a human decision. |
| SUR-DVO-044 | Deployment of a T0 component shall never reduce the number of healthy instances below the level that sustains the §46.2.6 peak throughput. |

### 47.7 Database migration strategy

This is the highest-risk routine operation in the platform. A bad migration on a 440-million-row table takes the service down and cannot be undone by redeploying the previous container.

#### 47.7.1 The expand/contract discipline

Every schema change is decomposed into up to four separately released phases. **A single release never contains both an expand and a contract phase for the same object.**

| Phase | What happens | Release |
|---|---|---|
| **E — Expand** | Add the new structure. New nullable column, new table, new index (built `CONCURRENTLY`), new enum value. Nothing is removed; nothing becomes required. | Release N |
| **M — Migrate** | Application writes to both old and new; a resumable, throttled backfill job populates the new structure for historical rows; reads still come from the old. | Release N (dual write) + background job |
| **S — Switch** | Reads move to the new structure, behind a feature flag so the switch is reversible in seconds without a deploy. Shadow-read comparison runs first, reporting any divergence. | Release N+1 |
| **C — Contract** | Old structure dropped, dual write removed. Only after a soak period. | Release N+2 or later |

**Worked example — renaming `attendance.check_in_ts` to `attendance.checked_in_at` on a 40-million-row table:**

1. **E (release N):** `ALTER TABLE attendance ADD COLUMN checked_in_at timestamptz;` — instantaneous, no rewrite, no lock beyond a moment's `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` acquired with `lock_timeout = 3s`.
2. **M (release N):** the write path sets both columns in the same transaction. A backfill job runs in batches of 5,000 rows ordered by primary key, with a 50 ms pause between batches, resumable from a checkpoint table, throttled automatically if replication lag exceeds 5 s or primary CPU exceeds 60%. 40 M rows at 5,000 per 100 ms ≈ 13 minutes of actual work spread over hours by the throttle.
3. **S (release N+1):** a shadow-read job compares the two columns for 24 hours and reports mismatches (expected: zero). Then the flag `attendance.read_checked_in_at` flips; reads use the new column. If anything is wrong, flip back in under 60 seconds.
4. **C (release N+3, ≥7 days later):** stop dual-writing, then in a subsequent release `ALTER TABLE attendance DROP COLUMN check_in_ts;`.

The entire sequence spans three to four weeks. That is the point: **schema changes are slow on purpose, because the alternative is fast and occasionally catastrophic.**

#### 47.7.2 Migration safety rules

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Session guards | Every migration session sets `lock_timeout = 3s` and `statement_timeout = 30s`. A migration that cannot acquire its lock fails fast and is retried in a quieter window rather than queueing behind a long query and blocking every subsequent request — the classic mechanism by which one `ALTER TABLE` takes down a service. |
| Index creation | Always `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, outside a transaction, with a post-check for an `INVALID` index left behind by a failed run. |
| NOT NULL | Never added directly. Add `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, backfill, `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` (which takes only a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock), then optionally convert. |
| Column type changes | Treated as a new column plus expand/contract, never as `ALTER TYPE` on a large table. |
| Defaults | Adding a column with a default is safe on modern Postgres, but adding a *volatile* default is not; volatile defaults are backfilled. |
| Enum changes | Additive only; removing an enum value requires expand/contract via a new type. |
| Partitioned tables | Migrations must be partition-aware; DDL is applied to the parent and verified on a sample of partitions; the `location` table's daily partitions mean a naive full-table DDL touches hundreds of objects (§32.4). |
| Foreign keys | Added `NOT VALID` then validated separately. |
| Backfills | Are jobs, not migrations: resumable, idempotent, checkpointed, throttled on replication lag and primary CPU, observable (progress metric, ETA), and cancellable. A backfill inside a migration transaction is prohibited. |
| N-1 compatibility | The previous release's code must run correctly against the new schema, verified in CI (stage 9). This is what makes a rolling deploy and a code rollback safe. |
| Review | Every migration requires a second reviewer; migrations touching money, tenancy or the `location`/`attendance` tables require the security/data reviewer. |
| Dry run | Every migration is applied to a restored copy of a recent production backup, timed, and its lock behaviour recorded, before it is approved for production. This is the single most valuable step in the list and it is cheap once the restore-test environment exists (§49.5). |

#### 47.7.3 The destructive-migration rollback problem

**State it plainly: you cannot roll back a `DROP`.** A deploy rollback restores code; it does not restore a dropped column, a truncated table or a deleted row. This asymmetry is the reason for the phase discipline above, and it deserves its own explicit policy.

| Policy | Detail |
|---|---|
| Separation | A destructive change (drop column, drop table, drop index that a query still needs, delete data) is **never** in the same release as the code change that stops using the object. |
| Soak requirement | A contract phase requires ≥7 calendar days since the switch phase, and at least one completed full backup cycle after the switch, so a restore point exists that contains both the old structure and post-switch data. |
| Proof of disuse | Before a contract phase, a query-log analysis and a shadow-read metric must show zero reads of the object for the full soak period. "I searched the codebase" is not proof; the database's own statistics are. |
| Dual approval | Contract-phase migrations require two approvals, one of which is the CTO or the designated data reviewer. |
| Rollback classification | **The rollback of a destructive migration is a disaster-recovery event, not a deployment rollback.** It means point-in-time restore of the affected tables into a side database and a reconciled merge — §49.8 scenario S4. It is scoped in hours, not minutes, and the change record must say so before approval, so the approver knows what they are approving. |
| Soft delete first | Canon §4 already forbids hard deletion of operational and financial records. Most "destructive" data changes are therefore status transitions, which are reversible. Genuine destruction is confined to schema objects and to retention-driven purges, which have their own dual-control process (§40.7.3, SUR-CMP-055). |
| Prohibited outright | `DROP TABLE` on any table containing D0 data (§46.4.1) without a retained, verified export in the archive store, and without a recorded 30-day waiting period. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-050 | All schema changes shall follow the expand/migrate/switch/contract discipline; a migration that both adds and removes structure for the same object in one release shall be rejected in review. |
| SUR-DVO-051 | Every migration shall be dry-run against a restored production-scale copy, with lock duration and wall-clock time recorded in the PR, before production approval. |
| SUR-DVO-052 | Migration sessions shall set `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout`; a migration without them shall fail the migration lint gate. |
| SUR-DVO-053 | Contract-phase migrations shall require a 7-day soak, documented proof of disuse from database statistics, dual approval, and a change record that explicitly states the rollback is a DR event. |
| SUR-DVO-054 | Backfills shall be resumable, idempotent, throttled on replication lag and primary CPU, and observable; a backfill shall never run inside a migration transaction. |
| SUR-DVO-055 | The previous release's application code shall be verified in CI to run correctly against the new schema (N-1 compatibility). |

### 47.8 Feature flags

#### 47.8.1 Flag taxonomy — and what is not a flag

| Type | Purpose | Lifetime | Who changes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Release toggle** | Ship incomplete work dark; enable per environment, then per tenant cohort, then everyone | ≤90 days, then removed | Engineering |
| **Operations toggle (kill switch)** | Disable a non-safety subsystem under load or during an incident; shed load in a defined order (§50.6) | Permanent, reviewed annually | On-call engineer, audited |
| **Experiment flag** | A/B or staged behaviour comparison | ≤60 days | Product, with analytics |
| **Migration switch** | The S phase of §47.7 | ≤30 days after the switch | Engineering |
| **Not a flag: entitlement** | Whether a tenant's plan includes a module (§1.4 Starter/Professional/Enterprise) | Permanent product structure | Belongs to the entitlement model (§31), evaluated server-side from the subscription — **never** a feature flag |
| **Not a flag: permission** | Whether this user may do this thing | Permanent | Belongs to the permission matrix (§31) |
| **Not a flag: tenant configuration** | Business settings, compliance rules, notification templates, thresholds | Permanent | Belongs to configuration data (§47.10, §40.1.5) |

Conflating these four is one of the most common ways a codebase becomes unreasonable: an entitlement expressed as a flag ends up with plan logic scattered through the code and no single answer to "what does Professional include".

#### 47.8.2 Where flags are forbidden

| Forbidden | Why |
|---|---|
| Any authorisation or tenant-isolation decision | A flag is a runtime toggle with a cache; an isolation boundary must be unconditional. A flag that can disable an isolation check is a vulnerability with a UI. |
| Financial correctness (rounding, ledger balancing, tax computation) | A flag here means two possible answers to "how much is owed", and both will exist in production data. |
| The SOS path's core function | **There is no flag that can disable SOS ingest, SOS alert creation, or SOS escalation.** Load shedding never reaches SOS (SUR-CMD-016). Flags may control SOS *enhancements* (client notification on SOS, audio streaming, AI summary) but never the path itself. |
| Audit logging | Audit must not be optional. |

#### 47.8.3 Lifecycle and hygiene

| Stage | Rule |
|---|---|
| Creation | A flag cannot be created without an owner, a type, a description, a default (always the safe/off value), and an expiry date. |
| Default | Off, everywhere, on creation. A flag whose default is "on" is not a release toggle; it is a kill switch and must be typed as one. |
| Targeting | Server-side evaluation only. Targeting axes: environment, tenant, branch, user, role, app version, and deterministic percentage bucketing (hash of a stable key, so a user's bucket does not flip between requests). |
| Evaluation performance | ≤1 ms p99, from an in-process cache refreshed every 30 s with a change-push for urgent flips; a flag service outage must fail to the last known value, then to the code default — never to an error. |
| Audit | Every flag change is an audit event with actor, before/after, reason and affected scope (§38.12). Kill-switch flips additionally raise a P2 notification to the engineering channel. |
| Expiry enforcement | A release toggle past its expiry fails the CI flag-hygiene gate. A weekly flag-debt report lists every flag by age, and any flag over 90 days requires an owner's decision: remove, convert to a kill switch with an annual review, or convert to configuration. |
| Removal | Removing a flag means removing both branches of the code, not just the condition. The PR that removes the flag also removes the dead branch, verified by coverage. |

#### 47.8.4 Build vs buy

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Self-hosted: a `feature_flag` table + Redis cache + a small admin UI** `[RECOMMENDED] for MVP` | Zero external dependency, zero data leaving the platform, sub-millisecond evaluation from an in-process cache, no per-seat cost, and roughly a week of engineering. The flag set at MVP is small (tens, not hundreds). Weakness: no built-in experimentation analytics, and we build the admin UI. |
| Unleash / Flagsmith (self-hosted open source) | More features, another service to run — which contradicts §47.1.2. Reasonable at Scale. |
| LaunchDarkly and similar SaaS | Excellent product, per-seat/per-MAU cost that becomes material, and flag evaluation context (which can include user and tenant identifiers) leaves the platform to a non-Indian region — which collides directly with §47.3.1. Would require careful context minimisation. |

`[DECISION REQUIRED: D-551]` — whether to adopt a managed flag platform at Scale, given the residency constraint on evaluation context.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-060 | Feature flags shall be typed, owned, defaulted-off, expiry-dated and audited; a flag without these attributes shall fail CI. |
| SUR-DVO-061 | Flags shall never gate authorisation, tenant isolation, financial correctness, audit logging, or the SOS path's core function. |
| SUR-DVO-062 | Flag evaluation shall be server-side, ≤1 ms p99, and shall degrade to the last known value then to the code default, never to an error. |
| SUR-DVO-063 | A weekly flag-debt report shall be produced; release toggles older than 90 days shall block the release until resolved. |
| SUR-DVO-064 | Entitlements, permissions and tenant configuration shall never be implemented as feature flags. |

### 47.9 Secrets management

§38.6 owns the control set (SUR-SEC-094 to 097). This subsection states only the operational practice.

| Aspect | Practice |
|---|---|
| Store | The cloud provider's managed secrets service, one namespace per environment, in separate accounts (SUR-SEC-141). Encryption keys in KMS with customer-managed keys; backup encryption keys are distinct from production data keys (SUR-SEC-102). |
| Injection | At container start, into memory, never into an image layer, never into an environment file on disk, never into IaC state. The application fails to start if a required secret is absent — fail fast, never fall back to a default credential. |
| Rotation | Automated where the provider supports it (database credentials, API keys with a rotation API). Manual rotation for third-party credentials without rotation APIs, on a documented calendar with an owner and a runbook. Rotation is exercised, not assumed: an annual rotation drill for each credential class. |
| Break-glass | A sealed emergency credential set exists for the case where the automated path is broken. It is stored under dual control (two custodians, neither of whom can use it alone), its use raises an immediate P0 security event, and it is rotated immediately after any use. |
| CI | The pipeline holds no long-lived production credentials (SUR-SEC-152); it assumes a short-lived workload identity per run. CI logs are scrubbed, and any secret that appears in a log is treated as compromised and rotated — not "removed from the log". |
| History scanning | Full-history secret scanning on first setup and diff scanning on every push; a detected secret triggers immediate rotation as an incident, before any discussion of whether it was "actually used". |
| Third-party consoles | Provider console credentials (Razorpay, FCM, SMS, WhatsApp, Zoho, app stores) are held in the secret store with named owners and MFA, and are covered by the joiner/leaver process (SUR-SEC-155). |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-070 | No secret shall exist in source control, IaC state, container images, CI logs, error reports or support tickets; detection triggers immediate rotation as a security incident. |
| SUR-DVO-071 | A secret rotation drill shall be performed annually for each credential class, with the elapsed time and any breakage recorded. |
| SUR-DVO-072 | Break-glass credentials shall be dual-custody, alarmed on use, and rotated immediately after use. |

---

### 47.10 Configuration management

Three layers, three lifecycles, three change processes. Confusing them is why systems end up requiring a deploy to change a reminder threshold.

| Layer | Contains | Changes via | Change speed | Audited as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Infrastructure configuration** | Instance sizes, scaling rules, network, buckets, queues, alarms | IaC + pipeline (§47.4) | Minutes to hours, reviewed | IaC commit + apply record |
| **Application configuration** | Feature flags, kill switches, provider endpoints, timeouts, rate-limit ceilings, sampling rates, log levels | Flag/config service, no deploy | Seconds | Audit event with actor and reason |
| **Business configuration** | Tenant settings, plan entitlements, compliance rules and lead times (§40.1.5), notification templates and routing (§36), rate cards, geofence tolerances, escalation ladders (§24.7), operational day boundary | Product UI, by authorised roles, with effective-dating and dry-run where consequential | Immediate or effective-dated | Domain audit log (§38.12), and for compliance rules the versioning of §40.1.4 |

**The governing rule:** if a non-engineer should be able to change it, it is business configuration and lives in the database with a UI, versioning and an audit trail. If changing it wrongly can break the service, it is application configuration with a flag-style audit and a rollback. If it defines the infrastructure, it is IaC. **Nothing operationally meaningful should require a code deploy to change** — that is the test of whether the boundary has been drawn correctly.

| Practice | Detail |
|---|---|
| Schema and validation | Every configuration layer has a schema. Application configuration is validated at boot; an invalid value prevents startup rather than producing undefined behaviour at 2 a.m. Business configuration is validated on save with the same rules the runtime uses. |
| Defaults | Every setting has a documented, safe default. A tenant that has configured nothing must still operate correctly. |
| Environment parity | Configuration *keys* are identical across environments; only values differ. A key that exists only in production is a bug. |
| Drift | Application configuration is compared against its declared expected state daily; unexplained divergence raises alert OA-09. |
| Secrets | Are never configuration. Configuration may reference a secret by name; it never contains a value. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-080 | Configuration shall be separated into infrastructure, application and business layers with distinct change processes, and the boundary shall be documented per setting. |
| SUR-DVO-081 | Application configuration shall be schema-validated at boot; an invalid configuration shall prevent startup. |
| SUR-DVO-082 | No business-meaningful threshold, template, rule or rate shall require a code deployment to change. |
| SUR-DVO-083 | Every configuration change at any layer shall be attributable to an actor with a timestamp and, for business configuration, a reason. |

---

### 47.11 Change management and deployment approval

#### 47.11.1 Change classes

| Class | Definition | Approval | Record |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Pre-approved, low-risk, automated and frequently repeated: routine application release with no migration and no T0 component change; dependency patch updates that pass all gates; scaling within pre-approved bounds | Pipeline gates + one code reviewer; no separate approval | Automatic from the pipeline |
| **Normal** | Anything with a schema migration, a T0 component change, a new external dependency, an infrastructure change, a provider configuration change, or a first-time deployment of a new component | Recorded approval from an authorised approver (CTO or a designated deputy) after reviewing the change record | Change record with risk, rollback plan, verification plan |
| **Major** | Contract-phase migrations, cutover of a data store, extraction of a service (§50.3), provider migration, tenant-cell moves, pricing/entitlement structural changes | Two approvals including the CTO; a scheduled window; a named rollback owner; a pre-agreed abort criterion | Full change record + post-implementation review |
| **Emergency** | Fixing a live P0/P1 | One approver, may be after the fact if the incident demands; retro-review within one business day (SUR-SEC-153) | Change record completed within 24 hours |

#### 47.11.2 Freeze windows

| Freeze | When | Scope | Exception |
|---|---|---|---|
| Payroll freeze | The tenant-configured payroll processing window (typically 1st–5th of the month) | Payroll, finance, ledger, invoicing modules | Emergency fixes only |
| Month-end billing freeze | Last 2 and first 3 days of the calendar month | Invoicing, GST, payments | Emergency fixes only |
| Shift-change freeze | Daily, 30 minutes either side of 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00 IST | T0 and T1 components | None — this is a hard rule; a deploy during shift change risks the check-in spike |
| Client-committed event freeze | Declared per contract (a large event deployment, an audit, a client go-live) | All | CTO approval |
| Festival/peak freeze | Declared in advance for periods with known operational load (major festivals with heavy event-security deployment) | T0/T1 | CTO approval |

#### 47.11.3 The lightweight change board

A five-person team does not need a change advisory board; it needs fifteen minutes a week. **A weekly 15-minute change review** covers: changes shipped last week and their outcomes, error-budget status per tier (§46.3.3), the change calendar for the coming week, freeze windows, and any Major change needing scheduling. It produces decisions, not minutes. As the team grows past ~15 engineers, this becomes a proper change process; it does not need to be one before then.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-090 | Every production change shall be classified, and its class shall determine its approval path; classification shall be automatic where derivable from the diff (migration present, T0 path touched, `/infra` touched). |
| SUR-DVO-091 | Freeze windows shall be enforced by the pipeline, not by memory; a deploy attempted during a freeze shall be blocked with the freeze's name and its exception path. |
| SUR-DVO-092 | Every Normal and Major change record shall contain a rollback plan and a verification plan before approval; "we would redeploy the previous version" is an acceptable rollback plan only where it is true. |
| SUR-DVO-093 | Emergency changes shall be retro-reviewed within one business day and shall be counted; a rising emergency-change rate is treated as a reliability signal, not as heroism. |

### 47.12 Rollback

#### 47.12.1 Decision criteria

The decision to roll back must be arithmetic, taken by whoever is on call, without needing to find a senior person. These are the pre-agreed triggers.

| Signal | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 5xx error rate on any T0/T1 endpoint | >2% for 3 minutes post-deploy | **Immediate automatic rollback** |
| p95 latency on a T0/T1 endpoint | >2× the pre-deploy baseline for 5 minutes | **Immediate automatic rollback** |
| Check-in success rate | Drops >5 percentage points vs the same window on the previous day | **Immediate automatic rollback** |
| SOS synthetic probe | Any failure, or >5 s end-to-end for two consecutive probes | **Immediate automatic rollback + page** |
| Mobile crash-free session rate | Drops below 99.0% on the new version with ≥200 sessions | Halt staged rollout; hotfix or roll forward (§47.13) |
| Any tenant-isolation or authorisation anomaly | One occurrence | **Immediate rollback + security incident** |
| Financial anomaly (ledger imbalance, duplicate payment, wrong invoice total) | One occurrence | **Immediate rollback + finance freeze on the affected module** |
| Data corruption suspected | Any credible signal | **Stop writes to the affected module, do not roll back blindly** — a rollback can compound corruption; escalate to §49 S3 |
| Elevated but sub-threshold errors | Anything ambiguous | Roll forward with a fix if the fix is understood and ≤30 minutes away; otherwise roll back. Ambiguity resolves in favour of rollback. |

**The one exception to "roll back when unsure":** suspected data corruption. Rolling code back does not un-write bad rows, and if the previous version interprets the corrupted data differently it can make things worse. That path goes to §49.8 S3.

#### 47.12.2 Rollback mechanics and time objectives

| Artefact | Mechanism | Time objective | Constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| API / workers / consoles | Redeploy the previous artefact digest (blue/green: switch traffic) | ≤5 min (≤60 s with blue/green) | Requires N-1 schema compatibility (SUR-DVO-055) |
| Application configuration / feature flag | Flip the flag | ≤60 s | The preferred mechanism — most "rollbacks" should be a flag flip, which is why risky changes ship behind flags |
| Expand-phase migration | No rollback needed; the added structure is unused by the previous code | N/A | This is the whole point of expand/contract |
| Switch-phase migration | Flip the read flag back | ≤60 s | Dual write must still be running |
| Contract-phase migration | **Not rollbackable.** Point-in-time restore + reconciliation | Hours (a DR event) | §49.8 S4; this is why the soak and dual approval exist |
| Infrastructure | Revert the IaC commit and re-apply | ≤20 min | Some resources (a deleted bucket, a rotated key) are not revertible; policy checks flag those at plan time |
| Mobile app | **Cannot recall an installed build.** Halt the staged rollout, publish a previous or fixed build, and use the **server-side kill switch** to disable the offending behaviour for already-updated devices | Rollout halt ≤5 min; a fixed build reaches users in hours-to-days | The server-side kill switch is the real mobile rollback mechanism, which is why risky mobile changes ship behind server-evaluated flags |
| Desktop app | Publish a superseding version and, if severe, set the security version floor to force the update (§20.30) | Hours | Users on machines that are off will update when they return |
| Third-party provider configuration | Manual revert per the documented baseline | ≤30 min | Why the baseline is documented (§47.4.3) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-100 | Rollback triggers shall be pre-agreed, automated where the signal is machine-observable, and shall not require a human decision for the automatic set. |
| SUR-DVO-101 | Every release shall be rollback-tested in staging as part of the release-candidate process: deploy N, deploy N-1, verify. |
| SUR-DVO-102 | Any change whose rollback is not a redeploy or a flag flip shall be classified Major and shall state its actual rollback procedure and duration in the change record. |
| SUR-DVO-103 | Every risky behavioural change on a mobile client shall be server-flag-controlled, so that a defect can be neutralised without waiting for an app store. |

### 47.13 Mobile release pipeline

#### 47.13.1 Build, signing and custody

| Aspect | Android | iOS |
|---|---|---|
| Signing | Play App Signing (Google holds the app signing key); the **upload key** is generated by us, stored in the secret store, backed up under dual custody, and never on a laptop | Distribution certificate and provisioning profiles managed via App Store Connect API key; the API key and the certificate private key are in the secret store with dual custody |
| Build environment | Ephemeral CI runner; no developer machine ever produces a store build | Same, on a hosted macOS runner |
| Reproducibility | Build inputs pinned (SDK version, NDK, dependency lockfile, base image); the build records its full input manifest with the artefact | Same |
| Custody risk | **The single highest-impact key custody item in the mobile pipeline is the Play upload key and the Apple distribution certificate.** Loss of the Apple certificate is recoverable (revoke and reissue); loss of the Play *upload* key is recoverable through Google support only if Play App Signing is enabled — which is precisely why it is enabled. | — |
| Versioning | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` plus a monotonically increasing build number derived from the CI run; the version and build number are visible in the app's About screen and are sent with every API request and crash report |

#### 47.13.2 Release channels and staged rollout

| Channel | Audience | Purpose | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Internal | Engineering + QA | Every merge to `main`, automatically | Continuous |
| Alpha / closed test | Suraksha's own guards at SURAKSHA-HQ sites | **Dogfooding on real shifts with real conditions** — the most valuable test this product has | ≥3 days per release train |
| Beta / open test | Opted-in pilot agencies' guards | Broader device and network diversity | ≥3 days |
| Production staged | Everyone | Percentage rollout | See below |

**Staged rollout percentages and halt criteria:**

| Step | Share | Minimum dwell | Halt if |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5% | 24 h | Crash-free sessions <99.0%, or ANR rate >0.5%, or check-in success rate down >3 pp vs the prior version, or any SOS submission failure attributable to the version |
| 2 | 20% | 24 h | Same thresholds |
| 3 | 50% | 24 h | Same |
| 4 | 100% | — | Monitored for 7 days; a regression at 100% triggers the kill switch and a hotfix train |

A halt is automatic where the store platform supports it and manual otherwise, driven by alert OA-19.

#### 47.13.3 Forced update for the Guard App

The Guard App is a safety tool used by workers who may have auto-update disabled to save data. A forced-update mechanism is necessary — and it is dangerous if built carelessly.

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Mechanism | The API returns, on every authenticated response and on an unauthenticated `/v1/app-config` call, `min_supported_version` and `recommended_version` per platform. The app compares on launch and on resume. |
| Soft prompt | Below `recommended_version`: a dismissible in-app card, at most once per 24 hours, explaining what the update fixes in plain language and in the guard's language. |
| Hard block | Below `min_supported_version`: a blocking screen with the reason, the store link, and a sideload link for tenants whose devices lack Play access. |
| **The safety carve-out** | **The hard-block screen must still expose SOS and the emergency call button.** A guard in danger on an out-of-date app must never meet a wall. This is non-negotiable and is a named test case. The screen also retains the offline check-in path if the device already has an open duty session, so a guard mid-shift is not stranded without an attendance record. |
| Raising the floor | `min_supported_version` may be raised only for: a security defect, a data-corruption defect, a safety-path defect, or the expiry of the 12-month compatibility window. It requires CTO approval and ≥7 days of soft-prompt lead time, except for a security defect, where the lead time may be shortened with a recorded justification. |
| Visibility | An OPS screen shows the active version distribution across the guard fleet, per tenant, so raising the floor is a decision made against data (how many guards would be blocked) rather than against a guess. |

#### 47.13.4 The offline-client compatibility window

This is where an offline-first field app imposes an obligation on the server that a web-only product never faces.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Server support window | The server accepts and correctly processes payloads from any Guard App version released in the **last 12 months** `[RECOMMENDED]` (SUR-NFR-198). A guard's device that has been offline in a basement for a week, or on a handset that stopped receiving store updates, must still be able to deliver its queued attendance and SOS records. |
| Why 12 months | Shorter (3–6 months) strands devices on constrained data plans and in tenants that manage updates centrally. Longer (24 months) means the server carries two years of payload-shape variants, which becomes a real maintenance tax and a security surface. Twelve months covers the observed update-lag distribution with margin `[ASSUMPTION: A-567]` and is re-evaluated from the version-distribution data at day 180. |
| Schema evolution rule | Within the window, changes to offline payload schemas are **additive only**: a field may be added; a field may never be removed, renamed or repurposed. Removing a field requires waiting for the window to expire past the last version that emitted it. |
| Enforcement | Each released version's payload schema is stored as a build artefact; CI replays a recorded corpus of payloads from every in-window version against the current server (SUR-NFR-199), and deleting an in-window schema fails the build. |
| Deprecation ladder | Month 0–6: fully supported, no prompts beyond the normal update card. Month 6–9: soft prompt escalates to every launch. Month 9–12: non-critical features (reports, profile edits, marketplace views) disabled with an explanatory message; duty-critical features remain. Month 12: hard block, with the SOS and emergency-call carve-out, and with any queued D0 data flushed to the server *before* the block engages — the app must never hold a guard's unsent attendance hostage behind an update wall. |
| Server-side telemetry | Version distribution, per-version error rate and per-version payload-parse failure rate are dashboarded, so the decision to expire a version is data-driven. |

#### 47.13.5 Store realities that shape release planning

| Reality | Consequence for planning | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Apple review latency is variable (typically 1–3 days, occasionally longer) `[ASSUMPTION: A-567]` | An iOS hotfix cannot be assumed to reach users same-day | Server-side kill switches are the primary hotfix mechanism; expedited review is requested only for genuine safety defects, and using it routinely burns the privilege |
| Google Play review is usually faster but staged rollout still takes days to reach everyone | Same | Same |
| Background location permission requires a declared, reviewed use case on both stores | Any change to the location model risks a review rejection that blocks an unrelated release | Location behaviour changes ship in their own release, never bundled with a feature release; the declaration text and the in-app disclosure screen are treated as release-critical assets |
| SMS-related permissions on Android are restricted, and an app requesting them without a qualifying use case can be rejected or removed | The SMS SOS fallback's *sending* path uses the platform's SMS composer/intent or a carrier-independent path rather than a permission that risks removal | `[RISK: R-571]` — the SOS SMS fallback design must be validated against current store policy before build; if the permission is unobtainable, the fallback becomes a one-tap pre-filled SMS the guard sends, which is slower but policy-safe and still functional |
| Foreground service types on modern Android require declaration and justification | The duty-time location service must declare the correct type or the app will be rejected or killed | Declared explicitly; tested on each new Android major version during the annual OS-compatibility pass |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-110 | Store builds shall be produced only by ephemeral CI runners from pinned inputs; a build produced on a developer machine shall never be published. |
| SUR-DVO-111 | Signing keys and store credentials shall be dual-custody in the secret store, covered by the joiner/leaver process, and their loss/recovery procedure documented and rehearsed annually. |
| SUR-DVO-112 | Every Guard App release shall pass through internal → alpha (Suraksha's own guards, ≥3 days on real shifts) → beta → staged production, with automatic halt criteria. |
| SUR-DVO-113 | The forced-update screen shall always expose SOS and emergency call, and shall flush queued D0 data to the server before blocking. |
| SUR-DVO-114 | The server shall support Guard App versions released within the last 12 months, verified by a version-replay corpus in CI. |
| SUR-DVO-115 | Guard App version distribution across the fleet shall be visible in OPS, per tenant, and shall inform every decision to raise the minimum supported version. |
| SUR-DVO-116 | Location-behaviour changes shall ship in a dedicated release, not bundled with feature work. |

---

### 47.14 Desktop application release and auto-update

§20.30 specifies the desktop app's behaviour; this subsection specifies how it is built, signed and shipped.

#### 47.14.1 Build and signing matrix

| Platform | Artefacts | Signing | The realities |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | `.exe` (NSIS) and `.msi` (managed deployment), x64 and ARM64 | Authenticode with an **OV or EV code-signing certificate** | An OV certificate is cheaper but accumulates SmartScreen reputation slowly — early users see "Windows protected your PC" until enough installs accumulate, which for a B2B product with a slow install curve can take months. An EV certificate grants immediate SmartScreen reputation but requires a hardware token or a cloud HSM, which means the CI signing step must call an HSM service rather than hold a file. **Recommendation: EV via a cloud HSM signing service**, because the first impression of a security product's installer showing a scary warning is a commercial problem, not just a technical one. `[ASSUMPTION: A-568]` cost ~₹25,000–60,000/year. Reputation resets on certificate change, so the certificate's renewal is planned, not last-minute. |
| macOS | `.dmg`, universal (Apple silicon + Intel) | Developer ID Application + Developer ID Installer, **hardened runtime**, then **notarisation** and **stapling** | Notarisation is a network call to Apple that can take minutes to hours and can fail *after* a successful build for reasons the build did not surface (an unsigned nested binary, a missing entitlement, a disallowed library). The pipeline therefore treats notarisation as a distinct, retryable stage with its own timeout and alert, and a release is not "built" until the ticket is stapled and verified with `spctl`. Apple Developer Program membership (~$99/year) is a hard dependency with a renewal date that, if missed, breaks releases and eventually breaks existing installs' update verification. |
| Linux | `.deb`, `.rpm`, `.AppImage` | GPG-signed repository for `.deb`/`.rpm`; published SHA-256 for all artefacts; AppImage is unsigned by nature | **AppImage is the primary supported artefact** because it removes distribution-version variance. The `.deb`/`.rpm` packages and their repository are a convenience for tenants with managed fleets. Desktop-environment variance (notifications, tray icons, credential storage via libsecret) is documented as best-effort per §20.30. |

#### 47.14.2 Auto-update pipeline

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Update manifest | A signed manifest per channel (stable, and a `pinned` channel for Enterprise tenants) listing version, artefact URLs, SHA-256 hashes, minimum-supported version, and release notes. Served from CDN, signed with a key distinct from the code-signing key, and verified by the client before any download. |
| Check cadence | On launch and every 6 hours (§20.30). |
| Delta updates | Where the packaging toolchain supports them, to respect office connections; full artefact as fallback. |
| Install timing | Download in background, install on quit, with a "Restart to update" prompt — never a forced restart during a working session, because the Agency Portal desktop app may be mid-invoice. |
| Staged rollout | The manifest supports a percentage gate keyed on a stable machine identifier, so a bad desktop build reaches 5% before 100%, with the same halt criteria as mobile (crash rate, error rate, failed-update rate). |
| Enterprise pinning | A tenant may pin a version; pinned tenants receive updates through an approved channel with release notes ahead of the general channel. |
| Security floor | A security version floor forces an update with 7 days' notice (§20.30); after the notice, the app blocks with an explanation and the download link. |
| Rollback | There is no uninstall-and-revert; rollback is publishing a superseding version. If the defective version cannot self-update (the worst case — a broken updater), the runbook is: publish a fixed version, notify tenants by email and in the web app, and provide a manual installer link. This scenario is the reason the updater itself is the most conservatively reviewed code in the desktop app. |
| Verification | Every release is installed and updated-from-previous on a clean VM per platform in CI before publication; an update that fails to apply from the previous version fails the release. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-120 | Desktop artefacts shall be signed per platform, notarised where required, and published with SHA-256 checksums and a signed update manifest. |
| SUR-DVO-121 | Notarisation shall be a discrete, retryable, alerted pipeline stage; a release shall not be publishable until stapling is verified. |
| SUR-DVO-122 | Every desktop release shall be verified by a clean-install test and an update-from-previous-version test on each supported platform before publication. |
| SUR-DVO-123 | Certificate and developer-account expiry dates shall be tracked as operational assets with 90/30/7-day reminders and a named owner. |
| SUR-DVO-124 | Desktop auto-update shall support percentage-staged rollout with automatic halt on elevated crash or failed-update rates. |

### 47.15 Environment cost management

#### 47.15.1 Indicative monthly cost at MVP

`[ASSUMPTION: A-569]` The figures below are professional estimates for an Indian-region hyperscaler at the §34.7.1 pilot topology, in INR per month, excluding usage-based communication costs (SMS/WhatsApp/voice, owned by §36) and AI model costs (owned by §25). They exist to make the cost conversation concrete, not to be quoted as a budget.

| Line | Monthly (₹) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Application compute (API + workers + real-time gateway) | 45,000 | 2–4 API, 2 worker, 2 gateway instances, small-to-medium sizes, with autoscaling headroom |
| Managed Postgres (primary + replica, 8 vCPU/32 GB, 500 GB SSD) | 50,000 | Per §32's estimate; the single largest line |
| Managed Redis (cache + streams + pub/sub) | 12,000 | Memory-sized for stream retention |
| Object storage + requests | 8,000 | Documents, photos, exports; grows fastest (§50.7) |
| CDN + WAF + DDoS | 10,000 | Fronting five web properties |
| Observability (logs, metrics, traces, error tracking) | 25,000 | The line most likely to surprise; capped by §46.10 SUR-NFR-164 |
| Backups + cross-region replication | 10,000 | Including the second-region copy |
| CI/CD (hosted runners, including macOS minutes for iOS builds) | 8,000 | macOS runner minutes are disproportionately expensive |
| Map tiles and geocoding | 15,000 | Heavily dependent on the geocode cache hit rate (§34.6) |
| Non-production (staging + UAT + preview + restore-test) | 25,000 | After auto-shutdown savings |
| Secrets, KMS, misc. managed services | 5,000 | |
| **Total (excluding communications and AI)** | **≈₹2,13,000** | Roughly ₹26 per active guard per month at 8,000 guards |

#### 47.15.2 Controls

| Control | Detail |
|---|---|
| Tagging and allocation | Every resource carries `env`, `service`, `cost_center` (SUR-DVO §47.4.2). A monthly cost report attributes spend to environment and to service, and an unallocated share above 5% is investigated. |
| Budgets and alerts | Per-environment monthly budgets with alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% of forecast, plus an anomaly alert on any single service rising >40% week-over-week (alert OA-38). Cost anomalies are frequently the first visible symptom of a bug — a runaway retry loop shows up on the bill before it shows up anywhere else. |
| Non-production shutdown | Staging, UAT and preview compute stop outside 08:00–22:00 IST on weekdays, restarting on demand via a self-service command. Saves roughly 60–65% of non-production compute. Databases in non-production are small and stay up to avoid restore complexity. |
| Ephemeral preview hygiene | Preview environments are destroyed on PR close and force-destroyed after 7 days regardless. |
| Right-sizing cadence | Quarterly review of instance sizes against observed utilisation; reserved capacity or committed-use discounts purchased only after 3 months of stable baseline (buying commitments on guessed capacity is how startups pre-pay for the wrong shape). |
| Log volume discipline | Log ingest is the observability cost driver; sampling rates and log levels are configuration (§47.10), adjustable without deploy, with a documented cost-per-GB so the trade-off is explicit. |
| Data-transfer traps | Cross-AZ chatter, NAT gateway processing charges, and object-storage egress are called out explicitly because they are the three lines that grow silently. Architecture reviews check them. |
| Cost per deploy / per tenant | A monthly report shows cost per tenant and cost per active guard, feeding the unit economics in §50.10. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-130 | Every resource shall be cost-tagged; unallocated spend above 5% of the monthly bill shall be investigated. |
| SUR-DVO-131 | Budget and anomaly alerts shall exist per environment; a >40% week-over-week rise in any service shall page during business hours as a possible defect, not only as a cost event. |
| SUR-DVO-132 | Non-production compute shall shut down outside working hours by default. |
| SUR-DVO-133 | Infrastructure cost per active guard per month shall be reported monthly and tracked against the §50.10 targets. |
