### 47.16 On-call and the runbook model

#### 47.16.1 The rotation — stated honestly

`[ASSUMPTION: A-566]` At MVP there are 5–8 engineers and no SRE. A 24/7 engineering rotation therefore looks like this:

| Element | MVP | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Primary on-call | 3 engineers rotating weekly | 6–8 engineers, weekly, split by domain (platform / application) |
| Secondary (escalation) | CTO, always | A senior rotation of 4 |
| Coverage | 24/7 for P0; 07:00–23:00 IST for P1; business hours for P2/P3 | 24/7 for P0/P1 |
| Response target | P0 acknowledge ≤5 min, engage ≤15 min. P1 acknowledge ≤15 min (in-hours), ≤30 min (out of hours) | P0 ack ≤5 min; P1 ack ≤15 min 24/7 |
| Compensation | On-call allowance plus time off in lieu for any out-of-hours engagement exceeding 30 minutes | Same, formalised |
| Alert budget | **≤2 pages per person per week.** Exceeding it for two consecutive weeks triggers a mandatory alert-review session (§48.14) — the alert is fixed or deleted | ≤2 pages/person/week |

**The honest statement, which belongs in this document rather than being discovered later: a three-person rotation is not sustainable indefinitely.** One person on call one week in three, being woken, is a known cause of attrition in small teams. The mitigations are real but partial:

1. **The Command Center is staffed 24/7 by humans** (§24.3) who are already awake and trained. They are **tier-0 triage**: they receive certain operational alerts, execute documented runbook steps that require no engineering judgement (restart a stuck worker via a purpose-built admin action, re-run a failed job, confirm whether an alert is real by checking a second source), and escalate to the engineer only when the runbook says to. This materially reduces engineering pages and is the single most valuable structural advantage this business has over a typical SaaS startup.
2. **Auto-remediation** for the recurring, well-understood conditions (§48.11's auto-remediation column) removes pages entirely rather than routing them.
3. **Severity discipline:** only genuine P0 conditions page out of hours. A queue backlog that will be fine in the morning is a ticket, not a page.
4. **Headcount trigger:** when out-of-hours pages exceed 4 per month sustained over a quarter, or when the rotation drops below 3 people, hiring a platform engineer becomes a stated business requirement, not a discussion. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-552]`

#### 47.16.2 Incident roles for a small team

| Role | Who | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Incident Commander | The on-call engineer initially; handed to the CTO for a sustained P0 | Owns the incident: decides, delegates, keeps the timeline. Does not debug. |
| Operations lead (fixer) | The engineer with the most context | Debugs and fixes. Does not communicate externally. |
| Communications | CTO or a designated non-engineer (COO for client-facing incidents) | Status page, client comms, internal updates on the cadence of §49.13 |
| Command Center liaison | The shift lead on duty | Manages operational continuity for guards and clients while the platform is being fixed; activates §49.12 if needed |

For a small incident these collapse into one person; the roles exist so that when an incident grows, the split is known rather than improvised.

#### 47.16.3 Runbook standard

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Coverage | Every P0 and P1 alert links to a runbook (SUR-NFR-147, SUR-NFR-162). An alert without a runbook does not ship. |
| Template | Symptom → Impact (which users, which tier) → Immediate containment → Diagnosis steps with the exact queries/commands/dashboards → Remediation options with their risks → Verification (how you know it is fixed) → Rollback → Escalation path and when to escalate → Related runbooks. |
| Executability | Written so that an engineer who did not build the system can execute it at 3 a.m. Every command is copy-pasteable; every dashboard is linked; no step says "investigate". |
| Availability during an outage | Runbooks are stored in the repository **and** mirrored to a location that does not depend on the platform or (for a provider-level incident) on the primary cloud account: a wiki on a separate provider, plus an offline PDF export refreshed weekly and held by the on-call rotation (§49.2). A runbook that is only readable when the system is up is not a runbook. |
| Testing | Runbooks for the top 10 alert conditions are exercised in a quarterly game day, with the elapsed time recorded and the runbook corrected from what actually happened. |
| Ownership | Each runbook has an owner and a last-verified date; a runbook not verified in 6 months is flagged. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DVO-140 | A documented on-call rotation with defined response targets, escalation path and compensation shall exist from launch. |
| SUR-DVO-141 | Command Center operators shall be trained and authorised to execute defined tier-0 runbook actions through purpose-built admin operations, with every action audited; they shall never be given shell or database access. |
| SUR-DVO-142 | Every P0/P1 alert shall link to a runbook that is readable when the platform is down. |
| SUR-DVO-143 | A blameless post-incident review shall be completed within 5 business days for every P0 and every P1 with customer impact, with tracked action items and an owner. |
| SUR-DVO-144 | Out-of-hours page volume shall be measured per person; sustained breach of the alert budget shall trigger an alert review and, at the defined threshold, a hiring decision. |
| SUR-DVO-145 | A quarterly game day shall exercise the top 10 runbooks against injected faults, with results feeding runbook corrections. |

## 48. Observability

### 48.0 Scope, and the four telemetry systems that must not be confused

SURAKSHA has four distinct alerting and telemetry systems. They serve different audiences, have different urgency semantics, and must never be merged "for simplicity" — merging them is how a guard-safety alert ends up in a channel an engineer has muted, or how a disk-space warning interrupts an operator handling an SOS.

| System | Owner section | Audience | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Engineering observability** (this section) | §48 | Engineers, on-call | "Is the platform healthy, and if not, why?" | GPS ingest lag p95 exceeded 30 s |
| **Operational security alerts** | §24 Command Center | Command Center operators, supervisors, field | "Is a guard, a site or a client in trouble?" | SOS raised; post unmanned; wake check missed |
| **Security detection** | §38.11 | Security responder (CTO at MVP), external assessor | "Is the platform under attack or misused?" | Impossible-travel login; bulk export anomaly |
| **Business analytics** | §42 | Management, agency owners, clients | "How is the business performing?" | Attendance %, fill rate, churn, ARPU |

**The line between §48 and §24 is the one most likely to blur, so it is drawn explicitly:**

- If the correct response is *"an engineer must fix the platform"* → §48, pages the on-call engineer.
- If the correct response is *"an operator must contact a human in the field"* → §24, appears in the Command Center alert queue.
- A single underlying event can legitimately produce both. When the GPS pipeline stalls, §48 pages an engineer (the pipeline is broken) **and** §24 must be told that the live map is stale so operators stop trusting it. These are two alerts with two audiences, generated from one condition, and the §24 one is created by the platform emitting a `platform.degraded` signal that the Command Center renders as a banner — it is not duplicated logic, it is one signal with two consumers.
- Guard-safety alert *content* (SOS, unmanned post, missed wake check, geofence exit, panic) is **never** defined in this section. §24 owns it entirely.

Normative IDs use `SUR-OBS-nnn`. Operational alert IDs use `OA-nn`.

---

### 48.1 Stance, tooling and the residency constraint

#### 48.1.1 Principles

| # | Principle | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Instrument with an open standard, store with a replaceable backend | OpenTelemetry SDKs and semantic conventions everywhere; the backend is a deployment decision, not an architectural one |
| 2 | Telemetry is a product surface, not exhaust | Domain metrics (GPS lag, check-in success, notification delivery) are specified by product requirement, not added when something breaks |
| 3 | Cardinality is a budget | Every label is a cost multiplier. Identifiers (guard_id, user_id, device_id, request_id) never become metric labels — they belong in logs and traces |
| 4 | No PII, ever, in telemetry | Restates SUR-SEC-159 as an implementation constraint on every pillar including error reports and traces |
| 5 | Every alert is actionable and has a runbook | An alert nobody acts on trains everyone to ignore alerts (§48.14) |
| 6 | Observe what users experience, not only what servers report | An internal health check that says "healthy" while every guard's check-in fails is the failure mode synthetic monitoring exists to catch |

#### 48.1.2 Backend selection — and why residency decides it

This is the one place where §47.3.1's residency stance materially constrains a tooling choice, and it should be decided consciously rather than discovered during procurement.

Application logs under our policy contain **no PII** (SUR-SEC-159). They do contain tenant identifiers, route names, error contents, and operational patterns — which is commercially sensitive and, more importantly, is subject to the same residency rule as everything else (SUR-PRV-091: "log stores… shall follow the same residency rule as the primary store"). Several leading observability SaaS products have no Indian region.

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Managed observability SaaS with an Indian region** `[RECOMMENDED] if available at acceptable cost` | Least operational burden — which is the decisive factor for a team with no SRE (§47.1.2). Requires verifying the Indian region covers logs, metrics, traces *and* error tracking, not just one of them. Cost scales with ingest volume and can become the third-largest infrastructure line; capped by SUR-NFR-164. Lock-in is moderate but mitigated by OpenTelemetry instrumentation — the agents and dashboards are the switching cost, not the code. |
| **Self-hosted open-source stack in-region** (Prometheus/Mimir + Loki + Tempo + Grafana, or SigNoz as a single integrated OTel-native deployment) `[RECOMMENDED] if no compliant SaaS` | Unambiguous residency, predictable cost (storage + compute, no per-GB ingest premium), full control. Cost: it is another production system to run, back up and upgrade — exactly what §47.1.2 warns against. SigNoz is called out specifically because it is OTel-native and deploys as one stack rather than four, which materially reduces the operational surface versus assembling LGTM by hand. |
| Non-Indian-region SaaS | Fastest to adopt, and it puts operational data outside the residency boundary. Would require a documented exception, a data-minimisation review, and a contractual position — for a benefit that the two options above already provide. Not recommended. |
| No dedicated backend (cloud provider's native logging/monitoring only) | Free-ish, in-region by construction, and genuinely adequate for infrastructure metrics. Inadequate for distributed tracing and for the domain metrics catalogue below, and provider-native log query languages are painful at incident time. Acceptable as a *supplement*, not as the whole. |

`[DECISION REQUIRED: D-553]` — the observability backend, decided at architecture selection against the residency test and a 12-month cost projection at Scale volumes.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-001 | All services shall be instrumented with OpenTelemetry SDKs using semantic conventions; vendor-specific agents may be used for collection but shall not be the source of instrumentation. |
| SUR-OBS-002 | The observability backend shall store logs, metrics, traces and error reports in an Indian region, or shall be covered by a recorded exception with a documented compensating control. |
| SUR-OBS-003 | A telemetry collector (OTel Collector) shall sit between applications and the backend so that the backend can be changed, duplicated or sampled without touching application code. |
| SUR-OBS-004 | Metric label cardinality shall be governed by an allowlist; adding a label requires an estimate of its cardinality, and a label capable of unbounded cardinality shall be rejected in review. |

---

### 48.2 Logs

#### 48.2.1 The log record schema

Every log line from every service is a single-line JSON object with these fields. Free-text logging is prohibited; the message is a stable, low-cardinality string and the variable parts are structured fields.

| Field | Type | Always present | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ts` | RFC3339 with milliseconds, UTC | Yes | Server clock; field events additionally carry `device_time` in the payload per canon §4 |
| `level` | enum | Yes | `debug` \| `info` \| `warn` \| `error` \| `fatal` |
| `service` | string | Yes | From the service catalogue |
| `module` | string | Yes | The modular-monolith module (§50.3) that emitted it |
| `env` | string | Yes | `prod` \| `staging` \| `uat` |
| `version` | string | Yes | Build version — makes "did this start with release N?" a query, not a guess |
| `trace_id`, `span_id` | string | Yes for request-scoped | W3C trace context (§48.2.3) |
| `request_id` | string | Yes for request-scoped | Echoed to the client as `X-Request-Id` (§33) so a user's support ticket carries the key |
| `tenant_id` | uuid | Where applicable | The single most useful filter in a multi-tenant system |
| `actor_ref` | string | Where applicable | **Pseudonymous** actor reference, not a name, phone or email |
| `route`, `method`, `status`, `duration_ms` | — | For API logs | |
| `event` | string | Yes | A stable, enumerated event name (e.g. `attendance.checkin.accepted`), never an interpolated sentence |
| `error.type`, `error.message`, `error.stack`, `error.code` | — | For errors | Stack traces only at `error` and above |
| `attrs` | object | Optional | Additional structured fields, subject to the redaction allowlist |

#### 48.2.2 Log categories, retention and volume

| Category | Contents | Level policy | Sampling | Hot retention | Total retention | Store |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Application | Business logic events, warnings, errors | `info` and above in production | 100% of `warn`+; `info` sampled per §48.2.4 | 14 days searchable | 90 days | Observability backend |
| API access | One record per request | `info` | 100%, except health checks (0%) and GPS ingest (1% + all errors) | 14 days | 90 days | Observability backend |
| Worker/job | Job start, end, duration, outcome, retry | `info` | 100% of terminal outcomes; 10% of routine progress | 14 days | 90 days | Observability backend |
| Security events | §38.11 event catalogue | — | 100%, never sampled | 90 days | 18 months | Separate security store with restricted access (§38) |
| Audit log | "Who did what to which record" | — | 100%, never sampled | Queryable indefinitely | 8 years, append-only, cold after 18 months (§40.7.3) | Separate append-only store — **not** the observability backend |
| AI interaction logs | Prompt metadata, tool calls, action class, approval outcome, model, tokens, cost, latency; **never** raw prompt content containing personal data | `info` | 100% of tool calls and approvals; content per §41.4.6 | 30 days | 24 months per §41.4.6 | Separate AI store with §41 access controls |
| Client logs (mobile/web) | Crash breadcrumbs, sync failures, permission denials, offline queue events | `warn`+ only, uploaded in batches | 100% of errors; breadcrumbs only attached to an error | 14 days | 30 days | Error tracking + backend |
| Migration/deploy | Migration timing, lock waits, deploy events | `info` | 100% | 30 days | 13 months | Observability backend |

**Audit is not logging.** This is a recurring source of confusion. Audit answers a legal and forensic question, must be immutable, must survive 8 years, and must never be sampled, rotated or lost when the log backend is swapped. It has its own store (§38.12). Operational logs are diagnostic, sampled, and disposable. A system that puts audit records in the log backend loses them the first time someone changes observability vendors.

#### 48.2.3 Correlation ID propagation — mobile → API → queue → job → provider

This is the requirement that makes an incident diagnosable. The chain must survive an asynchronous hop and, uniquely for this product, an *offline* hop that can be days long.

| Hop | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **1. Client originates** | Every client (Guard App, consoles, desktop) generates a W3C `traceparent` per user action and a stable `client_action_id` (UUID) for the logical operation. Both are attached to the request. For an **offline** event, the `client_action_id` and the original `device_time` are stored in the local queue, so an event created on Tuesday and delivered on Friday still carries the identity of the action that created it. |
| **2. Edge** | The load balancer/WAF assigns or preserves `X-Request-Id` and passes `traceparent` untouched. |
| **3. API** | The API adopts the incoming trace context (or starts a new trace and records the client's `traceparent` as a link if the incoming one is malformed — never trust client-supplied trace headers blindly). It binds `trace_id`, `request_id`, `tenant_id`, `actor_ref` and `client_action_id` into a request-scoped context that the logging library injects automatically into every line. |
| **4. Outbox** | When a domain event is written to the transactional outbox, the trace context is stored **as columns on the outbox row** (`trace_id`, `parent_span_id`, `client_action_id`). This is the critical link: the outbox is the boundary where synchronous becomes asynchronous, and a trace that dies at the outbox is a trace that cannot explain why a notification never arrived. |
| **5. Queue / Redis Stream** | The relay copies the trace context into the message headers. Consumers extract it and continue the trace as a new span with a link to the producer's span (a link, not a child, because the consumer may run much later — a child span with a 40-second gap misrepresents causality). |
| **6. Worker / job** | The job's span carries `trace_id`, `client_action_id`, `tenant_id`, plus job-specific attributes (attempt number, queue, scheduled vs triggered). |
| **7. External provider call** | The outbound call records the provider, the endpoint, the latency, the provider's own request/message identifier in the span, and the correlation is stored on the domain record (e.g. `notification.provider_message_id`) so a delivery receipt arriving hours later can be joined back to the originating action. |
| **8. Delivery receipt / webhook** | An inbound webhook looks up the domain record by the provider's identifier and re-attaches the original `trace_id` to its span as a link, closing the loop. |
| **9. Back to the user** | `X-Request-Id` is returned in every response and shown in the UI's error reference (§27.10.2's "Ref: 7K3-B2Q9"), so a support ticket contains the key that finds the trace. |

**Worked example.** A guard checks in at 06:03 with no signal; the event syncs at 06:41. The support question three days later is "why was Ravi marked late?" The answer is one query on `client_action_id`: the client log shows the action at 06:03 with the offline queue accepting it; the API log shows acceptance at 06:41 with `device_time=06:03, server_received_time=06:41`; the outbox row and the job span show the attendance rule evaluating against `device_time`; the notification span shows the "late" notice was never sent because the rule correctly used device time. The whole chain is one identifier.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-010 | W3C trace context shall be propagated across every hop including the transactional outbox, the queue and the job runner; the outbox schema shall carry trace columns. |
| SUR-OBS-011 | Every client action shall carry a `client_action_id` that survives offline queuing and is preserved on the resulting server-side records. |
| SUR-OBS-012 | Asynchronous consumers shall record a span **link** to the producing span, not a parent-child relationship, where the delay can exceed one second. |
| SUR-OBS-013 | Every API response shall return `X-Request-Id`, and every user-facing error shall display a reference derived from it. |

#### 48.2.4 Sampling

| Path | Policy | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Errors (any level ≥ `warn`) | **100%, never sampled** | The rare thing is the thing you need |
| SOS path (any span or log touching an SOS) | **100%, never sampled, never dropped under load shedding** | Non-negotiable |
| Payments, payroll, ledger, invoicing | 100% | Money must be reconstructable |
| Attendance writes | 100% | Payroll and billing depend on it |
| Authentication and authorisation decisions | 100% of denials; 5% of grants | Denials are the diagnostic signal; grants are the volume |
| GPS ingest | 1% of successful batches + 100% of failures, duplicates and mock-location detections | At 60–900 pings/s, 100% logging would cost more than the pings themselves |
| Health checks and static assets | 0% | Pure noise |
| Everything else at `info` | 100% at MVP; adaptive 10–100% at Scale, driven by volume budget | The budget is configuration (§47.10), adjustable without deploy |
| Under load-shedding | Sampling rates drop automatically for non-critical categories before any user-facing degradation | Telemetry must not be the reason the service falls over |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-014 | Sampling rates shall be runtime configuration, adjustable without deployment, with a documented cost-per-GB so the trade-off is explicit. |
| SUR-OBS-015 | Errors, SOS, financial and attendance paths shall be exempt from all sampling and from load-shedding-driven telemetry reduction. |

#### 48.2.5 The no-PII rule and how it is actually enforced

SUR-SEC-159 states the rule. A rule without enforcement machinery is a hope, so the enforcement is specified here.

| Layer | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| 1. Shared library | All logging goes through one library. It accepts structured fields against a **declared field allowlist per event type**; an undeclared field is dropped and counted, not logged. Logging an entire entity object is impossible by API design — there is no `log.info(guard)` overload. |
| 2. Serializer redaction | The serializer applies pattern-based redaction as a second net: 10-digit Indian phone numbers, email addresses, 12-digit identifier patterns, PAN-shaped strings, IFSC/account-shaped strings, bearer tokens, and anything under a key matching a sensitive-key list (`password`, `token`, `otp`, `secret`, `aadhaar`, `account`, `ifsc`, `dob`, `lat`, `lng`, `address`). Redacted values become `[redacted:phone]` so the *shape* of the problem survives without the value. |
| 3. CI lint | A static rule forbids passing an entity type, a request body, or a `params` object to the logger; forbids string interpolation into the `event` field; and requires new event types to declare their field allowlist. |
| 4. Pipeline detector | A detector runs on the log stream itself, matching identifier-shaped values. A hit raises **OA-30** at P1, identifies the emitting service, module and version, and the leak is treated as a privacy incident (SUR-NFR-125), not a cosmetic bug. |
| 5. Error tracking | Error reports are the most common accidental PII channel because they capture local variables and request bodies by default. A `before_send` scrubber runs the same redaction, request bodies are not captured for any route handling personal data, and breadcrumbs are allowlisted (§48.5). |
| 6. Coordinates | Exact coordinates are not application-log data (SUR-SEC-159). Where a location must be logged for diagnosis, a geohash truncated to ~5 km precision is logged instead. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-016 | All logging shall pass through a shared library with per-event field allowlists; direct serializer use shall fail the CI lint gate. |
| SUR-OBS-017 | A PII detector shall run continuously on the log stream; a detection shall raise a P1 privacy incident naming the emitting service, module and version. |
| SUR-OBS-018 | Error-tracking payloads shall be scrubbed before transmission; request bodies shall not be captured for routes handling personal data. |
| SUR-OBS-019 | Exact coordinates, document contents, credentials, tokens, OTPs and identifier numbers shall never appear in any log, trace attribute or error report. |

### 48.3 Metrics

#### 48.3.1 RED and USE

| Family | Applies to | Metrics |
|---|---|---|
| **RED** | Every request-serving component (API routes, WebSocket gateway, job consumers treated as request handlers) | **R**ate (req/s), **E**rrors (rate and ratio by class), **D**uration (histogram, p50/p90/p95/p99) — always labelled by route/handler, method, status class, and (bounded) tenant tier |
| **USE** | Every resource (compute, database, cache, queue, storage, connection pools) | **U**tilisation, **S**aturation, **E**rrors — CPU, memory, connections in use vs pool size, queue depth vs capacity, disk, IOPS, network |

Naming follows OpenTelemetry conventions: `suraksha.<module>.<object>.<unit>`, with units in the name (`_seconds`, `_bytes`, `_total`). Histograms, not averages — an average latency has never diagnosed anything. Exemplars link a histogram bucket to a representative trace, so "why is p99 bad" is one click, not an investigation.

#### 48.3.2 The domain metrics catalogue

These are the metrics that describe whether *this* product is working, as opposed to whether *a* web service is working. They are product requirements, not infrastructure afterthoughts.

| Metric | Type | Labels (bounded) | Why it matters | Alert |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gps.ingest.lag_seconds` | Histogram | partition | Difference between `recorded_at` and pipeline processing time. The core health signal for the live map. | OA-14 |
| `gps.ingest.rate` | Counter | source (live/replay) | Pings accepted per second; the replay split distinguishes a genuine load rise from a reconnection herd | OA-15 |

### 48.4 Distributed tracing

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Coverage | Every inbound request, every job execution, every outbound external call, every database query above 50 ms, every cache miss on a hot path, every queue publish/consume |
| The six critical traced paths | (1) SOS press → alert on console; (2) check-in submit → attendance row → outbox → notifications; (3) ping batch → stream → writer + signals → read model → WebSocket; (4) payment intent → gateway → webhook → ledger; (5) roster publish → fan-out → per-recipient delivery; (6) AI turn → retrieval → model → tool call → approval card |
| Span naming | `<module>.<operation>`, low cardinality; the variable parts are attributes |
| Required attributes | `tenant_id`, `module`, `actor_ref`, `client_action_id`, `app_version` where applicable, and outcome |
| Sampling | Head sampling at 10% for routine traffic; **tail sampling** retaining 100% of traces that contain an error, exceed the route's latency SLO, or touch SOS/payment/attendance paths. Tail sampling is the correct choice here because the interesting traces are defined by their outcome, which is only known at the end |
| Mobile continuity | The Guard App emits `traceparent` on requests; the cost is ~60 bytes per request, which is negligible against the 15 MB/shift budget (SUR-NFR-042) |
| Retention | 7 days for sampled traces; 30 days for error and SLO-violating traces |
| Known limitation | Traces cannot span the offline gap as a single trace — an event created offline on Tuesday and delivered Friday produces two traces joined by `client_action_id`, not one. This is stated so nobody spends an afternoon looking for a trace that cannot exist. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-030 | The six critical paths shall be traced end to end, and a trace-completeness check shall verify on sampled production traffic that no span in those paths is orphaned. |
| SUR-OBS-031 | Tail sampling shall retain all traces containing errors, SLO violations, or SOS/payment/attendance operations. |

---

### 48.5 Error tracking

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Tool | `[RECOMMENDED]` Sentry or a self-hosted equivalent (GlitchTip/Sentry self-hosted) chosen against the same residency test as §48.1.2. Alternatives: Bugsnag, Rollbar, or relying on log-based error aggregation — the last is rejected because release health, grouping and symbolication are exactly what a dedicated tool provides and what log aggregation does badly. |
| Grouping | By stack fingerprint with manual merge/split; an unbounded group count is itself a signal (usually an interpolated message that should be a structured field) |
| Release health | Every event carries the release version and environment; the tool reports crash-free sessions and crash-free users per release, which are the mobile rollout halt criteria (§47.13.2) |
| Symbolication | Source maps uploaded for web at build time and **not** served publicly; native symbols (dSYM, ProGuard/R8 mapping) uploaded for mobile; PDB for desktop. Without this, mobile crash reports are unreadable |
| PII scrubbing | A `before_send` hook applies the §48.2.5 redaction; request bodies are not captured for personal-data routes; breadcrumbs are allowlisted by category (navigation, network status, sync events) and never include form values |
| User context | A pseudonymous `actor_ref` and `tenant_id` only — never name, phone or email, even though the tool supports it and it would be convenient |
| Consent | Guard App and desktop crash reporting operates with the consent model of §18/§20.30; a user who declines still contributes anonymous crash counts (no stack, no breadcrumbs) so release health remains measurable |
| Alert integration | New-issue and regression alerts route to the engineering channel; a crash affecting >1% of sessions on a release pages (OA-19) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-040 | Error tracking shall be enabled for every client and server surface with symbolication configured; an unsymbolicated mobile release shall fail the release gate. |
| SUR-OBS-041 | Error payloads shall carry pseudonymous actor references only and shall be scrubbed before transmission. |
| SUR-OBS-042 | Crash-free session and user rates shall be published per release and shall gate staged rollout. |

### 48.6 Uptime and synthetic monitoring

Internal health checks answer "does the process think it is alive". Synthetics answer "can a user actually do the thing". Only the second is an availability measurement (SUR-NFR-061).

#### 48.6.1 Probe catalogue

| Probe | What it does | From | Interval | Threshold | Alert |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Public site | Fetch home page, assert content and TLS validity | 3 vantage points (2 Indian cities + 1 outside India) | 60 s | 2 consecutive failures, or LCP >4 s | OA-04 |
| API health | `GET /v1/health` with dependency status | 2 Indian | 30 s | 2 consecutive failures | OA-05 |
| **Login journey** | Full OTP login for a synthetic user, including OTP retrieval through a test channel | 2 Indian | 5 min | 2 consecutive failures | OA-06 |
| **Synthetic check-in** | Synthetic guard on a synthetic site submits a check-in with a valid position; assert acceptance, attendance row, and notification enqueue | 1 Indian | 5 min | 2 consecutive failures, or >4 s | OA-20 |
| **Synthetic SOS** | See §48.6.2 | 2 Indian | 5 min | **1 failure**, or >5 s end-to-end | OA-01 (P0) |
| Synthetic ping ingest | Submit a small ping batch; assert 202 and appearance in the read model | 1 Indian | 2 min | Lag >30 s | OA-14 |
| Synthetic notification | Trigger a test push and SMS to an internal test device; assert receipt callback | 1 Indian | 15 min | 2 consecutive failures | OA-23 |
| Synthetic payment | Gateway sandbox transaction end-to-end; plus **one real ₹1 transaction per day** on the live gateway, auto-refunded and reconciled | 1 Indian | 30 min (sandbox) / daily (live) | Any failure | OA-27 |
| WebSocket | Connect, subscribe, receive a heartbeat and a test event | 2 Indian | 60 s | 2 consecutive failures | OA-10 |
| Certificate expiry | TLS certificates on all five properties + API + status page | 1 | 6 h | <21 days remaining | OA-03 |
| Domain/DNS | Registrar expiry, NS records, MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC intact | 1 | 24 h | Any drift, or <60 days to domain expiry | OA-03 |
| Desktop update manifest | Fetch and verify manifest signature and artefact hashes | 1 | 1 h | Any failure | OA-40 |
| Mobile app-config | `GET /v1/app-config` returns valid version floors | 1 | 5 min | Any failure | OA-05 |

**On the daily real ₹1 payment probe.** A sandbox probe proves our integration works; it does not prove the *live* gateway account is healthy, that the settlement configuration is intact, or that a credential rotated last night still works. One real low-value transaction per day, auto-refunded, reconciled and excluded from revenue reporting by a flag on the record, catches the class of failure where everything looks fine until a client tries to pay. The trade-off is a tiny amount of gateway noise and a rule that finance reporting must exclude probe transactions — both cheap.

#### 48.6.2 The synthetic SOS probe — specified carefully

An SOS probe is the highest-value synthetic in the platform and the most dangerous to build carelessly. A probe that reaches a real operator, or worse a real emergency service, is a serious operational failure.

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Identity | A dedicated synthetic tenant (`SURAKSHA-SYNTHETIC`), a synthetic site, and a synthetic guard record, all flagged `is_synthetic = true` at the row level — not merely named "test" |
| Propagation | The `is_synthetic` flag propagates onto the SOS record and the alert; it is a first-class field, not an inference from the tenant |
| Routing | A synthetic alert is routed to a **separate synthetic lane** that is visible on an engineering dashboard and on a dedicated (silent) panel of the Command Center wallboard so operators can *see* the probe is healthy without being alerted by it. It never enters the live alert queue, never klaxons, never triggers escalation rungs, never notifies a client, and can never reach emergency services or a real phone number |
| Enforcement | A test asserts that a synthetic SOS produces zero outbound notifications to non-synthetic contacts; this test has no bypass |
| What it measures | End-to-end latency from probe submission to the alert being observable on the synthetic console lane via the WebSocket path — the same code path as a real SOS up to the routing decision |
| Coverage of the fallback | A separate hourly probe exercises the **SMS SOS gateway** from a real test SIM, measuring press-to-alert time on that path (SUR-NFR-023). This is the only way to know the SMS path still works, and it is the path we would need on our worst day |
| Alerting | Any single failure, or any result >5 s, raises OA-01 at P0 and pages immediately. A probe failure is treated as an outage of T0 until proven otherwise |
| The complement | The probe tests the *platform*. It does not test whether an operator responds. That is the monthly live SOS drill with real operators, owned by §24 and referenced by §49.14 |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-050 | Synthetic probes shall run continuously from at least two Indian vantage points and one outside India, and their results shall be the authoritative availability measurement for T0 and T1. |
| SUR-OBS-051 | A synthetic SOS probe shall run at 5-minute intervals against the production SOS path, isolated by an enforced `is_synthetic` flag that guarantees zero contact with real operators, clients or emergency services. |
| SUR-OBS-052 | A synthetic probe of the SMS SOS fallback shall run hourly from a real SIM. |
| SUR-OBS-053 | Probe infrastructure shall be independent of the platform being probed; a probe hosted inside the system it monitors is not a probe. |

### 48.7 Queue and job monitoring

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| Depth and age | Per queue: depth, oldest message age, enqueue rate, dequeue rate. **Oldest-message age is the alerting signal, not depth** — a deep queue draining fast is fine; a shallow queue with a 20-minute-old head is stuck |
| Outbox lag | Oldest unrelayed outbox row age. This is the master signal for asynchronous health: if the outbox is behind, notifications, webhooks, read models and alerts are all silently late |
| Consumer health | Per consumer group: lag, active consumers, pending entries, idle time. A consumer group with zero active consumers is a P1 regardless of queue depth |
| Job outcomes | Success/failure/retry counts, duration histogram, attempt distribution per job type |
| Retries and poison messages | Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, max attempts per job class, then DLQ. A message in the DLQ has an owner within one business day (SUR-NFR-087) |
| Scheduled job liveness | Every cron-style job (partition creation, retention purge, reconciliation, expiry ladders, digest sends) emits a heartbeat; a **missing** heartbeat alerts. Detecting a job that did not run is harder and more important than detecting one that failed |
| Idempotency | Job re-execution must be safe; a job that is not idempotent is a defect, because at-least-once delivery guarantees it will eventually run twice |

---

### 48.8 GPS pipeline health

| Signal | Threshold / purpose |
|---|---|
| Ingest lag (`recorded_at` → processed) | p95 and p99; the primary SLI for the live map (OA-14) |
| Stream length and consumer lag on `gps.ingest` | Redis stream backlog per consumer group; a growing "signals" lag means geofence/alert evaluation is falling behind — worse than a writer lag, because it delays operational alerts |
| Write batch efficiency | Rows per `COPY`, transactions per second, write latency |
| Read-model freshness | Age of the newest `guard_last_position` update vs wall clock |
| Live vs replay split | Proportion of pings arriving as offline replay; a jump indicates a field connectivity event |
| Devices reporting | Count of distinct devices sending in the last 10 minutes vs count of guards expected on duty. **A drop here is the clearest single indicator that something broke on the client side** |
| Accuracy and integrity distribution | Share of pings with `accuracy_m > 100`, share flagged `is_mock`, share flagged `implausible_movement` — a sudden shift usually means an app or OS change, not a change in guard behaviour |
| Partition health | Tomorrow's daily partition exists (a missing partition breaks all writes at midnight — a classic, entirely preventable outage), compression job status, downsampling job status |

#### 48.9 Notification health

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| Funnel per channel | Enqueued → attempted → accepted by provider → delivered (where receipts exist) → opened/actioned (where meaningful). Each stage's drop-off is a distinct failure mode |
| Latency per priority | Against §36.4.5; P0 measured individually, not statistically (SUR-NTF-066) |
| Provider health | Error ratio, latency, delivery-receipt ratio per provider; circuit-breaker state (SUR-NTF-063/064) |
| Template health | Send failures attributable to a specific template (an SMS template rejected by operator policy fails silently at the provider and is invisible without this) |
| Cost | Messages and spend per channel per day, against the tenant cost caps (§36.5) |
| Quiet-hours suppression | Count of messages suppressed and deferred, so a misconfiguration that suppresses everything is visible |
| Missing-language fallback | Count of sends that fell back to Tier 1 for a missing translation (SUR-FRQ-167) |

#### 48.10 Payment health

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| Success ratio | Per method (UPI/card/netbanking) over a rolling 30 minutes; UPI and card failure patterns differ and a blended number hides both |
| Webhook lag and gap detection | Gateway event → processing latency; and a **gap detector** comparing our event sequence against the gateway's, because a missed webhook is invisible by definition |
| Reconciliation mismatches | Local state vs gateway authoritative state, run continuously, not just at settlement (§35) |
| Intent-to-completion funnel | Intents created → attempted → succeeded → allocated to invoice → ledger entries written. A break between the last two is a silent money bug |
| Refunds and disputes | Volume and age |
| Settlement | Expected vs received settlement amounts, and settlement file processing status |
| Invoice generation | Success/failure at month start; numbering sequence integrity (a gap or reuse is a P0 — BR-003) |

---
### 48.11 The operational alert catalogue

Every alert below is an **operational** alert: its recipient is an engineer or an operator acting on the *platform*, not on a guard. Guard-safety alerts (SOS, unmanned post, missed wake check, geofence breach, panic, overdue patrol) are owned entirely by §24 and are deliberately absent here. Where an operational condition also degrades what operators can trust, the platform emits a `platform.degraded` signal that §24 renders as a console banner — one signal, two consumers, no duplicated logic.

**Who is paged** uses these targets: `ONCALL` = primary on-call engineer (pages 24/7 for P0, in-hours for P1); `ONCALL-BH` = business-hours ticket to on-call; `CTO` = secondary escalation; `CC` = Command Center shift lead (tier-0 triage per SUR-DVO-141); `FIN` = Finance; `SEC` = security responder; `TICKET` = queued, no page.

#### 48.11.1 Life-safety and real-time path (highest priority)

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-01** SOS path failure | Synthetic SOS probe fails once, or e2e >5 s on two consecutive probes | P0 | `ONCALL` + `CTO` immediately; `CC` notified | RB-SOS-01 | None — never auto-remediate the SOS path; failover to the retry endpoint is already automatic in the client |
| **OA-02** Escalation engine tick lag | `escalation.tick_lag_seconds` > 30 s for 2 min | P0 | `ONCALL` + `CC` | RB-ESC-01 | Restart the escalation worker once; if lag persists, page |
| **OA-10** Real-time gateway degraded | WebSocket probe fails 2× consecutively, or connection drop rate >20%/min, or gateway CPU >75% for 5 min | P1 | `ONCALL`; `CC` banner | RB-RT-01 | Scale gateway instances +1 (bounded); clients auto-fall-back to polling |
| **OA-14** GPS ingest lag | `gps.ingest.lag_seconds` p95 >30 s for 5 min | P1 | `ONCALL`; `CC` banner "map may be stale" | RB-GPS-01 | Scale the writer consumer group; if the signals group is the laggard, prioritise it |
| **OA-15** GPS ingest rate collapse | Ping rate drops >60% below the same-weekday, same-hour trailing 4-week baseline for 10 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-GPS-02 | None — this is almost always a client-side or ingest-endpoint fault needing diagnosis |
| **OA-20** Attendance write success drop | `attendance.write.success_ratio` < 98% over 10 min, or any 5-minute window <90% | P0 | `ONCALL` + `CC` | RB-ATT-01 | None |

#### 48.11.2 Infrastructure

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-41** Database primary CPU saturation | >80% for 10 min, or >90% for 3 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-DB-01 | Kill queries exceeding the statement timeout in the reporting role only; never kill OLTP queries automatically |
| **OA-42** Database connection saturation | Pool utilisation >85% for 5 min, or any connection wait >2 s | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-DB-02 | Recycle idle-in-transaction connections older than 5 min |
| **OA-43** Replication lag | Replica lag >30 s for 5 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-DB-03 | Route replica reads to primary with the reduced row cap (§46.3.4); throttle running backfills |
| **OA-44** Database storage headroom | <25% free, or projected exhaustion within 14 days at current growth | P1 (P0 at <10%) | `ONCALL` | RB-DB-04 | Trigger the partition-drop/archive job if a due one is pending; expand storage where the provider supports online expansion |
| **OA-51** Table bloat / autovacuum lag | Dead-tuple ratio >20% on a top-10 table, or autovacuum blocked >2 h | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-DB-05 | Schedule a manual vacuum in the next low-traffic window |
| **OA-50** Partition creation job missed | Tomorrow's `location` (and other daily-partitioned) partition does not exist by 18:00 IST | **P0** | `ONCALL` | RB-DB-06 | Create the missing partitions immediately, then alert regardless — this is a next-midnight total-write-failure condition and must never be silently fixed |
| **OA-45** Redis memory pressure | `used_memory` >80% of `maxmemory`, or any `evicted_keys` > 0, or stream length >90% of its cap | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-REDIS-01 | Trim non-critical streams to their cap; evict the lowest-priority cache namespace; **never** trim `gps.ingest` below the unacknowledged offset |
| **OA-46** Service instance unhealthy | Healthy instance count below the minimum for the tier's peak capacity, for 3 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-APP-01 | Replace the instance; scale out by one |
| **OA-47** API error-rate SLO fast burn | 5xx ratio consuming >2% of the monthly error budget in 1 h (multi-window burn, §48.13) | P0 | `ONCALL` | RB-APP-02 | Auto-rollback if within 30 min of a deploy (§47.12.1) |
| **OA-48** API latency SLO burn | p95 latency SLI consuming >5% of budget in 6 h | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-APP-03 | None |
| **OA-49** Object storage errors | Error ratio >1% for 5 min, or any 5xx on the upload path | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-OBJ-01 | Retry with backoff; client-side queueing already engaged |
| **OA-52** Worker pool starvation | Any queue's oldest message age >10× its normal p95, or a consumer group with zero active consumers | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-Q-01 | Restart the consumer group once; scale workers +1 |
| **OA-03** Certificate / domain / DNS expiry or drift | TLS cert <21 days; domain <60 days; any change to NS/MX/SPF/DKIM/DMARC vs the expected set | P1 (P0 at <7 days) | `ONCALL` + `CTO` | RB-DNS-01 | None — every remediation here is a deliberate human act |
| **OA-04** Public site down | 2 consecutive probe failures from 2 vantage points | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-WEB-01 | CDN serves stale-while-revalidate from cache automatically |
| **OA-05** API health endpoint failing | 2 consecutive failures | P0 | `ONCALL` | RB-APP-04 | Instance replacement |
| **OA-08** Infrastructure drift detected | Scheduled `terraform plan` shows any production diff | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-IAC-01 | None — codify or revert within 24 h (SUR-SEC-142) |
| **OA-09** Application configuration drift | Runtime config differs from declared expected state | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-CFG-01 | None |

#### 48.11.3 Application

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-06** Login / OTP failure | `login.success_ratio` <90% over 10 min, or `otp.delivery_ratio` <85% over 15 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-AUTH-01 | Fail over to the secondary OTP/SMS provider |
| **OA-07** Rate-limit rejection spike | Rejections >10× the trailing 7-day p95 for a scope, sustained 10 min | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-RL-01 | None — first determine whether it is abuse or a buggy client version (the `app_version` label answers this) |
| **OA-19** Mobile release health regression | Crash-free sessions <99.0% on a release with ≥200 sessions, or ANR >0.5%, or a crash affecting >1% of sessions | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-MOB-01 | Halt staged rollout automatically |
| **OA-22** Queue backlog / outbox lag / DLQ | Outbox oldest row >120 s; or any queue's oldest message >10 min; or `dlq.depth` > 0 for >1 h | P1 (P0 if outbox >10 min) | `ONCALL` | RB-Q-02 | Scale relay/consumers; DLQ items are never auto-replayed without inspection |
| **OA-32** Report job failures or backlog | Report failure ratio >5% over 1 h, or oldest queued report >15 min | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-RPT-01 | Scale the report worker lane; shed the lowest-priority scheduled reports |
| **OA-37** Document/OCR queue ageing | Oldest unprocessed document >2 h | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-DOC-01 | Scale the OCR lane; the manual verification path continues regardless |
| **OA-11** AI response latency breach | p95 exceeds the §25.11 budget for the interaction class by >50% over 15 min | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-AI-01 | Switch to the fallback model; degrade to the deterministic path |
| **OA-12** AI error ratio | >5% over 15 min, or provider 5xx/429 >2% | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-AI-02 | Circuit-break the provider; AI panels hide per §41.5.5 |
| **OA-16** GPS duplicate ratio rise | Duplicate ratio >5% for a single `app_version` over 1 h | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-GPS-03 | None — this is a client defect; the label names the culprit version |
| **OA-17/OA-18** Offline backlog growth | Median device backlog >500 events, or p95 sync completion >10 min, sustained 30 min | P2 (P1 if >20% of devices affected) | `ONCALL` | RB-SYNC-01 | Relax the replay rate limit if the cause is our throttle; otherwise none |
| **OA-21** Offline attendance share spike | Offline share of check-ins >3× the trailing 4-week same-weekday baseline | P2 | `ONCALL-BH`; `CC` informed | RB-SYNC-02 | None — usually a field network event, occasionally our ingest endpoint |

#### 48.11.4 Domain and data integrity

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-23** Notification delivery ratio drop | Accepted-by-provider ratio <95% for any channel over 15 min; or delivered-ratio <85% where receipts exist | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-NTF-01 | Circuit-break and re-route per §36.4.4 |
| **OA-24** Notification latency breach | P0/P1 latency SLA (§36.4.5) missed on >5% of sends over 15 min | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-NTF-02 | Prioritise the critical lane; shed P3 |
| **OA-25** Provider circuit breaker opened | Any notification/payment/SMS provider breaker opens | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-PRV-01 | Automatic re-route already engaged; alert exists so a human confirms the fallback is actually working |
| **OA-26** Fan-out duration breach | Roster-publish fan-out exceeds SUR-NFR-055 target | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-NTF-03 | Scale the fan-out lane |
| **OA-27** Payment success ratio drop | <90% over 30 min with ≥20 attempts | P1 | `ONCALL` + `FIN` | RB-PAY-01 | None — never retry payments automatically beyond the gateway's own retry semantics |
| **OA-28** Payment webhook lag or gap | Webhook processing lag >5 min, or a detected gap in the gateway event sequence | P1 | `ONCALL` + `FIN` | RB-PAY-02 | Trigger a reconciliation pull from the gateway API |
| **OA-29** Payment reconciliation mismatch | Any local-vs-gateway mismatch that survives one reconciliation cycle | **P0** | `ONCALL` + `FIN` + `CTO` | RB-PAY-03 | None — money discrepancies are never auto-corrected |
| **OA-35** Invoice generation failure | Any failure in the month-start invoice run, or a gap/reuse in an invoice number sequence | **P0** for numbering; P1 for failures | `ONCALL` + `FIN` | RB-FIN-01 | Retry the failed invoice generation once; numbering anomalies never auto-remediate (BR-003) |
| **OA-36** Payroll run duration or failure | Run exceeds SUR-NFR-056 target by 50%, or any run fails | P1 | `ONCALL` + `FIN` | RB-FIN-02 | Resume from checkpoint |
| **OA-31** Tenant resource hotspot | Any tenant >15% of database CPU-seconds over 7 days, or >30% over 1 h | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-TEN-01 | Apply the per-tenant query throttle at Scale; at MVP, investigate |
| **OA-34** Geofence rejection spike | Check-in geofence rejection ratio >3× the site's trailing 14-day baseline, for a single site, ≥5 occurrences | P2 | `ONCALL-BH`; `CC` informed | RB-GEO-01 | None — the usual cause is a geofence edited wrongly, and the runbook's first step is to check the geofence audit trail, not to suspect the guards |
| **OA-30** PII detected in logs | Log-pipeline detector matches an identifier-shaped value | P1 (privacy incident) | `ONCALL` + `CTO` | RB-PRIV-01 | Quarantine the affected log index from general access; never auto-delete (deletion destroys the evidence needed to find the leak) |
| **OA-53** Reconciliation job failure | Any `recon.*` job (§32.4) fails or reports an unexpected discrepancy | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-REC-01 | Re-run once; a second failure escalates |
| **OA-54** Retention/purge job anomaly | Retention job fails, or purges a row count >3× its 30-day average | **P0** on over-purge | `ONCALL` + `CTO` | RB-RET-01 | **Halt the purge job immediately on an over-purge signal** — a runaway retention job is an accidental mass deletion in progress (§49.8 S4) |
| **OA-55** Backup verification failure | Nightly automated restore-and-verify fails, or a backup is missing | **P0** | `ONCALL` + `CTO` | RB-DR-01 | Retry the backup immediately; failure to produce a verified backup for 24 h is a P0 that stays open |

#### 48.11.5 Operational security (response-side only — detection content is §38.11)

These four exist because a security detection needs an *operational* response path with a page and a runbook. The detection logic, the event catalogue and the investigation process belong to §38 and are not restated.

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-56** Security detection escalated to operations | Any §38.11 detection rated Critical by the detection layer | P0 | `SEC`/`CTO` + `ONCALL` | RB-SEC-01 (points into §38's incident process) | Per §38; typically session revocation or credential disablement |
| **OA-57** Authentication anomaly volume | Failed-login rate >20× the trailing 7-day p95, or credential-stuffing pattern detected | P1 | `ONCALL` + `SEC` | RB-SEC-02 | Tighten rate limits on the auth endpoints; enable step-up challenge |
| **OA-58** WAF / edge anomaly | WAF block rate >10× baseline, or a sustained volumetric attack signature | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-SEC-03 | Provider DDoS mitigation engages automatically; escalate rule set |
| **OA-59** Privileged or bulk-export action outside policy | A privileged administrative action or a bulk export exceeding the §38 threshold, outside declared hours or without an approval record | P1 | `SEC` + `CTO` | RB-SEC-04 | None — human judgement required |

#### 48.11.6 Business anomaly detection

These are the alerts that catch **silent** breakage: the system reports no errors, every dashboard is green, and yet something has stopped working. In a product where a missed attendance record becomes an unpaid guard, silent failure is the most expensive failure mode there is.

Every alert in this group compares against a **same-weekday, same-hour, trailing-4-week baseline**, because this business has a strong weekly shape (weekend site coverage differs from weekday) and a strong daily shape (shift bands). Comparing today against yesterday would fire every Monday and every Saturday and would be ignored within a fortnight.

| Alert | Condition / threshold | Severity | Who is paged | Runbook | Auto-remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OA-33** Attendance submission volume drop | Attendance submissions in a shift-change window fall **>40% below** the same-weekday, same-window trailing 4-week baseline, with ≥50 expected submissions | **P0** | `ONCALL` + `CC` | RB-ANOM-01 | None. First question the runbook asks: is this a platform fault, an app-version fault, or a genuine operational event (a bandh, a holiday, a large contract ending)? The `app_version`, tenant and geography breakdowns answer it in under two minutes. |
| **OA-60** Attendance volume spike | >200% of baseline | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-ANOM-02 | None — usually duplicate submission from a client defect |
| **OA-61** SOS volume anomaly — both directions | SOS count >5× baseline (possible mass event or a client bug generating false SOS) **or** zero SOS platform-wide for 72 h while >1,000 guards are on duty (possible silent SOS path breakage that the synthetic probe's narrow path did not catch) | P1 both directions | `ONCALL` + `CC` | RB-ANOM-03 | None |
| **OA-62** Notification volume collapse | Sends in an hour <40% of baseline | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-ANOM-04 | None — a collapse usually means the event source stopped, not the notifier |
| **OA-63** Payment/booking volume collapse | Successful payments or new bookings <40% of baseline over 3 h during business hours | P1 | `ONCALL` + `FIN` | RB-ANOM-05 | None |
| **OA-64** Guard onboarding / document verification throughput collapse | Verification completions <40% of baseline over a business day | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-ANOM-06 | None |
| **OA-65** Patrol / wake-check completion collapse | Completions <50% of baseline for a night, platform-wide | P1 | `ONCALL` + `CC` | RB-ANOM-07 | None — this is both a platform signal and a §24 operational signal, and the runbook explicitly requires informing the Command Center before assuming a bug |
| **OA-38** Infrastructure cost anomaly | Any service's daily spend >40% above its trailing 7-day mean | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-COST-01 | None — the runbook's first hypothesis is a defect (retry storm, runaway job, log flood), not a pricing change |
| **OA-39** AI cost budget breach | Daily AI spend >80% of the configured budget, or any interaction class exceeding its per-interaction ceiling on >5% of calls | P2 | `ONCALL-BH` | RB-AI-03 | Throttle the affected interaction class; degrade to the deterministic path |
| **OA-40** Desktop update manifest invalid | Manifest signature or artefact hash verification fails | P1 | `ONCALL` | RB-DESK-01 | None — serving a bad manifest to auto-updating desktop clients is worse than serving none |

**Total: 64 operational alerts** (OA-01 to OA-65, with OA-13 folded into OA-39). The catalogue is deliberately large because this system has more *silent* failure modes than a typical SaaS product — attendance that stops being recorded, notifications that stop being sent, a partition that was never created — none of which produce an error anywhere. §48.14's fatigue policy exists precisely to stop that number growing without discipline, and the 60-alert ceiling in that policy is already in force.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-060 | Every alert shall have a documented condition, severity, recipient, runbook link and auto-remediation stance before it is enabled. |
| SUR-OBS-061 | Business-anomaly alerts shall compare against a same-weekday, same-hour, trailing-4-week baseline, and shall require a minimum expected volume so that low-volume periods do not generate noise. |
| SUR-OBS-062 | No alert shall auto-remediate a financial, retention, deletion or security condition; those halt and page. |
| SUR-OBS-063 | Auto-remediation actions shall be logged as audit events with the triggering alert, and a remediation that fires more than twice in 24 hours shall escalate to a page rather than continue silently. |
| SUR-OBS-064 | Operational alerts shall never be delivered into the §24 Command Center alert queue; where operators need to know, the platform emits a `platform.degraded` signal rendered as a console banner. |

### 48.12 Engineering dashboards

Named dashboards with named panels, per the canon's concreteness rule. Each panel states what it shows and what a bad value looks like.

| Dashboard | Panels |
|---|---|
| **D1 — Platform overview** (the wallboard for engineering) | (1) SLO status tile per tier T0–T4 with error-budget remaining as a bar; (2) request rate and 5xx ratio, 24 h; (3) p50/p95/p99 latency, 24 h, overlaid with deploy markers; (4) active incidents; (5) synthetic probe grid — one square per probe, green/amber/red; (6) SOS e2e latency last hour; (7) attendance write success ratio; (8) outbox lag; (9) database primary CPU and connections; (10) current release version and time since deploy |
| **D2 — API and services** | Per-route RED table sorted by error rate then by p95; top 10 slowest routes; top 10 highest-traffic routes; error breakdown by class and code; rate-limit rejections by scope; per-tenant request share (top 10); dependency call latency (database, Redis, object storage, each external provider) |
| **D3 — GPS pipeline** | Ingest rate split live/replay; ingest lag p50/p95/p99; stream length and consumer-group lag per group; devices reporting vs guards expected on duty; accuracy distribution; mock-location and implausible-movement counts; read-model freshness; partition status for today and tomorrow; write batch size and duration |
| **D4 — Attendance and field operations** | Check-in/out volume vs baseline by shift band; success ratio by method; geofence rejection ratio; offline share; sync backlog distribution; wake-check and patrol-scan completion vs baseline; per-tenant top-10 failure counts |
| **D5 — Notifications** | Funnel per channel (enqueued → attempted → accepted → delivered); latency per priority against §36.4.5; provider error ratio and breaker state; fan-out job duration; cost per channel per day; suppressed-by-quiet-hours count; missing-translation fallback count |
| **D6 — Payments and finance** | Success ratio by method; funnel intent → success → allocated → ledgered; webhook lag and gap detector; reconciliation mismatch count and age; refunds and disputes; invoice generation status at month start; payroll run status and duration; settlement status |
| **D7 — Database** | CPU, memory, IOPS, connections, replication lag; slow-query top 20 with tenant attribution; lock waits and blocked queries; table and index sizes top 20; bloat and autovacuum status; partition inventory; per-tenant CPU-seconds share; WAL generation rate |
| **D8 — Queues and jobs** | Depth and oldest-age per queue; consumer lag; job success/failure/retry by type; DLQ contents with age; scheduled-job heartbeat grid (green = ran on time); longest-running jobs |
| **D9 — Mobile and desktop release health** | Version distribution across the fleet (Guard App, per tenant); crash-free sessions and users per release; ANR rate; staged-rollout position; payload-parse failure rate per app version; app-config fetch success; desktop update success/failure rate per platform and version |
| **D10 — AI operations** | Interactions by class; latency vs §25.11 budget; error ratio by model and type; cost per day vs budget and cost per interaction; guardrail block counts; approval-card acceptance/rejection rates (which is also an §41 governance signal); fallback-model usage |
| **D11 — SLO and error budget** | Per-SLO: current attainment, budget remaining, burn rate at 1 h/6 h/3 d windows, and time-to-exhaustion at current burn; a history of budget consumption by month |
| **D12 — Cost** | Daily spend by service and environment; spend per active guard; spend per tenant; observability ingest volume and cost; top movers week-over-week; non-production spend and shutdown compliance |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-070 | The twelve dashboards above shall exist, shall be defined as code alongside the SLO definitions, and shall be reviewed for usefulness quarterly; a panel nobody has looked at during any incident in two quarters is removed. |
| SUR-OBS-071 | Deploy markers shall be overlaid on every latency and error panel, because "did this start with a release?" is the first question in most incidents. |

### 48.13 SLOs and error budgets

#### 48.13.1 SLI definitions

An SLO without a precisely defined SLI is decoration. Each SLI states its numerator, denominator and data source.

| SLO | SLI definition | Target (MVP) | Target (Scale) | Window |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SLO-1 SOS availability** | Successful synthetic SOS probes ÷ total probes, where "successful" means the alert was observable on the synthetic console lane within 5 s | 99.9% | 99.95% | 28 d rolling |
| **SLO-2 SOS latency** | Probes completing within 5 s ÷ total probes | 95% | 95% | 28 d |
| **SLO-3 Attendance write success** | Check-in/out requests returning success (including offline-accepted) ÷ total attempted, measured server-side plus client-reported attempts | 99.5% | 99.9% | 28 d |
| **SLO-4 API availability (T1)** | Non-5xx responses ÷ total responses on T1 routes, excluding 4xx caused by client error | 99.5% | 99.9% | 28 d |
| **SLO-5 API latency (T1)** | Requests under the route's p95 target ÷ total | 95% | 95% | 28 d |
| **SLO-6 Console availability (T2)** | Successful synthetic journey completions ÷ attempts | 99.5% | 99.9% | 28 d |
| **SLO-7 GPS freshness** | Pings processed within 30 s of `recorded_at` ÷ total pings | 99% | 99.5% | 7 d |
| **SLO-8 Notification P0 delivery** | P0 notifications accepted by a provider within 5 s ÷ total P0 | 98% | 99% | 28 d |
| **SLO-9 Payment success** | Successful payments ÷ attempted, excluding customer-side declines (insufficient funds, cancelled) | 95% | 97% | 28 d |
| **SLO-10 Offline sync completeness** | Queued client events successfully persisted within 24 h of connectivity ÷ total queued | 99.9% | 99.9% | 28 d |

**On SLO-9's exclusion.** Excluding customer-side declines is a judgement call and it is stated openly: a bank declining a card is not our failure, and including it would make the SLO measure the Indian card ecosystem rather than our system. The *unfiltered* success ratio is still dashboarded, because it is what the business feels.

#### 48.13.2 Burn-rate alerting

Alerting on "SLO breached" is too late; alerting on every dip is noise. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting solves both.

| Burn rate | Budget consumed | Windows (long / short) | Action | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14.4× | 2% in 1 h | 1 h / 5 min | **Page** | At this rate the month's budget is gone in ~2 days |
| 6× | 5% in 6 h | 6 h / 30 min | **Page** | Gone in ~5 days |
| 3× | 10% in 1 d | 24 h / 2 h | Ticket | Gone in ~10 days |
| 1× | 10% in 3 d | 72 h / 6 h | Ticket | On pace to exactly exhaust the budget |

The short window is required to be breaching simultaneously, which prevents an alert firing on a burn that has already stopped.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-080 | Every SLO shall be defined as code with its SLI query, target, window and burn-rate alert thresholds, versioned in the repository. |
| SUR-OBS-081 | Burn-rate alerting shall use multi-window, multi-rate conditions; a single-window "SLO breached" alert shall not be used. |
| SUR-OBS-082 | Error-budget status shall gate release cadence per the policy in §46.3.3, automatically where the pipeline can evaluate it. |

---

### 48.14 The alert-fatigue policy

An alert that does not lead to action trains the team to ignore alerts, and the alert that matters arrives into that trained indifference. This policy exists to keep the catalogue small enough to be believed.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Every alert is actionable** | If the recipient's correct response is "nothing", it is not an alert. It may be a dashboard panel, a weekly report, or a ticket — but it does not page and does not go to the alert channel. |
| **Every alert has a runbook** | No runbook, no alert (SUR-NFR-147). Creating the alert and the runbook is one task, not two. |
| **Page budget** | ≤2 pages per on-call person per week (§47.16.1). Exceeding it for two consecutive weeks triggers a mandatory review of the firing alerts, at which each is fixed, tuned, downgraded to a ticket, or deleted. |
| **Page vs ticket** | Page only if it needs human action **now** and delay causes harm. Everything else is a ticket in business hours. A backlog that will drain overnight is not a page. |
| **Quiet hours** | P2 and P3 never page between 23:00 and 07:00 IST; they queue. P0 and P1 always page. |
| **The five-fires rule** | Any alert that fires more than five times in a quarter without a corrective action being taken is, by definition, either misconfigured or describing an accepted condition. At the quarterly review it is retuned, automated away, or deleted. There is no fourth option, and "we'll look at it later" is not permitted to survive two consecutive reviews. |
| **Every page is reviewed** | At the weekly on-call handover, every page from the past week is reviewed in one line: was it real, was it actionable, was the runbook correct, should it exist? The handover notes are the record. |
| **Flapping suppression** | An alert that resolves and re-fires within its evaluation window is grouped, not re-sent; an alert flapping more than three times in an hour is auto-suppressed for an hour with a single notification stating the suppression. |
| **Grouping and dependency** | When a root-cause alert fires (database down), dependent alerts (every API SLO burning) are grouped under it rather than paging separately. Dependency relationships are declared in the alert definitions. |
| **Maintenance silencing** | Silences are time-bounded (maximum 8 hours), require a reason, and expire automatically. An indefinite silence is not available; a permanently silenced alert should be deleted instead, honestly. |
| **Ownership** | Every alert has a named owner responsible for its precision. Ownership transfers with the module, not with the person who happened to create it. |
| **New alerts require a deletion candidate** | Once the catalogue exceeds 60 alerts, adding one requires nominating one for review. This is a blunt instrument and it works. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-OBS-090 | An alert that cannot state the action its recipient should take shall not be created. |
| SUR-OBS-091 | Every page shall be reviewed at the weekly handover; the review outcome shall be recorded. |
| SUR-OBS-092 | Any alert firing more than five times in a quarter without corrective action shall be retuned, automated or deleted at the quarterly alert review. |
| SUR-OBS-093 | Alert silences shall be time-bounded to a maximum of 8 hours and shall require a reason; permanent silencing is prohibited. |
| SUR-OBS-094 | Alert dependency grouping shall be declared, so that a single root cause produces a single page. |
