## 49. Backup & Disaster Recovery

### 49.0 Principles

| # | Principle | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **An untested backup is not a backup.** | Restore testing is a scheduled, automated, failing-loudly obligation (§49.5), not an annual intention. |
| 2 | **A replica is not a backup.** | A replica faithfully replicates a `DELETE FROM guard`. Replication protects against hardware failure; backups protect against *us*. |
| 3 | **A backup is not an archive.** | Backups exist to restore a system to a recent working state. Long-term legal retention (§40.7.3, 8 years) is an archive with its own store, its own format and its own access controls. Conflating them produces 8-year-old backups nobody can restore into a schema that no longer exists. |
| 4 | **Assume the attacker has our credentials.** | Backups are immutable, in a separate account, with separate keys (SUR-SEC-102). A backup an administrator can delete is a backup ransomware can delete. |
| 5 | **Restore is a business process, not a database operation.** | Bringing Postgres back does not bring the *business* back: gateways moved on, notifications were sent, guards kept working offline. §49.10 and §49.11 exist because of this. |
| 6 | **The safety function must survive the platform.** | If everything is down, SOS still has to work. §49.12 specifies how, on paper, with phones. |

Normative IDs use `SUR-DR-nnn`.

---

### 49.1 What is backed up, how, and what deliberately is not

| Asset | Method | Frequency | Retention | Encryption / location | Restore test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Transactional Postgres** | Managed automated backup + continuous WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery; plus a weekly independent logical dump (`pg_dump`, schema + data) as a format-independent safety net | Base: daily. WAL: continuous (≤5 min segments). Logical: weekly | Daily 30 d · weekly 12 w · monthly 12 m · yearly 8 y (financial and audit subsets) | Provider-managed encryption with a **backup-specific KMS key** distinct from the production data key (SUR-SEC-102); replicated to the second Indian region; a copy in a separate cloud account with object-lock | Automated nightly; full timed drill monthly |
| **Object storage** (documents, attendance photos, SOS audio/images, exports, generated PDFs) | Bucket versioning + lifecycle + **cross-region replication** to the second Indian region + object-lock (compliance mode) on the immutable classes (SOS evidence, signed invoices, audit exports) | Continuous replication | Per §40.7.3 record class; versions retained 90 d | Server-side encryption with a customer-managed key; replica bucket in a separate account | Monthly sampled object restore + checksum verification |
| **Audit log store** | Append-only store with its own backup chain, object-locked, replicated | Continuous | 8 years (§40.7.3), cold after 18 months | Separate key, separate account, write-once | Quarterly restore-and-verify of a sampled window |
| **Secrets and KMS key material** | Secret store's own backup, exported under dual control to an encrypted offline package held by two custodians; KMS keys replicated per provider capability; key metadata and rotation history documented | On change, and quarterly full export | 3 generations | Offline package encrypted with a key held separately from the package; stored in two physical locations | **Annual key-recovery drill** (§49.3) |
| **Infrastructure as code** | Git, mirrored to a second hosted provider and to an offline bundle refreshed weekly | On every commit | Full history | Repository provider encryption; the offline bundle encrypted | Included in the annual rebuild-from-scratch exercise |
| **Business configuration** (tenant settings, compliance rules and versions, notification templates, rate cards, escalation ladders) | Lives in Postgres — covered by the database backup. Additionally exported nightly as a human-readable JSON snapshot to object storage | Nightly | 90 days | As object storage | Included in the monthly drill's verification queries |
| **Application configuration and feature flags** | In Postgres + nightly JSON export | Nightly | 90 days | As above | Verified in drills |
| **Signed release artefacts** (container images, mobile builds, desktop installers, update manifests) | Registry/artefact store with immutability; retained for at least the compatibility window | On release | Container images 12 m; mobile/desktop builds ≥18 m (covers the 12-month compatibility window with margin) | Registry encryption; signatures verified on restore | Quarterly: pull an old artefact and verify signature + deployability |
| **Runbooks and DR documentation** | Repository + a wiki on an independent provider + **an offline PDF bundle refreshed weekly and held by every on-call engineer and by the Command Center** | Weekly | Current + 4 prior | Encrypted device storage; printed copy in the Command Center's sealed continuity folder | Verified at every quarterly drill by using only the offline copy |
| **Command Center continuity data** (guard/supervisor/site/client/police contact roster, site SOPs, gate instructions for Critical sites) | Nightly encrypted export to two operator workstations + a printed copy refreshed weekly | Nightly export, weekly print | Current + 1 prior | AES-encrypted file, passphrase under dual custody; printed copy in a sealed folder | Quarterly continuity drill (§49.12) |

#### 49.1.1 What is deliberately not backed up

| Not backed up | Why | Rebuild path and time |
|---|---|---|
| Redis cache namespaces | Derived; rebuilding is a cold-cache period, not data loss | Automatic on demand; ~15 min of elevated database load |
| Redis rate-limit and session-adjacent counters | Ephemeral by design; loss means a brief window of relaxed limits | Immediate |
| **Redis `gps.ingest` stream contents** | Bounded, in-flight ping data classified D2 (§46.4.1) | **Partially recoverable**: the Guard App retains its local buffer for 7 days and the server's acknowledgement is only issued after the writer consumer commits, so unacknowledged pings are re-sent by the client. Genuinely lost: pings acknowledged but not yet written — bounded to the stream's un-drained window, typically seconds. **Check-ins never travel this path** (§34.3.3), which is the whole reason the classification holds. |
| Derived read models (`guard_last_position`, dashboard aggregates, materialised views) | Rebuildable from source tables | Rebuild job; 10–40 min at MVP volume |
| Search index | Rebuildable from Postgres | Reindex job; ~30 min at MVP, ~4 h at Scale — **the rebuild time is the requirement**, and it is why search degrades to database `ILIKE` queries with a reduced result cap during a reindex rather than being unavailable |
| Analytical store / warehouse | Derived from the OLTP source and the event stream | Full rebuild; hours. Acceptable because no decision of record is made solely from it |
| Geocode cache | A cost optimisation only | Refills naturally; a temporary rise in map-provider spend |
| CDN caches, generated thumbnails, rendered map tiles | Derived | Regenerated on demand |
| Observability data (logs, metrics, traces) | Diagnostic, time-bounded, high volume, low restore value | Not restored. **Exception: security event logs and the audit store are backed up** — they are evidence, not diagnostics |
| Non-production environment data | Synthetic by construction (§47.2.2) | Regenerated by the seed generator in minutes |
| Preview and CI ephemeral state | Disposable | — |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-001 | Every data store shall be classified as backed-up or deliberately-not-backed-up, with the rebuild path and rebuild time recorded for the latter; an unclassified store shall be treated as a gap and remediated. |
| SUR-DR-002 | The classification shall be reviewed whenever a new data store is introduced, as part of the architecture review. |
| SUR-DR-003 | Rebuild times for non-backed-up derived stores shall be measured, not estimated, at least annually. |

---

### 49.2 Backup mechanics per store

| Store | Mechanism detail |
|---|---|
| Postgres PITR | Continuous WAL archiving to object storage in the primary region, replicated to the second region. Recovery to any second within the retention window. WAL archiving failure is alert **OA-55** at P0 — a PITR window silently stopping is the failure mode that is only discovered when you need it. |
| Postgres logical dump | A weekly `pg_dump` in custom format, per-schema, stored separately. This exists because a physical backup is bound to a Postgres major version and to the provider's backup format; a logical dump can be restored into a different provider, a different version, or a laptop. It is the insurance against provider-level catastrophe (§49.8 S6) and is the artefact used in the annual exit-readiness exercise (SUR-DVO-013). |
| Partitioned `location` table | Detached historical partitions are archived to object storage as compressed files at the 90-day tier boundary (§32.5) and are then outside the database backup entirely. Their restore path is documented and tested annually; restoring 13-month-old GPS history is an offline analytical operation, not a production one. |
| Object storage | Versioning protects against overwrite and delete; replication protects against regional loss; object-lock in compliance mode protects against a compromised administrator. Lifecycle transitions to infrequent-access at 90 days and archive at 365 days for eligible classes (§50.7). |
| Audit store | Append-only by construction (§38.12); backed up with the same immutability guarantees. Restoring audit data is a distinct procedure because it must never overwrite existing entries — restore is always into a separate namespace followed by a reconciled merge that can only add. |

---

### 49.3 Encryption and key custody

| Aspect | Specification |
|---|---|
| Keys | Backups are encrypted with KMS keys **distinct from the production data keys** (SUR-SEC-102), held in a separate account/project, with a separate key policy and separate administrators. |
| Access | Restoring requires two people: one who can access the backup store and one who can access the decryption key. Neither role alone can read a backup. This is dual control, and it is also why the annual drill must exercise both. |
| Immutability | Object-lock (compliance mode) for the retention window on the immutable classes, so that even the account root cannot delete within the window. |
| **The key-loss problem** | If the backup key is lost, the backup is a random-number generator's output. Mitigation: key material is replicated per the provider's multi-region key capability; key metadata, aliases, policies and rotation history are exported to the encrypted offline package (§49.1); and an **annual key-recovery drill** restores a backup using only the offline package and the documented procedure, with the elapsed time recorded. A drill that cannot complete is a P0 finding. |
| Rotation | Backup keys rotate annually. Rotation never re-encrypts old backups in place; older backups remain readable with their generation's key, and key generations are retained for the full backup retention period. This is stated because "we rotated the key" has destroyed more backups than any attacker. |
| Restoration into lower environments | Prohibited without the masking pipeline (SUR-SEC-100). The restore-test environment is the only exception, and it is isolated, unreachable and destroyed after verification (§47.2.1). |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-010 | Backups shall be encrypted with keys distinct from production data keys, held in a separate account under separate administration. |
| SUR-DR-011 | Restoration shall require dual control; no single identity shall be able to both access and decrypt a backup. |
| SUR-DR-012 | Key generations shall be retained for the full backup retention period; rotation shall never render an in-retention backup unreadable. |
| SUR-DR-013 | An annual key-recovery drill shall restore a backup using only the offline key package and documented procedure, with the result recorded. |

---

### 49.4 Retention schedule, and the tension with erasure rights

| Class | Daily | Weekly | Monthly | Yearly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full database | 30 days | 12 weeks | 12 months | 8 years for the financial/audit logical subset only |
| WAL / PITR | 30 days continuous | — | — | — |
| Object storage versions | 90 days | — | — | Per record class (§40.7.3) |
| Audit store | — | — | 18 months hot | 8 years cold |
| Secrets/key package | — | — | 3 generations | — |
| Configuration snapshots | 90 days | — | — | — |

#### 49.4.1 Erasure requests versus backups — the honest position

A data-subject erasure request (§39) deletes from live systems. It does not, and practically cannot, surgically edit an encrypted point-in-time backup. The platform's stated position:

1. Erasure is executed against all **live** stores within the SLA (SUR-NFR-121).
2. Backups are **not** edited. Editing a backup destroys its integrity and its restorability, and a backup with selectively removed rows is no longer a consistent snapshot.
3. A **suppression record** is created: an entry in a tamper-evident erasure ledger listing the subject identifiers erased and the date. Any restore of a backup taken before the erasure date **must** re-apply the suppression list as part of the documented restore procedure, before the restored data is used. This step is a mandatory, verified item in the restore runbook and in the restore verification checklist (§49.9).
4. Backups age out on the retention schedule, at which point the data is gone by expiry.
5. This position is documented in the privacy notice (§39) rather than being an internal secret, because a data subject is entitled to know that erasure from backups occurs by expiry, not by surgery.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-020 | Erasure shall be applied to live stores and recorded in a suppression ledger; backups shall not be edited. |
| SUR-DR-021 | Any restore from a backup predating an erasure shall re-apply the suppression ledger before the restored data is used, as a verified step in the restore procedure. |
| SUR-DR-022 | The backup-erasure position shall be documented in the privacy notice. |

---

### 49.5 Restore testing

**An untested backup is not a backup.** This subsection is the enforcement of that sentence.

| Test | Cadence | Scope | Pass criteria | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Automated restore-and-verify** | **Nightly** | Restore the previous night's base backup + WAL to a point 10 minutes before the backup completed, into the isolated ephemeral restore-test environment | All verification queries in §49.9 pass; row counts within expected tolerance; the restore completes within the RTO target | Automated; failure is **OA-55 at P0** |
| **Timed full-restore drill** | **Monthly** | Full production-sized restore, timed end to end, including application start-up against the restored database and a smoke suite | Completes within RTO (SUR-NFR-172); all verification queries pass; the elapsed time is recorded and trended | On-call engineer, rotating |
| **Object storage restore** | Monthly | Restore a sampled set of 100 objects across classes from the replica and from a prior version; verify checksums | 100% byte-identical | Automated |
| **PITR to an arbitrary point** | Quarterly | Restore to a randomly chosen timestamp in the retention window | Succeeds; data at that timestamp is internally consistent | On-call engineer |
| **Audit-store restore** | Quarterly | Restore a sampled window and verify the hash chain / append-only integrity | Chain intact, no gaps | CTO |
| **Key-recovery drill** | Annual | Restore using only the offline key package (§49.3) | Succeeds within 4 hours | CTO + second custodian |
| **Cross-account / exit-readiness restore** | Annual | Restore database and object storage into a different cloud account (and, at Scale, a different provider's object storage) | Succeeds; gaps documented | CTO |
| **Full DR game day** | Quarterly | A declared scenario from §49.8 executed end to end with the team, using only runbooks | Recovery achieved within the scenario's RTO; runbook corrections captured | CTO (as IC) |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-030 | An automated restore-and-verify shall run nightly; a failure shall raise P0 and shall remain open until a verified backup exists. |
| SUR-DR-031 | A timed full-restore drill shall run monthly, with the elapsed time recorded and trended; a drill exceeding the RTO target is a finding requiring a remediation plan. |
| SUR-DR-032 | A backup that has never been successfully restored shall not be counted as satisfying any RPO/RTO commitment, internally or in a client contract. |
| SUR-DR-033 | Restore drills shall be executed using only the runbooks, by an engineer who did not write them, at least once per quarter. |

---

### 49.6 RPO and RTO per component

The single most common error in DR planning is quoting one RPO/RTO pair for "the database". Different failure modes have completely different recovery mechanisms and therefore completely different numbers. The table below is organised by **failure mode**, which is what makes it usable at 3 a.m.

#### 49.6.1 MVP tier

| Failure mode | Recovery mechanism | RPO | RTO | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Database instance failure (hardware, process crash) | Managed automatic failover to the multi-AZ standby | ~0 (synchronous standby) | **≤15 min** | Provider-managed failover typically completes in 60–180 s; the remainder is connection-pool recovery, cache warm-up and verification. 15 minutes is what we will defend, not the best case we might see. |
| AZ loss | Same failover; application tier reschedules into surviving AZs | ~0 | **≤20 min** | Adds instance rescheduling and capacity acquisition in the remaining AZs |
| Logical corruption or accidental deletion | PITR restore to just before the event, into a side instance, then reconcile (§49.8 S3/S4) | **≤5 min** (WAL segment interval) | **≤4 h** for a full restore of ~500 GB; **≤1 h** for a targeted table-level restore-and-merge | The dominant cost is not the restore — it is *determining the correct point in time*. The runbook's first phase is establishing the timeline from the audit log, and it is budgeted at 30–60 minutes. |
| Redis loss | Rebuild; clients replay | Bounded to the un-drained ingest window (seconds of D2 data) | **≤10 min** | Cache rebuild plus stream re-creation; no D0 data at risk |
| Object storage object loss/corruption | Version restore or replica restore | ≤15 min (replication lag) | **≤30 min** for targeted objects | Versioning makes single-object recovery near-instant |
| Application tier failure | Redeploy from the immutable artefact | 0 | **≤10 min** | Stateless tier |
| **Full region loss** | Restore from cross-region backups into the second Indian region; rebuild infrastructure from IaC | **≤15 min** | **≤24 h** | **This is the honest number for MVP.** With backups replicated but no warm standby, recovery means: provision infrastructure from IaC (1–2 h), restore the database (3–4 h), restore/verify object storage access (1 h), DNS and certificate cutover (1 h), verification and smoke (2 h), plus decision time, coordination and the inevitable surprises. Quoting 4 hours here without a warm standby would be a lie, and the manual continuity protocol (§49.12) is what covers the gap. |
| Provider account compromise or lockout | Rebuild in a separate account from the out-of-account backup copy | ≤24 h (copy frequency) | **≤48 h** | §49.8 S6 |

#### 49.6.2 Enterprise / Scale tier

| Failure mode | Mechanism | RPO | RTO | What changes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Database instance failure | Same, with a pre-warmed connection pool and faster health detection | ~0 | **≤5 min** | Tuned failover detection; connection proxy that survives failover |
| Logical corruption / deletion | PITR with a continuously maintained delayed replica (1-hour lag) for instant "just before" access | **≤1 min** | **≤1 h** targeted, **≤3 h** full | The **delayed replica** is the single highest-value addition: it gives an already-running copy of the database as it was an hour ago, turning a 4-hour restore into a 10-minute table copy for most corruption events |
| Full region loss | Warm standby in the second Indian region with continuous replication; DNS failover | **≤5 min** | **≤4 h** | Requires the warm standby (§49.7); the residual 4 hours is verification, decision-making, and the deliberate refusal to automate a region failover |
| Provider compromise | Same, plus a third-party object-storage copy | ≤6 h | **≤24 h** | |

**Why region failover is not automated even at Scale.** An automatic cross-region failover on a false positive (a network partition between our monitoring and the primary region) causes split-brain: two regions accepting writes, with a reconciliation problem that is far worse than the outage it "prevented". Region failover is a human decision with a documented decision tree, made by the Incident Commander, with a named abort criterion.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-040 | RPO and RTO shall be stated per failure mode, not per component, and each shall carry its justification. |
| SUR-DR-041 | Stated RPO/RTO values shall be demonstrated in drills before being quoted to any client or included in any contract. |
| SUR-DR-042 | Cross-region failover shall require a human decision with a documented decision tree and abort criterion; it shall never be automated. |
| SUR-DR-043 | A delayed replica (1-hour lag) shall be introduced at the Scale tier as the primary defence against logical corruption. |

---

### 49.7 Geographic redundancy stance

| Stage | Stance | Cost delta (indicative) | Trigger to advance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MVP** | Single Indian region, multi-AZ. Backups replicated to the second Indian region **from day one** (cheap, and it is the difference between "we lost a region" and "we lost a region and everything in it). Infrastructure defined in IaC so the second region is buildable, and the build is exercised annually. | Baseline; cross-region backup replication adds ~₹6,000–10,000/month | — |
| **Warm standby** | Second Indian region running a continuously replicated database replica, a minimal application footprint, and pre-provisioned network/DNS. Not serving traffic. | +35–50% of production infrastructure cost | **Any of:** an Enterprise contract with a contractual RTO shorter than 24 h; >50,000 guards on the platform; a second region-level incident scare within 12 months; a regulator or major buyer requiring documented multi-region DR; the business reaching a revenue level where 24 hours of downtime is existential rather than painful `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-554]` |
| **Active-active** | Both regions serving | +100%, plus a very large increase in architectural complexity (write conflicts, data locality, cross-region consistency) | **Not recommended for this product at any foreseeable stage.** The latency argument does not apply (all users are in India, 20–110 ms to either region), so the only benefit is availability — which the warm standby already delivers at a fraction of the complexity. Active-active would be adopted only for a reason we do not currently have. |

**Residency note:** all three options stay within Indian regions, so geographic redundancy never conflicts with the §47.3.1 stance. This is precisely why a provider with two Indian regions was a selection criterion.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-050 | Backups shall be replicated to a second Indian region from launch. |
| SUR-DR-051 | The second region's infrastructure shall be buildable from IaC and shall be built and torn down at least annually as an exercise. |
| SUR-DR-052 | Advancement to a warm standby shall be triggered by the documented conditions, and the decision shall be recorded with its cost. |

---

### 49.8 Disaster scenarios and their runbooks

Each scenario states detection, immediate actions, the decision point, recovery, verification and an estimated duration. These are runbook summaries; the executable runbooks live in the repository and in the offline bundle (§49.1).

#### S1 — Availability-zone failure

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | OA-46 (instances unhealthy), OA-41/OA-42 (database), provider status page; synthetic probes degrade |
| Immediate | Confirm scope from the provider status page; verify database failover completed; verify application instances rescheduled into surviving AZs; check capacity headroom in the remaining AZs |
| Decision | None — this is designed for. The only decision is whether to over-provision temporarily |
| Recovery | Automatic. Scale out in surviving AZs if capacity is tight |
| Verification | Synthetic probes green; SLO burn arrested; no data gap (verify WAL continuity) |
| Duration | 10–20 min, mostly automatic |
| Comms | Internal only unless user-visible impact exceeded 5 minutes |

#### S2 — Region outage

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | All synthetic probes from all vantage points fail; provider status page confirms; internal monitoring (hosted in the same region) may itself be down — **which is why probes and the status page are external** |
| Immediate | Declare P0. Activate the §49.12 Command Center continuity protocol **immediately and in parallel** — do not wait for the technical recovery to fail first. Publish to the status page. Notify tenants by SMS from the out-of-region notification path |
| Decision | **The failover decision**, made by the Incident Commander against this tree: (a) Is the provider's ETA under 4 hours and credible? → wait, with continuity active. (b) Is the ETA unknown or over 4 hours? → begin the second-region rebuild. (c) Is data integrity in question? → rebuild regardless of ETA. **Abort criterion:** if the primary region recovers after the rebuild has begun but before cutover, the rebuild is completed to a verified state and then discarded; we do not attempt a partial cutover |
| Recovery | Build infrastructure in the second region from IaC → restore database from cross-region backup → point object storage to the replica bucket → restore secrets from the second-region copy → deploy the last-known-good artefacts by digest → DNS cutover with a pre-lowered TTL (300 s, maintained permanently for this reason) → certificate verification → smoke suite → open to traffic in stages (internal, then agency portals, then guard apps, then public) |
| Verification | Full §49.9 verification set; reconciliation with payment gateway; §49.11 offline replay management |
| Duration | MVP: 12–24 h. Warm standby: 2–4 h |
| Comms | §49.13 cadence: initial within 30 min, updates hourly |

#### S3 — Database corruption (logical)

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | OA-53 (reconciliation failure), OA-29 (payment mismatch), OA-91-class integrity check failures, or a human report of impossible data |
| Immediate | **Stop the bleeding first.** Identify the affected module and stop writes to it (kill switch, §47.8), rather than stopping the whole platform. Preserve evidence: snapshot the current state before any recovery action — you may need to compare |
| Decision | Scope: is the corruption confined to identifiable rows/tables, or is it structural? Confined → targeted restore-and-merge. Structural → full PITR. **Do not roll back application code reflexively**; if the previous version reads the corrupted data differently it can compound the damage (§47.12.1) |
| Recovery | Determine the corruption onset time from the audit log (§38.12) — this is the longest phase and the runbook budgets 30–60 min for it. Restore to just before onset into a **side instance** (never over the production database). Extract the correct rows. Merge into production with a reconciliation script that is reviewed by two people before execution and is run first in dry-run mode producing a diff report |
| Verification | §49.9 set, plus a targeted diff of the affected entity across the restored and live copies; financial reconciliation if money-adjacent (§49.10) |
| Duration | 2–8 h depending on scope; ≤1 h at Scale with a delayed replica |
| Comms | Affected tenants informed if their data was wrong at any point they could have seen it — this is not optional |

#### S4 — Accidental mass deletion

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | OA-54 (retention/purge anomaly), a spike in delete operations in the audit log, a user report, or a support action gone wrong |
| Immediate | Halt the responsible process immediately (the retention job's auto-halt on over-purge is the automated version of this). Revoke the actor's session if a human action. Snapshot current state |
| Decision | Was it a *soft* delete (status → Archived) or a *hard* delete? Canon §4 means operational and financial records are soft-deleted, so **most mass-deletion events are recoverable by a status update**, which is minutes of work. Hard deletion is confined to retention purges and schema operations, and those carry dual control (SUR-CMP-055) |
| Recovery — soft delete | Identify the affected rows from the audit log, restore status, re-emit any events that were suppressed. Minutes to an hour |
| Recovery — hard delete | PITR restore to before the deletion into a side instance; extract the deleted rows; re-insert with their original identifiers; repair foreign-key relationships; re-emit domain events where downstream state depends on them; run reconciliation. Note that re-insertion with original identifiers requires the sequence check in §49.9 |
| Verification | Row counts, referential integrity, and — critically — a check that the restore did not *resurrect* rows that were legitimately deleted before the incident, or rows covered by an erasure suppression record (§49.4.1) |
| Duration | Soft: <1 h. Hard: 3–8 h |

#### S5 — Ransomware or destructive compromise

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | §38.11 detections, mass encryption/deletion patterns, extortion contact, or OA-54/OA-55 |
| Immediate | **Assume all credentials are compromised.** Declare a security incident (§38's process governs; this runbook covers the recovery side). Isolate: revoke all sessions, rotate or disable all credentials, block outbound egress, freeze the CI/CD pipeline. **Do not** restore into the compromised account |
| Decision | Rebuild in a clean account is the default, not a fallback. The decision is only about scope and timing |
| Recovery | Stand up a clean account → rebuild infrastructure from IaC (reviewed for tampering — check the git history for unauthorised commits) → restore from the **immutable, object-locked backup copy** (this is why object-lock exists; a mutable backup is deleted by competent ransomware before the ransom note) → rotate every secret and key → rebuild container images from source rather than reusing registry artefacts (the registry may be poisoned) → verify image signatures against known-good signing → deploy → verify |
| Verification | Full §49.9 set + a forensic comparison of the restored data against the last known-good backup to identify what the attacker changed before the destructive phase |
| Duration | 24–72 h realistically |
| Comms | Per §38/§40 obligations, which this section does not restate; plus §49.13 operational comms |

#### S6 — Cloud provider account compromise or lockout

Two distinct causes, one recovery path.

| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| Compromise | Root/administrative credential compromise; overlaps with S5 |
| **Lockout** | Underrated and non-hypothetical: a failed payment method, a billing dispute, an automated fraud/abuse suspension, or a compliance action can suspend an account with very little warning. Mitigations: two payment methods on file with expiry monitoring; billing alerts at 50/80/100% (§47.15); a named billing owner and a backup; the account's contact addresses being a monitored distribution list rather than one person's inbox; and the out-of-account backup copy |
| Recovery | Rebuild in a new account (or with the alternate provider for object storage) from the out-of-account immutable backup copy and the git-mirrored IaC. Duration ≤48 h at MVP |
| Preventive requirement | The out-of-account backup copy is the entire mitigation. Without it, provider account loss is unrecoverable and the business ends. This is stated in exactly those terms so the line item is never cut for cost |

#### S7 — Third-party provider outage

Covered operationally by the degradation matrix in §46.3.4. The DR-specific additions:

| Provider class | DR consideration |
|---|---|
| Payment gateway | Extended outage (>4 h): switch to the documented offline collection path (client pays by bank transfer against the invoice), reconciled manually. Never fabricate a paid status |
| SMS / voice | ≥2 providers required (§36); an outage of both is treated as a T0 degradation because it removes the SOS SMS fallback — the Command Center is told explicitly and the continuity protocol's phone paths become primary |
| Push (FCM/APNs) | No alternative exists; SMS and voice are the fallback for P0 |
| AI provider | Fail-safe per §41.5.5; no operational dependency |
| Map provider | Degraded map per §46.3.4; operations continue |
| Email | Queue and delay; invoices remain available in-portal |

#### S8 — Key loss or KMS misconfiguration

| Phase | Actions |
|---|---|
| Detection | Decryption failures on restore, or a failed key-recovery drill |
| Immediate | Stop any process that might rotate or delete further key material. Identify which key generations are affected and which backups depend on them |
| Recovery | Restore key material from the offline package (§49.3); if unavailable, fall back to the newest backup encrypted with an available key generation, accepting the data loss between it and the present, and treat the gap as a data-loss incident with full disclosure |
| Prevention | The annual key-recovery drill is the only reliable prevention; a KMS key scheduled for deletion is a P0 alert regardless of intent |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-060 | Each of the eight scenarios shall have an executable runbook with a decision tree, an abort criterion and a verification checklist. |
| SUR-DR-061 | An immutable backup copy shall exist in a separate cloud account from production at all times; its existence and readability shall be verified weekly. |
| SUR-DR-062 | Recovery from a suspected compromise shall never restore into the compromised environment. |
| SUR-DR-063 | Cloud account billing and contact ownership shall be documented with a primary and a backup owner, two payment methods, and monitored expiry. |

---

### 49.9 Data-integrity verification after restore

A restore that completes is not a restore that worked. Every restore — nightly automated, drill, or real — runs this verification set, and the results are recorded. These are specific, executable checks, not a checklist of intentions.

| # | Check | Failure means |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Row counts per major table within expected tolerance of the pre-incident baseline (±0.5% for slow-changing, ±5% for high-churn) | Partial restore or wrong recovery point |
| 2 | **Sequence and identifier integrity**: every sequence's `last_value` is greater than the maximum existing id in its table | The classic post-restore bug — a restored sequence behind the data causes primary-key collisions on the first write, and it happens on almost every naive restore |
| 3 | **Invoice numbering**: the invoice number sequence is ahead of the maximum invoice number recorded in *external* evidence (gateway records, sent emails), not merely ahead of the restored table | Reusing an invoice number is a compliance and audit failure (BR-003) |
| 4 | **Ledger balance**: every transaction's debits equal its credits; the sum of all ledger entries per account reconciles to the account balance snapshot | Financial corruption |
| 5 | Invoice totals reconcile to their line items and to their ledger entries | Financial corruption |
| 6 | Payments reconcile against the gateway's authoritative record for the restore window (§49.10) | Missing or duplicated payments |
| 7 | Referential integrity: no orphaned assignments, attendance rows without assignments, invoices without clients, ledger entries without transactions | Partial restore |
| 8 | Attendance record count per day for the restore window compared against the expected count derived from published rosters | Silent attendance loss — the one that becomes an unpaid guard |
| 9 | No overlapping active assignments (BR-001 exclusion constraint validates) | Constraint state lost in restore |
| 10 | Tenant isolation spot-check: sample 100 rows across tenant-owned tables and verify `tenant_id` consistency with their parent records | Cross-tenant contamination during a merge |
| 11 | Audit-log continuity: no gap in the audit sequence except the declared restore gap, which must itself be recorded as a `restore_event` | Audit integrity |
| 12 | Erasure suppression list re-applied (§49.4.1) | Privacy failure |
| 13 | Partition inventory: all expected partitions present; tomorrow's partition exists | Next-midnight write failure |
| 14 | Object-storage reference integrity: sample 500 document/photo references from the database and verify the objects exist and their checksums match | Dangling references |
| 15 | Read models rebuilt and consistent with source (guard_last_position, dashboard aggregates) | Stale derived state presented as live |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-070 | The verification set shall run automatically after every restore, including nightly automated restores, and its results shall be recorded and trended. |
| SUR-DR-071 | A restore shall not be declared complete, and restored data shall not be served to users, until the verification set passes or every failure has a recorded, approved disposition. |

---

### 49.10 The special problem of restoring financial and audit data

A point-in-time restore gives an internally consistent database. It does **not** give a consistent *business*, because the outside world did not roll back with us. This is the hardest part of DR in this product and it deserves its own procedure.

| Problem | Procedure |
|---|---|
| **The gateway moved on** | Between the restore point T and now, Razorpay processed payments, refunds and settlements that our restored database does not know about. Procedure: after restore, run a **mandatory gateway reconciliation** over `[T, now]` pulling authoritative state from the gateway API (never from cached webhook payloads — a webhook proves origin, not truth, §33). Every gateway payment absent locally is created and flagged `restored_from_gateway`; every local payment absent at the gateway is investigated individually, never deleted. |
| **The outbox will re-emit** | Restoring to T resurrects outbox rows whose events already went out — notifications already sent, webhooks already delivered, ledger postings already made downstream. Procedure: on restore, the outbox relay enters **replay-suppression mode** for the window `[T, now]`: events are marked as processed rather than re-emitted, *except* for an explicit allowlist of events that are safe and useful to re-emit (read-model rebuilds). Consumer idempotency keys (§33.2) are the second net. Without this step, a restore sends every guard a duplicate roster notification and every client a duplicate invoice email — an embarrassment that also destroys trust in the notification channel. |
| **Invoice numbers must never be reused** | Verification check #3 above. Additionally, the invoice sequence is advanced past the maximum number found in any external evidence, and a `restore_gap` record documents any numbers that were issued but are no longer in the database, so an auditor's "where is invoice 2026-0417?" has an answer. |
| **The ledger must be re-balanced, not re-computed** | Financial history is append-only (BR-003). Corrections after a restore are made as **new, dual-approved journal entries of class `restore_adjustment`**, each referencing the incident, never by editing historical entries. The ledger therefore tells the truth about what happened including the incident, which is what an auditor needs. |
| **Payroll in flight** | A payroll run interrupted by the incident is never resumed blind. It is verified against the disbursement rail's authoritative record before any further disbursement, because a duplicated salary payment is both a financial loss and — for a guard who receives and spends it — an ugly recovery conversation. The rule: **verify first, pay second, always.** |
| **The audit log has a gap** | The window between the restore point and the incident contains audit entries that were written and then lost. That gap is itself auditable: a `restore_event` record is written stating the incident, the restore point, the recovery time, the affected window, the approver, and an explicit statement that audit entries in that window may be incomplete. Pretending the gap does not exist is the one thing that turns a technical incident into an integrity problem. |
| **Downstream reports** | Any report, statement or export generated from the affected window before the incident may be wrong. Procedure: identify them from the report job log, mark them superseded, and re-issue with a correction notice to anyone who received one. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-080 | Every restore affecting financial data shall trigger a mandatory gateway and disbursement-rail reconciliation over the affected window before any further financial processing is permitted. |
| SUR-DR-081 | The outbox shall support replay-suppression mode with an explicit re-emit allowlist, engaged automatically on restore. |
| SUR-DR-082 | Financial corrections after a restore shall be new dual-approved `restore_adjustment` entries; historical entries shall never be edited (BR-003). |
| SUR-DR-083 | Every restore shall write a `restore_event` audit record stating the recovery point, the affected window and the completeness caveat. |
| SUR-DR-084 | Interrupted payroll or disbursement runs shall be verified against the rail's authoritative record before resumption. |

---

### 49.11 In-flight offline guard data during an outage

While the platform is down, **guards keep working.** That is the whole point of offline-first, and it creates a specific recovery problem that a purely online product never faces.

| Aspect | Handling |
|---|---|
| During the outage | The Guard App continues to accept check-ins, check-outs, wake checks, patrol scans and incidents into its local queue. It shows the guard an honest status ("Not connected — your records are saved on this phone") and the pending-event count (SUR-NFR-217). SOS falls back to SMS or the displayed emergency number (§24.8.2). |
| The replay herd | When service returns, thousands of devices reconnect simultaneously and attempt to flush queues — a self-inflicted denial of service arriving exactly when the platform is at its most fragile. Handling: the server issues `Retry-After` with **jitter derived from the device id**, spreading replay over a configured window (default 30 minutes, extendable during recovery); ingest rate limits apply per device; **SOS and attendance are exempt from every throttle** (SUR-NFR-218). Rate-limit headroom is verified in the replay-herd load test (SUR-NFR-052). |
| Ordering | Sync is priority-ordered — SOS, attendance, incidents, patrol, pings, telemetry (SUR-NFR-214) — so a device with 20,000 buffered pings delivers its check-ins first. |
| Correctness of the record | Every replayed event carries both `device_time` and `server_received_time` (canon §4) and is flagged `delayed_sync`. Attendance rules evaluate against `device_time`, so a guard who checked in on time during the outage is not marked late by our failure. This is a correctness requirement and also a fairness one. |
| Derived signals | Per §34.3.5, geofence/idle/deviation signals are computed only for pings under 15 minutes old. Replayed history is stored and appears in the daily exception list; it does not fire live alerts. An operator receiving a geofence-exit alert six hours late is worse than receiving nothing. |
| Supervisor attestation | Attendance from an outage window is flagged for the supervisor's confirmation rather than auto-rejected or auto-verified. The rule is stated plainly: **the platform's outage is never treated as the guard's fault, and pay is never withheld on the basis of our downtime.** |
| Outage longer than the buffer | The Guard App buffers 7 days (§34.3.2). Beyond that, the oldest pings evict (D2, acceptable) but **D0 events never evict** (SUR-NFR-212) — if the D0 portion of the queue approaches its cap, the app warns the guard and the supervisor path takes over. For an outage exceeding the buffer's D0 capacity, the fallback is the manual muster: supervisors record attendance on the printed roster from the continuity pack (§49.12), and a bulk-import path with an attestation field brings it back into the system with `source=manual_continuity`. |
| Reconciliation after recovery | A post-recovery job compares expected attendance (from published rosters) against received attendance for the outage window and produces an exception list per site, which the operations team works through. Guards whose records are missing are contacted, not penalised. |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-090 | Replay after an outage shall be rate-controlled with device-derived jitter, exempting SOS and attendance, and shall be verified by the replay-herd load test. |
| SUR-DR-091 | Attendance and duty rules shall evaluate replayed events against `device_time`; a platform outage shall never cause a guard to be marked late, absent or unpaid. |
| SUR-DR-092 | Replayed events older than 15 minutes shall not generate live operational alerts; they shall appear in the exception list. |
| SUR-DR-093 | A manual muster fallback with a bulk-import path and an attestation field shall exist for outages exceeding the client buffer. |
| SUR-DR-094 | A post-recovery attendance reconciliation shall run automatically and produce a per-site exception list. |

---

### 49.12 Business continuity for the Command Center

**If the platform is down, SOS still has to work.** This is the requirement that distinguishes a security company's software from ordinary business software, and it is answered with a documented manual protocol, not with an architecture diagram.

§24 owns the SOS mechanics when the platform is up. This subsection owns what happens when it is not.

#### 49.12.1 The continuity tiers

| Tier | Condition | Protocol |
|---|---|---|
| **C0 — Console degraded, platform up** | The operator console is unusable (browser, network at the centre, gateway outage) but the platform is healthy | Operators switch to the **Admin App** on mobile (§23), which is a fully independent client. Alerts continue by push and voice. Recovery target: immediate. Drill: monthly, informally |
| **C1 — Platform down, telephony and SMS work** | The platform is unreachable but phone networks function | **The manual protocol below.** Recovery target: operating within 10 minutes of declaration (SUR-NFR-175) |
| **C2 — Command Center site unusable** | Power, network, fire, flood, or an access denial at the physical centre | Operators relocate to the secondary operating location or to home working, with softphone and VPN. The published Command Center number is cloud telephony with forwarding, so the number itself is portable — this is the single most important design decision for C2, and it must be verified quarterly |
| **C3 — Both platform and telephony down** (regional infrastructure event) | Extreme | Supervisors' local call trees and the printed emergency cards at Critical sites become the mechanism. Field supervisors are the recovery unit; the centre coordinates when it can |

#### 49.12.2 The C1 manual protocol, in detail

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Declaration** | The shift lead declares continuity mode. There is no approval step — waiting for permission during an outage is how the ten-minute target is missed. The declaration is logged (on paper if necessary) with time and reason |
| **How SOS reaches the centre** | Three paths, none of which depends on the application platform: (1) the **SMS SOS gateway number**, which is a separate number on a separate provider whose only function is to receive SOS SMS — during continuity it is monitored directly by an operator on a dedicated handset, reading the raw messages rather than relying on the platform to parse them; (2) the **published Command Center direct line**, which the Guard App displays on its SOS screen even with no data (§24.8.2) and which is printed on the guard's ID card and the site emergency card; (3) the supervisor call tree |
| **The continuity pack** | Exported nightly, encrypted, to two operator workstations, **and printed weekly** into a sealed folder held at the centre. It contains: every active site with address, gate access notes and site SOP summary; the on-duty roster for the next 24 hours by site and shift; every on-duty guard's name and phone; every supervisor and field officer with phone; every client site contact; the nearest police station and hospital per site with phone; the escalation contact list for Suraksha management; and the emergency-services numbers. The printed copy is the one that works when the workstations are also affected |
| **What operators do** | Log every event on the paper incident form (a defined layout: time, source, guard, site, nature, actions taken, outcome, operator initials). Handle SOS exactly as they would normally — call the guard, call the supervisor, dispatch, call emergency services if needed. The *response* does not degrade; only the tooling does |
| **Client communication** | Clients with active P0-notification contracts are called, not messaged, during continuity. A prepared script is in the pack |
| **Guard communication** | A broadcast SMS from the out-of-platform provider tells guards: the app may not sync, keep working, your records are saved, if you need help call this number. This message is pre-approved and pre-translated into Tier 1 and Tier 2 languages so it can be sent in one action without drafting under pressure |
| **Back-entry after recovery** | Paper records are entered into the platform with `source=manual_continuity`, the operator's identity, the original paper timestamp, and a scan of the form attached as evidence. Back-entry is completed within 24 hours of recovery and is reconciled against the §49.11 attendance exception list. Records entered this way are visibly marked in the UI so nobody mistakes them for system-captured data |
| **Practice** | **Quarterly, unannounced within a known week.** The drill measures: time from declaration to operating, whether the printed pack was current, whether the SOS SMS handset was charged and in the right hands, whether operators could find a site's gate access notes, and whether back-entry completed. Findings are tracked like any other finding |

#### 49.12.3 What makes this credible rather than decorative

| Requirement | Why it is listed separately |
|---|---|
| The SMS SOS gateway must be operable **without the platform** | If parsing the SMS requires our application, it is not a fallback. During continuity the messages are read by a human. The number, the SIM, the handset and the provider account must therefore be independent of the platform's infrastructure and independently funded |
| The Command Center number must be cloud telephony with forwarding | So that C2 (site loss) does not also mean losing the number every guard has been told to call |
| The pack must be **printed**, not only exported | A digital pack on a workstation is unavailable in a power or network event at the centre |
| The pack must be **current**, verified weekly | A continuity pack listing last quarter's rosters is worse than none, because it produces confident wrong action |
| Guards must know the number **before** they need it | Printed on the ID card, on the site emergency card at Critical sites, and displayed on the app's SOS screen offline |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-100 | A four-tier continuity model shall exist with a documented protocol per tier and a declaration authority that requires no approval. |
| SUR-DR-101 | The SMS SOS gateway shall be independently operable without the application platform, on a separate provider and account, and shall be monitored directly during continuity mode. |
| SUR-DR-102 | The Command Center's published number shall be cloud-telephony-based and forwardable, verified quarterly. |
| SUR-DR-103 | The continuity pack shall be exported nightly, printed weekly, and verified for currency at every drill. |
| SUR-DR-104 | A quarterly continuity drill shall measure time-to-operating, pack currency and back-entry completion, with findings tracked. |
| SUR-DR-105 | Records created during continuity shall be back-entered within 24 hours with `source=manual_continuity`, an evidence attachment, and a visible marker in the UI. |
| SUR-DR-106 | Every guard shall have the Command Center number available offline: on the app's SOS screen, on their ID card, and on the site emergency card at Critical sites. |

---

### 49.13 Incident communication plan

| Audience | Channel | Timing | Content rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| Internal engineering | Incident channel + page | Immediate | Facts, current hypothesis, current action, next update time |
| Suraksha management | Direct message to the CTO/COO/CEO group | Within 15 min for P0 | Impact, ETA if known, decisions needed |
| **Status page** (`status.surakshaguards.in`, **hosted off the primary infrastructure** — this is non-negotiable, a status page inside the failed system is worthless) | Public page + subscribers | Initial within **30 min** of a confirmed P0; updates at least hourly; a final update on resolution | What is affected, what is not, what users should do, when the next update comes. **No speculation about cause during the incident** |
| Affected agency tenants | In-app banner where the app is reachable; email; SMS for P0 | Initial within 30 min for P0; hourly | Same, plus tenant-specific impact where known |
| Affected clients | Account owner calls for enterprise clients; email otherwise | Within 1 h for P0 | Service impact and the operational continuity in place — clients care that their sites are still guarded, which is usually true even when the platform is down, and saying so early prevents panic |
| Guards | Broadcast SMS/push in Tier 1–2 languages | Within 30 min if the Guard App is affected | Pre-approved template: keep working, records are saved, call this number for help |
| Command Center operators | Direct, immediately | Immediate | Which systems to trust, which to distrust, whether to activate continuity |
| Regulators / contractual notifications | Per §38 and §40 obligations | Per those sections | Not restated here |

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| One voice | Communications come from the designated Communications role (§47.16.2), not from whoever is closest to a keyboard |
| Cadence discipline | Every update states when the next update will come, and that promise is kept even if the update is "no change" |
| No speculation | Cause is stated only when established. "We are investigating" is honest; a wrong cause published early is remembered longer than the outage |
| Post-incident report | For every P0 and every P1 with client impact: an internal blameless postmortem within 5 business days (SUR-DVO-143), and a client-facing incident report within 5 business days to affected tenants, stating what happened, impact, what was done, and what will change |
| Templates | Pre-written and pre-translated for the six most likely scenarios, so nobody drafts under pressure |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-DR-110 | The status page shall be hosted independently of the primary infrastructure and shall be updated within 30 minutes of a confirmed P0. |
| SUR-DR-111 | Every incident communication shall state when the next update will be issued, and that commitment shall be met. |
| SUR-DR-112 | Cause shall not be published until established; speculation during an incident is prohibited. |
| SUR-DR-113 | Client-facing incident reports shall be issued within 5 business days for every P0 and every client-impacting P1. |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nightly | Automated restore-and-verify | Automated | Pipeline | Verification set passes within RTO |
| Weekly | Out-of-account backup copy existence and readability check | Automated | Pipeline | Copy present, header readable |

|---|---|

| SUR-DR-121 | Every drill shall produce corrections to the runbooks it exercised; a drill that produces no corrections shall be scrutinised, because it usually means the drill was too easy. |

## 50. Scalability

### 50.0 Scope

This section sets out the growth path from pilot to pan-India with explicit volumetrics and the arithmetic behind them, the architectural evolution of the modular monolith, the database and caching scaling paths with their trigger metrics, queue and storage scaling, the command centre's read/write split, multi-region considerations, unit economics, a capacity-planning table, and the ten scaling bottlenecks specific to this system.

It does not restate the data model (§32), the real-time design (§34) or the security controls (§38). Where a scaling step has already been specified elsewhere — the tenancy models of §32.1.1, the real-time evolution of §34.7.2 — this section references the trigger and does not redefine the mechanism. Normative IDs use `SUR-SCL-nnn`.

---

### 50.1 The growth path

| Stage | Description and geography | Agencies (tenants) | Guards | Sites | Clients | Total user accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S0 — Pilot** | One city; controlled rollout of Suraksha's own operation plus early agency tenants `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` | 30 | 8,000 | 900 | 600 | ~9,500 |
| **S1 — City-dense** | 3–4 cities; the pilot city saturated plus adjacent ones | 80 | 25,000 | 2,800 | 1,900 | ~29,000 |
| **S2 — State** | 1 state, full coverage; district-level licence geography exercised | 150 | 50,000 | 5,500 | 3,800 | ~58,000 |
| **S3 — Multi-state** | 4–6 states; the Year-2 operating point `[ASSUMPTION: A-240]` | 400 | 120,000 | 12,000 | 9,000 | ~140,000 |
| **S4 — Pan-India** | 20+ states; the long-horizon target | 2,000 | 600,000 | 60,000 | 45,000 | ~690,000 |

**An honest note on S4.** The market is approximately 35,000 PSARA-licensed agencies (`A-001`). S4 assumes 2,000 of them — under 6% — and 600,000 guards. That is an ambitious but arithmetically sane target. A plan that assumed all 35,000 agencies would not be a plan; it would be a total-addressable-market slide wearing an engineering costume. Every number in this section is sized against S3 as the design point, with S4 as the direction of travel and an explicit re-baselining obligation at each stage transition (SUR-NFR-002).

---

### 50.2 Volumetrics, with the arithmetic shown

#### 50.2.1 The derivation assumptions

| Ref | Assumption | Value | Source / justification |
|---|---|---|---|
| V-1 | Shifts worked per guard per month | 26 | Standard 26-day working month in Indian private security; `[ASSUMPTION: A-562]` |
| V-2 | Average shift length | 10 h (mix of 8 h and 12 h posts) | §17/§20 rostering patterns |
| V-3 | Instantaneous on-duty concurrency, average | **36%** | Derived, not guessed: 8,000 guards × 26 shifts × 10 h = 2,080,000 guard-hours/month ÷ 720 hours in a month = **2,889 concurrently on duty**, i.e. 36% of the registered base |
| V-4 | Instantaneous on-duty concurrency, **peak** | **45%** | Day and evening shift bands overlap and are heavier than night; peak ≈ 1.25× average → 3,600 at S0 (matches B-2) |
| V-5 | Effective GPS ping interval, weighted across states | **~102 s** | Weighted from §34.3.1: 60% stationary-in-geofence @120 s, 20% battery-saver @300 s, 15% moving @60 s, 5% patrol @30 s → 3,600 × (0.6/120 + 0.2/300 + 0.15/60 + 0.05/30) = **35.4 pings/guard/hour** |
| V-6 | Night-shift share of shifts | 35% | Drives wake-check volume |
| V-7 | Share of shifts running patrols | 30%, at 4 rounds × 6 checkpoints = 24 scans/shift | §18 patrol module |
| V-8 | Attendance photos per shift | 2 (check-in and check-out) | §18 |
| V-9 | Documents per guard (lifetime) | 6 | §40.2.3 KYC set |
| V-10 | SOS rate | ≤5 per 1,000 guards per day (target ceiling) | §34.3 stated target |

#### 50.2.2 The volumetrics table

| Metric | Arithmetic | S0 | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guards on duty (peak) | guards × 45% | 3,600 | 11,250 | 22,500 | 54,000 | 270,000 |
| **GPS pings/second (average)** | on-duty(avg) × 35.4 ÷ 3600 | **28** | 89 | 177 | 425 | 2,126 |
| **GPS pings/second (peak)** | on-duty(peak) × 35.4 ÷ 3600 | **35** | 111 | 221 | 531 | 2,657 |
| GPS pings/second (replay burst, 10×) | peak × 10 | 350 | 1,110 | 2,210 | 5,310 | 26,570 |
| GPS pings/day | avg/s × 86,400 | 2.4 M | 7.7 M | 15.3 M | 36.7 M | 183.7 M |
| Shifts/day | guards × 26/30 | 6,933 | 21,667 | 43,333 | 104,000 | 520,000 |
| **Attendance events/day** | shifts × 2 | **13,867** | 43,333 | 86,667 | 208,000 | 1,040,000 |
| Attendance events/second in a shift-change window | shifts × 2 × 0.6 ÷ 3 ÷ 1,800 | 1.5 | 4.8 | 9.6 | 23.1 | 115.6 |
| Wake checks/day | shifts × 35% × 6 | 14,560 | 45,500 | 91,000 | 218,400 | 1,092,000 |
| Patrol scans/day | shifts × 30% × 24 | 49,918 | 156,000 | 312,000 | 748,800 | 3,744,000 |
| Incidents/day | ~1 per 100 shifts | 69 | 217 | 433 | 1,040 | 5,200 |
| SOS events/day | guards ÷ 1,000 × 5 | 40 | 125 | 250 | 600 | 3,000 |
| **Notifications/day** | (shifts × 3) + (sites × 5) + (clients × 2) | **26,500** | 84,300 | 158,600 | 390,000 | 1,935,000 |
| Attendance photos/day | shifts × 2 | 13,867 | 43,333 | 86,667 | 208,000 | 1,040,000 |
| Documents (cumulative) | guards × 6 | 48,000 | 150,000 | 300,000 | 720,000 | 3,600,000 |
| AI interactions/day | (console users × 0.2 × 5) + (guards × 0.1) | ~2,300 | 7,000 | 14,000 | 33,000 | 165,000 |
| Concurrent console sessions (peak) | tenants × ~4 + Suraksha + clients | ~120 | 370 | 700 | 1,600 | 8,000 |
| Concurrent WebSocket connections | consoles + command views + wallboards | ~200 | 620 | 1,200 | 2,800 | 14,000 |
| API requests/second (peak) | modelled from the above, 6× shift-change factor | 250 | 780 | 1,550 | 3,000 | 15,000 |

#### 50.2.3 Reconciling with §34's figures — and why the difference matters

§34.3.3 quotes GPS ingest at **~15 writes/second average and ~150/second peak** at V1. The arithmetic above gives **28/s average and 35/s peak** (350/s on replay burst). Both are defensible; the entire divergence is in two assumptions:

- **On-duty concurrency.** §34's figure is consistent with roughly 20% instantaneous concurrency; V-3 derives 36% from shifts × hours ÷ month, which is the more defensible route because it is arithmetic rather than intuition.
- **Effective ping interval.** §34's figure implies ~200 s effective; V-5 derives ~102 s from the published sampling policy's state mix. The mix itself is a guess about how much time guards spend stationary versus patrolling.

**We size infrastructure for the higher number and we instrument the assumption.** `A-562` (on-duty concurrency and the sampling state mix) is one of the two or three assumptions in this entire document whose error propagates furthest — it drives ping volume, storage, database write load, and therefore the largest infrastructure line item. It is measured directly from production within the first 30 days and this table is re-derived (SUR-NFR-002).

Note also that §34's "peak" is a burst peak while ours is a steady-state peak; the replay-burst row is the comparable figure, and there the two are within the same order of magnitude.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-001 | The volumetrics model shall exist as a maintained spreadsheet/notebook with its inputs as named parameters, so that changing one assumption re-derives every downstream number rather than requiring a manual rewrite. |
| SUR-SCL-002 | On-duty concurrency, the sampling state mix, and the peak-to-average ratio shall be measured continuously in production and compared against the model monthly; a divergence >25% triggers a re-derivation and a capacity review. |

### 50.3 Architectural evolution

#### 50.3.1 The starting point: a modular monolith

Canon §4 settles the stance. This subsection specifies **how the modules are bounded so that extraction is possible later without a rewrite** — which is the only thing that makes "start as a monolith" a responsible choice rather than a deferred problem.

| Module | Owns (primary tables) | Depends on | Extraction difficulty | Extraction trigger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `identity` | person, user, session, credential, device | — | Medium | Only if a separate identity product is sold |
| `tenancy` | tenant, branch, membership, plan, entitlement | identity | **Never extract** — it is the isolation boundary; splitting it multiplies the isolation risk across services | — |
| `workforce` | guard, employment, skill, document links, verification state | identity, tenancy | Medium | Team boundary only |
| `client` | client, site, post, contract, rate card | tenancy | Medium | Team boundary only |
| `scheduling` | roster, shift, assignment, leave, replacement | workforce, client | Hard (transactional with attendance) | Team boundary only |
| `fieldops` | attendance, wake check, patrol, scan, checkpoint | scheduling, workforce | Hard (money-adjacent) | Team boundary only |
| **`tracking`** | location (pings), guard_last_position, geofence evaluation | workforce (read-only reference) | **Easy — designed for extraction** | **First extraction.** See below |
| `incident` | incident, SOS, alert, escalation, evidence | fieldops, tracking, workforce | Medium — but the **SOS path is isolated first**, before the module is extracted | See below |
| **`notification`** | notification, template, delivery record, provider adapters | all (as an event consumer) | **Easy — already event-driven** | **Second extraction** |
| `billing` | invoice, payment, ledger, transaction, wallet | client, fieldops | Hard (transactional, BR-003) | Team boundary only; extract last if ever |
| `payroll` | payroll run, payslip, component, disbursement | workforce, fieldops | Hard | Team boundary only |
| `marketplace` | listing, lead, quotation, tender, bid | client, tenancy | Easy | Product boundary |
| `compliance` | licence, rule, evaluation, finding, evidence pack | workforce, tenancy | Medium | — |
| **`document`** | document, extraction job, OCR result | all | **Easy — already a job queue** | **Fifth extraction** |
| **`ai`** | interaction, tool call, approval, model adapters | all (read via their APIs) | **Easy — already an orchestration layer** | **Fourth extraction** |
| **`analytics`** | read models, aggregates, report jobs | all (read-only) | **Easy — already read-only** | **Third extraction** |
| `admin` | platform administration, tenant lifecycle, support tooling | all | Medium | — |

#### 50.3.2 The rules that keep extraction possible

These are the load-bearing rules. Without them, "modular monolith" is just "monolith".

| Rule | Enforcement |
|---|---|
| A module never queries another module's tables | Architecture lint in CI (SUR-NFR-142); every table has a declared owning module |
| A module is called only through its published in-process interface | Same lint; internals are not importable |
| Cross-module writes go through the owning module's interface or through a domain event | Code review + the outbox pattern |
| No shared mutable state between modules except the database, and that only through owners | Design review |
| Dependency direction is declared and acyclic | Lint fails on a cycle |
| Every module publishes its domain events with a versioned schema | Event registry; contract tests |
| Every module owns its own metrics, logs, alerts and runbooks | §48 module label; alert ownership |
| Module interfaces are designed as if remote: no shared transactions across module boundaries except where explicitly documented and justified | Review checklist item — this is the rule that makes the eventual network hop a change of transport rather than a change of semantics |

**The transactional exception is stated honestly.** `scheduling`, `fieldops` and `billing` genuinely share transactions today (publishing a roster, recording attendance and generating an invoice line must be consistent), and pretending otherwise would produce a distributed-transaction problem we do not need. Those three are therefore marked "hard to extract" and are extracted last, if at all — which is fine, because they are not the modules whose load forces extraction.

#### 50.3.3 What must be separated first, and the exact trigger

| Order | Component | Why it goes first | **Trigger metric** | What separation means |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | **The SOS path** (not a module — a path through `incident`) | It is the only life-safety function, and no amount of unrelated load may be allowed to delay it | **Any single incident in which SOS latency exceeded its target because of unrelated load. One occurrence is enough** (§34.7.2) | Dedicated compute, dedicated database connection pool, dedicated provider credentials, dedicated rate-limit exemption path. Not a separate codebase initially — a separate *execution lane* |
| **1** | **`tracking` — GPS ingest** | Highest write volume by an order of magnitude, most independent data, already behind a queue, and its failure mode (a slow database) must never stall the guard's app | **Sustained ping rate >1,500/s**, or **ingest lag p95 >10 s for 3 consecutive days**, or **ingest processing >50% of application-tier CPU** (§34.7.2) | Own service, own database (or own Postgres instance holding only the ping partitions), own scaling policy. `guard_last_position` becomes a published read model |
| **2** | **`notification` — fan-out** | A single roster publish to a 5,000-guard tenant is a burst of tens of thousands of sends that, in a shared worker pool, starves everything else | **>500,000 messages/day**, or **fan-out queue depth p95 >10,000**, or **any fan-out job blocking the shared worker pool for >5 minutes** | Own service, own worker pool, own provider connection pools and rate-limit budgets per provider |
| **3** | **`analytics` — reporting** | Read-heavy, long-running, and the workload most likely to interfere with operational queries | **Replica CPU >60% sustained for 7 days**, or **report queries accounting for >2% of OLTP wait time**, or **>50 concurrent report jobs at peak** | Own service reading from a dedicated replica or the columnar store (§32.6); operational reads never share a connection pool with reports |
| **4** | **`ai` — inference orchestration** | Latency-variable, cost-variable, dependent on an external provider whose outage must not affect anything else | **>10,000 interactions/day**, or **AI worker memory pressure causing evictions**, or **any incident in which a model-provider outage or latency spike affected a non-AI path** | Own service with its own concurrency limits, its own cost budget enforcement, and a hard circuit breaker at the boundary |
| **5** | **`document` — OCR/extraction** | CPU/memory-heavy, bursty at onboarding, entirely asynchronous | **>2,000 documents/day**, or **OCR backlog wall-time >30 minutes**, or **document jobs causing worker-pool contention twice in a month** | Own service, own worker pool, own scaling policy (scale-to-zero between bursts) |

Each trigger is a live metric with an alert (SUR-NFR-104), so the decision to extract is made from data at a review, not from architectural enthusiasm during a sprint.

#### 50.3.4 Why not microservices from the start

| Cost of premature microservices, for this system specifically | Detail |
|---|---|
| Distributed transactions where the domain is genuinely transactional | Publishing a roster creates assignments, which produce attendance, which produce invoice lines and payroll inputs. In one database this is a transaction with constraints (including the BR-001 exclusion constraint). Across services it becomes sagas, compensating actions and eventual consistency in the exact place where the business demands correctness: pay and billing |
| Tenant isolation multiplied | Isolation is currently enforced at one data-access layer with row-level security and one tested suite (SUR-SEC-133). With N services it must be enforced, and tested, N times. Multi-tenant data leakage is the company-ending risk (R-362); multiplying its surface to buy scalability we do not yet need is a bad trade |
| Operational surface per engineer | With 5–8 engineers (A-566), each service adds a deploy pipeline, an on-call surface, a set of dashboards, a set of alerts and a version-compatibility matrix. The §47.1.2 analysis applies directly: we cannot run Kubernetes; we certainly cannot run twelve services on it |
| Latency added to every read | A dashboard card that today joins across three modules in one query becomes three network calls. At p95 that is real, and it lands squarely on §46.2's targets |
| Observability cost | Distributed tracing becomes mandatory rather than valuable; telemetry volume multiplies; §46.10's 15% cost cap becomes hard to hold |
| The actual scaling problem is data volume in one table | 36.7 million pings/day at S3 in one partitioned table. That is a *data* scaling problem solved by partitioning, compression, tiering and eventually a separate ingest service — none of which requires decomposing the business logic |
| Team boundaries do not exist yet | The strongest argument for microservices is organisational: independent teams shipping independently. With one team, service boundaries create coordination cost without buying independence |

**When the argument flips:** more than ~20 engineers organised into teams with distinct ownership; or any of the §50.3.3 triggers firing; or a component whose scaling profile genuinely diverges (GPS ingest is the clearest example, which is why it is extraction #1). Not before, and never because a diagram looks tidier.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-010 | Module boundaries shall be declared, table ownership shall be explicit, and cross-module data access shall be prevented by an automated architecture check. |
| SUR-SCL-011 | Module interfaces shall be designed as if remote — no cross-module transactions except the three documented exceptions, each of which shall carry a recorded justification. |
| SUR-SCL-012 | Each extraction trigger in §50.3.3 shall have a live metric and an alert; extraction shall be proposed only when a trigger has fired and been reviewed. |
| SUR-SCL-013 | The SOS path shall be isolated as an execution lane from launch, and shall be physically separated on the first occurrence of load-induced latency breach. |

### 50.4 Database scaling path

| Step | Change | **Trigger** | Effort | Reversible? | Principal risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Baseline: one primary + one replica, partitioned `location`, governed indexes (§32.4) | — | — | — | — |
| 1 | **Vertical scale** the primary | Primary CPU >65% sustained over 7 days, or connection saturation | Hours (a failover) | Yes | Brief failover; hits a ceiling quickly and expensively |
| 2 | **Add read replicas** and route read-only workloads | Read:write ratio >4:1 **and** primary CPU >60%, or replica CPU >70% | Days | Yes | Replication lag becomes user-visible; requires explicit read-your-writes handling on the paths that need it |
| 3 | **Separate the high-volume append tables** (`location`, `audit_log`, `notification_delivery`) onto their own instance | Any of these exceeding **30% of database size**, or vacuum/WAL pressure from them measurably affecting OLTP latency (§34.7.2) | 2–4 weeks | Hard | Cross-instance joins must be removed first — which is why they were designed not to exist |
| 4 | **Partition further** (sub-partition `location` by tenant; partition `attendance` by month) | A single tenant exceeding 20% of daily ping volume (§32.4); `attendance` exceeding ~200 M rows | 1–2 weeks | Yes | Query plans change; the CI `EXPLAIN` suite is the safety net |
| 5 | **Dedicated instance for the largest tenants** (Model C, §32.1.1.4) | Tenant >5,000 active guards, or >15% of database CPU-seconds over 7 days, or a contractual requirement | 2–4 weeks per tenant | Yes (move back) | The routing indirection (SUR-DAT-014) must already exist — it does, from V1 |
| 6 | **Cell/pod topology, sharded by tenant** (Model D, §32.1.1.5) | >500 tenants, or primary >4 TB, or a single incident affecting >20% of tenants twice in a quarter | Months | No, practically | The largest single architectural change in the roadmap; the control plane, routing and cross-cell analytics all become new systems |
| 7 | **Columnar analytical store** | Triggers in §32.6.5 | Weeks | Yes | Duplication and freshness semantics |

**Connection pooling.** PgBouncer (or the provider's equivalent) in **transaction mode** sits in front of Postgres from S1 onward. The specific caution that must be recorded: transaction-mode pooling breaks session-level state, which matters here because §38 uses row-level security. Setting the tenant context with `SET` at session level would be silently wrong under transaction pooling; the implementation must use `SET LOCAL` inside the transaction, or pass the tenant through a function parameter. This is a named test in the tenant-isolation suite, because it is exactly the kind of bug that produces cross-tenant data exposure and passes every functional test.

**Query governance.** Statement timeouts per role (short for OLTP, long for reporting), a slow-query budget reviewed weekly, the CI `EXPLAIN` gate (§32.4), and per-tenant query attribution so that "the database is slow" resolves to "this tenant's report is slow" in one query.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-020 | Each database scaling step shall have its trigger instrumented and alerted; steps shall be taken in order, and skipping a step shall require a recorded justification. |
| SUR-SCL-021 | Tenant context under transaction-mode pooling shall be set transactionally, never at session level, and this shall be a named case in the tenant-isolation suite. |
| SUR-SCL-022 | Read-your-writes requirements shall be identified per flow; flows requiring it shall read from the primary explicitly rather than relying on replication timing. |
| SUR-SCL-023 | Cross-instance joins shall not be introduced; a query spanning two database instances is a design failure, not an optimisation problem. |
