### 50.5 Caching strategy

#### 50.5.1 The layers

| Layer | Contents | TTL | Invalidation |
|---|---|---|---|
| CDN | Static assets, marketing pages, public marketplace listings, public tender lists | Assets: immutable, content-hashed. Pages: 5 min with stale-while-revalidate | Purge on publish |
| HTTP / ETag | API GET responses for slow-changing reference data | Conditional, validated | ETag change |
| Redis — reference data | Status vocabularies, plan definitions, rate cards, compliance rule sets, notification templates, geofence polygons | 5–60 min | Event-driven purge on change (`site.geofence_changed`, `rule.published`) |
| Redis — computed read models | Dashboard aggregates, KPI tiles, list counts | 30 s–5 min | Time-based; recomputed by a job |
| Redis — session and rate limits | Token deny-list, rate counters, idempotency keys | Per purpose | Natural expiry |
| In-process | Geofence polygons per site in the signals consumer (§34.6.2), feature flags, permission definitions | 30 s–5 min | Push-invalidated |
| Client | Guard App local database; console query cache | Per surface | Explicit; always labelled with age (SUR-UIX-004) |

#### 50.5.2 What must never be cached

| Never cached | Why |
|---|---|
| **Authorisation decisions** beyond a very short, explicitly invalidated window | A stale "allow" is a security failure. Permission *definitions* may be cached (with push invalidation on role change); a per-request *decision* is evaluated fresh |
| Anything keyed without `tenant_id` in the cache key | The single most dangerous cache bug in a multi-tenant system. Cache keys are constructed by a shared helper that always includes the tenant; a hand-built key is a review failure |
| **Tenant-scoped responses in a shared CDN cache** | The classic tenant-leak vector. Authenticated responses are marked `private, no-store` at the edge; the CDN caches only genuinely public content, and cache keys never vary on a header an attacker controls |
| Money: balances, ledger totals, amount due, payment status | A cached balance is a wrong balance the moment a payment lands |
| Compliance status used for a **blocking** decision | Deployment gating (§40.6) reads live; a cached "compliant" that is 5 minutes stale can put an unverified guard on a site |
| Live guard position beyond ~10 seconds | It is a safety surface; stale position with a "live" label is worse than no map |
| SOS state, alert state, escalation state | Operational truth, read live, always |
| OTPs, tokens, credentials, signed URLs beyond their own short lifetime | Obvious, stated because caching layers are added by people who were not in this conversation |

#### 50.5.3 Cache discipline

| Concern | Handling |
|---|---|
| Stampede | Request coalescing (single-flight) per key, plus jittered TTLs so a thousand keys do not expire in the same second |
| Negative caching | Short-TTL caching of "not found" to prevent a missing-key hammer, but never for authorisation or compliance results |
| **Cache as a crutch** | If losing the cache takes the service down, it was never a cache — it was an undeclared database. Every cache must have a working (slower) fallback path, and this is verified by a quarterly chaos exercise that flushes Redis in staging under load (§46.3.4) |
| Cache hit-rate monitoring | Per namespace; a falling hit rate is an early warning of a key-cardinality bug |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-030 | All cache keys for tenant-scoped data shall be constructed by a shared helper that includes `tenant_id`; hand-constructed keys shall fail review. |
| SUR-SCL-031 | Authenticated responses shall never be cacheable at a shared CDN layer; edge cache configuration shall be tested for tenant leakage in CI. |
| SUR-SCL-032 | Money, live position, compliance-blocking status, and authorisation decisions shall not be served from cache. |
| SUR-SCL-033 | Every cached path shall have a verified uncached fallback, exercised by a quarterly cache-flush chaos test. |

### 50.6 Queue scaling and load shedding

| Step | Change | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Redis Streams with consumer groups, partitioned by `guard_id` hash (§34.3.3) | — |
| 1 | Separate worker lanes: `critical` (SOS, alerts, attendance side effects), `default`, `heavy` (reports, OCR, payroll), `bulk` (imports, exports) | From launch |
| 2 | Independent scaling per lane | Lane utilisation >70% sustained |
| 3 | More stream partitions | Per-partition consumer lag rising while total consumer count is at its efficient maximum |
| 4 | Dedicated Redis instance for streams, separate from cache | Redis memory >60% or stream operations >40% of Redis CPU |
| 5 | Replace Redis Streams with Kafka or a managed equivalent | **>2,000 events/s sustained**, or a requirement for >7-day replay, or **>6 independent consumer groups** (§34.7.2) |

#### 50.6.1 The load-shedding order

When the system is saturated, something must be dropped or delayed. Deciding what, under pressure, is how the wrong thing gets dropped. The order is fixed in advance and implemented as ops toggles (§47.8):

| Shed order | What | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Analytics event ingestion, telemetry sampling | Dashboards lag; no user impact |
| 2 | Scheduled report generation and exports | Reports queue; users see "queued" |
| 3 | AI interactions | AI panels disappear (§41.5.5) |
| 4 | Document OCR / extraction | Manual verification path continues |
| 5 | P3 notifications, digests, marketing | Delayed or dropped per TTL |
| 6 | Non-critical read-model refreshes | Dashboard figures show their age |
| 7 | P2 notifications | Delayed |
| 8 | GPS ping *storage* (signals evaluation continues) | Trail gaps, recorded honestly |
| **Never shed** | **SOS, alert creation and escalation, attendance writes, check-in/out, incident creation, payment processing, audit logging** | — |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-040 | Worker lanes shall be separated from launch so that a heavy job class cannot starve the critical lane. |
| SUR-SCL-041 | The load-shedding order shall be implemented as ops toggles, tested under load, and shall never reach the never-shed set. |
| SUR-SCL-042 | Shedding shall be announced in the UI where it changes what a user sees (report queued, figure stale, assistant unavailable) — never silent. |

### 50.7 Storage growth and cost projection

#### 50.7.1 Growth arithmetic

| Class | Per-unit size | S0/year | S3/year | S4/year | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPS pings (raw) | ~120 B/row + index | ~55 GB (per §32.4) to ~110 GB at our higher ping rate | ~1.6 TB | ~8 TB | Compresses to 8–12% (§32.5) |
| GPS pings (compressed, retained 13 months) | — | ~6–12 GB | ~180 GB | ~900 GB | The compression is what makes this a non-problem |
| **Attendance photos, uncompressed originals (2 MB)** | 2 MB | **10.1 TB** | **152 TB** | **760 TB** | **Unaffordable — see the lever below** |
| **Attendance photos, policy-compressed (60 KB)** | 60 KB | **304 GB** | **4.6 TB** | **23 TB** | The single largest storage lever in the platform |
| Documents (KYC etc.) | ~300 KB | 14 GB cumulative | 216 GB | 1.1 TB | Slow-growing, long-retained |
| Incident and SOS evidence (photos, 30 s audio segments) | ~1.5 MB/incident | 38 GB | 570 GB | 2.8 TB | Long retention (7 y), immutable |
| Attendance/patrol/wake operational rows | ~250 B | 20 GB | 300 GB | 1.5 TB | |
| Notification delivery records | ~200 B | 2 GB | 28 GB | 140 GB | Candidate for the separate-instance step |
| Audit log | ~400 B | 15 GB | 220 GB | 1.1 TB | 8-year retention; cold-tiered after 18 months |
| Generated documents (invoices, payslips, reports) | ~150 KB | 30 GB | 450 GB | 2.2 TB | |
| **Total object storage (with photo policy)** | | **~390 GB/yr** | **~6 TB/yr** | **~30 TB/yr** | |
| **Total database (compressed, retained)** | | **~60 GB** | **~1 TB** | **~5 TB** | |

#### 50.7.2 The levers, ranked by impact

| Lever | Saving | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Attendance photo policy: resize to 640 px longest edge, JPEG q70, strip EXIF except the fields we need** | **~97%** of photo storage — 10 TB/year becomes 304 GB/year at S0 | A 640 px face photo is entirely sufficient for "is this the right person at the gate"; it is not sufficient for forensic identification, which is not what it is for. Originals are kept for 7 days only, then replaced by the derivative |
| GPS compression + downsampling + 13-month purge (§32.5) | ~90% | Historical trail precision beyond 30 days is reduced — disclosed, and a privacy control as much as a cost one (§39) |
| Object lifecycle tiering (standard → infrequent-access at 90 d → archive at 365 d) | 40–70% on the aged portion | Retrieval latency and cost on archive; acceptable for evidence that is rarely read |
| Actually running retention purges (§40.7.3) | Prevents unbounded growth entirely | Requires the retention engine to work — which is why OA-54 monitors it in both directions |
| Deduplication of identical documents (same file uploaded for multiple guards) | 5–15% | Content-hash addressing; small implementation cost |
| Log and telemetry retention discipline (§48.2.2) | Large, on the observability bill rather than storage | Shorter forensic window; mitigated by the security store's separate longer retention |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-050 | Attendance and incident photos shall be stored as policy-compressed derivatives; originals shall be retained no longer than 7 days unless flagged as evidence. |
| SUR-SCL-051 | Object lifecycle policies shall be applied per record class and verified quarterly against actual storage-class distribution. |
| SUR-SCL-052 | Storage growth shall be projected monthly against the model, and a deviation >30% shall trigger a review before it becomes a budget event. |

### 50.8 Read/write split for the Command Center

The Command Center is the most read-intensive surface in the platform and the one that must remain trustworthy under degradation. Its data sources are specified panel by panel so that no panel accidentally queries the wrong thing.

| Panel | Read source | Write path | Behaviour when the replica is down | Behaviour when the primary is degraded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Live map — guard positions | `guard_last_position` read model (Redis-backed, Postgres-persisted) + WebSocket deltas | — | Unaffected (not on the replica) | Unaffected; positions continue from the ingest path |
| Live map — site/geofence overlays | In-process cache from the reference cache | — | Unaffected | Unaffected |
| Alert queue | Primary (operational truth, read live) | Primary | Unaffected | Read-only mode with an explicit banner; acknowledgements queue locally and are marked pending |
| Alert detail / SOS workspace | Primary | Primary | Unaffected | Read-only with banner; the operator's phone-based response continues regardless |
| Escalation state | Primary | Primary | Unaffected | Read-only; escalation continues server-side |
| Attendance board | Read model, refreshed on interval | — | Unaffected | Stale, labelled with age |
| Historical replay / trail | **Replica** (or the ping partitions' instance after step 3) | — | Falls back to primary with a reduced row cap and a shorter timeout | Unavailable, stated plainly |
| Reports and SLA views | **Replica** | — | Queued as async jobs | Queued |
| Wallboard KPIs | Read model | — | Unaffected | Stale, labelled |
| Shift handover notes | Primary | Primary | Unaffected | Read-only; handover falls back to the paper form (§49.12) |

**The governing rule: nothing an operator must act on immediately is read from a replica.** Replication lag on a safety surface is a correctness bug wearing a performance costume. Everything an operator merely reviews may come from a replica, labelled with its age.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-060 | Every Command Center panel shall declare its read source; safety-critical panels shall read from the primary or from an ingest-path read model, never from a replica. |
| SUR-SCL-061 | The Command Center shall remain usable in a primary-degraded read-only mode, with an explicit banner and with operator actions queued and marked pending. |
| SUR-SCL-062 | Any displayed figure not read live shall carry its age (SUR-UIX-004). |

### 50.9 Multi-region considerations

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does latency require multi-region? | **No.** All users are in India; RTT from anywhere in India to a Mumbai or Hyderabad region is 20–110 ms (B-7/B-8). A second region would remove perhaps 30 ms for users in the far north-east, which is not a product problem worth a distributed-database problem |
| Does residency require multi-region? | No — it *constrains* it. Any second region must be Indian (§47.3.1), which is why a provider with two Indian regions was a selection criterion |
| Does availability require multi-region? | **Eventually, for DR.** Owned by §49.7, with its triggers and cost delta. Warm standby, not active-active |
| Does scale require multi-region? | No. A single Indian region has more capacity than S4 requires |
| What would break in active-active? | Write conflicts on rosters and attendance; the ledger's ordering guarantees; the `guard_last_position` compare-and-set (§34.3.5) becoming a distributed CAS; the escalation engine's timers running twice. Each is solvable and none is worth solving for a benefit we can get from a warm standby |
| Read replicas in a second region? | Only at the §34.7.2 trigger: read latency p95 >300 ms from a distant region **and** >30% of reads originating there. Neither is expected within S4 |
| What is multi-region from day one? | Backups (§49.7) and the CDN. Both cheap, both valuable |

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-070 | Multi-region shall be pursued for disaster recovery only, per §49.7, and shall remain within Indian regions. |
| SUR-SCL-071 | Active-active multi-region shall not be adopted without a documented requirement that a warm standby cannot satisfy. |

### 50.10 Cost-per-unit economics

#### 50.10.1 Infrastructure cost per guard per month

`[ASSUMPTION: A-569]` Built from the §47.15.1 baseline and scaled with the volumetrics above. Excludes communications (SMS/WhatsApp/voice — §36) and AI model spend (§25), which are usage-priced and are shown separately because they behave differently.

| Stage | Guards | Monthly infra (₹) | **₹ per guard/month** | Why it falls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S0 | 8,000 | 2,13,000 | **₹26.6** | The fixed floor (one database, one Redis, observability, non-production, CI) dominates at pilot scale |
| S1 | 25,000 | 4,20,000 | **₹16.8** | Fixed costs amortise; compute grows sub-linearly |
| S2 | 50,000 | 6,60,000 | **₹13.2** | Reserved-capacity discounts become available on a stable baseline |
| S3 | 120,000 | 12,60,000 | **₹10.5** | Extractions allow right-sized scaling per component; storage tiering matures |
| S4 | 600,000 | 42,00,000 | **₹7.0** | Cell topology; storage and ingest dominate and both are heavily optimised by then |

| Variable cost class | S0 (₹/guard/month) | S3 | Lever |
|---|---|---|---|
| Notifications (SMS-heavy) | ~₹8 | ~₹3 | Migrating transactional traffic from SMS (₹0.15–0.25/message `[ASSUMPTION: A-569]`) to push and WhatsApp is the single largest variable-cost lever; SMS remains the P0 fallback and the OTP path |
| AI | ~₹2 | ~₹4 | Per-interaction ceilings (§25.11); intent matching locally so navigation costs nothing; small models for simple reads |

| **Total variable** | **~₹12** | **~₹8** | |
| **All-in infrastructure** | **~₹38.6/guard/month** | **~₹18.5/guard/month** | |

#### 50.10.2 The honest margin picture at pilot

At S0, SaaS revenue from 30 agency tenants is ₹1.5–3.0 lakh/month (Starter ₹5,000 to Professional ₹10,000, canon §1.4) against ₹2.13 lakh of infrastructure plus ~₹1 lakh of variable cost. **The SaaS line alone does not cover infrastructure at pilot scale.** That is not a defect in the plan; it is the normal shape of an infrastructure-heavy platform before amortisation, and it is stated here so that nobody discovers it in month five.

Three things change it, and they are business decisions belonging to §52, not engineering ones:
1. Suraksha's own guarding operation (₹18,500–38,000 per guard per month of service revenue, canon §1.5) is the dominant revenue line at pilot; the platform's infrastructure cost of ~₹39/guard/month is a rounding error against it.
2. Agency tenants' guard counts matter more than tenant counts: a Professional tenant with 1,500 guards costs ~₹58,000/month of infrastructure against ₹10,000 of subscription. **Per-guard pricing components, or plan limits by guard count (D-003), are therefore not a pricing nicety — they are the difference between positive and negative unit economics on large tenants.** This is flagged here because it is an engineering observation with a direct commercial consequence.
3. Amortisation: by S2 the per-guard cost has halved.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-080 | Infrastructure cost per active guard per month shall be computed and reported monthly, split into fixed and variable components (SUR-DVO-133). |
| SUR-SCL-081 | Cost per tenant shall be computed monthly; a tenant whose infrastructure cost exceeds its subscription revenue shall be reported to management with its cost drivers. |
| SUR-SCL-082 | Every scaling decision shall state its cost delta per guard per month. |

### 50.11 Capacity planning

| Resource | Headroom metric | Review trigger | Action trigger | Lead time to add | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| API compute | CPU at peak, p95 latency margin | >50% peak CPU | >65% for 7 days | Minutes (autoscale) / days (limit raise) | Raise autoscale ceiling; right-size instances |
| Database primary CPU | Peak CPU, active connections | >50% | >65% for 7 days | Hours (vertical), weeks (step 2/3) | §50.4 ladder |
| Database storage | % free, growth rate | <40% free | <25% free or 14-day projection | Hours (online expansion) | Expand; verify retention jobs are running |
| Database connections | Pool utilisation | >60% | >85% | Hours | Add pooler capacity; audit connection leaks |
| Replica capacity | Replica CPU, replication lag | >50% CPU | >70% or lag >10 s | Days | Add replica; move reporting to its own |
| Redis memory | used/max, evictions | >60% | >80% or any eviction | Hours | Scale up; split streams onto their own instance |
| Redis throughput | ops/s, CPU | >50% | >70% | Hours | Split by workload |
| Queue capacity | Consumer lag, oldest-age | Oldest-age >2× normal p95 | >10× normal p95 | Minutes | Scale consumers; add partitions |
| WebSocket gateway | Concurrent connections vs tested ceiling | >50% of tested ceiling | >70% | Minutes | Scale out; re-run the connection load test |
| Object storage | Growth rate vs projection | >20% above model | >30% above model | N/A (elastic) | Investigate; apply levers (§50.7.2) |
| Worker pool | Lane utilisation | >50% | >70% | Minutes | Scale the lane |
| Notification provider throughput | Provider rate-limit headroom | >50% of contracted rate | >70% | **Weeks** — provider contract negotiation | Raise contracted throughput; add a second provider |
| Map/geocoding quota | Quota consumed | >50% | >70% | Days | Raise quota; improve cache hit rate |
| AI provider quota | Tokens/min against limit | >50% | >70% | Days–weeks | Raise limits; add a fallback provider |
| Team on-call capacity | Pages per person per week | >1 | >2 for 2 weeks | **Months** — hiring | §47.16.1 |

**The two long-lead items are provider throughput contracts and hiring.** Both are measured in weeks-to-months while everything else is minutes-to-days, which is precisely why they are on this table: the constraint that takes longest to relieve must be watched earliest.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-090 | Capacity headroom shall be reviewed monthly against this table; a resource crossing its review trigger shall have a documented plan before it crosses its action trigger. |
| SUR-SCL-091 | Long-lead capacity items (provider throughput, hiring) shall be reviewed quarterly with a 2-stage-ahead horizon. |

### 50.12 The top 10 scaling bottlenecks in this system

Not generic bottlenecks — these are the ten places where *this* product breaks first, in order of how soon they bite.

| # | Bottleneck | Why it bites here specifically | **Leading indicator** | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Shift-change write burst on the primary** | 60% of the day's attendance writes land in three 20–30 minute windows (B-9). Each check-in is a transaction with constraint evaluation, an outbox insert and a commit. The system is idle for 22 hours and then does everything at once | p95 check-in write latency **inside the 06:00 window specifically**, trended day over day; WAL generation rate during the window | Pre-warm connections before the window; batch outbox inserts; ensure the exclusion constraint's index is hot; **never deploy during shift change** (§47.11.2); at scale, shard attendance writes by tenant |
| **2** | **`location` table write and vacuum load** | 2.4 M rows/day at S0 rising to 36.7 M at S3, all append, all partitioned daily. Autovacuum on a table this shape, plus daily partition maintenance, plus compression jobs, compete with OLTP | Autovacuum lag on `location`; dead-tuple ratio; **whether tomorrow's partition exists** (OA-50); WAL rate attributable to the table | `FILLFACTOR=100`, no spatial index on raw pings (§32.4), `COPY` batching, compression at 2 days, extraction #1 when the trigger fires |
| **3** | **Notification fan-out for a large tenant** | One roster publish at a 5,000-guard tenant generates 5,000+ push sends, an SMS subset and possibly WhatsApp — in a shared worker pool this starves every other job for minutes | Fan-out job duration p95; critical-lane queue oldest-age *during* a fan-out; provider 429 rate | Dedicated fan-out lane from launch; chunked fan-out with fair scheduling across tenants; per-tenant concurrency cap; extraction #2 |
| **4** | **External provider rate limits** | FCM, the SMS aggregator, WhatsApp BSP and the map provider all impose per-second and per-day caps. Ours is a bursty workload against providers that price and limit for steady state. A cap breach is invisible until messages silently fail | 429/throttle rate per provider; **headroom against contracted rate**, not just current usage | Token-bucket shaping per provider; multi-provider routing (§36); contracted rate increases with a **weeks-long** lead time (§50.11); priority lanes so P0 always fits within the cap |
| **5** | **Real-time fan-out per topic** | A Command Center watching a 5,000-guard tenant's map receives every position update. Naively that is 5,000 × updates/minute per connected operator; ten operators multiply it | Messages/second per connection; gateway CPU; viewport subscription cardinality | Viewport-scoped geohash subscriptions (§34.2); server-side aggregation above a density threshold (render clusters, not dots); update coalescing at 1 Hz maximum per topic; extraction of the gateway at the §34.7.2 trigger |
| **6** | **Offline replay thundering herd** | Unique to this product. A regional network event or a platform outage means thousands of devices reconnect within minutes, each flushing up to 7 days of buffered events, arriving exactly when the system is least healthy | Device backlog distribution reported in each batch (OA-17); ratio of replay to live ingest (D3 panel); reconnect rate | Server-issued `Retry-After` with device-derived jitter; per-device replay rate limits exempting SOS and attendance (SUR-NFR-218); priority-ordered sync (SUR-NFR-214); verified by the replay-herd load test |
| **7** | **Reporting and export queries competing with operational reads** | Agency owners run month-end reports at exactly the time the finance module is generating invoices, on the same replica the Command Center uses for historical trails | Replica CPU; replication lag; report job queue depth; share of replica wait time attributable to reports | Separate reporting replica; async job model above 50k rows (SUR-NFR-026/027); statement timeouts by role; extraction #3 |
| **8** | **Redis as a single point of multiplexed load** | Cache, rate limits, the GPS ingest stream, the pub/sub backplane, distributed locks and idempotency keys all on one instance. Memory pressure from stream retention evicts cache entries, which increases database load, which slows ingest, which grows the stream — a genuine feedback loop | `used_memory` vs `maxmemory`; **any** `evicted_keys` > 0; stream length vs cap; ops/s split by namespace | Namespace-level memory budgets; bounded stream lengths; split streams onto their own instance at the §50.6 trigger; verified uncached fallback paths (SUR-SCL-033) |
| **9** | **Single-tenant hotspot** | One 20,000-guard Enterprise agency can consume more resource than the other 399 tenants combined, and its report at 09:00 becomes everyone's outage | Per-tenant database CPU-seconds share (OA-31); per-tenant request share; per-tenant ping rate | Per-tenant query throttling; the §32.1.1 isolation ladder (dedicated instance at 5,000 guards or 15% CPU share); fair-scheduling in the worker lanes |
| **10** | **Month-end financial cliff** | Payroll for 120,000 guards and invoicing for 9,000 clients both land in the first five days of the month. Payroll is CPU-heavy and transactional; invoice numbering is sequential and cannot be trivially parallelised | Payroll run duration trend (OA-36); invoice generation duration; the queue depth of the heavy lane on the 1st | Spread tenants' payroll windows across the month by configuration rather than everyone on the 1st; chunked, checkpointed, resumable runs; a dedicated heavy lane with pre-scaled capacity for the first 5 days; per-tenant invoice number sequences so parallelism is possible |

**Watch list (not yet top-10, but on the same trajectory):** object-storage request rate during photo-upload bursts at shift change; document OCR backlog during a large agency's onboarding migration; search index rebuild time (§49.1.1) becoming a multi-hour degradation at S3; the audit log's growth forcing the §50.4 step-3 separation earlier than the ping table does; and WebSocket reconnection storms after every deploy, which the 60-second drain with spread `reconnect_after` hints is designed to prevent but which must be re-verified as connection counts grow.

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| SUR-SCL-100 | Each of the ten bottlenecks shall have its leading indicator instrumented, dashboarded and thresholded before the stage at which it is predicted to bite. |
| SUR-SCL-101 | The bottleneck list shall be reviewed at each stage transition and re-ordered from observed data, not from this document's predictions. |
| SUR-SCL-102 | Load tests shall include the five named scenarios of §46.2.6, each of which exercises at least one of the top-five bottlenecks. |

## 51. Roadmap

This section converts the product specification in §7–§50 into a build sequence with gates. It does not re-describe any module, screen or workflow — it says **when** each is built, **why then**, **what must be true before** it starts, and **what must be true before** the next phase is funded. Screens are referenced by their `SUR-SCR-nnn` identifiers from §28; workflows by `WKF-nn` from §29; goals by `GOAL-nn` from §5; metrics by their `ANL-` identifiers from §42.

### 51.1 How to read this roadmap

#### 51.1.1 What a phase is

A phase is a funded block of work that ends in a **decision**, not a date. Each phase in this section is specified on ten points: objective and the business question it answers · scope · out-of-scope · dependencies · team shape · duration and its assumption · risks · acceptance criteria · go/no-go decision · demonstrable outcome. A phase that cannot pass its acceptance criteria does not proceed by adding a caveat; it is either extended or descoped, and the decision is recorded.

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-RDM-001 | Every phase shall end with a recorded go/no-go decision naming the decision-maker, the acceptance criteria met and unmet, and the disposition of unmet criteria (extend, descope, accept as debt with an owner and a date). | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-RDM-002 | No phase shall begin before its stated dependencies are demonstrably complete; a dependency declared "nearly done" shall be treated as not done for gating purposes. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-RDM-003 | Acceptance criteria shall be measurable from instrumented data (§42) or from a scripted test (§44), never from an opinion that a phase "feels complete". | [RECOMMENDED] |

#### 51.1.2 The three horizons this roadmap serves

The roadmap is simultaneously a build plan, a hiring plan and a cash plan. Phase durations therefore carry an explicit team-size assumption (§51.13); halving the team does not halve the output, and the section says what actually happens instead.

#### 51.1.3 Reconciling the phase labels used elsewhere in this PRD

§28 tags each screen `Ph1`–`Ph4` and §29.41 tags each workflow `Ph1`–`Ph3`. Those are coarse three-band groupings written before this section existed; §8.1 and §28.1 both state that phase definitions are **owned by §51**. The mapping is:

| Label in §28 / §29 | Roadmap phase in this section | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Ph1 | Phase 0 · Phase 1 · Phase 2 | "Can we run a real deployment end to end" |
| Ph2 | Phase 3 · Phase 4 | "Commercial completeness" |
| Ph3 | Phase 5 | "Scale and depth" |
| Ph4 | Beyond Phase 5 | `[FUTURE]`, see §51.11 |

**One deliberate exception, stated openly.** §28 marks 41 Agency Portal web screens as `Ph1`. In this roadmap the Agency Portal is a **Phase 3** surface. Those screens are `Ph1` in §28's sense of "cannot ship *that product* without them" — they are the Agency Portal's own minimum set, not the platform's. The domain services beneath them (Guard, Site, Post, Shift, Roster, Assignment, Attendance) are built multi-tenant in Phase 0–2 and consumed by OPS for tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ`; Phase 3 surfaces the same services to agency tenants. This is the single most important structural decision in the roadmap and it is defended in §51.9.3.

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-RDM-004 | Every domain service shall be built tenant-scoped from its first commit (canon §3 tenancy), even when its only consumer in Phase 1 is tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ`. Retrofitting tenancy is prohibited. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-RDM-005 | No Phase 3 work shall require a rewrite of a Phase 1 domain service to introduce tenancy, entitlements or branch scoping; if such a rewrite is discovered, it is a Phase 0 defect and is fixed as a P0. | [RECOMMENDED] |

---

### 51.2 Phase 0 — Foundation

#### 51.2.1 Objective and the business question it answers

**Objective:** build the substrate that every later phase stands on — identity, tenancy, the design system, the security baseline and the core database — and nothing that a customer can see.

**Business question answered:** *"Can we build this at all, safely, multi-tenant, without discovering in month nine that tenancy, permissions or money handling were bolted on?"* Phase 0 exists because the three defects that are unfixable later — cross-tenant leakage, an ad-hoc permission model and floating-point money — are all decided in the first eight weeks.

#### 51.2.2 Scope

| Area | In scope | Canonical spec |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Central identity service; phone-first OTP; email+password; Google/Apple; mandatory phone verification; session policy (30-day client, short privileged); MFA framework | canon §4, §38 |
| Tenancy | `tenant_id` on every tenant-scoped row; `branch_id` as the second axis; row-level enforcement at the data layer; `SURAKSHA-HQ` seeded as tenant zero | canon §3, §32 |
| Permissions | Role catalogue for all four role families; permission resolution service; entitlement service reading plan entitlements as data (SUR-FIN-166) | §31, §35.8.1 |
| Core database | Entity model for Organization, Agency, Branch, Client, Site, Post, Shift, Guard, Assignment, Document, Audit Log; migration tooling; soft-delete and archive semantics | §32 |
| Money primitives | Integer-paise money type; double-sided ledger primitives; idempotency keys on money-moving operations | §35.1 |
| Design system | Tokens, type scale, colour (#F6F7F9 base, Suraksha navy/steel), component library, density modes, mobile-first and desktop-density variants, accessibility baseline | §27 |
| Security baseline | Secrets management, encryption at rest and in transit, audit-log append-only store, dependency scanning, SAST in CI, tenancy test harness | §38, §43 |
| Platform ops | CI/CD, environments (dev/stage/prod), observability skeleton (logs, traces, metrics), backup and restore proven once | §47, §48, §49 |
| API contract | OpenAPI contract-first discipline, versioning policy, error envelope, pagination and idempotency conventions | §33 |
| Screens | None customer-facing. `SUR-SCR-400` (OPS login & MFA), `SUR-SCR-478` (System configuration & feature flags), `SUR-SCR-479` (Users, roles & access review) as the internal shell | §28 |

#### 51.2.3 Explicitly out of scope

Any booking flow. Any guard-facing surface. Any agency-facing surface. Any AI. Any payment integration beyond a sandbox credential check. Any marketing site content. Any mobile application. Any analytics dashboard. Reporting. Notifications beyond a transactional email/SMS smoke path. Anything with a screen a customer would recognise.

#### 51.2.4 Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Prior phase | None — this is the origin | — |
| External | Cloud account, domain control of `surakshaguards.in` and subdomains, SMS/OTP provider account, Zoho email tenancy | OTP cannot be tested end to end; identity work stalls |
| External | Razorpay sandbox credentials | Money primitives cannot be validated against a real gateway shape |
| Decision | D-005 serviceable cities (needed only as a config shape, not a final list) | Serviceability model can be built; the list can be filled later |
| Organisational | Founder sign-off on the role catalogue (canon §3) and the permission philosophy (§31) | Permission model churns and every later phase inherits the churn |

#### 51.2.5 Team shape

| Role | Count | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Product lead | 1 | Owns the entity model and role catalogue decisions |
| Design (systems) | 2 | Design system is a Phase 0 deliverable, not a Phase 1 side-effect |
| Backend | 4 | Identity, tenancy, entity model, money primitives — four parallel tracks |
| Frontend (web platform) | 2 | Component library implementation, OPS shell |
| DevOps/SRE | 1 | Environments, CI/CD, backup/restore proof |
| Security | 1 | Threat model, baseline controls, tenancy test harness |
| QA/automation | 1 | Test framework, tenancy test suite |
| **Total** | **12** | |

#### 51.2.6 Duration

**8 weeks** `[ASSUMPTION: A-580]` at the team shape above, assuming the team is available from week 1 and the role catalogue is signed off by end of week 2. The assumption most likely to break is design-system scope: a design system built for eleven surfaces is a larger artefact than a design system built for one, and §27's component set is not small.

#### 51.2.7 Key risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Design system over-scoped, becomes a 16-week project | Phase 1 starts late with no UI foundation | Ship tokens + 25 highest-frequency components in Phase 0; the long tail lands during Phase 1 behind the same tokens |
| Tenancy implemented at the application layer only | A single missed `WHERE tenant_id` becomes a P0 breach (GOAL-13) | Enforce at the data layer; automated tenancy test on every tenant-scoped endpoint before any feature merges |
| Permission model designed for Suraksha roles only, then bent for agency roles | Phase 3 rewrite | Model all four role families in Phase 0 even though three have no UI yet |
| "Foundation" becomes a euphemism for indefinite architecture work | Nothing demonstrable for two months, confidence drops | Hard 8-week timebox with the acceptance criteria below; anything unfinished moves into Phase 1 as named debt |

#### 51.2.8 Acceptance criteria

| # | Criterion | How it is tested |
|---|---|---|
| A0-1 | A user can register with a phone number, receive an OTP, verify it, and hold a session; sessions expire per the configured policy | Automated end-to-end test in CI |
| A0-2 | Two seeded tenants exist; an authenticated principal of tenant A receives 404/403 (never 200) on every tenant-scoped endpoint for tenant B's data | Automated tenancy suite covering **100%** of tenant-scoped endpoints; zero failures |
| A0-3 | The permission service resolves a decision for every (role × resource × action) triple in §31 with no "default allow" path anywhere | Matrix test derived from §31, 100% coverage |
| A0-4 | A ledger entry cannot be created without a balancing counter-entry; a money value cannot be stored as a float anywhere in the schema | Schema assertion + unit tests |
| A0-5 | The design system publishes tokens and ≥25 components with light-theme and density variants, documented, consumed by the OPS shell | Component inventory reviewed against §27 |
| A0-6 | A production-shaped database is backed up and restored to a new environment with zero data loss, timed | Documented restore drill (§49) |
| A0-7 | CI blocks a merge on: failing tenancy test, SAST high finding, missing migration, contract-breaking API change | Deliberate red-build test of each gate |
| A0-8 | Every write to a tenant-scoped or money-scoped entity produces an append-only audit record with actor, tenant, before/after and timestamp | Audit coverage test |

#### 51.2.9 Go/no-go decision

**Proceed to Phase 1 if and only if** A0-1 through A0-8 pass with zero open P0 defects and the tenancy suite is green at 100%. **Do not proceed** on a partial tenancy result — the correct response to a failing tenancy suite is to extend Phase 0, because every week of Phase 1 built on leaky tenancy multiplies the remediation cost. Decision owner: CTO, recorded with the CEO and COO informed.

#### 51.2.10 What is demonstrable

To an investor or a technical due-diligence reviewer, not to a customer: a live login with OTP; a screen recording of tenant A being denied tenant B's data across the whole API surface; the design system documentation site; a restore drill report; the CI gates failing a deliberately bad commit. This is a credibility demo, not a product demo, and it should be presented as such rather than dressed up.

### 51.3 Phase 1 — Core MVP

#### 51.3.1 Objective and the business question it answers

**Objective:** make it possible for a real client to buy real guarding from Suraksha online, and for Suraksha to fulfil it, on a system rather than on WhatsApp.

**Business question answered:** *"Will a client buy a guard online without a phone call, and can we run the resulting deployment on our own software?"* This is GOAL-02 and the operational half of GOAL-10. It is also the phase that makes the ten `P1–P10` defects in the current live site (canon §1.8) go away, because a booking flow that works replaces P10 and a truthful site replaces P1–P8.

#### 51.3.2 Scope

| Module group | Screens (§28) | Workflows (§29) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main website — marketing, trust, legal | `SUR-SCR-001`–`005`, `007`, `012`–`014`, `026`–`033`, `039`, `040`, `043`, `044`, `047`–`050`, `052`–`057`, `059` | — | Replaces all fabricated content (GOAL-14); every published number query-backed (SUR-PLT-020) |
| Booking engine | `SUR-SCR-015`–`022` | `WKF-06` B2C booking, `WKF-01` customer registration, `WKF-22` payment | Razorpay live; GST invoice PDF |
| Enterprise capture | `SUR-SCR-023`, `024` | `WKF-07` B2B lead, `WKF-08` quotation, `WKF-09` contract | Quote → contract, no self-serve enterprise checkout |
| Client portal | `SUR-SCR-061`–`065`, `067`–`069`, `072`, `073`, `076`, `079`, `081`–`084`, `086`–`089`, `093`–`096`, `101`, `102` | — | Attendance dashboard is ops-entered data in Phase 1 (see dependency below) |
| OPS — clients, bookings, sales, contracts | `SUR-SCR-401`–`404`, `414`–`421`, `423`, `425`, `426` | `WKF-07`–`WKF-09` | The internal engine that fulfils a booking |
| OPS — sites, workforce, deployment | `SUR-SCR-428`–`435`, `437`, `440`–`443`, `445`, `446` | `WKF-10` site setup, `WKF-11` guard allocation, `WKF-12` shift creation, `WKF-13` attendance (manual capture path), `WKF-18` replacement | Roster and allocation for `SURAKSHA-HQ`, multi-tenant-ready |
| OPS — compliance & support | `SUR-SCR-469`, `SUR-SCR-471`–`474` | `WKF-05` guard verification, `WKF-29` document expiry, `WKF-25` complaint | Licence register and document expiry from day one; BR-002 enforced |
| Guard platform (web) | `SUR-SCR-138`, `139`, plus guard self-service records and document upload | `WKF-02` guard registration | Guard onboarding without the app; the app arrives in Phase 2 |

| Platform | Notification transport (push scaffold, SMS, WhatsApp where permitted, email) for booking, verification and complaint events (§36) | — | Full notification architecture arrives with the alerting load in Phase 2 |

Indicative screen count committed in Phase 1: **110** of the 503 in §28.

#### 51.3.3 Explicitly out of scope

The Guard App. GPS attendance. Live tracking. Patrol. Wake checks. SOS. The Command Center console. Payroll. Invoicing automation (the first invoices are produced by Finance from the locked attendance register — see §29.41's note). The Agency Portal in any form. The marketplace directory. Any mobile application. AI. Analytics dashboards beyond the operational counters on `SUR-SCR-401`/`402`. Tenders. Recruitment. Assets. Visitor management.

#### 51.3.4 Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Prior phase | Phase 0 complete, all criteria green | Tenancy or permission rework mid-phase |
| External | Razorpay production account, activated, with the correct business category | No online payment; booking flow ends at "we will call you", defeating GOAL-02 |
| External | GST registration and the invoicing series configuration | Invoices cannot be issued legally to B2B clients |
| External | At least one valid PSARA licence in the launch state or district | Nothing can be legally deployed; the whole phase becomes a demo |
| External | SMS/WhatsApp sender approvals and template registration | OTP and booking notifications throttled or blocked |
| Decision | **D-005** serviceable cities for V1 | The booking serviceability check has nothing to check against |
| Decision | **D-210** advance vs full first-month payment (raised in §29) | The payment step cannot be built to a final shape |
| Organisational | A real bench of verified guards in the launch city | The system works and there is nobody to deploy |

#### 51.3.5 Team shape

| Role | Count | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Product | 2 | One on client-side (website/booking/portal), one on OPS |
| Design | 3 | Two product designers, one content/UX writer for the truthful-content rewrite |
| Backend | 7 | Booking, contracts, workforce/deployment, notifications, payments, verification, platform |
| Frontend web | 5 | Marketing site, booking, portal, OPS |
| QA/automation | 3 | Regression suite grows fastest here |
| DevOps/SRE | 1 | |
| Data/analytics | 1 | Event taxonomy (§42.4) instrumented as features ship, not after |
| **Total** | **22** | Plus operational headcount (city ops, verification) which is not an engineering cost |

#### 51.3.6 Duration

**14 weeks** `[ASSUMPTION: A-581]`, assuming the team above, the design system carried forward from Phase 0, and no change to the booking commercial model mid-phase. The largest schedule risk is not engineering: it is the truthful-content rewrite (GOAL-14), which requires the founders to produce real photographs, real case material, real coverage claims and legally reviewed policy pages. That work is frequently the last thing done and the first thing to slip.

#### 51.3.7 Key risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Content and legal pages are not ready, so the site launches with placeholder text | Repeats the exact failure mode of the current site (canon P1–P8) | Content is a tracked deliverable with named owners from week 1; a page without approved content does not ship, the route 404s cleanly |
| Booking conversion is far below GOAL-02's 60% | The central B2C thesis is wrong or the flow is wrong | Instrument `ANL-B03` per step from day one; a 6-step flow with per-step drop-off is diagnosable, a "quote form" is not |
| Attendance is manual in Phase 1, and manual attendance becomes normalised | Phase 2's Guard App is treated as optional | State the Phase 1 attendance path as explicitly temporary in the product itself (a banner in OPS naming the Phase 2 replacement) |
| The launch city has too few clients to produce signal | Acceptance criteria pass on a sample of three | Set a minimum sample in the acceptance criteria (below) rather than a percentage on a tiny base |

#### 51.3.8 Acceptance criteria

| # | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| A1-1 | ≥25 real bookings created through `SUR-SCR-015`–`021` by real customers (not staff, not test accounts) | Booking records with distinct verified phone numbers |
| A1-2 | ≥60% of those bookings complete booking → payment → confirmation with **zero** manual intervention | `ANL-B04` ≥ 60% (GOAL-02) |
| A1-3 | Payment success rate ≥92% on attempted checkouts | `ANL-B05` |
| A1-4 | ≥1 client with ≥1 site, ≥4 guards, deployed and running for ≥30 consecutive days entirely on-platform | Contract, Site, Post, Shift, Assignment and Attendance records exist for every day |
| A1-5 | 100% of deployed guards have a Verified licence-relevant document set before their first shift; zero deployments of an unverified guard | `ANL-K03`, `ANL-K04`; BR-002 enforcement log shows zero overrides |
| A1-6 | Zero fabricated team members, clients, testimonials, tenders, awards or statistics on any public surface | Manual content audit against canon P1–P5, signed off |
| A1-7 | Zero P0 tenancy defects; tenancy suite green throughout | GOAL-13 |
| A1-8 | The first client invoice is produced from platform data (even if Finance issues it manually) and is accepted by the client without dispute | Invoice + client acceptance record |
| A1-9 | Median quote turnaround ≤8 business hours on B2B enquiries | `ANL-B07` |

#### 51.3.9 Go/no-go decision

**Proceed to Phase 2 if** A1-1, A1-4, A1-5, A1-6 and A1-7 are met, **and** A1-2 is either met or its failure is diagnosed to a specific step with a fix in hand. A booking completion rate below 40% with no diagnosis is a **no-go**: it means either the market does not buy this way or the flow is wrong, and building the Guard App on top of a demand hypothesis that has not been validated is the most expensive possible mistake. In that case the correct action is a 4-week Phase 1b focused solely on the funnel.

Decision owner: CEO (demand question) with CTO (delivery question), both required.

#### 51.3.10 What is demonstrable

A customer can be shown: a live website with no fabricated content, a working six-step booking that ends in a paid confirmation, and a client portal showing their own deployment, guards, documents and invoices. An investor can be shown: real bookings, real revenue, a real client running 30 days on-platform, and a funnel with per-step conversion. This is the first phase where "we have a product" is a true statement.

### 51.4 Phase 2 — Operations

#### 51.4.1 Objective and the business question it answers

**Objective:** put the field into the system. Build the Guard App, GPS attendance, patrol, wake checks, SOS and the Command Center, so that duty becomes provable rather than asserted.

**Business question answered:** *"Can we prove, to a client and to ourselves, that the guard we billed for was actually on post — and can we respond when he is not?"* This is GOAL-01, GOAL-04 and GOAL-05, and it is the phase that converts Suraksha from a staffing vendor into a monitored-security company. Every claim on the live brand — 24/7 command center, live GPS tracking, GPS attendance, night anti-sleep wake-checks (canon §1) — becomes true in Phase 2 and is a marketing lie until then.

#### 51.4.2 Scope

| Module group | Screens (§28) | Workflows (§29) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guard App — onboarding & auth | `SUR-SCR-164`–`169` | `WKF-02` | Language pack select, permission primer, battery-optimisation guide, device binding, face enrolment |
| Guard App — duty | `SUR-SCR-170`–`173` | `WKF-11`, `WKF-12` | Today's duty, shift detail, post orders, roster, site brief |
| Guard App — attendance | `SUR-SCR-174`–`176` | `WKF-13` | GPS + geofence + face check-in/out with exception reasons; `device_time` **and** `server_received_time` (canon §4) |
| Guard App — patrol | `SUR-SCR-180`–`183` | `WKF-14` | QR/NFC checkpoint scan with a manual fallback that is auditable, not silent |
| Guard App — wake check | `SUR-SCR-185` | `WKF-15` | The differentiator; D-213 governs window and randomisation |
| Guard App — emergency & incident | `SUR-SCR-187`–`193` | `WKF-16`, `WKF-17` | SOS raise, active state, debrief; incident with evidence |
| Guard App — profile & system | `SUR-SCR-203`, `204`, `211`, `212` | `WKF-29` | Offline queue status and degraded-state banner are first-class screens, not error states |
| Command Center | `SUR-SCR-405`–`411` | `WKF-16`, `WKF-17`, `WKF-18` | Console, wallboard, live national map, alert detail and escalation ladder, SOS workspace, handover log, on-call tree |
| OPS — operations depth | `SUR-SCR-449`–`451`, `443`, `446` | `WKF-15`, `WKF-17`, `WKF-18` | Wake-check compliance, incident queue and investigation, replacement workspace |
| Client portal — live surfaces | `SUR-SCR-075`, `077`, `078`, `074` | `WKF-13`, `WKF-14`, `WKF-18` | Live tracking map, attendance detail & dispute, patrol report, replacement request — all only meaningful once the Guard App is live |
| Customer App | `SUR-SCR-106`–`119`, `121`–`124`, `127`, `128`, `130`, `131`, `135`, `137` | `WKF-01`, `WKF-06`, `WKF-13`, `WKF-17` | Full booking + monitoring on mobile (§8.3 stance) |
| Admin App | `SUR-SCR-480`–`495` band (alert, triage, approve, assign) | `WKF-16`, `WKF-17`, `WKF-18` | The on-call surface; wins the first 60 seconds of an alert |
| Guard platform (web) | `SUR-SCR-140`–`155` band | `WKF-02`, `WKF-05`, `WKF-29` | Guard records, documents, payslip-ready shell |
| Real-time platform | Ingest path, presence, location stream, alert pipeline (§34, §24.6) | — | The separate real-time path anticipated in canon §4 |

Indicative screen count committed in Phase 2: **99**.

#### 51.4.3 Explicitly out of scope

Payroll execution. Invoicing automation. The Agency Portal. The marketplace directory. The Agency App. Tenders. Recruitment. AI in any form, including the Guard App voice assistant (`SUR-SCR-206`, Ph2 in §28, deferred here to Phase 4 — see §51.11). Biometric device integration. Visitor management. Body-worn cameras or video streaming. iOS Guard App (Android-first per §8.1; iOS is a Phase 4/5 question).

#### 51.4.4 Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Prior phase | Phase 1 — Site, Post, Shift, Assignment must exist before an attendance event has anything to attach to | Attendance becomes an orphan event stream |
| Prior phase | Phase 0 identity, because a guard's identity is the same central identity (canon §4) | Two identity systems, permanently |
| **External — the gating one** | **Guard App adoption.** Live tracking, wake checks, patrol compliance and attendance-driven billing are all downstream of guards actually installing, keeping installed, and using the app on their own low-end Android devices | Every client-facing "live" surface shows nothing. This is the longest pole (§51.8.3) |
| External | Play Store listing approval; background-location permission justification; per-OEM battery-optimisation behaviour (Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo, Realme, Samsung all differ) | Location stops when the screen sleeps, and the product silently fails at night — exactly when it matters |
| External | Push infrastructure with a delivery guarantee good enough for wake checks and SOS; iOS Critical Alerts entitlement is `A-146` (raised in §25) and must not be depended on | Wake checks miss; the design must work without the entitlement |
| Decision | **D-103** Guard App target device profile and data budget (raised in §8) | The app is built for a phone the workforce does not own |
| Decision | **D-213** wake-check window and randomisation policy | The control is either trivially gamed or punishes a guard walking a legitimate round |
| Organisational | Command Center staffing — 24×7×365 with no unmanned minute (SUR-CMD-001). Minimum viable rota is ~6 operators + 1 supervisor | The console exists and nobody is watching it, which is worse than not claiming it |

#### 51.4.5 Team shape

| Role | Count | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Product | 2 | One field/mobile, one command centre |
| Design | 3 | Including one designer dedicated to the Guard App — low literacy, gloves, night, glare |
| Backend | 8 | Real-time ingest, alerting, attendance/patrol/wake-check domain, offline sync reconciliation |
| Frontend web | 5 | Command Center console and wallboard are dense, high-stakes UI |
| Mobile | 6 | 4 on Guard App (offline-first is expensive), 2 on Customer App + Admin App |
| QA/automation | 4 | Including one dedicated to device-lab testing across the OEM matrix |
| DevOps/SRE | 1 | Real-time path has its own scaling and alerting profile |
| Data/analytics | 1 | |
| Ops SME (field) | 1 | A real supervisor, embedded, full-time — not a consultant |
| **Total** | **31** | Plus 7 Command Center operational staff (not engineering) |

#### 51.4.6 Duration

**16 weeks** `[ASSUMPTION: A-582]`, assuming a device lab covering the five dominant Android OEMs in the target wage band, an embedded field SME, and that offline-first sync is designed in week 1 rather than retrofitted. The assumption most likely to break is field trial time: a wake-check system can only be validated at 02:00 on a real night post, and there is no way to compress the calendar for that.

#### 51.4.7 Key risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Guards do not install or keep the app | The entire phase's value evaporates; live surfaces stay empty | Make attendance-to-payslip the guard's incentive (GOAL-06): no app, no verified attendance, no payslip line the guard can see and trust. Ship the app-download screen (`SUR-SCR-163`) into onboarding, not as an afterthought |
| Battery drain kills adoption after week 2 | Silent uninstall wave | Adaptive location sampling; measure and publish battery cost per shift as an acceptance criterion (below) |
| Offline sync produces duplicate or conflicting attendance | Payroll and billing disputes, and BR-003 violations if corrected badly | Idempotent event IDs generated on-device; server-side reconciliation with an explicit conflict queue; never silently overwrite |
| Face check-in fails for a specific demographic or in low light | Guards blocked from duty; discrimination risk | Exception path with supervisor vouching (`SUR-SCR-209`) is mandatory, not optional; failure rates monitored by site and time-of-day |
| Command Center is understaffed and alerts age out | SUR-CMD-004 violated; the brand promise is false | Roster gating (SUR-CMD-005); an alert that cannot be picked up escalates automatically |
| False SOS floods desensitise operators | The one alert that matters is missed | Confirm-step on `SUR-SCR-187`, per-guard false-alarm tracking, and a debrief on every SOS (`SUR-SCR-189`) |

#### 51.4.8 Acceptance criteria

| # | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| A2-1 | ≥90% of deployed guards have the app installed and active in the last 7 days | Device registry vs deployed-guard count |
| A2-2 | Proof completeness ≥95% of rostered shifts on Suraksha-operated sites produce a GPS+face check-in and check-out | GOAL-01 / `ANL` service-delivery family |
| A2-3 | Wake-check acknowledgement rate ≥97% on night posts | GOAL-04 |
| A2-4 | Median wake-check escalation-to-resolution <10 minutes | GOAL-04 |
| A2-5 | Median time-to-fill on a replacement <45 minutes urban daytime, <90 minutes at night | GOAL-05 |
| A2-6 | 100% of P0/P1 alerts terminate in a resolution with an outcome code or an incident record; zero silent expiries | SUR-CMD-004 |
| A2-7 | Guard App functions for a complete 12-hour shift with no connectivity and syncs without data loss or duplication | Scripted offline field test, repeated on 5 OEM devices |
| A2-8 | Battery consumption ≤18% of a 4,000 mAh battery over a 12-hour shift with location active `[ASSUMPTION: A-583]` | Device lab measurement |
| A2-9 | Client portal live map and attendance dashboard render field-sourced data with <60s end-to-end latency at p95 | Synthetic probe |
| A2-10 | Zero attendance records exist without both `device_time` and `server_received_time` | Schema + data audit |

#### 51.4.9 Go/no-go decision

**Proceed to Phase 3 if** A2-1, A2-2, A2-3, A2-7 and A2-10 are met. A2-1 is the hard gate: **below 75% Guard App adoption, do not start Phase 3.** Selling an operations platform to agencies whose guards will use the same app, when your own guards will not use it, is a proposition that dies in the first reference call. In that case the right move is a Phase 2b of 6–8 weeks focused exclusively on adoption — device support, incentive design, supervisor enforcement, app weight and battery.

Decision owner: COO (field adoption) with CTO (technical criteria).

#### 51.4.10 What is demonstrable

To a client: a live map showing their guard on their site right now; last night's wake-check log with timestamps; an SOS raised on a test device that appears on the Command Center console in seconds and escalates on a visible ladder; a month of attendance with photographic and geographic evidence per shift. To an investor: the Command Center wallboard with real deployments, and the proof-completeness metric trending. This is the demo that sells both businesses — it is the single most valuable artefact the roadmap produces.

### 51.5 Phase 3 — Agency SaaS

#### 51.5.1 Objective and the business question it answers

**Objective:** surface the domain services built in Phases 0–2 to agency tenants as the Agency Portal (ERP, payroll, billing, CRM, compliance), open the Trinetra marketplace, and start subscription revenue.

**Business question answered:** *"Will a PSARA-licensed agency pay ₹5,000 or ₹10,000 a month for this, and will they still be paying in month four?"* This is GOAL-07 and GOAL-09. It is also the phase where the business model changes shape: until now every rupee of revenue costs a guard's wage; from here some revenue has a 70%+ contribution margin (§52.2).

#### 51.5.3 Explicitly out of scope

Tenders and tender discovery (`SUR-SCR-342`–`345`) — Professional feature, Phase 4. OCR migration (`SUR-SCR-355`) — Enterprise, Phase 4. Workflow automation. Advanced analytics and the report builder. Asset and visitor management. Biometric integration. Multi-branch depth beyond basic branch scoping. Custom roles and SSO. The Enterprise API. Marketing tools and website/profile management. AI copilot in the portal. Settlement runs and marketplace subcontracting money flows (`WKF-23`, Ph3 in §29.41).

This out-of-scope list is deliberately aggressive. Canon §1.4 places a long list on Professional and a longer list on Enterprise; Phase 3 ships **Starter completely and Professional partially**, and the plan comparison page must say so rather than sell a Professional plan whose headline features arrive later. See SUR-RDM-012.

#### 51.5.4 Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Prior phase | Phase 0 tenancy and entitlements. Every Phase 3 screen is a tenant-scoped, entitlement-gated view over Phase 1–2 services | Phase 3 becomes a rewrite instead of a surfacing exercise |
| Prior phase | Phase 2 Guard App — an agency tenant's guards use the **same app**. Without it the Agency Portal is a roster spreadsheet with a login | The core differentiator versus incumbent agency software disappears |
| Prior phase | Phase 1 booking/CRM primitives reused for the agency's own clients | Duplicate implementations of Client, Site, Contract |
| External | Verified supply for the marketplace — agencies willing to be listed and verified (GOAL-08) | An empty directory converts nobody and damages credibility |

| Decision | **D-580** whether Suraksha operates guarding in the same cities where it sells SaaS | Determines how the conflict of interest is disclosed and priced (§52.5.5) |
| Organisational | An onboarding/customer-success function. A 60-guard agency does not self-serve onto an ERP | Trial-to-paid and 90-day retention both collapse |

#### 51.5.6 Duration

**20 weeks** `[ASSUMPTION: A-584]`, assuming the Phase 0 entitlement service genuinely works as data (SUR-FIN-166) so gating is configuration rather than code, and assuming payroll is scoped to "basic" on Starter as canon §1.4 says rather than quietly built to full depth for everyone. Payroll is the schedule risk: statutory computation, salary structures, advances, deductions and payslip generation are individually simple and collectively a 6–8 week block that cannot be parallelised much.

#### 51.5.7 Key risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Agencies want their **existing** data in the system on day one, and OCR migration is Phase 4 | Onboarding stalls at "we have 400 guards in a register" | Ship a CSV/Excel bulk import (`SUR-SCR-260`) in Phase 3 and a hands-on migration service; OCR is for the genuinely paper-based Enterprise case |
| Payroll produces a wrong number once | Trust is lost permanently; payroll is the least forgiving module in the product | Parallel-run for two cycles against the tenant's existing process before it becomes the system of record; a documented variance report per run |
| Starter is good enough and nobody upgrades | ARPA flat, `ANL-P14` near zero, the ₹10,000 tier is decorative | Design the upgrade triggers into the product (§52.3.5) rather than hoping |
| The conflict of interest surfaces in a sales call before it is addressed | Agencies decline to put their client list into a competitor's system | Publish the position first (§52.5.5); make the data commitments contractual, not aspirational |
| Marketplace launches empty | GOAL-08 stalls; the SaaS funnel has no top | Seed the directory with unclaimed, publicly-sourced listings and a claim flow (`SUR-SCR-232`, `SUR-SCR-233`) before the SaaS launch, during Phase 2 |

#### 51.5.8 Acceptance criteria

| # | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| A3-1 | ≥30 agency tenants on a paid plan (any tier), acquired without founder-led selling on more than half | Subscription records; `ANL-P13` plan mix reported |
| A3-2 | ≥70% of onboarded Starter tenants have ≥80% of their active guards rostered in the portal by day 30 | GOAL-07 |
| A3-3 | 90-day retention ≥80% for the first paid cohort | GOAL-09 / `ANL-P10` inverse |
| A3-4 | Trial-to-paid conversion ≥25% | `ANL-P11` |
| A3-5 | ≥2 tenants complete a full payroll cycle on-platform with zero disputed payslips | `WKF-20` completion; dispute count |
| A3-6 | ≥500 marketplace listings live with ≥200 licence-verified | `ANL-M01`, `ANL-M02` (interim milestone toward GOAL-08's 5,000/2,000) |
| A3-7 | Entitlement enforcement: zero instances of a tenant accessing a capability outside its plan | Automated entitlement test per plan per endpoint |
| A3-8 | Zero cross-tenant data exposure incidents | GOAL-13 |
| A3-9 | Median onboarding time from payment to first roster published ≤7 days | Onboarding milestone timestamps |
| A3-10 | Subscription billing runs a full cycle including a failed payment, dunning, suspension and reactivation without manual repair | `WKF-32`; scripted test in production-shaped staging |

#### 51.5.9 Go/no-go decision

**Proceed to Phase 4 if** A3-1, A3-3 and A3-7 are met. The decisive one is **A3-3 retention**: 30 signups with 50% 90-day retention means the product was bought and abandoned, and the correct response is not more features (Phase 4) but a retention investigation. If A3-1 is met but A3-2 is not — tenants pay but do not actually roster in the product — the business is selling a subscription to a shelf, and Phase 4's intelligence features have no data to be intelligent about.

Decision owner: CEO with the Agency SaaS product lead; COO consulted on onboarding capacity.

#### 51.5.10 What is demonstrable

To an agency prospect: their own competitor-shaped peer running rosters, attendance and payroll live; the marketplace listing that brings them enquiries; the desktop app installing on the office PC that currently runs legacy software. To an investor: MRR with a plan mix, a cohort retention curve, and a second revenue engine with a materially different margin profile from the guarding business.

### 51.6 Phase 4 — Intelligence

#### 51.6.1 Objective and the business question it answers

**Objective:** add the AI platform, analytics depth, OCR-based migration and workflow automation — and complete the depth of every surface that Phases 1–3 shipped at breadth.

**Business question answered:** *"Now that we have real operational data, can we make the product decide, summarise and act — and does that measurably change what a user does?"* This is GOAL-12, and commercially it is the phase that justifies the Professional tier and unlocks Enterprise.

**An honest structural note.** Phase 4 carries the largest screen count of any phase (**~178 of 503**) because it does two jobs: the intelligence layer *and* the depth completion of every surface. That is too much for one gate. `[RECOMMENDED]` split it into **Phase 4a — Intelligence core** (AI platform, analytics, OCR, automation; ~70 screens) and **Phase 4b — Surface depth** (the remaining ~108 screens across all surfaces), each with its own gate. This section specifies them as one phase with two named gates; formal adoption of the split is `D-589`.

#### 51.6.2 Scope

| Module group | Screens (§28) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| AI platform | `SUR-SCR-353`, `354` (agency), `SUR-SCR-476`, `477` (OPS), `SUR-SCR-206` (Guard App voice), `SUR-SCR-134` (Customer App assistant) | `WKF-34` AI request, `WKF-35` AI approval; four action classes and the prohibition list are canon §1.7 and §41 — not restated here |
| AI languages | Hindi + English at launch of the phase; additional Indian languages rolled out behind a per-language readiness gate toward the ≥19 target | canon §1.7; GOAL-12 |
| Analytics & reporting | `SUR-SCR-351`, `352` (agency), `SUR-SCR-099`, `100` (client), OPS analytics depth | §42 dashboards; curated-first then self-serve (§42.5.1) |
| OCR migration | `SUR-SCR-355` | `WKF-33`; **Enterprise-only** per canon §1.4 |
| Workflow automation | Agency Portal automation module | **Professional+** per canon §1.4 |
| Tenders | `SUR-SCR-342`–`345` | **Professional+**; `WKF-26`, `WKF-27`. Government portal APIs are uncertain — manual/assisted discovery with a documented fallback (§37) |
| Assets, visitors, leave, expenses | `SUR-SCR-299`, `308`–`312`, `329` | Professional depth |
| Compliance depth | `SUR-SCR-346`, `348`, `350`, `SUR-SCR-470` | Compliance dashboard is Professional per canon §1.4 |
| Surface depth completion | The `Ph2` remainder across main website (17), client portal (16), Customer App (8), Guard App (17), guard web (8), Trinetra (12), Agency Portal (50), Agency App (15), Admin App (7), desktop (7) | Each surface reaches its designed depth |
| Benchmarking | Cross-tenant benchmarks per §42.7, opt-in, aggregate-only | Gated on minimum cohort sizes |

#### 51.6.3 Explicitly out of scope

Autonomous AI action outside the four permitted classes — permanently, not just in this phase (canon §1.7). Predictive models that require more history than exists (attrition and absconding scoring need ~12 months of clean data; see §51.11). Facial recognition beyond the enrolled-guard check-in already built. Body-worn video. Enterprise API and SSO (Phase 5). Custom integrations (Phase 5, and sold per §52.6). Pan-India expansion.

#### 51.6.4 Dependencies

| Type | Dependency | Consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Prior phase | **Data volume.** Analytics and AI over three tenants and 200 guards produce confident nonsense | Every insight is a coin flip presented as a recommendation |
| Prior phase | Phase 3 entitlements — AI and analytics are tier-differentiated ("basic AI"/"basic analytics" on Starter; advanced on Professional per canon §1.4) | Gating becomes code, violating SUR-FIN-166 |
| Prior phase | §41 AI governance controls operational: action classes, approval queues, interaction logging | AI ships without a guardrail and the prohibition list is unenforceable |
| External | LLM/ASR provider contracts with data-residency and non-training terms acceptable under §39 | Cannot process tenant data through the model at all |
| External | Indian-language ASR quality in the target languages, on noisy field audio | GOAL-12's ≥19 languages is technically infeasible for some; the canon already says "where technically feasible" |
| External | Government tender portal access — no reliable public API assumed (canon §0) | Discovery is assisted/manual; the product must say so rather than imply a feed |
| Decision | **D-589** whether Phase 4 splits into 4a/4b | Determines the gate structure and funding tranche |

#### 51.6.5 Team shape

| Role | Count | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Product | 3 | AI, analytics, surface depth |
| Design | 3 | AI interaction patterns are a design problem before they are a model problem |
| Backend | 8 | |
| Frontend web | 6 | |
| Mobile | 3 | |
| AI/ML engineering | 4 | Retrieval, prompt/agent orchestration, evaluation harness, permission-aware context assembly |
| Data engineering | 3 | Analytics read model (§42.5.5), event pipeline, benchmark aggregation |
| QA/automation | 4 | Including AI evaluation and red-teaming against the prohibition list |
| DevOps/SRE | 2 | Inference cost and latency management |
| **Total** | **36** | |

#### 51.6.6 Duration

**16 weeks for 4a + 12 weeks for 4b = 28 weeks combined** `[ASSUMPTION: A-585]`, run with partial overlap so the elapsed figure is ~22 weeks. The assumption most likely to break is language coverage: each additional Indian language is an ASR quality problem, a prompt problem, a UI string problem and a QA problem, and the ≥19 target is a multi-quarter programme, not a phase deliverable.

#### 51.6.7 Key risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| AI inference cost per tenant exceeds the plan's contribution margin | A Starter tenant at ₹5,000 becomes unprofitable (§52.3.7) | Per-tenant AI interaction quotas as an entitlement (`D-003`); cheap-model routing for read-only classes; cost per tenant tracked as a first-class metric |
| AI produces a confident wrong answer about a guard's attendance or pay | Trust collapse, and a potential dispute with legal consequences | Read-only and recommendation classes cite their source records; approval-required class for anything with consequence; §41 governance |
| Analytics restatements confuse users | The dashboard stops being believed | §42.6.4 restatement policy applied from the first release |
| Benchmarking leaks a competitor's number | Contractual and reputational breach | §42.7.2 thresholds enforced in the aggregation job, not the UI |
| Phase 4 becomes an unbounded "make it smart" project | No gate is ever passed | The 4a/4b split with independent acceptance criteria |

#### 51.6.8 Acceptance criteria

| # | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| A4-1 | ≥40% of agency-tenant weekly active users invoke AI at least once a week | GOAL-12 |
| A4-2 | Hindi and English fully supported across AI surfaces; ≥6 additional Indian languages live with a published readiness level | GOAL-12 (progress toward ≥19) |
| A4-3 | Zero AI actions executed outside the four permitted classes; zero instances of a prohibited action (canon §1.7) | §41 audit; red-team suite green |
| A4-4 | Every AI recommendation surface cites the underlying records; a spot audit of 100 responses finds ≥95% correctly sourced | Manual audit |
| A4-5 | AI inference cost per active tenant ≤₹620/month at Professional and ≤₹240 at Starter `[ASSUMPTION: A-586]` | Cost telemetry per tenant |
| A4-6 | OCR migration ingests a 5,000-record legacy set at ≥92% field-level accuracy with a human review queue for the remainder | `WKF-33` acceptance test |
| A4-7 | Analytics dashboards reconcile to source systems within the tolerances in §42 (e.g. `ANL-F02` to `ANL-F01` ±2%) | Data-quality checks (§42.6.3) |
| A4-8 | Benchmark publication suppresses every cohort failing the §42.7.2 thresholds; a deliberate under-threshold cohort is verified suppressed | Automated disclosure-control test |
| A4-9 | Plan-tier differentiation of AI and analytics is enforced by entitlement, not code | Entitlement test suite |

#### 51.6.9 Go/no-go decision

**Gate 4a → 4b:** A4-3, A4-4 and A4-5 must pass. An AI that is unsafe or unaffordable does not proceed regardless of how popular it is. **Gate 4b → Phase 5:** A4-1, A4-7 and A4-9. If A4-1 fails badly (<15% weekly AI usage), the correct conclusion is that AI is not the differentiator for this user and Phase 5 investment should shift to enterprise integrations and scale. Decision owner: CTO with the AI governance owner named in §41; CEO for the commercial reallocation.

#### 51.6.10 What is demonstrable

To an agency owner: asking "who is absent at my Andheri site right now and who can cover it" in Hindi, by voice, and getting a correct answer with the records cited and a one-tap approval. To an Enterprise prospect: a paper register from 2019 turned into a searchable guard database. To an investor: usage-weighted engagement data and the first credible expansion-revenue story.
