### 52.6 Additional revenue lines to evaluate

Each line is assessed on revenue potential, effort, strategic fit, and a decision. "Park" means revisit at a stated trigger; "reject" means stop asking.

#### 52.6.1 Enterprise onboarding and migration fees

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | A one-time, priced engagement for Enterprise tenants: data migration (including OCR of paper records), configuration, role design, training and go-live support. Canon §1.4 already commits "dedicated onboarding" and "large-scale migration" as Enterprise entitlements |
| Revenue potential | **₹150,000–₹500,000 per Enterprise tenant** `[A-599]`. At 10 Enterprise tenants a year, ₹15–50 lakh |
| Effort | Low-to-medium. The capability is being built anyway (Phase 4 OCR migration, `WKF-33`); this is a pricing and packaging decision, not a build |
| Strategic fit | High. §52.3.7 shows Enterprise contribution margin at 48.1% **precisely because** ₹300,000 of onboarding is amortised into cost to serve. Charging it separately moves Enterprise contribution to ~66% and makes the segment properly attractive |
| Risk | Fee friction can lose a deal; a large migration that goes wrong is a reputational event |
| **Decision** | **PURSUE.** Price as a mandatory line item with a published floor, discountable only under §52.8. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-583]` on whether it is mandatory and what the floor is |

#### 52.6.2 Custom integration fees

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Building or supporting a tenant-specific integration — an ERP, an access-control system, a biometric device family, a client's ticketing system. Canon §1.4 lists "custom integrations" as Enterprise |
| Revenue potential | **₹100,000–₹400,000 per integration**, plus an annual support fee at ~20% of build `[A-599]` |
| Effort | High per integration, and it competes directly with roadmap capacity (see the Phase 5 risk in §51.7.7) |
| Strategic fit | Medium. Necessary to close enterprise deals; dangerous if it becomes the business |
| Risk | Engineering becomes a services organisation; each integration is a permanent maintenance liability |
| **Decision** | **PURSUE, with a hard rule:** priced above fully-loaded cost, delivered by a solutions-engineering function that is separate from the product team, with an annual support fee attached, and refused below a price floor. Never absorbed into a subscription |

#### 52.6.3 Training and certification for guards

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Structured training content and a platform-verifiable certification for guards, sold to agencies (or, in the worst version, to guards) |
| Revenue potential | **Low in the near term.** ₹200–500 per guard per certification `[A-599]`; at 5,000 guards, ₹10–25 lakh a year, but with high content production cost |
| Effort | High. Content production, assessment design, per-state statutory alignment, and translation into the workforce's languages are all separate disciplines |
| Strategic fit | Medium-high strategically, low commercially. A verified skill record makes the marketplace and the guard profile more valuable, and it supports GOAL-06's dignity argument |
| Risk | **Charging the guard is unacceptable.** A workforce earning ₹10,500 a month must never be a revenue source for the platform that employs them |
| **Decision** | **PARK** until Phase 5. Build the *records* (`SUR-SCR-205`, `273`, `274`) which cost little and serve compliance; defer content. Trigger: a state mandates platform-verifiable training, or ≥10 tenants request content. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-594]` — recommended default: the platform never charges a guard for anything, ever |

#### 52.6.4 Recruitment marketplace

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Charging agencies to access the verified guard supply on the Guard platform — job postings, candidate access, placement fees |
| Revenue potential | **₹500–2,000 per placement** `[A-599]`; meaningful at scale given industry attrition, plausibly ₹50 lakh+ a year at 30,000 guards on-platform |
| Effort | Medium. The recruitment pipeline module and guard profiles already exist for Professional tenants |
| Strategic fit | High — attrition is the industry's defining operational problem, and being the place guards are found is a durable position |
| Risk | **Severe if handled badly.** Suraksha would be monetising the movement of guards between its own tenants, and could be seen as poaching from the agencies that pay it. A guard's data belongs to the guard (SUR-GRD-003), so consent is the gating constraint, not a formality |
| **Decision** | **PARK to Phase 5**, and only in a guard-initiated form: a guard opts in to being discoverable, controls what is visible, and can withdraw. Never an agency-initiated database search of another tenant's roster. Trigger: ≥20,000 guards on-platform with ≥30% opted in |

#### 52.6.5 Payment and float economics

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Economics arising from money held in transit: client advances and wallet balances (`ANL-F14`), and the gap between collecting from a client and paying a partner agency or guard |
| Revenue potential | Low and legally constrained. At ₹2 crore of average float, a 5% return is ₹10 lakh a year `[A-599]` — real but small relative to the risk |
| Effort | Low to earn, high to govern |
| Strategic fit | **Low.** This is a financial-services activity attached to a security company |
| Risk | High. Client money used as working capital is a solvency and regulatory exposure, and one liquidity event destroys the business |
| **Decision** | **REJECT as a revenue line.** `[RECOMMENDED]` client advances and wallet balances are treated as a liability, reconciled daily to the ledger with zero drift (`ANL-F14`), and are **not** used as working capital. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-586]` — recommended default: full segregation. The legitimate adjacent benefit — negotiating better gateway rates at volume — is pursued as a cost reduction, not a revenue line |

#### 52.6.6 Insurance and benefits partnerships

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Distribution partnership for group personal accident cover, term life, health top-ups or micro-benefits for guards, and liability cover for agencies |
| Revenue potential | **Commission of 5–15% of premium** `[A-599]`. At 20,000 guards × ₹600 annual premium × 10% = ₹12 lakh a year; larger with agency liability products |
| Effort | Low to medium — the partner underwrites and administers; the platform provides distribution, enrolment and payroll deduction |
| Strategic fit | **High.** It improves the guard's actual life, strengthens the agency's compliance posture, and creates a retention hook that is not a feature |
| Risk | Mis-selling risk; regulatory requirements for insurance distribution; a bad partner damages Suraksha's brand with a workforce that has little recourse |
| **Decision** | **PURSUE from Phase 5**, with a regulated partner, transparent commission disclosure, no default enrolment, and no deduction from a guard's wage without explicit, revocable consent |

#### 52.6.7 Data and benchmarking products

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| What it is | Two distinct things: (a) in-product benchmarks for tenants (§42.7), and (b) a published industry report or a sold dataset |
| Revenue potential | (a) Not a separate line — it is a Professional-tier retention feature. (b) Modest: a subscription industry report might earn ₹5–15 lakh a year `[A-599]` |
| Effort | (a) Already scoped in §42.7. (b) Low incremental, using the same aggregates |
| Strategic fit | (a) High. (b) Medium — it builds category authority |
| Risk | **The privacy constraint from §39 and §42.7.2 is absolute**: opt-in only, aggregate-only, minimum 10 contributing tenants per cohort, no single tenant above 25% of a cohort, no individual guard data at any aggregation, no client-identifying slices, disclosure-control checks before publication. Selling row-level or re-identifiable data is not a product decision — it is prohibited |
| **Decision** | (a) **PURSUE** as a Professional/Enterprise retention feature, not as a priced line. (b) **PARK** to Phase 5 as a marketing asset — published free, not sold — because the category authority is worth more than the subscription revenue. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-595]`; `D-365` in §42 governs whether rate benchmarking is offered at all |

#### 52.6.8 Summary

| Line | Potential | Effort | Fit | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Enterprise onboarding & migration fees | Medium | Low | High | **Pursue** — Phase 3/4 |
| Custom integration fees | Medium | High | Medium | **Pursue** with a price floor and a separate delivery function — Phase 5 |
| Training & certification | Low | High | Medium | **Park** — records now, content later; never charge the guard |
| Recruitment marketplace | Medium-high | Medium | High | **Park** to Phase 5; guard-initiated and consent-gated only |
| Payment & float economics | Low | Low | Low | **Reject** as revenue; segregate client money |
| Insurance & benefits partnerships | Medium | Low-medium | High | **Pursue** from Phase 5 with a regulated partner |
| Data & benchmarking (in-product) | Indirect | Low | High | **Pursue** as a retention feature, not a priced line |
| Data & benchmarking (published) | Low | Low | Medium | **Park**; publish free for authority rather than sell |

### 52.7 Unit economics and the model

Everything in this sub-section is an **illustrative structural model on stated assumptions**. It is not a forecast, not a plan, and not a commitment. Its purpose is to show which variables the business is actually sensitive to, so that the right three things are measured obsessively.

#### 52.7.1 Customer acquisition cost by channel and segment

`[ASSUMPTION: A-599]` for every figure. Definitions follow `ANL-B13`; attribution follows `ANL-B14` (first-touch and last-touch both reported).

| Engine | Segment | Channel | Cost basis | **CAC** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A — guarding | B2C individual/RWA | Paid search + local SEO | ₹450 CPL ÷ 10% lead-to-booking | **₹4,500** |
| A — guarding | B2C individual/RWA | Referral / word of mouth | ₹900 incentive + attribution overhead | **₹900** |
| A — guarding | B2C individual/RWA | Marketplace / organic | Content and SEO cost allocated | **₹1,800** |
| A — guarding | B2B corporate | Field sales | ₹280,000 loaded AE cost/month ÷ 3.3 contracts | **₹85,000** |
| A — guarding | B2G / tender | Bid team + tender fees | ₹420,000 per win at a 15% win rate on ₹63,000 avg bid cost | **₹420,000** |
| B — SaaS | Starter | Self-serve from marketplace listing | Marketing allocation ÷ activations | **₹6,000** |
| B — SaaS | Starter/Professional | Inside sales (call + demo) | ₹180,000 loaded rep/month ÷ 6.4 closes | **₹28,000** |
| B — SaaS | Professional | Partner / referral from an existing tenant | Referral credit + overhead | **₹9,000** |
| B — SaaS | Enterprise | Field sales + pre-sales + pilot | ₹350,000 fully loaded per closed deal | **₹350,000** |

#### 52.7.2 Payback period

Payback = CAC ÷ monthly contribution.

| Segment | CAC | Monthly contribution | Arithmetic | **Payback** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B2C guarding (self-serve, 1.6 positions avg `[A-599]`) | ₹4,500 | 1.6 × 2,445 = ₹3,912 | 4,500 ÷ 3,912 | **1.2 months** |
| B2C guarding (referral) | ₹900 | ₹3,912 | 900 ÷ 3,912 | **0.2 months** |
| B2B guarding (12 positions avg) | ₹85,000 | 12 × 2,445 = ₹29,340 | 85,000 ÷ 29,340 | **2.9 months** |
| SaaS Starter (self-serve) | ₹6,000 | ₹3,902 | 6,000 ÷ 3,902 | **1.5 months** |
| SaaS Professional (inside sales) | ₹28,000 | ₹7,412 | 28,000 ÷ 7,412 | **3.8 months** |
| SaaS Enterprise (field) | ₹350,000 | ₹21,667 | 350,000 ÷ 21,667 | **16.2 months** |

`ANL-B13`'s target is payback ≤6 months. Every segment except Enterprise clears it comfortably; Enterprise clears it only on a multi-year contract, which is why §52.8 requires Enterprise terms of at least 12 months.

#### 52.7.3 Lifetime value

LTV = monthly contribution × expected life. Expected life = 1 ÷ monthly churn rate, capped at 36 months because a longer projection is arithmetic rather than evidence.

| Segment | Monthly contribution | Churn assumption `[A-599]` | Expected life | **LTV** | **LTV : CAC** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B2C guarding | ₹3,912 | 7.1% monthly (14-month avg contract) | 14 months | 3,912 × 14 = **₹54,768** | 12.2 : 1 |
| B2B guarding | ₹29,340 | 3.3% monthly (30-month avg contract) | 30 months | 29,340 × 30 = **₹880,200** | 10.4 : 1 |
| SaaS Starter | ₹3,902 | 4.0% monthly (`ANL-P10` target ≤3%) | 25 months | 3,902 × 25 = **₹97,550** | 16.3 : 1 |
| SaaS Professional | ₹7,412 | 2.0% monthly | 36 months (capped) | 7,412 × 36 = **₹266,832** | 9.5 : 1 |
| SaaS Enterprise | ₹21,667 | 1.0% monthly | 36 months (capped) | 21,667 × 36 = **₹780,012** | 2.2 : 1 |

**Read this table sceptically.** The ratios above 10:1 are not evidence of a wonderful business; they are evidence that the churn assumptions are unvalidated. Nothing in this table should be quoted externally until at least two full cohorts have been observed (`ANL-P09`, `ANL-P10`). The one number that is defensible today is the *shape*: Starter pays back in weeks, Enterprise pays back in over a year.

#### 52.7.4 The three variables that matter most

| # | Variable | Why it dominates | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Guard wage relative to bill rate (Engine A)** | It is 65% of the cost stack and it is set by state notification, not by Suraksha | A ₹1,000 wage increase absorbs ₹1,294 of contribution (wage + 29.39% statutory load). At ₹2,445 base contribution, that is **53% of the margin gone** for a 9.5% wage move |
| **2** | **SaaS logo churn (Engine B)** | It is the multiplier on every LTV figure, and it compounds | At 3% monthly churn, Starter LTV is ₹130,067 (3,902 ÷ 0.03). At 6%, it is ₹65,033. A 3-point churn difference **halves the value of the entire SaaS business** |
| **3** | **Deployed guard utilisation / fill rate** | Bench guards, unfilled posts and slow replacement all destroy contribution while the fixed base runs | A 10% unfilled-post rate on 500 posts is 50 × ₹2,445 = **₹122,250/month of contribution lost**, against a fixed base of ₹870,000 — 14% of the entire fixed cost, gone |

| Variable | −10% | Base | +10% |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guard wage (₹10,500 base) | contribution ₹3,801 (+55%) | ₹2,445 | contribution ₹1,089 (−55%) |
| SaaS monthly churn (4.0% base) | Starter LTV ₹108,389 (+11%) | ₹97,550 | Starter LTV ₹88,682 (−9%) |
| Fill rate (100% base) | 90% fill: contribution −₹122,250/mo on 500 posts | — | n/a (cannot exceed 100%) |

*(Wage sensitivity arithmetic: at ₹9,450 wage, statutory = 9,450 × 0.2939 = 2,777; total cost = 9,450 + 2,777 + 2,469 = 14,696; contribution = 18,500 − 14,696 = ₹3,804. At ₹11,550: statutory = 3,394; total = 11,550 + 3,394 + 2,469 = 17,413; contribution = ₹1,087. Small rounding differences from the table above.)*

#### 52.7.5 A worked 12-month illustrative scenario

**Read this as a structural illustration, not a forecast.** Month 1 here is the first month of commercial operation after Minimum Viable Launch (Phase 2 exit, ~roadmap week 38). SaaS revenue begins in commercial month 5, corresponding to the Phase 3 exit. All inputs `[ASSUMPTION: A-599]`:

- Blended guarding bill rate ₹19,500/position (90% unarmed at ₹18,500, 10% armed at ₹38,000 gives a mix rate above ₹18,500 — the ₹19,500 used here is deliberately conservative)
- Blended guarding contribution ₹2,680/position (§52.2.5 arithmetic)
- SaaS ARPA ₹6,400 in months 5–9 (early mix 80% Starter / 20% Professional: 0.80 × 5,400 + 0.20 × 10,400 = 4,320 + 2,080), rising to ₹7,200 in months 10–12 as the mix shifts
- SaaS contribution at 63% of ARPA (§52.3.7 blended)
- Fixed cost includes engineering, command centre, city operations, G&A and sales & marketing across both engines

**Part A — Engine A (guarding).** Guarding revenue = guards × 19,500 · guarding contribution = guards × 2,680.

| M | Guards | Guarding revenue (₹) | Guarding contribution (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40 | 780,000 | 107,200 |
| 2 | 70 | 1,365,000 | 187,600 |
| 3 | 110 | 2,145,000 | 294,800 |
| 4 | 160 | 3,120,000 | 428,800 |
| 5 | 220 | 4,290,000 | 589,600 |
| 6 | 290 | 5,655,000 | 777,200 |
| 7 | 370 | 7,215,000 | 991,600 |
| 8 | 460 | 8,970,000 | 1,232,800 |
| 9 | 560 | 10,920,000 | 1,500,800 |
| 10 | 670 | 13,065,000 | 1,795,600 |
| 11 | 790 | 15,405,000 | 2,117,200 |
| 12 | 920 | 17,940,000 | 2,465,600 |

**Part B — Engine B (SaaS) and the combined result.** MRR = tenants × ARPA · SaaS contribution = MRR × 0.63 · net = total contribution − fixed cost.

| M | Tenants | MRR (₹) | SaaS contrib (₹) | Total contrib (₹) | Fixed cost (₹) | **Net (₹)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | — | — | — | 107,200 | 1,450,000 | −1,342,800 |
| 2 | — | — | — | 187,600 | 1,500,000 | −1,312,400 |
| 3 | — | — | — | 294,800 | 1,600,000 | −1,305,200 |
| 4 | — | — | — | 428,800 | 1,750,000 | −1,321,200 |
| 5 | 6 | 38,400 | 24,192 | 613,792 | 1,950,000 | −1,336,208 |
| 6 | 14 | 89,600 | 56,448 | 833,648 | 2,150,000 | −1,316,352 |
| 7 | 25 | 160,000 | 100,800 | 1,092,400 | 2,400,000 | −1,307,600 |
| 8 | 40 | 256,000 | 161,280 | 1,394,080 | 2,650,000 | −1,255,920 |
| 9 | 58 | 371,200 | 233,856 | 1,734,656 | 2,900,000 | −1,165,344 |
| 10 | 80 | 576,000 | 362,880 | 2,158,480 | 3,200,000 | −1,041,520 |
| 11 | 106 | 763,200 | 480,816 | 2,598,016 | 3,500,000 | −901,984 |
| 12 | 136 | 979,200 | 616,896 | 3,082,496 | 3,800,000 | −717,504 |

**Results read off the model:**

| Result | Value | Arithmetic |
|---|---|---|
| Month-12 monthly revenue | ₹18,919,200 | 17,940,000 + 979,200 |
| Month-12 annualised revenue run-rate | ₹22.70 crore | 18,919,200 × 12 |
| Month-12 ARR from SaaS alone | ₹1.17 crore | 979,200 × 12 (`ANL-P02`) |
| Cumulative operating deficit over 12 months | **₹1.43 crore** | Sum of the Net column = −14,324,032 |
| Contribution shortfall at month 12 | ₹717,504/month | Still loss-making at 920 guards and 136 tenants |
| **Contribution break-even** | **~1,188 guards** at month-12 SaaS levels | (3,800,000 − 616,896) ÷ 2,680 = 1,187.7 |

**Working capital, which the profit-and-loss above does not show and which is the number most likely to be underestimated:**

> Direct cost at month 12 = 920 × (19,500 − 2,680) = 920 × 16,820 = **₹15,474,400/month**
> Guards are paid monthly; clients pay at ~45 days (`ANL-F05` target ≤45)
> Working capital tied up ≈ 1.5 months of direct cost = 15,474,400 × 1.5 = **₹2.32 crore**

> **Indicative total funding requirement for these 12 months ≈ ₹1.43 Cr (operating) + ₹2.32 Cr (working capital) ≈ ₹3.75 crore**, before any buffer, capex or the pre-launch build cost of Phases 0–2.

**The strategic reading of this model.** The guarding engine produces 95% of the revenue and 80% of the contribution at month 12, and consumes 100% of the working capital. The SaaS engine produces 5% of the revenue and 20% of the contribution, and consumes none. Every additional SaaS tenant improves the cash position; every additional guard worsens it in the short term and improves it over 45 days. That asymmetry — not the margin percentage — is the real argument for building the SaaS engine, and it is the reason §51.9.3 recommends leading with guarding but running hard at the SaaS timeline rather than letting it drift.

### 52.8 Pricing governance

#### 52.8.1 Discount authority

| Role | May discount | Maximum duration | Additional condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sales (Agency Sales / Sales) | 0% | — | May offer only published list price and published annual terms |
| Sales Manager | up to **10%** | 3 billing periods | Recorded reason code |
| Head of Sales | up to **20%** | 6 billing periods | Recorded reason code + monthly discount report |
| Founder/Management (any one) | up to **35%** | Any | Recorded reason, reviewed at the monthly commercial review |
| Founder/Management + Finance (both) | above 35%, or free periods | Any | Must model the contribution margin; below the floor in SUR-MON-012 requires an explicit written rationale |

The same ladder governs **guarding** pricing, with an additional absolute constraint: no quotation may be issued below the computed minimum viable bill rate for the city (SUR-MON-003) without Founder/Management approval, because a discount there is not a margin decision — it is a decision to lose money on every guard-month for the life of the contract.

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-MON-041 | Discounts shall be entitlements on the subscription object (§35.8.1) with a type, a value, a duration and an approver, never a manually edited invoice amount. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-MON-042 | Every discount shall carry a reason code from a fixed list (competitive, pilot, volume, goodwill, migration incentive, strategic reference) and shall appear in a monthly discount report by approver, by reason and by realised value. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-MON-043 | Discounts shall expire automatically at their stated duration and shall notify the tenant 30 days before expiry with the new price. A discount that silently becomes permanent is a pricing failure. | [RECOMMENDED] |
| SUR-MON-044 | Enterprise negotiated pricing shall be visible only to the tenant and to authorised Suraksha roles (SUR-FIN-167) and shall never be exposed in any comparative, benchmark or analytics surface. | [CONFIRMED] |

#### 52.8.2 Contract terms

| Term | Standard position |
|---|---|
| SaaS Starter / Professional | Monthly rolling, cancel any time, or annual paid upfront with two months free (§52.3.8) |
| SaaS Enterprise | Minimum 12 months, typically 24–36; annual or milestone invoicing; termination for convenience with 90 days' notice, termination for cause per the agreement |
| Auto-renewal | On by default for annual terms, with notice at 60/30/7 days before renewal and a one-click switch to monthly or to cancel. Renewal without notice is prohibited |
| Guarding B2C | Monthly rolling with a 30-day notice period; deposit or first-month advance per `D-210` |
| Guarding B2B | 12-month term standard, 30–90 day notice, SLA credits per §35.4.6, rate revision clause tied to statutory wage revision |
| **Wage revision clause** | Every guarding contract shall contain a rate-revision clause linked to a statutory minimum-wage revision, with a defined notice period. Without it, a mid-contract wage notification converts a 13% margin into a loss (§52.2.3) |
| Payment terms | B2C on invoice; B2B 30 days standard, 45 maximum, credit-checked above a configured exposure |

#### 52.8.3 Price-increase policy and grandfathering

| Rule | Position `[RECOMMENDED]` |
|---|---|
| Frequency | At most once per 12 months for any given tenant |
| Notice | Minimum 60 days, in-product and by email, to the Agency Owner |
| Cap for existing tenants | 10% per increase |
| Grandfathering | Existing subscriptions remain on their **plan version** (§35.8.1) until explicitly migrated; a price change creates a new plan version and does not retroactively alter an active one |
| Grandfathering window | Existing tenants keep their price for at least 12 months from the change date; annual subscribers keep it for their full paid term |
| Enterprise | Contractual escalation clauses govern; no unilateral increase within a term |
| Feature removal | A capability listed in the tenant's plan version shall not be removed from that version. If a capability must be retired, affected tenants are notified 90 days ahead and offered either a migration path or a price adjustment |
| Public price change | Announced on Trinetra with the effective date, and applied to new customers only from that date |
| **The one thing never done** | An increase applied silently at renewal, discovered on the invoice. This is the fastest available method of converting a retained customer into a churned one plus a public complaint |

`[DECISION REQUIRED: D-590]` on ratifying the 10% cap and the 12-month grandfathering window.

| ID | Requirement | Label |
|---|---|---|
| SUR-MON-045 | Price changes shall be implemented as new plan versions, never as edits to an active plan version; a tenant's price shall be reconstructible for any historical date. | [CONFIRMED] |
| SUR-MON-046 | Every price-change notification shall state the old price, the new price, the effective date, the reason, and the tenant's options (accept, downgrade, switch to annual, cancel with no penalty before the effective date). | [RECOMMENDED] |

### 52.9 The KPI set that tells you monetization is working

All definitions, formulas, data sources, grains, owners and targets are owned by §42 and are **not** redefined here. This is the selection and the reading order.

#### 52.9.1 The five questions, and the metric that answers each

| Question | Primary metric | Supporting metrics |
|---|---|---|
| Are we selling? | `ANL-P03` New MRR · `ANL-B04` Booking completion rate | `ANL-B02`, `ANL-B06`, `ANL-B08`, `ANL-M03` |
| Are we keeping what we sold? | `ANL-P09` Net revenue retention | `ANL-P10`, `ANL-P08`, `ANL-P06`, `ANL-P16` |
| Are we growing accounts, not just adding them? | `ANL-P04` Expansion MRR | `ANL-P14`, `ANL-P12`, `ANL-P13`, `ANL-P05` |
| Is each unit profitable? | `ANL-F09` Gross margin per contract | `ANL-F10`, `ANL-F12`, `ANL-F13`, `ANL-F08` |
| Are we collecting the money? | `ANL-F03` Collections | `ANL-F05`, `ANL-F04`, `ANL-F06`, `ANL-F16` |

#### 52.9.2 The monetization scorecard

| # | Metric (§42) | What a bad reading means | Escalation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ANL-P01` MRR / `ANL-P02` ARR | The SaaS engine is not compounding | Founder/Management |
| 2 | `ANL-P07` Net MRR movement | Growth is being cancelled by churn and contraction | Founder/Management |
| 3 | `ANL-P09` Net revenue retention (target ≥105%) | Existing tenants are shrinking; expansion design (§52.3.5) is not working | Product + Sales |
| 4 | `ANL-P10` Logo churn (target ≤3%/month) | The product is bought and abandoned; check `GOAL-07` activation | Product |
| 5 | `ANL-P11` Trial-to-paid (target ≥25%) | The trial (D-002) is the wrong shape or onboarding is failing | Growth |
| 6 | `ANL-P13` Plan mix | Professional is decorative; upgrade triggers are not firing | Product |
| 7 | `ANL-P14` Upgrade rate (target ≥2%/month) | Gating is either too generous or invisible (§52.4.2) | Product |
| 8 | `ANL-P15` Payment failure rate (target ≤4%) | Billing friction, not intent, is causing churn | Finance |
| 9 | `ANL-P16` Involuntary churn share (target ≤20% of churn) | Dunning and card-expiry pre-warning are failing | Finance |
| 10 | `ANL-F09` / `ANL-F10` margin per contract and per site | Contracts priced below the computed floor (SUR-MON-003) | Finance + Sales |
| 11 | `ANL-F08` Payroll as % of revenue | Wage drift is eating the guarding margin (§52.7.4 variable 1) | Finance |
| 12 | `ANL-F05` DSO (target ≤45 days) | Working capital is expanding faster than revenue | Finance |
| 13 | `ANL-F06` Ageing buckets (90+ ≤5%) | Receivables are becoming bad debt | Finance |
| 14 | `ANL-F16` Bad debt rate (target ≤1%) | Credit control is failing | Finance |
| 15 | `ANL-B13` CAC blended, payback ≤6 months | Acquisition is outrunning value | Marketing + Finance |
| 16 | `ANL-B14` Channel attribution | Spend is being allocated blind | Marketing |
| 17 | `ANL-M01` / `ANL-M02` listings and verified share | The marketplace supply that feeds GOAL-09 is not building | Marketing + Verification |
| 18 | `ANL-M06` Marketplace conversion (target ≥12%) | The directory generates traffic but not business | Sales |
| 19 | `ANL-F15` Settlement timeliness (target ≥98%) | Partner agencies are being paid late; brokerage supply will disappear | Finance |
| 20 | `ANL-F14` Wallet balance and float | Client money position; must reconcile daily with zero drift (§52.6.5) | Finance |

## 53. Risk Register

This register consolidates every risk raised across sections 1–52 and 57–60, plus the material risks those sections did not raise. **IDs are permanent.** They are referenced inline throughout the document; a risk is never renumbered, only re-scored or closed.

**How to read it.** Probability and Impact are scored H / M / L against a 12-month horizon at the scale described in §51 (Phases 0–3, up to ~400 tenants and ~120,000 guards, per A-240). Impact is scored on the worst credible outcome, not the average one. Owner role is the accountable role, not the working team — accountability is singular. Where a harvested item arrived without a probability, impact, mitigation or owner, one has been supplied and marked `[RECOMMENDED]`; those scores are the registers author's judgement and are the first thing management should challenge.

**Scoring definitions.**

| Score | Probability (within 12 months) | Impact (worst credible) |
|---|---|---|
| H | More likely than not to occur at least once | Threatens the business, a life, or a licence; or costs >₹50 lakh / >6 weeks of roadmap |
| M | Plausible; would not surprise an informed observer | Material damage to a client, tenant cohort, or quarter; recoverable with effort |
| L | Requires an unusual combination of events | Contained; absorbed within normal operating tolerance |

Categories used: **Product · Operational · Security · Compliance · Financial · Vendor · AI · Privacy · Adoption · Scaling.** Every risk carries exactly one primary category; several are cross-cutting and the secondary lens is named in the mitigation text.

---

**What the shape of this map says.** There is no low-impact column. That is not a scoring failure — it is the honest character of a business that puts a person on a gate at night and moves other people's wages. Every risk in this document either endangers a person, endangers money, or endangers a licence. The practical consequence is that "accept and move on" is available for only 18 of 137 risks (the L/H and L/M cells, which are managed by drill, insurance and contract rather than by engineering), and the 52-item M/H cell is where most of the platform's control design actually lives. Distribution by category: Operational 33 · Financial 20 · Compliance 16 · Product 13 · AI 11 · Adoption 10 · Security 9 · Vendor 9 · Privacy 8 · Scaling 8.

### 53.13 Risk review cadence

| Cadence | Forum | Scope | Output | Chair |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weekly, 30 min | Founders' operating review | The 10 leading indicators in §53.12 only. No discussion of any other risk unless an indicator has tripped | Trip/no-trip per indicator; an owner and a date for each trip | CEO |
| Fortnightly, 45 min | Engineering risk review | All Security, AI, Scaling and Product risks with an open mitigation task; new risks raised by incidents or reviews | Mitigation status; any re-score; new IDs raised in the R-620–R-649 band | CTO |
| Monthly, 60 min | Full register review | All 137 risks. Every risk is either *unchanged*, *re-scored*, *mitigated to a lower cell*, or *closed with evidence*. `[RECOMMENDED]` scores older than 90 days must be confirmed or replaced with measured data | Updated register; heat map regenerated; list of risks whose scores are still unevidenced | Founder/Management |
| Monthly | Compliance and privacy pack | Compliance and Privacy categories, plus R-302 veto usage, R-303 holder count, R-330 export anomalies, R-333 erasure resolution | Reported to Founder/Management in writing, whether or not anything changed | Compliance |
| Quarterly | Drill cycle | One live drill per quarter from: SOS end-to-end (R-626), DR/region loss (R-637), backup key recovery (R-577), break-glass (R-146), Command Center continuity pack currency (R-575) | Drill report with the observed time against the committed figure; a committed figure not demonstrated in three consecutive drills may not be sold (D-559) | COO |
| Per phase gate | Phase gate review | Every risk tagged to the entering phase must have a named owner and a mitigation in progress. Any H/H risk without an active mitigation blocks the gate | Gate decision recorded with the risk position at the time | Founder/Management |
| Event-driven | Post-incident review | Every P0 and P1 incident asks: which register entry predicted this? If none did, a new risk is raised in the R-620–R-649 band before the review closes | New or re-scored risk; a leading indicator added if one was missing | CTO or COO by incident class |

**Three standing rules.**
1. **A risk without an owner role is not in the register.** The registers author has supplied an owner for every harvested item that lacked one; those are marked `[RECOMMENDED]` in the mitigation column and must be confirmed at the first monthly review.
2. **A mitigation that is only a document is not a mitigation.** At the monthly review each mitigation must name either a shipped control (with a requirement ID), a test (with a TC- ID), or a recurring calendar event with a named owner. Anything else is re-scored as unmitigated.
3. **Closing a risk requires evidence, not opinion.** The evidence is a measurement, a drill report, a signed contract, or a released control. "We no longer think this will happen" is a re-score, not a closure, and it is recorded as such with the reasoning.

## 54. Assumption Register

Every `[ASSUMPTION: A-xxx]` tag in this document resolves here. **IDs are permanent.** An assumption is not a decision: nobody chose it, we simply cannot proceed without taking a position, and being wrong has a cost. The register's job is to make that cost visible and to attach a cheap test to it.

**Column meanings.** *Why we are assuming it* is the evidential basis, honestly stated — "observed", "inferred", "no source found", or "planning placeholder". *Risk if wrong* names the consequence, and cross-references the risk register where one exists. *Validation required* is the specific action, not "investigate". *Validate by* is the phase from §51 by which the assumption must be replaced with a measurement, an evidenced answer, or an accepted permanent uncertainty.

**Phase tokens.** P0 = Foundation · P1 = Core MVP · P2 = Operations · P3 = Agency SaaS · P4a/P4b = Intelligence · P5 = Scale. "Pre-P0" means it must be settled before the first sprint.

### 54.1 Market assumptions

| ID | Assumption | Why we are assuming it | Risk if wrong | Validation required | Validate by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-001 | ~35,000 PSARA-verified licensed private security agencies exist pan-India | Canon §1; widely repeated industry figure with no primary source held by us | Every TAM, funding and acquisition-cost model is sized off a number we cannot source; a 3× error changes the business case, not the product | Reconstruct bottom-up from state/district controlling-authority lists for the D-005 launch states; publish our own number with its method and treat the national figure as an estimate | P1 |
| A-162 | At least a handful of genuine reference agencies exist at Trinetra launch | Required for the home page's credibility blocks to be real | The proof blocks stay hidden, weakening the marketplace's first impression (R-102, R-162) | Sign 10 reference agencies before the Trinetra page ships; never fabricate (canon P1/P2/P4) | P3 |
| A-627 | The V1 serviceable cities (D-005) each contain enough demand density to carry a city's ~₹870,000/month fixed base `[RECOMMENDED]` | Inferred from the §52 city model; not measured in any specific city | A city is opened that can never break even at ~325 guards, consuming the working capital in R-582/R-623 | Before opening each city: count addressable sites from public directories, test 20 outbound conversations, and require a signed anchor client before the fixed base is committed | P1 per city |
| A-628 | B2B and enterprise clients will contract a young vendor with a short track record for a security service `[RECOMMENDED]` | Assumed by the §12 pipeline; unproven, and directly weakened by the honest-empty-state position (R-123) | The enterprise segment does not open, and the entire margin case for Engine A rests on B2C and society contracts | Track win/loss reason codes from the first 30 qualified opportunities; specifically count losses attributed to references or vintage | P2 |

### 54.2 Business-model assumptions

| ID | Assumption | Why we are assuming it | Risk if wrong | Validation required | Validate by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-101 | No measured baseline exists for the twelve §4 problems (absenteeism, dispute value, payroll error rate, attrition) | Honest statement of what we do not know | Every ROI claim, GOAL target and pricing argument rests on unmeasured numbers | Instrument Suraksha's own operation first; publish internal baselines before quoting any number externally | P2 |
| A-102 | All numeric targets GOAL-01…GOAL-15 are planning placeholders | Set before any operating data existed | Teams measured against wrong targets misallocate effort for a full quarter | Re-baseline every GOAL target after one quarter of live operation | P2 |
| A-103 | Agencies will accept a monthly SaaS fee at the stated price points against thin margins, and the owner alone decides | The entire B2B revenue model depends on it; ₹5,000/month is real money to a 20-guard agency | The SaaS engine has no revenue; R-583 and R-584 both materialise | 20 paying pilots across size bands before scaling acquisition spend | P3 |
| A-363 | Initial KPI targets in §42.2 are professional estimates, not observed benchmarks | No operating data exists | Managing to wrong targets is worse than managing to none | Label all targets provisional; set from the observed 75th percentile after 90 days (D-369) | P3 |
| A-598 | Marketplace pricing: premium profile ₹2,500/mo, sponsored placement ₹6,000/mo per state×service slot, brokerage 6–8% | Modelled, not tested | The marketplace revenue line is fiction and D-165 is decided on air | Test with the first 20 verified listings; the result resolves D-165 | P3 |
| A-624 | Agencies will pay specifically ₹5,000 (Starter) and ₹10,000 (Professional) per month, and the feature split between the two actually drives upgrades `[RECOMMENDED]` | Canon §1.4 fixes the prices as a foundation rule; the *willingness* at those points and the discrimination of the ladder are untested | Either the price is too high (no supply, R-583) or the ladder does not discriminate (everyone stays on Starter and ARPA collapses) | Price-sensitivity interviews with 30 agencies across size bands using the actual plan comparison screen; measure Starter→Professional upgrade rate in the first two cohorts against the 32% mix in A-596 | P3 |
| A-630 | The marketplace listing audience and the SaaS buying audience are the same person, so acquisition cost is shared across both revenue lines `[RECOMMENDED]` | Central to the §52 CAC model and to Trinetra's role as the acquisition engine | If listing agencies are a different, smaller or non-buying population, SaaS CAC is understated and the marketplace is a cost centre | Measure listing→trial→paid conversion by agency size for the first 200 listings; report CAC separately per source before scaling spend | P3 |

### 54.6 Regulatory assumptions

Nothing in this group is a legal conclusion. Each is a statement about what interfaces and permissions we believe exist, in the sense of canon §0 — jurisdiction rules remain configurable data.

| ID | Assumption | Why we are assuming it | Risk if wrong | Validation required | Validate by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-122 | Identity-verification APIs (Aadhaar/PAN) may not be available to us on permissible terms | Depends on an authorised-entity relationship we do not hold | Verification stays manual, at manual cost and turnaround (R-602) | Manual verification as the guaranteed path; any API is an accelerator only | P1 |
| A-142 | No reliable public API exists for PSARA licence verification | No such service found at national level | Verification TAT, marketplace trust and Verification staffing are all set by manual throughput | Manual/assisted workflow as the primary design; confirm with two state controlling authorities (A-210) | P1 |
| A-144 | E-invoice / e-way requirements applicable to Suraksha's turnover and client mix are as modelled | Turnover-dependent and changeable | Invoices are rejected by client AP systems | Build the invoice engine to emit required references as configurable fields (D-270) | P3 |
| A-145 | No reliable public API exists for government tender portals | No confirmed public API | The Professional plan's tender feature is an operations service, not a product feature (R-276) | Manual entry plus document extraction; a commercial aggregator only if procured (D-274) | P4b |
| A-163 | No dependable pan-India programmatic PSARA licence verification exists (restates A-142 for Trinetra) | Same | Marketplace verification is capacity-bound (R-162) | Document-based manual verification; per-state automation as optional configuration | P3 |
| A-164 | No dependable programmatic interface for police-verification status exists | No such service found | Verification tracking is manual data entry forever | Manual-entry tracker with document evidence | P2 |
| A-165 | E-invoicing/e-way is handled through the agency's chosen provider, not a direct government integration | Keeps a mandatory external dependency out of the issue path | Enterprise expectations exceed scope | Generate the required payload; integrate with the agency's provider | P4b |
| A-166 | No uniform public API exists for government tender portals (restates A-145 for the agency module) | Same | Tender discovery is a curated pipeline with staffing cost | Curated corpus + manual entry + per-source connectors where lawful | P4b |
| A-210 | Agency and licence verification remain assisted-manual because the regulator operates at state/district level | No known national digital verification service | The verification SLA cannot be committed | Confirm with two state controlling authorities before committing the SLA | P1 |
| A-211 | Government tender data is obtainable via a licensed feed or permitted access, not an official API | No confirmed public API | Coverage claims outrun the data (R-276) | Commercial evaluation of available feed vendors | P4b |
| A-241 | 13 months of location retention is operationally sufficient for dispute resolution | Balances evidence against privacy exposure | Either a dispute cannot be defended or we hold sensitive data too long (R-106, D-242) | Review after the first 3 client disputes involving location evidence | P3 |
| A-271 | Suraksha's WhatsApp use cases fit approved utility/service template categories | Determines whether WhatsApp is operational or marketing-only | A channel the client experience depends on disappears (R-275) | Assume approval for booking/payment/duty utility templates; design every event to work without WhatsApp | P1 |
| A-332 | Face-verification vendors in India will accept storing the template on their side or on-device | Determines whether SUR-PRV-011 is achievable as written | The platform ends up holding biometric material and DP-09 risk (R-277) | Validate at vendor selection; a vendor requiring central template storage is disqualified | P2 |
| A-360 | Suraksha's ISO 9001:2015 and government certification claims are backed by current, in-date evidence | Claims are already published on the live ops portal | Public claims without substantiation are a compliance and brand risk (canon P4, R-103) | Verify and load evidence, or remove the claims from public content | Pre-P0 |
| A-361 | No public API exists for PSARA licence or police-verification lookup (restates A-142/A-164 for compliance) | Same | Verification capacity and cost are structurally fixed | Design for manual verification; treat any API as future enrichment | P1 |
| A-362 | Protected-attribute data sufficient for disparate-impact analysis is not held for most attributes | We deliberately do not collect it | The fairness programme's scope is narrower than its claim (R-364) | Monitor on available axes; disclose the limitation; do not collect attributes solely to monitor | P4a |
| A-523 | No government tender portal offers a stable public API at V1 | Same as A-145/A-166, stated for QA | Tests are written for the wrong integration shape | Build the assisted path first; treat any API as an optimisation | P4b |

Ranked not by likelihood of being wrong, but by how much of the plan depends on them. A wrong assumption here is not a defect to fix — it is a different company.

Every proof claim — GPS attendance, live tracking, wake checks, patrol, SOS — becomes supervisor-mediated data entry, which is precisely the fraud surface the product exists to remove | The product's entire differentiator; Phase 2 gate; §11–§13 marketing claims; R-580, R-161 |

| 9 | A-001 | The market is materially smaller than 35,000 agencies | TAM, funding narrative, acquisition-spend ceiling |
| 10 | A-330 / A-570 | In-region managed services are unavailable. Compensating controls must be designed after commitments are made | Security posture, DR integrity, residency claims to Enterprise clients |

## 55. Decision Register

195 open decisions. **IDs are permanent.** This is the section management works from: every row is written so that it can be approved or rejected in a single sentence. A recommended default that cannot be approved or rejected as written is a defect in this register, not a decision.

**Grouping is by accountable owner**, because the fastest way to clear a decision backlog is to hand each owner their own list. Within each group, decisions are ordered by ID. The owner is who *decides*; the register is maintained by Product.

**Column meanings.** *Recommended default* is what will be built if nobody decides — it is safe, reversible where possible, and concrete. *Alternatives* is the realistic set of other answers, not an exhaustive list. *Impact if deferred* states what happens if the decision is still open when its phase arrives. *Decide by* uses the §51 phase tokens (Pre-P0, P0, P1, P2, P3, P4a, P4b, P5).

**Deferral has a default.** If a decision passes its "decide by" phase unanswered, the recommended default is deemed adopted and recorded as such, with the owner notified. Silence is a decision; it is just a worse one.

The 14-day Professional trial (D-002) plus a free marketplace listing provide the on-ramp | Free tier capped at 10 guards; free listing-only account | Signup and entitlement design may need a third shape added later | P3 |
| D-592 | Which additional revenue lines in §52.6 are funded in Phase 5? | Phase 5 scope is otherwise unbounded | Fund enterprise onboarding/migration and insurance partnerships; park the rest against their triggers | Fund all; fund none | Phase 5 has no scope boundary | P5 |
| D-593 | Ratify the §52.8.1 discount authority thresholds, and who holds the Head of Sales authority before that role is filled? | Discount authority without a named holder defaults to whoever is in the room (R-589) | Ratify; the CEO holds unfilled tiers explicitly, with the same reporting obligations | Founder approval for all discounts; no thresholds | Discount drift begins with the first deal | P1 |
| D-594 | Adopt "the platform never charges a guard for anything" as policy? | Training, certification and recruitment lines all create a temptation to monetise the lowest-paid participant | Adopt as an absolute published policy | Charge for optional certification; charge for premium profiles | The temptation arrives with the first revenue shortfall and there is no rule to point at | P1 |
| D-595 | Is a published industry benchmark report pursued free, sold, or not produced? | Category authority versus a small revenue line, against §42.7.2 privacy constraints | Published free, subject to §42.7.2 thresholds and Founder/Management approval; not sold | Sold as a product; not produced | Marketing plans a report the privacy constraints may not permit | P5 |
| D-602 | Does B2G become a dedicated business line with its own compliance staffing, or remain a feature of the agency SaaS? | Determines whether tender capability gets an owner or stays a side feature nobody is accountable for | Feature of the SaaS until ≥5 tenants derive material tender revenue | Dedicated line from Phase 3; drop B2G | §13 scope has no owner and drifts | P4b |
| D-603 | Two-gate launch (Phase 1 soft, Phase 2 marketing) versus a single launch gate | Changes which §58 rows are blocking and what may be claimed publicly on day one | Two gates, per §51.10 | Single gate; three gates | Launch criteria are ambiguous and marketing claims outrun capability (R-588) | P1 |
| D-612 | Body-worn cameras: build, partner, or decline | Storage cost, privacy exposure and evidentiary obligations all step-change with video | Partner if pursued; own only the evidence chain and access control | Build in-house; decline permanently | A client request forces an unplanned answer | P5 |
| D-616 | First international market, if expansion is pursued | Determines residency architecture, compliance authoring and support model | Choose on regulatory similarity and partner availability; not before the domestic operation is repeatable | Named market now; never | Architecture may be over-generalised for an expansion that never comes | P5 |
| D-617 | Alarm-monitoring convergence: build, partner or acquire | Adding a high-false-positive stream to the SOS desk would degrade the core safety promise (R-141) | Partner first; never share a queue with SOS | Build; acquire; decline | An opportunistic deal puts alarm traffic on the SOS desk | P5 |
| D-620 | What is the wage-reserve policy — the minimum number of payroll cycles held in cash before a new guarding contract is signed? `[RECOMMENDED]` | Wages are paid on a fixed date; client collections are not. This is the single control on R-623 | **≥1.5 payroll cycles of the deployed workforce held in a segregated reserve at all times; signing beyond the reserve requires an explicit Founder/Management decision recorded with the cash position at the time** | 1 cycle; 2 cycles; no formal reserve, monthly review only | Payroll is funded from whatever cash exists, including client float (contradicting D-586) | P1 |
| D-623 | Client concentration ceiling and what happens when it is breached `[RECOMMENDED]` | The first phase's revenue depends on very few contracts; losing one removes both the reference and the cash (R-632) | **No single client above 25% of guarding revenue after month 12; breach triggers a written diversification plan at the next phase gate and blocks further concentration in that account** | 40% ceiling; no ceiling, report only | Concentration is discovered at renewal, when there is no time to diversify | P2 |

### 55.2 CTO / technical decisions

| ID | Question | Why it matters | Recommended default | Alternatives | Impact if deferred | Decide by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-103 | Minimum supported Android device profile and monthly data budget for the Guard App | Drives image compression, location cadence, offline store size, sync strategy and photo-evidence policy | Android 9+, 2 GB RAM, ≤150 MB/month at normal duty; validate on real guard devices before build (A-621) | Android 8+; Android 11+; device-issued fleet only | Guard App is built for a device population we have not measured | P1 |
| D-122 | Map provider: Google vs Mappls/MapMyIndia vs OSM | Cost at scale, Indian address/pincode quality, offline tiles for the Guard App | Mappls for geocoding/serviceability, Google for rendering, pending a cost model | Single provider; OSM self-hosted | Geocoding quality and map cost are both unknown at launch (R-248) | P1 |
| D-125 | Customer App technology: React Native vs Flutter vs two native builds | Team hiring, performance on low-end Android, shared code with the Guard App | React Native, sharing infrastructure with the Guard App (see D-600 for the Guard App exception) | Flutter; native; PWA | Mobile hiring cannot start; the shared-code story is undefined | P0 |
| D-162 | Will the iOS apps pursue the critical-alert entitlement for wake checks and SOS? | Without it, iOS cannot reliably wake a guard or an owner at night, forcing Android-only night operations | Pursue the entitlement; ship Android-first for night-shift roles meanwhile | Skip it and rely on SMS/voice fallback | iOS night operations ship with an undeclared reliability gap | P2 |
| D-194 | Does the platform offer a formal SLA on identity-service availability to Enterprise tenants, and at what number? | Identity is the single point of failure for all ten surfaces (R-191); an SLA drives architecture cost | 99.95% monthly for the identity service, contractual only on Enterprise | 99.9%; no SLA; SLA for all plans | Enterprise contracts are signed without an availability position | P4b |
| D-241 | Is TimescaleDB available on the chosen managed Postgres platform, and is its licence acceptable? | Determines whether ping compression and continuous aggregates are built-in or hand-written (~800 lines) | Confirm before the ingest consumer is written; fall back to native partitioning if unavailable | Hand-rolled partitioning always; a separate time-series store | Ingest is built twice | P1 |
| D-246 | Do we support client-supplied webhook mTLS for Enterprise integrators? | Some enterprise security teams require it; certificate rotation is real operational work | HMAC signing only in V1; mTLS on request as an Enterprise engagement | mTLS from V1; never | An Enterprise security review blocks at integration time | P4b |
| D-247 | Which map provider for V1 — Google, Mapbox or Mappls (restates D-122 for the real-time layer)? | Coverage quality in tier-2/3 cities affects geofence usability; cost scales with console usage | Run a coverage test on 20 real sites plus a cost model, then decide; keep the abstraction layer regardless | As D-122 | Geofences are built against unmeasured coverage | P1 |
| D-305 | Does revoke-on-non-response in periodic access review apply to agency tenants, or only to Suraksha internal roles? | Auto-revoking an Agency Owner's finance user because they ignored an email could stop a payroll run | Apply to Suraksha internal roles immediately; for tenants, notify and flag rather than auto-revoke in V1, with auto-revoke as a tenant opt-in | Apply everywhere; apply nowhere | Access review tooling is built with the wrong default and stops a tenant's payroll | P3 |
| D-330 | Which managed SIEM / log-analytics platform, and when does a dedicated SIEM replace scheduled queries? | Detection quality, cost and the staffing model for security monitoring | Cloud-native log platform with scheduled detections at MVP; dedicated SIEM before the first Enterprise tenant | Dedicated SIEM from day one; no SIEM | Detection coverage is undefined when the first Enterprise security review arrives | P2 |
| D-331 | Who holds the security on-call pager at MVP, and is out-of-hours coverage internal or contracted? | P0 response time is meaningless without someone who answers (R-601) | CTO plus one engineer on a two-person rotation, with a documented escalation to a retained partner | Contracted MDR; founders only; no formal rota | Security incidents have no defined responder | P1 |
| D-332 | Is a paid bug-bounty programme adopted, and at what phase? | Bounty without triage capacity produces noise and reputational risk | Responsible disclosure with recognition at MVP; paid bounty only after a dedicated security owner exists | Paid bounty from launch; never | Researchers report through unmanaged channels | P4b |
| D-338 | Are agency tenants permitted to configure integrity mode "Block", and under what conditions? | Blocking rooted devices can lock a guard out of their own attendance on a legitimate cheap handset (R-332) | Permitted only where the agency issues devices, and never for the SOS path | Never permitted; permitted for all tenants | Guards on cheap devices are locked out by a tenant's configuration choice | P2 |
| D-364 | Do Enterprise tenants get direct read access to their analytics read model, and on what terms? | Affects data architecture, isolation model and support burden | Offer a scoped, contracted, read-only export API before direct warehouse access | Direct warehouse access; export files only | An Enterprise deal forces an architecture concession under time pressure | P4b |
| D-520 | The exact Tier-1 mobile device list (models, not classes) for release blocking, and who refreshes it quarterly | Without named models the mobile gate is unenforceable | Two named low-end Androids on 10/11, two mid on 12/13, one current, two iPhones (current and current−2); refreshed quarterly by Mobile QA from field-trial data | Class-based definition; market-share-based list | Gate G7 is unenforceable and "low-end Android" means whatever is on the shelf | P2 |
| D-521 | Who owns the synthetic data generator — QA or the platform team? | It is the single dependency that makes the no-production-data rule workable (R-521) | QA owns it, platform engineers contribute; it lives in the application repository and its CI runs on every schema change | Platform owns; nobody owns, ad hoc fixtures | The generator rots and the no-production-data rule is broken "just once" | P1 |
| D-523 | Is the third-party penetration test annual, per major release, or both, and who owns the budget? | Gate G4 depends on it and the cadence changes the gate's meaning | Annual full-scope plus a targeted test per major release touching auth, payments or tenancy | Annual only; per release only | G4 passes on an undefined artefact | P2 |
| D-526 | Acceptable word error rate for voice recognition per language, and who signs it off | AIQ-10 has no threshold without this | Set per language from a baseline field measurement; the emergency-keyword rule stays at 100% regardless | Single global WER target; no target | Voice ships without a quality bar (A-564) | P4a |
| D-527 | The exact SOS end-to-end latency target, and whether it differs online vs queued-offline | §43.10 and §43.12.3 both reference it as a rollback trigger | Two published targets: online trigger-to-operator-queue, and offline trigger-to-transmit-on-reconnect, measured separately | One combined target; no published target | The most safety-critical rollback trigger has no number | P2 |
| D-528 | Does the platform operate an SMS fallback for SOS where data is unavailable, and at what cost per message? | SUR-EDG-008 specifies it as a transport with a real recurring cost and a carrier dependency | Enable it for the SOS path only, with per-tenant cost visibility | No SMS fallback; SMS fallback for all safety events | One of three SOS transports is unfunded (R-571) | P2 |
| D-532 | Maximum permitted unsynced-queue age before a supervisor is alerted | It bounds the data loss in SUR-EDG-046 | 4 hours for telemetry, 30 minutes for any safety event still queued | Single threshold; no alerting | Offline data loss is unbounded and invisible | P2 |
| D-539 | Release-blocking crash-free-session floor per device tier | G7 and the staged-rollout gates cite it without a number | 99.5% on Tier 1, 99.0% on Tier 2, measured over the rollout stage | Single floor; no floor | The staged-rollout gate cannot fail, so it cannot pass | P2 |
| D-541 | Is a QA canary tenant permitted in production, and what data may it hold? | §43.12.2 smoke tests depend on it, and it is a permanent tenant in the live system | Yes, two canary tenants holding only synthetic data, excluded from all business reporting and clearly marked | No production canary; canary with real data | Production smoke tests cannot run, or run against real tenant data | P1 |
| D-550 | Primary backend language/framework and mobile framework (links to D-125) | Determines hiring, the shared-code story across four apps, and the CI toolchain; changing it later is a rewrite | One backend language for API + workers and one cross-platform mobile framework; record as an ADR before the first sprint | Polyglot backend; per-app frameworks | Hiring cannot start; the first sprint writes code in whatever the first hire knows | Pre-P0 |
| D-551 | Adopt a managed feature-flag platform at Scale, given tenant/user identifiers in the evaluation context? | Whether flag evaluation data leaves India, and whether we build or buy | Self-host at MVP; re-evaluate at 100+ flags with a data-minimisation review | Managed from day one; no flag system | Flags proliferate in config files and cannot be audited | P4b |
| D-552 | Headcount trigger for hiring a dedicated platform/SRE engineer | A three-person on-call rotation is a known attrition risk; an implicit trigger is never pulled (R-601) | Hire when out-of-hours pages exceed 4/month sustained over a quarter, or when the rotation drops below 3 | Fixed date; fixed headcount; never | The rota degrades silently until someone resigns | P2 |
| D-553 | Observability backend selection (managed-in-India vs self-hosted OSS vs provider-native) | Residency, cost at scale and operational burden on a team with no SRE pull in different directions | Prefer a managed backend with a verified Indian region for logs, metrics, traces and errors; otherwise a single integrated OTel-native self-hosted stack | Provider-native; self-hosted OSS; multiple backends | Telemetry is scattered across tools and R-573 arrives early | P1 |
| D-554 | When to fund the warm standby in the second Indian region | Moves region-loss RTO from 24 h to 4 h at +35–50% infrastructure cost; also the answer to enterprise DR questions | Fund at the first of: an Enterprise contract with an RTO clause, 50,000 guards, or a second region-scare within 12 months | Fund from day one; never | R-637 stays open and DR answers in procurement are improvised | P4b |
| D-555 | Cloud provider and region pair | Determines the managed-service catalogue the whole §47 operating analysis rests on | AWS Mumbai primary, Hyderabad for DR, with an out-of-account immutable backup copy | Another provider; single region; multi-cloud | No IaC can be written (see D-601) | Pre-P0 |
| D-556 | Is the daily real ₹1 payment probe acceptable to finance and to the gateway's terms? | The only way to detect a live-gateway failure before a client does; creates transactions finance must exclude | Run it, flag the records, exclude from all revenue reporting | Sandbox probe only; no probe | Gateway failures are discovered by customers (R-625) | P1 |
| D-557 | SMS SOS fallback implementation given mobile-platform SMS permission restrictions | If the permission is unobtainable the fallback becomes a one-tap pre-filled SMS — slower, and it changes the §46.2 target | Validate against current store policy before build; design for the policy-safe variant and treat automatic send as an enhancement | Assume the permission; drop the transport | R-571 materialises during store review, late | P2 |
| D-558 | Guard App server compatibility window — 12 months confirmed or adjusted from real update-lag data | Too short strands guards on constrained data plans; too long is a permanent maintenance and security tax | Ship with 12 months; re-derive from the fleet version distribution at day 180 | 6 months; 24 months | API versioning policy is set on an unmeasured assumption (A-567) | P2 |
| D-560 | Payroll window staggering across tenants to flatten the month-end cliff | Concentrating all tenants on the 1st–5th creates a monthly capacity spike that is pure waste to provision for (R-524) | Make the payroll window a tenant configuration with a default distributed across the month; incentivise off-peak windows | Fixed window for all; no staggering | Month-end capacity must be provisioned for a peak that could have been flattened | P3 |
| D-589 | Is Phase 4 split into 4a (intelligence core) and 4b (surface depth) with independent gates? | Phase 4 as specified carries 178 of 503 screens — too much for a single go/no-go (R-587) | Split, with the gate criteria in §51.6.9 | Keep as one phase; split three ways | The phase runs indefinitely and delivery discipline is lost | P3 |
| D-600 | Guard App native Android versus React Native for all four mobile apps | Battery, OEM process kills, exact alarms and SOS cold start sit under the safety-critical path; modifies D-125 | Native Kotlin for the Guard App, RN for the other three; decide by an 8-week measured prototype | RN for all four; native for all four | Mobile hiring and the safety-path reliability model are both unresolved | P0 |
| D-601 | Cloud provider and primary Indian region, fixed before any IaC is written (restates D-555) | Late reversal costs 6–10 weeks of migration dominated by data transfer, not code | One cloud, Indian primary region, managed containers, managed Postgres/Redis/storage | As D-555 | Infrastructure work cannot begin | Pre-P0 |
| D-605 | On-call compensation, time-off-in-lieu, and when founders stop being the escalation path of last resort | A permanently on-call CTO is a single point of failure for the whole company (R-601, A-605) | Allowance plus TOIL; third engineer on the rota by day 90 | No allowance; outsourced first line | The CTO burns out within 90 days of launch | P1 |
| D-606 | Certify a short list of third-party GPS/OBD trackers, or accept any device posting to the ingest endpoint? | An open endpoint pushes device data-quality problems into operations | Certify a short list | Open endpoint with validation; no third-party devices | Telematics support burden is unbounded | P5 |
| D-610 | Mobile release cadence: fortnightly train versus monthly | Determines how fast field defects reach guards, against store review turnaround | Fortnightly, with an out-of-band lane for safety-path fixes | Monthly; continuous | Safety-path fixes queue behind feature releases | P2 |
| D-618 | Partner ecosystem: curated app directory versus open marketplace | A third-party token is the most likely future cross-tenant leak vector | Curated indefinitely, given data sensitivity | Open with review; open with sandboxing | An open ecosystem is launched before the isolation model can support it | P5 |
| D-619 | Who may call a rollback at each of the three layers, and can they act unilaterally? | Reverting must be cheaper and less career-risky than pressing on | Engineer/CTO for software; Command Center lead/COO for operational mode; any single founder for launch rollback | Founder approval for all rollbacks; automated only | Rollbacks are delayed by escalation during an incident | P1 |
| D-624 | Is a second payment gateway adapter maintained warm from Phase 1, or deferred until migration is forced? `[RECOMMENDED]` | R-278 and R-625 both depend on it; a cold adapter is not a mitigation | **Warm from Phase 1: the second adapter carries at least 1% of live traffic continuously and is exercised in the monthly reconciliation drill** | Cold adapter maintained in code only; single gateway with a documented manual fallback | The migration playbook exists on paper and fails when it is first used | P1 |
| D-626 | Which single artefact is the source of truth for the requirement ID index in §56.2, and who maintains it as requirements are added? `[RECOMMENDED]` | Without an owner the index in §56.2 is accurate on the day it is written and wrong two sprints later | **A generated index: a CI job parses all `SUR-`, `BR-`, `WKF-` and `TC-` IDs from the specification repository and regenerates §56.2 on every merge; Product owns the job, and a duplicate or gap fails the build** | Manually maintained by Product; maintained per section by each author; not maintained | Traceability degrades silently and the §56.6 completeness review cannot be repeated | P0 |
| D-631 | Where do `TC-` IDs for the §57–§60 capabilities live, given §44 predates those sections? `[RECOMMENDED]` | Launch readiness, drills, health scores and incident classes are asserted but untested (finding F-25) | **Extend §44 with a `TC-OPS-` range; do not create a parallel test-ID scheme** | A separate operations test suite; no formal tests for §57–§60 | Launch and post-launch capabilities ship with no test coverage and no gate | P1 |

### 55.3 COO / operational decisions

| ID | Question | Why it matters | Recommended default | Alternatives | Impact if deferred | Decide by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-104 | Lead-time and urgency rules per city and per guard category for B2C bookings | Determines what deployment window the site may promise and how SLA is measured | 48h standard, 24h urgent with surcharge, event blocks 72h — as configuration, per city | Fixed national lead times; no published lead time | Booking promises a window operations cannot meet (R-122) | P1 |
| D-108 | Default wake-check cadence, acknowledgement window and escalation thresholds for night duty | The headline differentiator; too frequent exhausts guards and burns battery, too sparse is not proof | 90-minute cadence, 5-minute acknowledgement window, escalation on the second consecutive miss; contract-overridable | 60-minute cadence; guard-initiated only | The differentiator ships with parameters nobody owns | P2 |
| D-143 | Is immediate client notification on SOS default-on or default-off, per contract tier? | Client trust, false-alarm noise and contractual drafting | Default-on for Tier-1 and government clients, default-off (t+5 min) for others, always overridable per contract | Always on; always delayed; client-configured only | Contract templates and the SOS flow both stall | P2 |
| D-145 | Command Center regional model: single national watch vs regional rooms, and at what scale a second room opens | Capital and hiring plan; affects seat design and handover process | Single national watch until 2,500 concurrent on-duty guards, then a second regional room | Regional from day one; permanent single room | The hiring plan has no trigger and the second room is opened late | P3 |
| D-146 | May operators hold a duress-code convention with guards, and how is it trained and stored? | A safety control that is also a secret which must not sit in a queryable field | Adopt it; store as a per-operation convention in the SOP, never as a per-guard database field | Per-guard code in the database; no duress convention | A safety control is either absent or implemented as a data field | P2 |
| D-163 | What contact response-time commitment does Trinetra publish? | A published promise operations cannot meet damages trust more than no promise | Publish "within 1 working day" only once staffed | Publish same-day; publish nothing | The page ships with a promise nobody is accountable for | P3 |
| D-169 | Support response targets for Starter and Professional plans | Sets expectation and staffing; Enterprise SLA is already promised in the plan definition | Starter next-working-day, Professional same-working-day, both business hours | Same target for all; no published target | Support is staffed against an unstated expectation (D-604) | P3 |
| D-213 | Final wake-check acknowledgement window and randomisation policy | Too short punishes a guard walking a round; too long defeats the control | 120 s window, randomised firing within ±20 min of the scheduled slot, minimum 45 min spacing | Fixed schedule; 60 s window | BR-416 and BR-450 have no parameters | P2 |
| D-529 | Configured over-strength pay rule when an unassigned guard works a post | SUR-EDG-030 leaves it configured but undefined | Pay requires supervisor approval with a reason; client billed contracted strength | Never pay; always pay; bill the client | An edge case resolves inconsistently and becomes a payroll dispute | P3 |
| D-530 | Short-notice release payment, if any, to guards released when a client cancels hours before deployment | Affects agency economics and guard trust (R-622) | A configurable per-shift release payment defaulting to zero until commercially decided | Fixed half-shift payment; none, non-configurable | Guards absorb the cost of client cancellations with no policy | P3 |
| D-537 | Which client roles receive SOS notifications by default, and can a client opt every contact in? | TC-CMD-013 depends on the default | Security Head and Site Manager opted in by default; others opt in explicitly and are recorded | All contacts by default; none by default | SOS notification routing is undefined at the moment it matters | P2 |
| D-540 | Who signs off UAT on behalf of the guard participant class? | §43.13.2 requires a signature per class and guards individually cannot give it | The Suraksha COO plus the participating agency's Operations Manager, against the published field-trial thresholds | Agency owner alone; no guard-class sign-off | UAT cannot be closed | P2 |
| D-604 | Committed support response/resolution targets per plan, and whether Starter gets a contractual commitment | Support SLAs signed before staffing exists become breaches; S1 must not vary by plan | Publish the §59.2.2 defaults; S1 identical for everyone | Plan-differentiated S1; no published targets | Contracts commit to targets nobody has staffed | P3 |
| D-607 | The committed guard payment date (T+n) and whether missing it carries an internal penalty | Late wages at this wage level drive attrition faster than any other factor (R-603, R-622) | Commit to a comfortably achievable date; treat a miss as a P1 incident | Aggressive date with best effort; no commitment | Payday slips without consequence and the launch cohort leaves | P2 |
| D-609 | Verification queue staffed in-house or partly outsourced, and how quality is sampled | The queue is the deployment bottleneck; a backlog is a revenue and coverage problem (R-602) | In-house decisions; outsource only the mechanical completeness pass | Fully outsourced; fully in-house | The bottleneck is discovered when it is already blocking deployments | P2 |
| D-622 | Minimum bench-depth ratio, and who may authorise deploying below it `[RECOMMENDED]` | Bench depth is the only real defence against replacement-SLA failure and single-site concentration (R-604, R-215) | **Minimum 1.5× the deployed strength per city; deploying below 1.3× requires a recorded COO authorisation per contract; below 1.2× no new contract may start** | 1.2× minimum; no formal ratio, judgement per city | Contracts are signed that cannot be covered when two guards are absent | P1 |
| D-632 | Is there an operational runbook set maintained separately from this specification, and who owns it? `[RECOMMENDED]` | §59 references runbooks that no artefact currently holds; a runbook inside a product specification is never updated at 03:00 (finding F-32 context) | **Yes — the COO owns the runbook set, versioned alongside SOPs rather than inside the product specification, and referenced from §59** | Runbooks inside the PRD; no formal runbooks | Operators improvise during incidents and the §53.13 drill cycle has nothing to test against | P1 |

### 55.4 Compliance / legal decisions

Nothing in this group is a legal conclusion; each is a product position taken pending qualified advice, held as configuration where possible (canon §0).

| ID | Question | Why it matters | Recommended default | Alternatives | Impact if deferred | Decide by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-105 | Which KYC documents are required for which client service categories and value thresholds? | Affects conversion friction directly and is compliance-sensitive | Minimal KYC for standard residential; full KYC for PSO/armed and for GST-invoiced business accounts | Uniform full KYC; no KYC below a value | Booking cannot define its document step | P1 |
| D-123 | E-signature for contracts and quotes — provider and sufficiency | Determines whether quote acceptance is fully digital | Click-accept with an audit trail in V1; an e-sign provider in V2 | E-sign from V1; wet signature | Contract acceptance stays manual and slows every deal | P2 |
| D-126 | Are prior-employer disciplinary notes ever surfaced to a prospective agency? | Fairness, defamation exposure, and workforce-marketplace value | Not surfaced as free text; aggregate integrity signal only, with the guard able to see and respond | Full history visible; nothing visible | A livelihood-affecting data flow is built without a position | P3 |
| D-144 | Retention period for SOS audio/photo evidence and GPS track history | Balances dispute defence against privacy and storage cost | SOS evidence 36 months; GPS tracks 90 days full resolution then downsampled to 24 months | Uniform 12 months; longer for all | Retention jobs cannot be written; R-370 exposure grows | P2 |
| D-160 | Is an Aadhaar-based eKYC route available, and under what authorised-entity relationship? | Determines whether guard onboarding is minutes or days, and how identity numbers may be stored | Assume no eKYC; capture a masked reference + verification outcome only, document-based | Pursue authorised-entity status; full number storage | Onboarding is designed twice | P1 |
| D-166 | May an adverse record on one tenant be surfaced as a signal to another tenant? | Real safety value versus a serious privacy and fairness exposure | Do not surface across tenants in V1; revisit with legal and a due-process design | Cross-tenant with appeal; cross-tenant freely | A shared blacklist emerges informally through support channels | P3 |
| D-167 | How are government identity numbers stored — full, masked, or verification-outcome only? | Determines the blast radius of any breach and the platform's obligations | Store a masked reference + verification outcome only, unless a specific lawful basis is configured | Full encrypted storage; no storage at all | The most sensitive field in the platform is stored by default rather than by decision | Pre-P0 |
| D-192 | Data-retention period for login history and device records | Security investigation capability vs privacy minimisation and storage cost | 24 months for login history; 12 months after last use for device records | 12/6 months; indefinite | Retention jobs are written against an unstated policy | P2 |
| D-196 | Cross-tenant benchmark publication: opt-in or opt-out for agencies? | Determines the usefulness of market benchmarks and the trust posture of the marketplace | Opt-out with k≥10 anonymity, disclosed at onboarding | Opt-in only; no benchmarks | The benchmark feature is built on an untested consent basis | P4b |
| D-197 | May Suraksha staff impersonation ever be write-enabled, and under what authority? | Support effectiveness vs the integrity of tenant audit trails (R-142) | Write-enabled impersonation only with an in-session tenant approval, dual authorisation, and a 30-minute cap | Read-only always; write-enabled for Support leads | Support builds workarounds that are worse than the controlled path | P3 |
| D-221 | Is a guard's final settlement withheld pending asset return, and to what limit? | Employment fairness vs asset loss; affects WKF-36 and payroll | Recover assessed asset value from final settlement up to a configured cap; never withhold the whole settlement | Withhold in full until return; never recover | Offboarding resolves inconsistently and unfairly | P3 |
| D-223 | May a guard be deployed while police verification is outstanding, and must the client be told? | Trust promise vs supply reality; directly affects the "VERIFIED" brand claim | Provisional deployment off by default; where a tenant enables it, the client sees the pending state | Never permitted; permitted silently | The brand's central claim is decided by an operational shortcut | P2 |

(restates D-166 for the data model) | Cross-tenant visibility helps agencies avoid an unfit guard but creates a livelihood-affecting shared blacklist | Tenant-local in V1; cross-tenant only as an aggregate verification status with an appeal process | As D-166 | Same as D-166 | P3 |
