#### 57.2.2 Scaling characteristic per component

| # | Component | Scales with | Scaling shape | First bottleneck | Lever |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C-01 | edge | Page views, tile loads | Horizontal (managed) | Tile spend, not capacity | Cache TTL, clustering |
| C-02 | api | Concurrent users × request rate | Horizontal, stateless | DB connections, then CPU on report endpoints | Add instances; move reports to replica; PgBouncer |
| C-03 | rt-gateway | Concurrent open sockets | Horizontal; memory-bound per instance | ~10–20k sockets/instance | Add instances; shard topics by tenant |
| C-04 | ingest | Guards on duty ÷ ping interval | Horizontal, stateless, cheap | Redis write throughput | Add instances; increase stream partitions |
| C-05 | signals-consumer | Ping rate | Horizontal by stream partition | Postgres write amplification on `location` | Partition count; batch inserts; extract to own DB (§34.7.2) |
| C-06 | worker-critical | Open alerts × escalation steps | Horizontal; must never queue behind heavy work | Provider send latency | Dedicated queue + provider account |
| C-07 | worker-default | Events, notifications, webhooks | Horizontal by queue partition | Provider rate limits | Concurrency per provider; more partitions |
| C-08 | worker-heavy | Tenants × payroll/invoice cycle (spiky, monthly) | Horizontal, burst | Postgres CPU during month-end | Schedule windows; replica reads; per-tenant fairness |
| C-09 | scheduler | Job count (not load) | **Singleton by design** | None at our scale | Split domains into 2 leaders if job runtime overlaps |
| C-10 | ai-orchestrator | AI interactions | Horizontal; provider-token-bound | Provider rate/quota and cost | Per-tenant quotas, caching, model tiering |
| C-11 | media-processor | Uploads (enrolment spikes, incident media) | Horizontal, burst | Object-storage throughput, OCR quota | Autoscale, queue depth-based |
| C-12–C-16 | Web apps | Sessions | Horizontal / static-CDN | SSR CPU on the marketing site | Static generation + CDN |
| C-17–C-20 | Mobile apps | Installed base | Client-side | App size + battery on low-end Android | Payload discipline; §57.3.3 |
| C-21 | desktop-ap | Installed base | Client-side | Auto-update bandwidth | CDN, delta updates |
| C-22 | postgres-primary | Writes: pings, attendance, audit, ledger | **Vertical first**, then partition/extract | Write IOPS from `location` + `audit_log` | Bigger instance → partition pruning → extract ingest DB |
| C-23 | postgres-replica | Report concurrency | Horizontal (add replicas) | Replication lag under month-end load | More replicas; move to warehouse (§32.6.5) |
| C-24 | redis | Streams + cache working set | Vertical, then cluster | Memory | Bounded stream length; eviction policy; cluster mode |
| C-25 | object-storage | Cumulative documents/media | Effectively unlimited | Cost, not capacity | Lifecycle tiering, retention (§39) |
| C-26 | observability | Log volume × retention | Managed | Ingest cost | Sampling, cardinality control |

**Note on C-02.** The monolith is one *deployable*, not one *process pool*. It is deployed as three separately scalable pools sharing the same image and code: `api-web` (interactive traffic), `api-enterprise` (partner API, isolated so a partner's batch job cannot starve the console), and `api-admin` (OPS/back-office). Same binary, different resource limits, different rate-limit profiles, different scaling triggers. This gives most of the blast-radius benefit of service extraction at none of the distributed-systems cost, and it is the single most useful piece of architectural preparation for the day extraction is genuinely justified.
---

### 57.3 Technology recommendations

#### 57.3.0 How to read these

Every decision below is presented on the seven lenses the brief requires. Read them as follows:

| Lens | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Why** | The specific property of *this* product that makes the choice correct. Not "it is popular". |
| **Alternatives** | Real candidates that were considered, with the reason each lost. |
| **Trade-offs** | What we are giving up. Every choice gives something up; if a row says "none", it is wrong. |
| **Cost implication** | Direction and rough magnitude, in operating cost and in engineering time. Absolute rupee figures are indicative only and must be re-quoted at contract time. |
| **Scaling implication** | What happens to this choice at 10× and at 100× the pilot. |
| **Vendor lock-in** | How hard it is to leave, measured in weeks of engineering, not in adjectives. |
| **Security impact** | What this choice does to attack surface, data residency and the §38/§39 posture. |
| **If this changes** | The single constraint that would flip the decision, and to what. |

Two standing constraints apply to all of them, from the canon and from §39: **India-first data residency** unless there is a documented reason otherwise, and **no guard location data leaves our infrastructure** for any convenience feature.

---

#### 57.3.1 Backend language and framework

**[RECOMMENDED] TypeScript on Node.js (LTS), with NestJS as the module framework, inside one modular-monolith repository.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Three forces point the same way. (1) The frontend is unavoidably TypeScript across five web properties plus React Native apps; one language means shared types generated from the OpenAPI spec (§33), shared validation schemas, shared money/date/i18n utilities, and one hiring pool for a small team. (2) The workload is overwhelmingly I/O-bound — database round trips, provider calls, fan-out — which is exactly what an event-loop runtime is good at. (3) NestJS imposes module boundaries, dependency injection and a decorator-based interceptor chain, which is precisely the discipline a modular monolith needs to avoid becoming a big ball of mud; the cross-cutting mechanisms in §57.4 are implemented once as guards/interceptors and applied declaratively. |
| Alternatives | **Go** — better CPU efficiency, lower memory, superb for the ingest path; loses on shared types with the frontend, on ORM/migration maturity for a schema this size, and on hiring at Indian startup salary bands. **Python (Django/FastAPI)** — best AI/ML ecosystem and admin scaffolding; Django's ORM is excellent for this domain, but async maturity and per-request overhead are weaker, and split-language teams of five engineers lose more to context-switching than they gain. **Java/Kotlin (Spring Boot)** — strongest for a system this transactional and the natural fit if we hired from enterprise fintech; heavier to operate, slower to iterate at pilot stage. **PHP (Laravel)** — genuinely fast to build and cheap to hire for in India; rejected because the real-time and offline-sync work sits awkwardly and the long-term ceiling is lower. |
| Trade-offs | Node is the wrong runtime for CPU-heavy work. We accept that and route it away: PDF rendering, image processing, payroll arithmetic over large tenants and OCR post-processing run in `worker-heavy` where a hot loop blocking the event loop is contained, and any genuinely CPU-bound routine is allowed to be a separate small Go or Python binary invoked as a job — explicitly permitted, not forbidden. Second trade-off: JavaScript's numeric type is unsafe for money, which is why canon §4's integer-paise rule is enforced by a `Money` value type and a lint rule banning raw arithmetic on monetary fields. |
| Cost | Lowest total for our shape: one language, one CI toolchain, one dependency scanner, one set of hiring criteria. Node's memory footprint is higher than Go's — roughly 1.5–2× the instance size for the same throughput, which at pilot scale is a rounding error (single-digit thousands of rupees per month) and becomes a real number only past the ingest volumes in §34.7.2, at which point the ingest path is the thing to rewrite, not the monolith. |
| Scaling | Horizontal and stateless to the limits of the database. The known ceiling is the ingest path; §34.7.2 already names the trigger for splitting it, and Go is the natural language for that one extracted service. |
| Lock-in | None. Node, NestJS and Postgres drivers are open source and portable across any host. |
| Security | Large transitive dependency tree is the main risk — mitigated by lockfiles, `npm audit`/SCA in CI, a dependency-addition review rule, SBOM generation per release, and runtime allow-listing of outbound egress (§38). Node's ecosystem also has the best-maintained libraries for the specific security primitives we need (Argon2id bindings, JOSE, OpenAPI validation). |
| **If this changes** | If the ingest path exceeds the §34.7.2 trigger, or if a CPU-bound workload becomes the dominant cost, **extract that path to Go** — do not rewrite the monolith. If the team we can actually hire is Java-heavy, **Spring Boot** is a fully acceptable substitute for the monolith; nothing else in this document changes. |

---

#### 57.3.2 Frontend framework

**[RECOMMENDED] React with TypeScript. Next.js (App Router) for surakshaguards.in and trinetra.surakshaguards.in; a Vite + React SPA for ops., ap. and guards.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The five properties have two genuinely different jobs. The marketing/marketplace surfaces need SEO, fast first paint on mobile networks, server rendering and image optimisation — Next.js exists for that. The three application consoles are authenticated, dense, long-session, real-time surfaces where SEO is irrelevant and SSR is a liability (it complicates WebSocket state, permission-aware rendering and offline-ish behaviour); a plain SPA with aggressive code-splitting is simpler, cheaper to host and faster to iterate. Using React for both means one design system implementation (§27), one component library, one set of engineers. |
| Alternatives | **Next.js everywhere** — one framework, but SSR overhead and hosting complexity for consoles that will never be crawled. **Vue/Nuxt** — smaller bundles and a gentler learning curve; loses on ecosystem depth for the specific hard parts (virtualised dense tables, map integration, complex forms) and on shared code with React Native. **Angular** — genuinely good for large enterprise consoles with strong conventions; rejected because it shares nothing with the mobile stack and narrows hiring. **Svelte/SvelteKit** — best runtime performance and smallest bundles; the smallest talent pool of the four and the thinnest component ecosystem for operator-grade tables. **Server-rendered HTML + htmx** — very attractive for the back-office surfaces and would cut a lot of code; rejected because the Command Center and map surfaces are irreducibly stateful and would end up as a second frontend stack anyway. |
| Trade-offs | Two build setups to maintain instead of one. Mitigated by sharing the design system, API client, i18n catalogue and analytics SDK as internal packages in a monorepo, so the divergence is confined to routing and rendering. Next.js also carries a real upgrade tax across major versions; we pin, and we do not adopt experimental APIs in the App Router. |
| Cost | Marketing/marketplace on a managed static+SSR host or a container behind the CDN; consoles are static bundles on object storage + CDN, which is close to free. Engineering cost is dominated by the design system, not the framework. |
| Scaling | Console performance scales with *rendering discipline*, not with servers: virtualised tables, viewport-scoped map subscriptions (§34.2), and pagination everywhere are the actual levers. SSR pages scale on the CDN. |
| Lock-in | Low for React itself. Next.js has moderate lock-in to its routing/rendering model and, if hosted on its vendor's platform, to that platform — which is why the recommendation is to run Next.js in a container we control, not on a proprietary edge runtime. |
| Security | Standard browser posture: strict CSP with nonces, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitisation, HttpOnly/SameSite cookies for the session where possible, tokens never in `localStorage` for privileged consoles, subresource integrity for third-party scripts, and permission-aware rendering that never relies on client-side hiding for authorisation (the server re-checks — §31). |
| **If this changes** | If bundle size on low-end devices becomes the binding constraint for `guards.`, move that one property to **SvelteKit or server-rendered HTML**; it is the smallest and least coupled property and can diverge without cost. |

---

#### 57.3.3 Mobile approach — the Guard App decision

This is the most consequential client-side decision in the document, so it is argued at length rather than asserted.

**The constraints, stated plainly.** The Guard App runs on the cheapest Android phone its user could buy — typically 2–3 GB RAM, an entry-level SoC, 32 GB storage that is usually 85% full, Android 10–13, frequently with an aggressive OEM battery manager (Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo, Realme, Samsung all ship their own process killers). It must: hold a foreground location service for a 12-hour shift within a ≤6% battery budget (§18); fire exact local alarms for wake checks that must work with no network (§18, `AlarmManager` exact alarms + a watchdog); run a durable encrypted local queue of attendance, patrol, incident and media events; capture and compress camera images; run a face/liveness template locally; deliver an SOS within seconds from a cold or backgrounded state; and survive OEM battery optimisation that will kill a poorly-configured background process without warning. iOS is nearly irrelevant for this audience in India today.

**The options.**

| Option | Background location & alarms | Battery control | App size (low-end impact) | Cold-start / SOS latency | Team cost | Fit for the other three apps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Native Android (Kotlin)** | Direct, complete: foreground service, `AlarmManager` exact alarms, `WorkManager`, OEM whitelisting flows, Doze handling | Full — every wake-up, sensor and interval is ours | Smallest (~8–15 MB) | Best | Needs an Android engineer; iOS would be a second build | Poor — no reuse |
| **React Native** | Requires native modules for exactly the hard parts; the JS thread is not where the location loop lives | Good *if* the native module is written well — which means writing Kotlin anyway | +12–20 MB Hermes/RN runtime | Adds JS bundle load to cold start; SOS must be a native path to be safe | Best reuse with the web stack (TypeScript, React) | Excellent |
| **Flutter** | Mature plugins, good background support, but still native code underneath for exact alarms and OEM quirks | Good | +10–18 MB engine | Good; AOT compiled | Dart — a separate language and hiring pool from everything else we build | Good, but shares nothing with web |
| **WebView / PWA shell** | Not viable | Not viable | Smallest | Poor | Cheapest | — |
| **KMP (Kotlin Multiplatform)** | Native on Android by construction | Full | Small | Best | Newer, thinner ecosystem for UI | Moderate |

**The argument.** The decisive observation is that *the hard 30% of the Guard App must be written in Kotlin regardless of framework choice.* Background location with adaptive intervals, exact alarms surviving Doze, OEM battery-manager handling, a foreground service notification that a guard cannot accidentally dismiss, a boot-completed receiver, a durable local queue and a cold-start SOS path are all native concerns. React Native does not remove that work; it wraps it, and then adds a JS runtime, a bridge and a second failure mode on top of the exact code path where failure means a guard's SOS did not send. For an app whose *entire* value is background reliability on hostile devices, adding an abstraction layer over the reliability-critical part is the wrong direction.

Against that: React Native gives us one team building four apps, shared TypeScript with the web, over-the-air-style iteration on non-native surfaces, and a much lower total headcount — which for a company at this stage is not a small thing. And §16 has already recorded `D-125` with a working default of React Native for the Customer App "sharing infrastructure with the Guard App".

**The recommendation splits the apps, because the apps are not alike.**

| App | [RECOMMENDED] approach | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Guard App (Android)** | **Native Android, Kotlin + Jetpack Compose** | Background reliability, battery budget, exact alarms, OEM quirks, app size on a full 32 GB phone, and a cold-start SOS path with no runtime in front of it. This app is 80% of the platform's field risk; it gets the approach with the fewest layers between intent and OS. |
| Guard App (iOS) | **Deferred**; native Swift when justified | iOS penetration among Indian guards is very low. Building it "because cross-platform is free" is the classic reason to pick RN — but the free build would be the *unreliable* one. Revisit on evidence of demand (a PSO/close-protection segment is the plausible case). |
| **Customer App** | **React Native** | Booking, tracking view, invoices, support. No background service, no exact alarms, no battery budget. Cross-platform is straightforwardly correct here, and iOS matters for this audience. |
| **Agency App** | **React Native** | Admin-format companion to the Agency Portal; shares the web app's TypeScript models. |
| **Admin App** | **React Native** | OPS in hand for authorised staff; needs push and good tables, not background services. |

This modifies the working default in `D-125` (which assumed the Guard App and Customer App would share a stack) and is raised as `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-600]`. The cost of the split is one Android engineer who is not shared with the web team, plus a duplicated implementation of shared concerns — API client, auth, i18n, offline queue — for one app. The mitigation is that the Guard App's API surface is deliberately narrow (§33.3.9 and the `/guard/today` bundle), so "duplication" here is a few thousand lines, not a parallel product. The benefit is that the one app where failure is a safety event has no framework between it and the operating system.

| Lens | Position (Guard App = native Android; other three = React Native) |
|---|---|
| Why | Above. In one line: put the fewest possible layers under the SOS button and the location loop, and take the cross-platform win everywhere it costs nothing. |
| Alternatives | React Native everywhere (one team, more risk on the critical path); Flutter everywhere (better background story than RN, but a third language for a five-person engineering team and no web reuse); native everywhere (best quality, roughly double the mobile headcount). |
| Trade-offs | We lose Guard App code sharing and gain an Android-specific hiring dependency. We accept a delayed iOS Guard App. We accept that two mobile toolchains must be maintained in CI. |
| Cost | +1 Android engineer (or contractor) versus the all-RN plan; roughly ₹15–25 lakh/year `[ASSUMPTION: A-600]`. Set against the cost of a single SOS that did not send, this is the cheapest insurance in the document. |
| Scaling | Client-side; scales with installs, not servers. The relevant scaling risk is *release* scaling — forced-update enforcement (§58) and staged rollouts matter more than runtime performance. |
| Lock-in | None to a vendor; a real lock-in to Android platform APIs, which is inherent to the requirement. |
| Security | Native gives direct access to the Android Keystore for key material, hardware-backed attestation for device binding (§38 device binding for guards), Play Integrity, and a smaller third-party dependency surface than an RN app of equivalent function. |
| **If this changes** | If a measured RN prototype holds the ≤6%/12h battery budget and passes an OEM-kill matrix on the five most common Indian budget devices with SOS cold-start under target, **switch the Guard App to React Native** and collapse to one mobile team. That test is the deciding evidence, and it should be run in the first eight weeks — see D-600. |

---

#### 57.3.4 Desktop application approach

**[RECOMMENDED] Tauri (v2) wrapping the existing Agency Portal web bundle, with a native shell for updates, notifications, file access and the local export folder.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The desktop app's requirement (canon §1.3, §20) is "same account, same data, same modules" plus OS-native notifications for P0/P1 alerts, native file dialogs for bulk import/export, scheduled export to a local folder, and installers for Windows/macOS/Linux. That is a web application in a native shell — no more. Tauri gives that shell using the OS's own webview, so the download is ~5–15 MB instead of ~90–150 MB, memory footprint is a fraction of Electron's, and agencies on modest office PCs (which is most of them) get an app that starts fast and does not eat 400 MB of RAM alongside their accounting software. Auto-update, code signing, notarisation and tray/notification APIs are first-class. |
| Alternatives | **Electron** — the safe, boring choice: bundled Chromium means one rendering engine to test, the deepest ecosystem, and the most StackOverflow answers; costs 10× the download size, much higher memory, and the maintenance burden of shipping a browser (including its security patches) with every release. **Native per OS (WPF/.NET, SwiftUI, GTK)** — best experience, triple the work, no code sharing with `ap.` — clearly wrong for a module-for-module mirror of a web app. **PWA install** — nearly free, but weak on OS notifications for critical alerts, weak on local file/folder automation, no signed installer to hand an IT department, and no controlled auto-update. **Flutter desktop** — plausible, but a fourth UI stack for this codebase. |
| Trade-offs | Tauri renders in the *system* webview: WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux. That means three rendering engines to test, and Linux WebKitGTK is the known weak spot (older distributions lag on CSS/JS features). Mitigations: target a defined baseline, run the desktop bundle through the same browser test matrix as the web app, avoid bleeding-edge CSS in the Agency Portal, and treat Linux as a supported-but-second-tier target with an AppImage that bundles a known-good runtime where feasible. Also: Tauri's Rust core means the (small) native layer is Rust, which is a language the team may not otherwise have — the surface is small enough to be manageable, but it is real. |
| Cost | Build and signing cost is similar to Electron; Apple Developer Program and a Windows code-signing certificate (OV or EV) are required either way — budget roughly ₹40–90k/year for certificates and enrolment `[ASSUMPTION: A-601]`. Bandwidth cost of updates is an order of magnitude lower than Electron's. Engineering: ~3–5 weeks for the shell, packaging, signing, notarisation and auto-update across three OSes, plus ongoing per-release CI time. |
| Scaling | Scales with installed base only. The real scaling concern is release engineering: three platforms × signing × notarisation × auto-update channels. Automate it in CI on day one or it will not get done. |
| Lock-in | Low. The app *is* the web bundle; abandoning Tauri for Electron later is a shell swap, not a rewrite. |
| Security | Smaller attack surface than Electron (no bundled Chromium to patch), a capability-based permission model for filesystem and shell access that we can lock down to exactly the export folder, and mandatory signing/notarisation so an agency's IT can verify provenance. Counterpoint: relying on the OS webview means we depend on the user patching their OS — an argument Electron wins on, and the reason the app must enforce a minimum OS/webview version and refuse to run below it. |
| **If this changes** | If Linux WebKitGTK rendering defects consume more than a sprint of remediation, or if an Enterprise client requires a single audited runtime version across their fleet, **switch to Electron** — same web bundle, bigger installer, problem gone. |

---

#### 57.3.5 Primary database

**[RECOMMENDED] PostgreSQL 16, managed, single primary + one read replica — settled in §32.0.1 and restated here only for completeness.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | See §32.0.1. In summary: the domain is relational and integrity-critical (rosters, assignments, contracts, invoices, ledger), it needs real transactions and foreign keys, row-level security is our tenant-isolation backstop, PostGIS covers geospatial in-engine, JSONB covers the genuinely variable parts, and declarative partitioning covers GPS and audit volume — one engine, one operations story, matching the modular-monolith stance. |
| Alternatives | Rejected in §32.0.1: MySQL (weaker JSON/geospatial/partitioning story), MongoDB (wrong for a ledger), a NewSQL distributed store (solves a scale problem we do not have, at a cost we cannot absorb), separate stores per domain (premature). |
| Trade-offs | Single-writer ceiling; vertical scaling is the first answer and it is a real ceiling. Accepted deliberately, with the escape route documented in §34.7.2. |
| Cost | The largest single infrastructure line item. Pilot-scale managed Postgres with a replica and PITR sits in the low tens of thousands of rupees per month; it grows with storage (dominated by `location` and `audit_log`) far faster than with CPU, which is why partitioning, compression and retention (§39) are cost controls, not hygiene. |
| Scaling | Vertical → partition pruning → move `location` to its own instance → read replicas per workload → cell topology. Every step has a named trigger in §34.7.2. |
| Lock-in | Very low, provided we avoid provider-proprietary extensions. The one thing to watch is any managed variant that is Postgres-compatible rather than Postgres — those trade portability for elasticity and must be evaluated on extension support (PostGIS, TimescaleDB, `pg_trgm`) before selection. |
| Security | RLS as defence-in-depth for tenancy, `pgcrypto`/application-level envelope encryption for the small set of columns that need it, TLS enforced, no public network exposure, IAM-based access for humans with break-glass audited (§38). |
| **If this changes** | If write volume on `location` alone breaches the §34.7.2 trigger, **move that table to its own instance** (still Postgres) before considering any other engine. |

---

#### 57.3.6 Geospatial capability

**[RECOMMENDED] PostGIS in the primary instance — settled in §34.6.1.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The workload is a handful of point-in-polygon and distance tests per ping against fences already resolved from the assignment, plus "which guards are near this point" over a small `guard_last_position` table. That belongs in the transaction, next to the data. |
| Alternatives | Tile38 / Redis GEO (faster moving-object queries; adds a second source of truth for position), managed geofencing APIs (sends the most sensitive data we hold to a vendor — rejected on §39 grounds), H3/geohash-only in application code (we already use geohash for map fan-out topics; it is a complement, not a replacement). |
| Trade-offs | Geospatial queries share the OLTP instance's resources. Contained because §34.6.2 keeps evaluation in-process and out of the database entirely for the hot path. |
| Cost | Zero incremental. |
| Scaling | Does not scale with fence count (§34.6.2); scales with position-table size, which partitioning handles. |
| Lock-in | None — open source, and PostGIS is portable across every managed Postgres worth using. |
| Security | Keeping location evaluation first-party is a material privacy advantage and is one of the few architectural facts worth stating to guards directly. |
| **If this changes** | If "nearest deployable guard" over a very large live fleet becomes a p95 latency problem, **add Tile38 as a derived index** — never as the source of truth. |

---

#### 57.3.7 Cache

**[RECOMMENDED] Redis (managed, single primary + replica, AOF persistence, TLS, auth).**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Redis is already required by §33 (sliding-window rate limits, `jti` deny-list), §34 (Streams for ingest and jobs, Pub/Sub for socket fan-out) and §34.3 (10-minute dedupe sets). Adding a *second* technology for caching when the one already deployed does it well is unjustified. Its uses here: session/permission-resolution cache (short TTL, invalidated on role change), reference-data cache (plans, entitlements, jurisdiction rule sets, geofence definitions), reverse-geocode result cache (the single most valuable cache we have — it directly reduces metered map spend), dashboard aggregate cache, and distributed locks for the scheduler. |
| Alternatives | **Memcached** — simpler and slightly faster for pure key-value, but no streams, no pub/sub, no sorted sets; we would still need Redis. **In-process caching only** — free and fastest, but incoherent across instances; used *in addition*, for immutable reference data with short TTLs, never for anything permission-related. **Dragonfly/KeyDB/Valkey** — drop-in compatible with better multi-core utilisation; a legitimate substitute if the managed Redis price becomes objectionable. |
| Trade-offs | Redis is memory-bound and, in the Streams role, our least durable component. This is why §34.4 draws the line explicitly: **Redis carries delivery, Postgres carries truth**. Nothing whose loss is unacceptable exists only in Redis. Second trade-off: cache invalidation on permission change must be immediate, which is why permission caches are keyed by a `permission_version` per principal that increments on any role or scope change — an invalidation strategy, not a TTL hope. |
| Cost | Small at pilot scale (a few thousand rupees per month for a 1–4 GB managed instance). Cost grows with stream retention, which is bounded by design. |
| Scaling | Vertical, then cluster mode. The trigger to worry is memory pressure from stream backlog, which is itself an alert (a growing backlog means a consumer is down). |
| Lock-in | None; the Redis wire protocol has multiple compatible implementations. Avoid provider-proprietary Redis-adjacent features. |
| Security | Never internet-exposed; TLS in transit; ACL users per component (the `rt-gateway` gets pub/sub only, `ingest` gets stream-write only); no PII in cache values beyond what the requesting principal may already read; cache keys include `tenant_id` so a key-construction bug cannot cross tenants. |
| **If this changes** | If durability requirements rise (for example, notifications must survive a total Redis loss), **move the affected queue to Postgres-backed jobs** or to a managed broker — do not try to make Redis durable enough. |

---

#### 57.3.8 Queue and streaming

**[RECOMMENDED] Redis Streams for ingest/notifications/webhooks/jobs, plus a transactional outbox in Postgres as the durability layer — settled in §34.4; Kafka explicitly deferred with a named trigger.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Sustained message volume at pilot is under 100/second. Redis Streams give consumer groups, acknowledgement, replay within a bounded window and partitioning by key, on infrastructure already deployed. The outbox pattern means every event that *matters* is written in the same transaction as the state change that produced it, so a total queue loss costs delivery latency, not correctness. |
| Alternatives | **Kafka / Redpanda** — the right answer at 10–50× this volume or with a genuine need for long replay and many independent consumer groups; today it is a cluster, a schema-registry conversation and an on-call surface for a problem we do not have. **Managed cloud queues (SQS/Pub-Sub/Service Bus)** — operationally free and durable; adds per-message cost, cloud coupling, and awkward ordering semantics for the per-guard ordering we want. **RabbitMQ** — excellent routing, weaker replay, another cluster. **Postgres-only job queue (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`)** — genuinely good and worth keeping in mind; rejected as the *primary* path only because ping ingest at peak would put avoidable write load on the OLTP primary, which is exactly what §34.3 is designed to prevent. |
| Trade-offs | Weaker durability than a real broker; bounded replay window; memory-bound backlog. All three are accepted explicitly and all three are alerted on. |
| Cost | Zero incremental infrastructure. Engineering cost is the outbox drain and the DLQ replay screen, both of which we need under any option. |
| Scaling | Partition count is the lever. The migration trigger to Kafka is written in §34.7.2 (>2,000 events/s sustained, >7-day replay need, or >6 consumer groups) and must be observed for 7 days before acting (SUR-RT-014). |
| Lock-in | None. Consumers are written against a thin queue interface so the broker swap is an adapter, not a rewrite — this is worth the small abstraction cost precisely because the migration is anticipated. |
| Security | Same Redis ACL posture as above. Ping payloads on the stream contain location data: the stream is not readable by any component other than the signals consumer, and stream retention is bounded so location does not accumulate in a second store outside the §39 retention regime. |
| **If this changes** | If a regulator, an Enterprise contract or an incident requires provable, durable, replayable event history, **adopt Kafka/Redpanda for the affected topics only** — not for everything. |

---

#### 57.3.9 Search

**[RECOMMENDED] PostgreSQL full-text search (`tsvector`) plus `pg_trgm` fuzzy matching in V1. No dedicated search engine until a named trigger fires.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Search in this product is overwhelmingly *scoped lookup*, not discovery: find a guard by name/phone/employee code within my tenant, find a site, find an invoice, find a client, find a ticket. These are filtered, permission-scoped, small-result queries where the tenant filter already reduces the candidate set by orders of magnitude. Postgres FTS with trigram similarity handles Indian name spelling variance (the actual hard problem — "Rajesh/Rajeshh/Rajes", transliteration variants) well enough with a good similarity threshold, and it does so inside the same permission and tenant boundary as everything else, which is the property that matters most. The one genuinely discovery-shaped surface is TRINETRA's agency directory, which is public-ish, small (tens of thousands of rows) and heavily faceted — still comfortably Postgres. |
| Alternatives | **OpenSearch/Elasticsearch** — the real answer for large-scale relevance-ranked search and log analytics; costs a cluster, an index pipeline, a re-index story and, critically, a *second place where tenant data lives* that must independently enforce isolation. **Typesense / Meilisearch** — much lighter, excellent typo tolerance, genuinely attractive for the guard-name problem; still a second data store with its own sync and isolation obligations. **Managed search APIs (Algolia and similar)** — best relevance and speed per engineering hour, but sends tenant data to a third party and prices per operation, which is wrong for an internal lookup that runs constantly. |
| Trade-offs | Relevance ranking is cruder than a real engine; multi-field weighted scoring is manual; cross-entity "search everything" is a UNION over a few targeted queries rather than one index. Indexing cost is paid on write in the OLTP database. All acceptable for scoped lookup; none acceptable if search becomes a headline feature. |
| Cost | Zero incremental. A dedicated engine would add roughly ₹15–40k/month plus setup and ongoing sync engineering `[ASSUMPTION: A-602]`. |
| Scaling | Fine to millions of rows *per tenant filter*. The trigger to reconsider: any search endpoint p95 above 500 ms after index tuning, or a product requirement for cross-tenant relevance ranking (marketplace discovery at scale), or full-text search over documents/OCR text at volume — that last one is the most likely trigger and is where Typesense/Meilisearch would enter. |
| Lock-in | None. |
| Security | Decisive advantage: one store, one RLS policy, one tenant boundary. Every external search engine introduces a second isolation surface, and search indexes are a classic cross-tenant leak vector. Deferring the engine defers that risk entirely. |
| **If this changes** | If document/OCR full-text search across large tenants becomes a product requirement, **add Typesense or Meilisearch for that corpus only**, with tenant ID as a mandatory filter enforced server-side, never client-supplied. |

---

#### 57.3.10 Object storage

**[RECOMMENDED] The primary cloud's S3-compatible object storage in an Indian region, behind a first-party storage adapter, with signed short-lived URLs and lifecycle tiering (aligned with §37 and §39).**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | We store guard documents, selfies and face templates, incident photos and video, patrol evidence, invoices and payslips (PDF), report exports, OCR migration source files and desktop installers. Volume is dominated by media and grows monotonically. Object storage is the only sane home; the S3 API is the de-facto standard, and writing to it through our own adapter keeps the provider replaceable. |
| Alternatives | **Self-hosted MinIO** — full control and no egress fees; adds a storage system to operate, with durability that is now *our* problem. **Wasabi / Backblaze B2** — much cheaper for cold archive with no egress charges; fewer Indian regions and weaker IAM integration. **Storing files in Postgres** — genuinely convenient for small documents and transactional consistency; rejected because it destroys backup economics at media volume. |
| Trade-offs | Egress and request costs are the hidden line item, driven by document and image *views* in the verification queue and the client portal. Mitigated by CDN in front of frequently-read derived assets (thumbnails), never in front of originals, and by generating thumbnails at ingest so the verification queue never fetches full-resolution originals. |
| Cost | Storage is cheap; requests and egress are not. Model it per 1,000 guards: ~8–12 documents + 1 selfie + periodic incident media each, at a few MB after compression, is single-digit GB per 1,000 guards — trivially cheap. The cost driver is incident **video**, which is why §39's retention schedule for media is a cost control as much as a privacy control. |
| Scaling | Effectively unlimited. Operational scaling concerns are lifecycle policy correctness and the legal-hold exception path. |
| Lock-in | Low with an adapter and the S3 API; the real switching cost is data transfer of the accumulated corpus, which grows over time — a reason to make the archive-tier choice early rather than late. |
| Security | Buckets private by default with public access blocked at the account level; every read via a short-lived signed URL issued only after a §31 permission check; server-side encryption with customer-managed keys for the sensitive prefixes (identity documents, biometric templates); versioning and object-lock on the audit/evidence prefixes; virus scanning on upload before an object becomes readable; EXIF/GPS stripping on user-supplied images except where the geotag *is* the evidence, in which case it is retained deliberately and labelled. |
| **If this changes** | If archive volume (incident video, OCR sources) makes primary-tier storage the dominant cost, **move cold prefixes to Wasabi/B2** behind the same adapter. |

---

#### 57.3.11 Real-time transport

**[RECOMMENDED] WebSocket for consoles, push (FCM/APNs) for the Guard App, polling for client-facing live views — settled in §34.2, with the per-use-case matrix there.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Different clients have genuinely different needs and §34.2.2 assigns each the cheapest transport that meets it. The key asymmetries: operator consoles are few, long-lived and latency-critical (WebSocket); guard phones are many, backgrounded and battery-constrained (push, never a background socket — SUR-RT-005); client live views are many, casual and tolerant of a minute's staleness (polling). |
| Alternatives | SSE everywhere (simpler, one-directional, a good future move for the client live view); a managed real-time service (Pusher/Ably/managed WebSocket) — removes the gateway from our on-call at a per-connection/per-message price and puts operational alert content through a third party, which is wrong for the SOS path; MQTT — a good fit for device telemetry in principle, but a second protocol stack for a benefit our HTTP batch ingest already achieves. |
| Trade-offs | We own a stateful component (`rt-gateway`) and everything that comes with it: sticky routing, deploy-time connection drain, thundering-herd reconnects, and the fact that "the socket is connected" is not "the user is seeing the truth" — which is why §34.2.3's `seq`-gap-plus-snapshot recovery exists and why SUR-RT-007 mandates a polling fallback within 10 seconds. |
| Cost | Two small gateway instances at pilot. Managed alternatives would cost more per month and much less engineering. |
| Scaling | Sockets per instance is the ceiling; topics shard by tenant and geohash (§34.2). |
| Lock-in | None. |
| Security | Every subscription authorised at subscribe time against §31 scope, re-authorised on token refresh, terminated on revocation (SUR-RT-006). The gateway holds no data of its own, which keeps it out of the blast radius. |
| **If this changes** | If the gateway becomes an on-call burden disproportionate to its value, **move non-SOS topics to a managed real-time provider** and keep the SOS channel first-party. |

---

#### 57.3.12 API gateway

**[RECOMMENDED] No standalone gateway product in V1. Edge (CDN/WAF) handles coarse protection; the application's own middleware chain handles authentication, tenant resolution, per-tenant rate limits, idempotency and validation, per §33.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | A gateway product earns its keep when it routes to many services, terminates many protocols, or enforces policy that services cannot be trusted to enforce. We have one application, one protocol and a permission model (§31) far too tenant- and scope-aware to express in gateway configuration. Putting authorisation in a gateway would split the permission model across two systems — the single worst outcome available. Rate limiting must be per *tenant and principal* against entitlement data the gateway does not have, so it belongs in the app too. |
| Alternatives | **Kong / Tyk** — good developer-portal and plugin story; worth revisiting when the Enterprise API has real external volume. **Envoy / Traefik / NGINX** — excellent L7 proxies, and one of them is present anyway as the ingress; we use them for routing and TLS, not policy. **Cloud-managed API gateways** — attractive quota/key management, strong coupling, per-request pricing. |
| Trade-offs | Cross-cutting API policy lives in application code, so it ships on the application's release cadence rather than being changed at the edge in seconds. Accepted; the mitigation is that the limits themselves are *configuration* (per-plan entitlements, §57.4), changeable without a deploy. |
| Cost | Zero. |
| Scaling | Scales with the app. The one thing to keep at the edge is protection that must work when the app is overloaded: connection limits, body-size caps, IP reputation, WAF rules. |
| Lock-in | None. |
| Security | Fewer places to enforce authorisation is more secure, not less, provided the middleware chain is mandatory-by-construction — the framework must make it impossible to register a route that skips the auth/tenant/audit interceptors, and a CI check must fail the build if a route lacks an explicit permission declaration (see §57.4.3). |
| **If this changes** | If the Enterprise API grows past ~10 active integrators needing self-service keys, quotas and a developer portal, **adopt Kong (or the cloud equivalent) for `/enterprise` only** — never in front of `/api/v1`. |

---

#### 57.3.13 Identity and authentication — build vs buy

**[RECOMMENDED] Build the identity service in-house (canon §4 already fixes the *behaviour*: one central identity, phone-OTP-first, email/password, Google, Apple, mandatory phone verification, MFA, 30-day client sessions, shorter privileged sessions), using vetted libraries for every cryptographic primitive and a third-party OTP/SMS aggregator for delivery only.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The requirement is not "log a user in". It is: one identity spanning four audience families and five properties; a person who may simultaneously be a guard in one tenant and a client contact in another; device binding with approval-gated device change for guards; role assignment scoped to tenant → branch → site; impersonation with consent and audit; guard offboarding that revokes across app, portal and device; and permission evaluation against a matrix of the depth in §31. Every hosted IdP models the first 30% of that well and the rest via custom claims, hooks and workarounds — and the parts they do not model (scope resolution, entitlement gating, device binding, tenant-crossing identity) are exactly the parts that are load-bearing here. The authentication primitives themselves — Argon2id, TOTP, JWT/JOSE, WebAuthn — are library calls, not research. |
| Alternatives | **Auth0/Okta** — fastest to a working login, excellent enterprise SSO, strong security posture; expensive at hundreds of thousands of MAU (guards are MAU), and pricing scales exactly with the population we least monetise. **AWS Cognito** — cheap at scale, but a rigid model, awkward custom flows, and painful migration out. **Keycloak (self-hosted)** — full-featured, free, standards-compliant; a substantial Java service to operate, patch and scale, and its data model still needs a shadow user table on our side. **Ory (Kratos/Hydra)** — clean, API-first, self-hostable; several services to run and a young operational story for a five-person team. **Supabase Auth / Firebase Auth** — very fast for phone OTP; ties identity to a platform we are not otherwise using. |
| Trade-offs | We own authentication security forever: password hashing parameters, OTP brute-force resistance, enumeration resistance, session fixation, token rotation, revocation gaps, MFA recovery. §38 already specifies these controls (SUR-SEC-012 to 034), so the design work is done — but the *vigilance* is a permanent obligation, and a mistake here is a company-ending class of bug. This is the single biggest "we chose the harder path" decision in the document and it should be revisited if the team cannot staff security review properly. Mitigations: use audited libraries only, never hand-roll crypto, put the auth module under mandatory two-reviewer rules, include auth in every pentest scope, and buy enterprise SSO rather than build it (below). |
| Cost | Build cost is roughly 6–9 engineer-weeks for the core plus ongoing maintenance. Buy cost at 100,000 monthly-active guards would be substantial and recurring, and rises exactly as the guard population grows — the wrong cost curve for a workforce platform. Note the asymmetry: the *delivery* cost (SMS OTP) is unavoidable either way and is the dominant per-login cost in India regardless of IdP choice. |
| Scaling | Stateless verification (JWT + Redis deny-list, §33.2) scales horizontally. The scaling risk is OTP delivery cost and deliverability, not compute — which is a provider problem (§57.3.18), and a reason to make WhatsApp OTP and (later) passkeys real cost-reduction projects. |
| Lock-in | Building avoids IdP lock-in entirely, which matters because migrating an identity provider with hundreds of thousands of users and no password material to export is one of the worst migrations in software. |
| Security | Higher risk if built carelessly, lower attack surface if built carefully. Standards followed exactly: OAuth 2.1/OIDC shapes for third-party sign-in, JOSE for tokens, Argon2id with pepper, TOTP with drift window, WebAuthn-ready. **Explicit carve-out: enterprise SSO (SAML/SCIM) for large agencies and enterprise clients is [FUTURE] and should be *bought*** — a SAML implementation is a specialised, high-risk build with no strategic value to us, and a hosted broker for that one flow is the right trade. |
| **If this changes** | If a security review finds the team cannot sustainably own authentication, **move to Keycloak self-hosted** (keeps data residency, avoids per-MAU pricing) with our permission/scope layer remaining first-party on top of it. |

---

#### 57.3.14 AI model strategy

**[RECOMMENDED] A provider-abstracted, multi-model strategy: hosted frontier APIs for reasoning and generation, hosted Indian-language specialists for ASR/TTS/translation, and a small self-hosted model only where privacy or unit cost forces it. All calls pass through the orchestrator's permission pre-check and action-class gate (§25, §41).**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The AI requirement (canon §1.7) is voice + text in Hindi, English and at least 19 Indian languages, strictly role- and permission-aware, across four action classes. Two distinct capability needs follow. (1) **Reasoning/generation** — summarising an incident, drafting a roster suggestion, explaining a payroll variance, answering "which sites are short-staffed tonight". Frontier hosted models are far ahead of anything self-hostable for instruction-following and structured output, and the volume at pilot is low enough that hosted inference is dramatically cheaper than a GPU. (2) **Speech and Indian languages** — this is where the interesting choice sits. General-purpose ASR degrades badly on Indian-accented, code-mixed, noisy field audio from a low-end phone microphone. India-specialised providers (Bhashini/AI4Bharat-derived stacks, Sarvam and comparable vendors) are materially better on exactly our audio and cover the long tail of languages that global providers do not. A single vendor will not be best at everything, so the orchestrator routes per capability. |
| Alternatives | **Self-host open-weight models** (Llama/Mistral class for text, Whisper-derivatives for ASR) — no per-token cost, full data control, no third-party processing of tenant data; costs a GPU fleet (a single always-on inference GPU in an Indian region is a meaningful monthly line item), an MLOps capability we do not have, and lower quality on multilingual instruction-following. Justified later at high, steady volume, and justified *earlier* for any workload where data must not leave our infrastructure. **Single-vendor** — simplest contracts and one SDK; unacceptable concentration risk for a capability embedded in the product, and no single vendor leads on both frontier reasoning and Indian-language ASR. **No AI in V1** — a legitimate scope cut, but canon §1.4 sells "basic AI" in the Starter plan, so it is contractual. |
| Trade-offs | Hosted APIs mean tenant text and audio leave our infrastructure. This is the trade-off, and §39/§41 constrain it: zero-retention/no-training contractual terms are a hard procurement requirement; PII is minimised and redacted before the call where the task allows; guard location is never sent; the context assembler retrieves only what the *requesting principal* may already read, so the model can never become a permission-bypass; every interaction is logged with model, version, prompt hash, cost and outcome. Second trade-off: model behaviour drifts between versions, so prompts are versioned, pinned to model versions, and regression-tested against a golden set before any model upgrade. |
| Cost | Per-interaction, small and directly attributable; the risk is not unit cost but *unbounded* cost. Controls: per-tenant AI quotas tied to plan entitlement (Starter = basic AI, canon §1.4), model tiering (a cheap small model for classification/extraction, a frontier model only for genuine reasoning), aggressive caching of deterministic outputs, streaming to reduce abandoned-generation waste, and a hard monthly circuit breaker per tenant. Voice is the expensive modality: ASR per audio-minute at guard-population scale can exceed text cost by an order of magnitude, so voice is capability-gated by plan and by role, and long recordings are transcribed once and reused. |
| Scaling | Hosted APIs scale by contract; the constraint is provider rate limits and regional availability. Self-hosting becomes economic when a single high-volume workload (most likely ASR, or OCR-adjacent extraction) is steady enough to keep a GPU busy — that is the trigger, not a philosophical preference. |
| Lock-in | Contained by a provider adapter with a capability interface (`generate`, `classify`, `extract`, `transcribe`, `translate`, `speak`) rather than a vendor SDK sprayed through the codebase. Prompts, evaluation sets and the guardrail layer are ours and portable; switching a provider should be days, not months. Real residual lock-in is prompt tuning per model family — mitigated by keeping the golden-set evaluation harness (§41) so a swap is measurable. |
| Security | AI is the newest and least-understood attack surface here. Mandatory: prompt-injection defences on any content-derived input (documents, OCR text, client messages are untrusted input, never instructions); the **permission pre-check happens before retrieval, not after generation** (§57.4.8); action-class enforcement in code, not in the prompt; no tool the model can call has more authority than the calling user; and the canon §1.7 prohibitions are enforced as code paths that simply do not exist for the model, rather than as instructions it is asked to obey. |
| **If this changes** | If a client contract or a regulator requires that no tenant content leaves our infrastructure, **self-host an open-weight model for that tenant's workloads** and degrade the feature set accordingly — the capability interface already allows a per-tenant routing policy. |

---

#### 57.3.15 OCR and document extraction

**[RECOMMENDED] A hosted document-AI service as primary (per §37: Google Document AI or AWS Textract, with Azure Document Intelligence as an alternative), plus self-hosted PaddleOCR/Tesseract as a fallback for bulk and for documents that must not leave our infrastructure. Run a bake-off against Indian-document specialists before committing.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Two very different OCR jobs exist here. (a) **Identity and compliance documents** at guard enrolment — Aadhaar-shaped IDs, PAN, licences, certificates, police-verification letters: photographed at an angle, in bad light, often laminated and glare-affected. Accuracy directly determines verification-queue workload, so a few points of extraction accuracy is worth real money in staffing. (b) **Legacy data migration** for Enterprise onboarding (canon §1.4) — decades of registers, muster rolls and spreadsheets-printed-to-PDF, high volume, one-off per tenant, tolerant of a human review pass. Hosted document AI wins clearly on (a); self-hosted is competitive on (b) where volume is bursty and cost matters more than the last few points of accuracy. |
| Alternatives | Pure self-hosted (PaddleOCR is genuinely strong on Indic scripts; Tesseract is weaker) — cheapest, no data egress, needs tuning and a GPU for reasonable throughput. Indian identity-document specialists (IDfy, Signzy and similar) — often materially better on exactly our document types and may bundle verification workflows; less general, per-document pricing. Manual data entry — the honest baseline, and the fallback that must always exist. |
| Trade-offs | Sending identity documents to a third-party processor is a privacy decision, not just a technical one: it needs a processor agreement, a documented purpose, retention limits at the processor, and disclosure in the privacy notice (§39). Data-minimisation applies — §20 already rules that Aadhaar-type numbers are stored masked with only the verification outcome retained (D-167); the same rule applies to what we send: crop to the needed region where possible, and never retain the full-resolution original at the processor. |
| Cost | Per-page pricing, concentrated at enrolment and at Enterprise migration. Controls: OCR only on document types where extraction saves real time; never re-OCR on re-upload if a hash matches; batch migration through the cheaper self-hosted path with sampled human QA. |
| Scaling | Bursty by nature (a 500-guard agency onboarding in a week). Queue-isolated in `worker-heavy` so a migration cannot starve interactive work; per-tenant concurrency caps. |
| Lock-in | Low behind an extraction adapter that returns a normalised field set with per-field confidence. The valuable, portable asset is our **field-mapping and confidence-threshold configuration**, plus the human-correction dataset — which we should retain deliberately, as it is what makes a future self-hosted model viable. |
| Security | Documents are among the most sensitive objects we hold. Requirements: processor agreement with no-training and short-retention terms; transport over TLS to a regional endpoint; no document ever public-URL-accessible; extraction results treated as *untrusted input* to the AI layer (an OCR'd document is a prompt-injection vector); and a per-tenant configuration flag that forces the self-hosted path for tenants who contractually require it. |
| **If this changes** | If per-document cost or a residency requirement dominates, **move enrolment OCR to self-hosted PaddleOCR** and absorb the accuracy loss as verification-queue workload — a decision that should be made on a measured accuracy-versus-staffing-cost comparison, not on principle. |

---

#### 57.3.16 Maps and geocoding

**[RECOMMENDED] A first-party map abstraction layer with one provider behind it, starting with Google Maps Platform for coverage, and aggressive caching of reverse-geocoding results — per §34.6.3 and §37, with the provider decision itself pending a coverage bake-off (D-247).**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The product needs street-level India coverage including small roads, industrial estates and tier-2/3 addresses; address autocomplete during site setup; polygon drawing for geofences; marker clustering for 200–500 markers on the console; and reverse geocoding for display. Coverage quality in exactly the places our sites are — industrial areas and outer suburbs — is the deciding factor, and it is a factual question answered by a test, not by a preference. |
| Alternatives | Mappls/MapMyIndia (strongest Indian addressing, domestic vendor, a genuine data-residency and cost advantage; less familiar tooling), Mapbox (good vector rendering economics and styling, patchier Indian small-road data), self-hosted OSM tiles + Nominatim/Photon (no per-view cost, full control, real operational work and weaker address quality). |
| Trade-offs | Provider APIs price per load and per call, so cost scales with *console usage* — a cost that grows with our own operational headcount, not with revenue. Hence the §34.6.3 disciplines: cache reverse-geocodes permanently keyed by rounded coordinates, never reverse-geocode on ingest, pause map refresh on hidden tabs, cluster markers, and never re-initialise a map on tab switch. |
| Cost | Potentially the second-largest third-party line item after SMS if left uncontrolled; near-negligible if the caching rules above are enforced. Set a monthly budget alert per API key from day one. |
| Scaling | Scales with console sessions and site-setup activity, not with guard count — a favourable curve, provided ping-time geocoding stays prohibited. |
| Lock-in | Contained by the abstraction layer: switching is a frontend adapter plus a geocode-cache refill, measured in weeks. Do not use provider-proprietary geofencing, distance-matrix or place-ID semantics in stored data — store coordinates and address components, never opaque provider IDs, or the abstraction is a fiction. |
| Security | Geofence evaluation is first-party (§34.6.1), so guard positions are never sent to the map provider — only the operator's viewport and occasional geocode lookups. API keys are referrer/IP-restricted and separated per property so a leaked marketing-site key cannot be used against the operational quota. |
| **If this changes** | If the D-247 coverage test shows Mappls is equal or better on our real sites, **switch to Mappls** — a domestic vendor with better Indian addressing and lower cost is strictly preferable at equal coverage. |

---

#### 57.3.17 Payment gateway

**[RECOMMENDED] Razorpay for all inbound client payments and SaaS subscription billing (canon §4, fixed), behind a payments adapter; the *payout* rail remains open (D-243) and must be chosen before payroll disbursement is built.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Settled by the canon. It is also the right call on merits for an India-first product: UPI, cards, netbanking, subscriptions/mandates (e-mandate/UPI AutoPay for the ₹5,000/₹10,000 SaaS plans), an invoicing API, good documentation and predictable settlement. §35 already specifies the ledger, GST invoice and reconciliation behaviour around it. |
| Alternatives | Cashfree, PayU, CCAvenue, Stripe India (weaker local coverage), or direct bank integration. Retained as *contingency*, not as a parallel integration — a second live gateway doubles reconciliation complexity for a failure mode that has never yet cost us a day. |
| Trade-offs | Single-gateway dependency: an outage stops inbound collection. Accepted because collection is not life-safety and the mitigation (manual bank transfer with a reference, reconciled later) already exists in §35. MDR is a cost of doing business; UPI-first routing keeps it low. |
| Cost | Percentage MDR on transaction value, plus subscription/mandate fees. Material at B2C volumes (₹18,500–₹38,000 per contract per month) — so payment-method routing (UPI over card where the customer is indifferent) is a real margin lever and should be measured. |
| Scaling | Provider-scaled. Our scaling concerns are webhook idempotency, reconciliation at volume and settlement-file ingestion — all specified in §35. |
| Lock-in | Moderate: stored mandates/tokens are the sticky part, since migrating recurring mandates to another gateway is genuinely hard and customer-visible. The adapter keeps *code* portable; it cannot make mandates portable. Record this honestly rather than pretending otherwise. |
| Security | We never touch raw card data — hosted checkout/tokenisation only, keeping PCI scope at SAQ-A. Webhooks are signature-verified and idempotent; refunds require an approval (§30/§35) and can never be initiated by AI (canon §1.7). |
| **If this changes** | If MDR at scale or a mandate-success-rate problem becomes material, **add a second gateway for a specific method only** (for example a UPI-optimised provider) rather than migrating wholesale. |

---

#### 57.3.18 Notification providers

**[RECOMMENDED] Multi-provider by channel, exactly as §36 specifies: FCM + APNs for push; two SMS aggregators (one high-tooling, one cost-optimised) with DLT-registered templates and priority routing; one WhatsApp BSP; Zoho for email (canon §4) with proper domain authentication; all behind one notification service with per-channel failover.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Notification is on the critical path for the T0 SOS flow and for the entire wake-check mechanic, so single-provider dependency is unacceptable there. India adds a hard constraint that has no equivalent elsewhere: **transactional SMS requires DLT-registered headers and pre-approved templates**, so template approval lead time is a launch-blocking dependency and must be started weeks before go-live (§58). WhatsApp adds its own template-approval regime and category rules. |
| Alternatives | Single aggregator (cheaper, simpler, unacceptable concentration risk on the SOS path); Twilio-only (best tooling and reliability, highest cost, and Indian DLT compliance still applies); direct operator connections (best price at very high volume, worst operational overhead). |
| Trade-offs | Two SMS providers means two DLT registrations, two template sets kept in sync, two sets of delivery-report semantics to normalise, and a routing policy to maintain. This is real work and it is justified only because SMS is the fallback that carries life-safety messages when push fails. |
| Cost | SMS is the largest per-message cost and OTP is the largest volume driver — which makes OTP delivery the single most expensive recurring per-user cost in the product. Levers: WhatsApp OTP where permitted (materially cheaper), SMS Retriever API to reduce re-sends, rate limits to stop abuse, and eventually passkeys/device-bound sessions to remove routine OTPs entirely for returning guards. |
| Scaling | Provider-scaled; our concern is per-provider throughput caps, per-template throttles and the fan-out cost of a mass event (a city-wide alert to 5,000 guards must be rate-shaped, not fired at once). |
| Lock-in | Low per provider; the sticky asset is the DLT template registry and approved WhatsApp templates, which are per-provider artefacts and take weeks to re-approve. Keep the canonical template content in our own store with provider-specific IDs mapped alongside (§36) so a re-approval is a data migration, not a content rewrite. |
| Security | Message content follows §39 minimisation — no sensitive detail in an SMS or push payload beyond what is needed to act ("SOS at Site X, tap to open"), never salary figures, never document numbers, never precise location in a message body. Webhooks from providers are signature-verified. Provider credentials are scoped and rotated (§38). |
| **If this changes** | If WhatsApp template categories are rejected for our operational use cases (A-271), **the affected notifications fall back permanently to SMS/push** and the cost model must be re-run — this is a commercial risk, not a technical one. |

---

#### 57.3.19 Analytics stack

**[RECOMMENDED] Three separated concerns, per §42.5 and §37: (a) in-product/business analytics computed from Postgres read models and served in-product; (b) product-behaviour analytics via PostHog (self-hosted or EU/India-region hosted); (c) error and crash reporting via Sentry. Marketing/web analytics on a consent-gated tool, kept entirely separate from product data.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The numbers that appear on a customer's or agency's dashboard are *product*, not analytics: they must be permission-scoped, auditable, definition-versioned (SUR-ANL-001..004) and computed from the same truth as invoices. They belong in Postgres read models, not in an analytics vendor. Separately, we need behavioural product analytics (funnels, activation, feature adoption) that no OLTP query answers well — that is PostHog's job, on events defined in §42.4. Keeping the two apart prevents the classic failure where a vendor's number contradicts the invoice. |
| Alternatives | Mixpanel/Amplitude (better polish, data leaves the country, per-event pricing at guard-population scale is unattractive); GA4 for product (wrong tool, consent-encumbered, sampling); building product analytics ourselves (a distraction); a warehouse + BI stack (ClickHouse/BigQuery + Metabase) from day one — the right Year-2 answer, with triggers already defined in §32.6.5. |
| Trade-offs | Self-hosting PostHog is a real operational commitment (it is a heavy application). If we cannot staff that, a regional hosted plan is acceptable, and the enterprise-sales argument for self-hosting ("no behavioural data leaves our infrastructure") is worth weighing against the ops burden explicitly. Second trade-off: two systems means two definitions of "active user" unless the metric registry (§42.1) governs both — it must. |
| Cost | PostHog self-hosted is infrastructure cost only; hosted is per-event and grows with guard app usage, which is high-volume and low-value per event — so client-side event volume must be curated, not fire-hosed. Sentry has a generous free/low tier; error volume, not user count, drives cost. |
| Scaling | Event volume from the Guard App is the dominant term. Mitigation: sample high-frequency low-value events, batch on-device, and never send an analytics event on a code path that also produces an audit or domain event (the audit trail is the record; analytics is the sample). |
| Lock-in | Low: events are defined in our own taxonomy (§42.4) and sent through our SDK wrapper, so redirecting them to another sink is a configuration change. |
| Security | Behavioural events carry no PII beyond a pseudonymous ID plus tenant and role; no guard names, no coordinates, no document numbers. Marketing analytics runs only after consent and never on authenticated product surfaces. Sentry must have PII scrubbing and source-map upload restricted to CI. |
| **If this changes** | If self-hosting PostHog costs more operational attention than it returns, **move to a regional hosted plan** and document the data-flow change in the §39 processing register. |

---

#### 57.3.20 CI/CD

**[RECOMMENDED] GitHub Actions as the CI/CD engine, trunk-based development with short-lived branches, containerised builds, and progressive delivery (canary for `api`, staged rollout for mobile). §47 owns the pipeline detail; this is the tooling selection.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The code already lives where the team collaborates; a separate CI system is a second permission model and a second secret store. Actions covers everything we need: matrix builds for three desktop OSes, Android and iOS runners for the mobile apps, OIDC federation to the cloud so no long-lived cloud credentials sit in CI, environment protection rules for production approvals, and a marketplace of maintained actions for signing and notarisation. |
| Alternatives | GitLab CI (excellent, integrated, better self-hosted story — correct if the repo moves to GitLab); Jenkins (maximum control, maximum maintenance); CircleCI/Buildkite (good runners, another vendor); ArgoCD/Flux for GitOps deployment — worth adopting *if and when* Kubernetes is adopted, not before. |
| Trade-offs | macOS runners for desktop/iOS builds are the expensive minutes; mitigated by building those only on release branches and tags, not on every push. Actions' YAML becomes unwieldy at scale — mitigated by composite actions and reusable workflows, kept under the same review discipline as application code. |
| Cost | Low: mostly free minutes for Linux, with macOS minutes as the main charge. Self-hosted runners are an option if minutes become material. |
| Scaling | Scales with team size and build frequency. The real scaling issue is *test* time; §43/§44 own the test pyramid, and the pipeline must keep the pre-merge suite under ~10 minutes or engineers will route around it. |
| Lock-in | Moderate but shallow — workflow YAML is portable in shape if not in syntax, and everything meaningful (Dockerfiles, migration commands, deployment scripts) is provider-neutral by construction. |
| Security | Signing keys, notarisation credentials and store credentials are the crown jewels in CI: they live in environment-scoped secrets with required reviewers, never in repository-level secrets. Third-party actions are pinned to commit SHAs, not tags. SBOM generation, dependency scanning, secret scanning, container scanning and IaC scanning all run in-pipeline and block on high severity (§38). Production deploys require an approval from a role that did not author the change. |
| **If this changes** | If the codebase moves to a self-hosted VCS for compliance reasons, **switch to GitLab CI** — the pipeline stages translate directly. |

---

#### 57.3.21 Hosting, cloud provider and region

**[RECOMMENDED] One primary cloud provider with an Indian region as the default (AWS `ap-south-1` Mumbai as the working assumption, with `ap-south-2` Hyderabad as the secondary), running containers on a managed container service — not Kubernetes — in V1.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | Three requirements drive this. (1) **Data residency**: guard identity documents, biometric templates and location history are the most sensitive data in the system, and an Indian region is both the defensible privacy posture (§39) and the answer an enterprise or government-adjacent buyer expects. (2) **Latency**: every user is in India. (3) **Managed everything**: a five-person engineering team should operate zero databases, zero brokers and zero clusters by hand. AWS is the working assumption because its Indian regions are mature, managed Postgres with PostGIS is well understood there, and the operational documentation and hiring pool are the deepest. The compute choice — a managed container runtime such as ECS/Fargate or an equivalent app platform — is deliberate: **Kubernetes is not justified for eight container types and one team**, and adopting it early costs a full-time person's attention indefinitely. |
| Alternatives | **GCP** (`asia-south1` Mumbai) — arguably better managed Postgres ergonomics and a stronger AI/document-AI story; slightly thinner Indian enterprise familiarity. **Azure** (Central/South India) — the right answer if a large enterprise or government-adjacent buyer standardises on it, and the strongest compliance-certification story for Indian public-sector-adjacent work. **Indian sovereign providers (E2E, ESDS, CtrlS, Jio Cloud)** — a genuine data-sovereignty and cost advantage and a real selling point for some buyers; thinner managed-service catalogues, which means more of §57.2's components become our own to operate. **Multi-cloud from day one** — rejected outright: it doubles the operational surface to hedge a risk that has not materialised. |
| Trade-offs | Single-provider dependency, and managed services are the sticky part. We accept it and contain it: every managed service we use has an open-source equivalent (Postgres, Redis, S3 API, containers), so the exit is a migration project rather than a rewrite. We also accept that a managed container runtime is less flexible than Kubernetes — deliberately, because that inflexibility is what keeps the operational surface small. |
| Cost | Pilot-scale monthly infrastructure is dominated by (1) the Postgres instance and its storage, (2) egress and object storage, (3) observability ingest. Reserved/committed-use pricing is worth taking once traffic is predictable — but not before, since committing early to the wrong instance shape is a classic waste. Cost per guard per month is the unit metric to track (§59.12), and it should fall as the base grows. |
| Scaling | Vertical first, horizontal for stateless tiers, then the §34.7.2 progression. Multi-AZ from day one for the database (this is not optional); multi-region is a DR decision owned by §49 and triggered by contract, not ambition. |
| Lock-in | Real but bounded, and the biggest single lock-in in this document. Mitigations that must actually be followed: no proprietary serverless-function framework as an architectural dependency; no vendor-specific database dialect; no vendor-only queue semantics; containers everywhere so the compute layer is portable; IaC that describes the system rather than clicking it into existence. |
| Security | Cloud-native controls we depend on: IAM with least privilege and no long-lived keys (OIDC federation from CI), KMS for envelope encryption, private subnets with no public database exposure, security groups as the default deny, VPC flow logs, GuardDuty-class threat detection, and CloudTrail-class API audit retained per §38. Region choice is itself a security control: data residency reduces both legal and reputational exposure. |
| **If this changes** | If a major buyer requires a specific cloud or a sovereign Indian provider, **the container-plus-managed-Postgres shape ports**; budget a migration of roughly 6–10 weeks, dominated by data transfer and IaC rewrite, not by application changes. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-601]` — the provider must be fixed before any IaC is written, because the cost of deciding late is the cost of writing it twice. |

---

#### 57.3.22 Infrastructure as code

**[RECOMMENDED] Terraform (or OpenTofu) for all cloud infrastructure, with remote state, per-environment workspaces and mandatory plan review in CI. No manual console changes in any environment, including the first one.**

| Lens | Position |
|---|---|
| Why | The system has three environments (dev, staging, production) plus ephemeral preview environments, and a DR obligation (§49) that is meaningless unless the infrastructure can be recreated from source. Terraform is the default for a reason: the largest provider ecosystem, the largest hiring pool, and a plan/apply model that makes change review possible. OpenTofu is a drop-in fork worth adopting if licence terms matter. |
| Alternatives | **Pulumi** — real languages, better abstractions, excellent for teams that dislike HCL; smaller ecosystem and a state service to consider. **AWS CDK / cloud-native IaC** — good ergonomics, maximal provider coupling. **Ansible** — configuration management, not infrastructure provisioning; complementary at most. **ClickOps** — how most startups actually begin, and the reason their DR plan is fiction. |
| Trade-offs | Terraform slows the first two weeks and repays it every week after. State management requires discipline: remote state with locking, no shared state across environments, and a documented recovery procedure for a corrupted state file. Drift is the standing risk — mitigated by a scheduled `plan` that alerts on any difference between code and reality. |
| Cost | Engineering time only. Roughly 2–3 weeks of initial investment for the full topology, then marginal. |
| Scaling | Scales well if modules are written per concern (network, data, compute, observability) and composed per environment. |
| Lock-in | Terraform itself: low. The *provider modules* are cloud-specific, so a cloud migration rewrites the IaC — which is the honest cost noted in §57.3.21. |
| Security | IaC is where security posture becomes reviewable: security groups, IAM policies, encryption settings and public-access blocks are all code, all diffed, all reviewed. `tfsec`/`checkov`-class scanning runs in CI and blocks on high severity. Terraform state contains secrets and is treated as a secret store: encrypted, access-controlled, never in the repository. |
| **If this changes** | If the team is materially more productive in TypeScript than HCL and the ecosystem gap closes, **Pulumi is an acceptable substitute** — the requirement is "all infrastructure in reviewed source", not a specific tool. |
