#### 57.3.23 Summary of recommendations

| Area | [RECOMMENDED] | If this constraint changes, pick instead |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | TypeScript / Node LTS / NestJS, modular monolith | Ingest volume or CPU-bound cost → extract that path to **Go**; Java-heavy hiring → **Spring Boot** |
| Frontend | React + TS; Next.js for public, Vite SPA for consoles | Bundle size on low-end devices for `guards.` → **SvelteKit / server-rendered HTML** for that property |
| Mobile — Guard App | **Native Android (Kotlin + Compose)**; iOS deferred | RN prototype meets the battery + OEM-kill + SOS cold-start bar → **React Native**, one mobile team |
| Mobile — Customer/Agency/Admin | React Native | Team is Dart-strong or RN performance disappoints → **Flutter** |
| Desktop | **Tauri v2** wrapping the AP web bundle | Linux WebKitGTK defects or a fleet-standard runtime requirement → **Electron** |
| Primary database | PostgreSQL 16 managed, primary + replica | `location` write volume breaches §34.7.2 → **separate Postgres instance for ingest** |
| Geospatial | PostGIS in-instance | Nearest-guard latency at large fleet → add **Tile38 as a derived index** |
| Cache | Redis managed | Durability required for a queue → **Postgres-backed jobs** for that queue |
| Queue/stream | Redis Streams + Postgres outbox | §34.7.2 triggers or durable replay requirement → **Kafka/Redpanda for those topics** |
| Search | Postgres FTS + `pg_trgm` | Document/OCR full-text at volume → **Typesense/Meilisearch** for that corpus |
| Object storage | Cloud S3-compatible, Indian region, adapter | Archive cost dominates → **Wasabi/B2** for cold prefixes |
| Real-time transport | WS (console) / push (guard) / poll (client) | Gateway on-call burden → **managed real-time provider** for non-SOS topics |
| API gateway | None; edge + app middleware | >10 Enterprise integrators needing a portal → **Kong for `/enterprise` only** |
| Identity | **Build**, with bought SSO later | Team cannot own auth security → **Keycloak self-hosted** under our permission layer |
| AI models | Multi-provider hosted, capability-routed, abstracted | Contractual no-egress requirement → **self-hosted open-weight** per tenant |
| OCR | Hosted document AI + self-hosted fallback | Cost or residency dominates → **PaddleOCR self-hosted**, absorb accuracy loss in the queue |
| Maps | Abstraction + Google to start (D-247) | Coverage test parity → **Mappls** (domestic, cheaper, better addressing) |
| Payments | Razorpay (canon) + adapter | MDR or mandate success rate → **add a second gateway per method** |
| Notifications | FCM/APNs + 2 SMS aggregators + 1 WhatsApp BSP + Zoho | WhatsApp categories rejected (A-271) → **SMS/push permanently**, re-run cost model |
| Analytics | Postgres read models + PostHog + Sentry | PostHog ops burden → **regional hosted plan**; Year-2 → **warehouse per §32.6.5** |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions, trunk-based, progressive delivery | VCS moves for compliance → **GitLab CI** |
| Hosting | One cloud, Indian region, managed containers (not K8s) | Buyer mandates a cloud/sovereign provider → **port the container + managed-Postgres shape** (6–10 weeks) |
| IaC | Terraform/OpenTofu, remote state, CI plan review | Team productivity in TS → **Pulumi** |

### 57.4 Cross-cutting mechanisms — built once, used everywhere

Eight mechanisms must have exactly one implementation. Every one of them, implemented twice, becomes a security incident or an audit failure eventually. They are listed here with their single home, their enforcement point, and the CI rule that prevents a second implementation appearing.

| # | Mechanism | Single implementation | Enforcement point | Guard against drift |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Identity | Identity module (L4) | Middleware: token → principal | No route may read a token directly; lint rule bans raw JWT decoding outside the module |
| 2 | Tenancy | `tenant_id` on every tenant row + RLS + a request-scoped tenant context | Repository layer sets the session tenant; RLS is the backstop | Migration CI fails if a new table lacks `tenant_id` or an explicit exemption |
| 3 | Permissions | One `can(principal, action, resource)` evaluator over the §31 matrix | Route decorator + service-layer re-check | Build fails on any route without a declared permission; a test enumerates every route against the matrix |
| 4 | Audit | One `audit.record()` writing append-only entries | Interceptor on all mutating routes + explicit calls for domain events | Test asserts every mutating endpoint produces an audit row |
| 5 | Feature flags | One flag service with tenant/role/percentage targeting | Evaluated server-side; client receives resolved flags | Flags registered in code with an owner and an expiry date; stale-flag report weekly |
| 6 | Entitlements | One entitlement resolver over plan → features → limits | Checked before the permission check on gated capability | Plan matrix is data (canon §1.4), never `if plan == 'starter'` in a module |
| 7 | Notifications | One notification service: event → template → channel policy → provider (§36) | Domain modules emit events; they never call a provider | Lint rule bans provider SDK imports outside the notification module |
| 8 | AI permission-checking | Permission pre-check **before** retrieval; action-class gate before execution (§41) | AI orchestrator; tools inherit the caller's principal | No AI tool may accept a `tenant_id` parameter — it is always taken from the principal |

#### 57.4.1 Identity

One identity per human being, not per role or per product. A person is one `account`; their relationships are `membership` rows binding the account to a tenant, a role and a scope. This is what allows the real case: a person who is a guard employed by Agency A, a supervisor at Agency B's site under a mutual-aid arrangement, and separately a residential customer with a home guard contract. Sessions carry the account; **scope is chosen per session context**, and switching context is an explicit, audited act, never an inference.

Tokens follow §33.2: short-lived access token carrying `account_id`, `session_id`, `permission_version` and the active context (`tenant_id`, `branch_id` where applicable); refresh tokens rotate in a family; revocation is a `jti` deny-list in Redis with a TTL equal to the access-token lifetime. `permission_version` is the mechanism that makes permission changes take effect within seconds without making every request hit the database: when a role or scope changes, the account's version increments, and any token carrying an older version is forced to re-resolve.

#### 57.4.2 Tenancy

Three layers, in order of strength:

1. **Application context** — every request resolves exactly one active tenant; the repository layer refuses any query without a tenant context except in an explicitly marked cross-tenant path (marketplace search, Suraksha OPS oversight, platform analytics), each of which is enumerated, permission-gated and audited.
2. **Row-level security** — Postgres RLS policies keyed on a session variable set per connection checkout. This is the backstop that catches the query someone wrote by hand.
3. **Test enforcement** — the tenant-isolation suite (§44) runs a matrix of "principal from tenant A attempts every read and write against a resource in tenant B" and must be 100% green to ship. This is a launch blocker in §58 and a release blocker forever after.

Branch (`branch_id`) is a scoping axis inside a tenant, never a substitute for it (canon §3). Suraksha's own guarding operation is tenant `SURAKSHA-HQ` and gets no special-case code path — it is a tenant like any other, which is the only way the multi-tenant paths stay honest.

#### 57.4.3 Permissions

One evaluator, one matrix (§31). Signature: `can(principal, action, resource) → Allow | Deny(reason)`. Inputs are the principal's roles within the active tenant, the scope of each role (tenant / branch / site set), the resource's own tenant and scope, the entitlement state of the tenant's plan, and any temporal condition (for example, a supervisor's access to a site limited to their assignment window).

Two rules make it reliable. First, **declare-or-fail**: every route declares its required permission in a decorator; the application refuses to start if any route lacks one. Second, **check twice, deny once**: the route-level check is a fast rejection, and the service layer re-checks against the *loaded* resource, because the route can only check what the URL claims. Client-side hiding is presentation, never authorisation.

#### 57.4.4 Audit

One append-only trail (canon §4). Every entry: who (account, role, active tenant, impersonation chain if any), what (action, entity type, entity ID), when (`server_received_time`, plus `device_time` where the event is field-originated), where (IP, user agent, device ID, app version), why (correlation to the request ID, and a reason string where the action requires one), and the before/after diff for mutations, with sensitive fields redacted to a change-marker rather than a value.

Audit is written in the same transaction as the change it records. If the audit write fails, the change fails — this is deliberate and it is the reason audit cannot be a queue. The trail is separately readable by the Auditor role with no ability to write, and retained per §39/§40.

#### 57.4.5 Feature flags

One flag service, evaluated server-side, with targeting on tenant, plan, role, percentage and explicit allow-lists. Flags exist for three legitimate purposes: progressive rollout of a risky change, per-tenant pilots (an Enterprise tenant trialling a workflow), and kill-switches for a degrading dependency. They are not a permission system and not an entitlement system — a CI check fails any flag whose name matches a plan name, because that is entitlement wearing a costume.

Every flag is registered with an owner and a removal date. A weekly report lists flags past their date; a flag older than 90 days without a documented reason is a defect.

#### 57.4.6 Entitlements

The plan ladder (canon §1.4) is **data**: a `plan` has `features` (capability keys) and `limits` (numeric caps — guards, users, sites, API calls, AI interactions, storage, per D-003). The resolver answers `entitled(tenant, capability) → Allowed | Blocked(reason, upgrade_path)` and `withinLimit(tenant, limit_key, requested) → Allowed | Blocked(current, cap)`.

Two rules: entitlement is checked **before** permission (a user may be permitted to do a thing their plan does not include, and the correct response is an upgrade prompt, not "access denied"), and a limit breach never destroys data — exceeding a guard cap blocks *adding* guards, never disables existing ones, because a subscription lapse must not strand people mid-shift (§30, and the subscription-expiry workflow WKF-32).

#### 57.4.7 Notifications

Domain modules emit domain events. They never know a channel, a provider or a template. The notification service (§36) resolves: event → applicable recipients (by role, scope and subscription preference) → template (per language, per channel) → channel policy (severity-driven: P0 uses push + SMS + in-app simultaneously and does not wait for the first to fail) → provider (with failover) → delivery record. Quiet hours, digesting and preference are applied for P2/P3 and explicitly bypassed for P0/P1.

The single most important architectural property here: **notification failure never blocks the domain transaction**, and domain success never depends on notification success — but for T0 events, a *delivery* failure raises its own alert, because "the SOS was recorded but nobody was told" is the worst possible silent failure.

#### 57.4.8 AI permission-checking

The rule that makes the AI layer safe is ordering, and it is worth stating precisely because it is easy to get backwards:

```
user utterance
   → intent classification (no data access)
   → permission pre-check: what may THIS principal read/do for THIS intent?
   → context retrieval, restricted to that answer  ◄── the model never sees
   → model call                                        data the user cannot see
   → proposed action + action class
   → action-class gate:
        Read-only        → return
        Recommendation   → return, labelled, never auto-applied
        Approval-required→ create an Approval for a human with authority
        Automated        → execute ONLY if in the low-risk allow-list
   → execute through the SAME service methods a human would use
     (same permission checks, same validation, same audit)
   → log the interaction (§41)
```

Two invariants: the model is never a permission boundary (retrieval is filtered before the call, so a jailbreak cannot exfiltrate what was never retrieved), and AI never has a privileged code path (it calls the same services with the same principal, so an AI action is indistinguishable from a human action at the enforcement layer and distinguishable in the audit log by its actor annotation). The canon §1.7 prohibitions are enforced by the absence of the tool, not by instruction.

---

#### 57.4.9 Request lifecycle traced end to end

**Scenario.** Guard Ramesh (tenant `AGY-4471`, branch Jaipur-North) arrives at Site "Vaishali Warehouse", Post "Main Gate", night shift 20:00–08:00. He is on a ₹6,500 Android phone with one bar of 2G at the gate. He opens the Guard App and taps the single primary action: *Check in*. The client's Facility Manager has the live view open on a laptop in Gurugram. Suraksha's Command Center has the city board open. Twenty-two minutes later he has still not checked in from the *second* post he was also rostered to — and the alert path fires.

| # | Step | What happens | Mechanism used |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **App open, offline** | The duty screen renders entirely from the cached `/guard/today` bundle (SUR-GAP-008). No network is required to know the shift, the post, the checkpoint list or the gate instructions. | Offline-first (canon §4, Guard App only) |
| 2 | **Tap Check in** | The app captures: GPS fix (with accuracy radius), `device_time`, a selfie if the post requires it, the device ID and app version. It writes an event to the encrypted local queue with a client-generated `idempotency_key` (UUIDv7 + device ID) and **immediately shows "Checked in — syncing"**. The guard's job is done in under three seconds regardless of network. | Local durable queue; idempotency key generated at source |
| 3 | **Queue drain attempt** | The sync worker attempts an HTTP POST. On 2G it may take 20 seconds or fail. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter; the media (selfie) is uploaded separately and lazily, so a heavy image never blocks the attendance fact. | Batched HTTP, never a background socket (SUR-RT-005) |
| 4 | **Edge** | TLS terminates; the WAF applies coarse limits; a request ID is injected and returned in the response header so the app can log it for support. | L2 |
| 5 | **Gateway/middleware** | Token validated (signature, expiry, `jti` not in the deny-list, `permission_version` current). Principal resolved: account → membership in `AGY-4471` → role Guard → scope = own assignments. Tenant context set on the request and on the database session (RLS). Idempotency key checked in Redis: if seen, the prior response is replayed and no second attendance row is created. Per-principal rate limit applied. | §57.4.1, §57.4.2 |
| 6 | **Permission + entitlement** | `can(principal, 'attendance.check_in', assignment)` — allowed only for the guard's own current assignment, within the configured early/late tolerance window. Entitlement check is a no-op here (attendance is in every plan). | §57.4.3, §57.4.6 |
| 7 | **Business validation** | Assignment exists, is `Active`, belongs to this guard, this post, tonight. Geofence check: the reported point is inside the site fence (or outside it, which does not reject the check-in — it *flags* it, because rejecting a real guard standing at a real gate because of GPS drift is the worst possible product behaviour). Time integrity: both `device_time` and `server_received_time` are stored; a large skew is recorded and flagged, never silently trusted (canon §4). Compliance gate: is the guard deployable (documents valid, no hard block)? A failure here does not block the check-in either — it records the check-in and raises a compliance exception, because the person is already at the post and safety comes before paperwork. | §30 business rules; canon §4 time integrity |
| 8 | **Transaction** | In one transaction: insert `attendance` (status `Present` or `Present-Late`), update the assignment's derived state, write the **audit** entry, and write **outbox** rows for `attendance.checked_in` and, if flagged, `attendance.geofence_exception`. Commit. Everything after this point is asynchronous and cannot corrupt the fact. | §57.4.4; transactional outbox |
| 9 | **Response** | `201` with the canonical attendance record and a `next_config` block telling the device its new ping interval (on duty, stationary, inside fence → 120 s). The app marks the queued item done and clears it. If the response never arrives, the app retries with the same idempotency key and step 5 makes the retry harmless. | §34.3 server-steered sampling |
| 10 | **Outbox drain** | `worker-default` reads the outbox, publishes to `events.fanout` (Redis Pub/Sub) and to `notifications.send` (Redis Stream). | §34.4 |
| 11 | **Command Center board** | `rt-gateway` receives the pub/sub message, matches it to subscriptions on `tenant:AGY-4471:site:<id>` and on the Suraksha oversight scope, re-verifies that each subscribed socket still has permission, and pushes the event with a per-topic `seq`. The operator's board flips the post from amber to green within roughly a second of commit. | §34.2.3 |
| 12 | **Client live view** | The Facility Manager's browser is **polling at 60 s** (§34.2.2 — clients do not get a socket in V1). Within a minute the site card shows "Main Gate — on duty, checked in 20:03". The client sees a *status*, not the guard's live coordinates, because §39 restricts precise location sharing with clients to what the contract and the guard's consent actually permit. | §34.2.2, §39 |
| 13 | **Notification fan-out** | Notification service resolves recipients by rule: the Supervisor gets an in-app update only (P3 — no one needs an SMS because a guard arrived on time). If it had been a late check-in beyond tolerance, the Operations Manager would get a P2. Nothing is sent to the client unless their contract configures arrival notifications. | §36, §57.4.7 |
| 14 | **Analytics** | An `attendance_checked_in` event is emitted to the product-analytics sink with tenant, role, surface and latency — no name, no coordinates. The KPI path is separate: ANL-D01/D02 are computed from the `attendance` table, not from the analytics event, so the dashboard and the invoice can never disagree. | §42.4, §42.6 |
| 15 | **Ping stream begins** | The device starts sending batched pings every 120 s to `/ingest`. Each batch: validated, deduped against a 10-minute Redis set, published to `gps.ingest`. `signals-consumer` evaluates 1–5 cached fences in-process, applies hysteresis, writes to the partitioned `location` table, and emits geofence events only on a *confirmed* transition. No ping is ever reverse-geocoded. | §34.3, §34.6.2 |
| 16 | **The alert path** | Ramesh's second rostered post has no check-in. `worker-critical` holds an escalation timer created when the shift became due. At T+20 minutes with no attendance row, it raises alert `post.unmanned` at severity **P1** against the Command Center rules engine (§24). The rules engine resolves the escalation ladder from configuration: (a) push + in-app to the Supervisor with a 5-minute acknowledgement clock; (b) unacknowledged → push + **SMS** to the Operations Manager and the post appears in the Command Center's active queue with an audible cue; (c) still unacknowledged at 15 minutes → the Branch Manager, and the client-facing SLA clock starts. Each step writes an audit entry and each outbound message writes a delivery record. If the *delivery* fails on the P1 path, that failure is itself an alert. | §24, §36, C-06 |
| 17 | **Resolution** | The operator opens the alert, sees Ramesh checked in at his first post 22 minutes ago, and dispatches a replacement (WKF-18) or reassigns. The alert closes with a reason code that feeds ANL-W07 and the SLA measurement. | §29, §42 |

**What this trace demonstrates:** the guard's experience is bounded by his device, not by our network; correctness is established in one transaction; everything downstream is derived and recoverable; the client sees the truth without seeing more than they should; and the life-safety path (step 16) runs on a queue that report generation can never occupy.

**What it also exposes honestly:** between step 2 and step 8 the platform does not know the guard is present. If his phone stays offline for six hours, the Command Center's board is wrong for six hours, and the `post.unmanned` alert in step 16 will fire for a guard who is standing at his post. This is inherent to offline-first field software, and the product's answer is a design choice rather than a technical fix: alerts of this class are labelled "no signal from device" versus "confirmed absent", and the supervisor's confirmation — a phone call — is what resolves the ambiguity. Any design that claims to resolve it technically is lying about physics.

---

### 57.5 Build versus buy

Scored on four factors: is it core to our differentiation; is it a solved commodity; what is the cost curve as guards/tenants grow; and what does buying do to data exposure.

| Capability | Decision | Reasoning | Cost curve if bought | Data exposure if bought |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guard/roster/attendance/patrol domain | **BUILD** | This *is* the product. No vendor models Indian private-security operations at this depth. | — | — |
| Command Center & escalation | **BUILD** | Life-safety logic and the core of the brand promise. | — | — |
| Multi-tenant permission model | **BUILD** | Too specific to §31 to buy; buying splits the model. | — | — |
| Authentication primitives | **BUILD** (see §57.3.13) | Per-MAU pricing scales with the population we monetise least; custom flows are the load-bearing part. | Bad: linear in guards | Full identity graph at a vendor |
| Enterprise SSO (SAML/SCIM) | **BUY** `[FUTURE]` | Specialised, high-risk, zero strategic value, low volume. | Flat, per-enterprise | Limited to enterprise staff |
| Payments (collection) | **BUY** — Razorpay | Regulated, commodity, PCI scope avoidance. | % of revenue | Payment data at a regulated processor |
| Payout rail | **BUY** — pending D-243 | Regulated rails; building is not an option. | Per payout | Bank details at processor |
| GST invoice generation | **BUILD** (format), **BUY** (nothing) | The invoice is a legal artefact tied to our ledger (§35); templating it is trivial, outsourcing it is not. | — | — |
| Accounting/books | **BUY** — export to the tenant's own system | Agencies already have accountants and tools; competing is a distraction. | Per tenant, theirs | Their choice |
| SMS/WhatsApp/Email delivery | **BUY** | Carrier relationships and DLT compliance are not buildable. | Per message — the largest variable cost | Message content at provider (minimised per §39) |
| Push delivery | **BUY** — FCM/APNs | No alternative exists. | Free | Device tokens only |
| Maps & geocoding | **BUY** (tiles/geocode) + **BUILD** (geofencing) | Tiles are a commodity; geofence evaluation on guard positions is privacy-critical and stays first-party. | Per load/call | Viewport and address lookups only |
| OCR | **BUY** primary + **BUILD** fallback | Accuracy gap is real; the fallback protects cost and residency. | Per page | Identity documents — the highest-sensitivity outbound flow |
| LLM/ASR/TTS | **BUY**, abstracted | Frontier quality is unbuyable at our scale by building. | Per token/minute | Text and audio, minimised and redacted |
| Face matching / liveness | **BUY** (SDK) where used, per-post optional | Specialised CV; never platform-wide (§34.7.3, §39). | Per verification | Biometric — treated as the highest bar |
| Background verification (police/criminal/employment) | **BUY** — agency vendors | Regulated, human-process-heavy, relationship-based. | Per check | Candidate PII at vendor |
| Video storage/streaming (body cams) | **BUY** `[FUTURE]` (§60) | Media infrastructure is a business of its own. | Per GB/hour | Footage — a major new obligation |
| Observability (logs/metrics/traces) | **BUY** managed | Running an observability stack is a full-time job. | Per GB ingested | Logs — must be PII-scrubbed before egress |
| Error/crash reporting | **BUY** — Sentry (self-host optional) | Commodity. | Per event | Stack traces — scrubbed |
| Product analytics | **BUY** — PostHog (self-host preferred) | Commodity with a self-host escape. | Per event | Behavioural events, pseudonymous |
| BI/reporting for tenants | **BUILD** (curated) + **BUY** later (self-serve) | §42.5's stance: curated first; a BI tool bolted on early exposes the schema and the tenant boundary. | Per seat | Query access to tenant data |
| Support ticketing (internal) | **BUY** initially, **BUILD** the in-product surface | In-product tickets must be tenant-scoped and permission-aware (§20); the agent-side console is a commodity. | Per agent | Ticket content |
| Help centre / knowledge base | **BUY** | Commodity, and content is the value. | Flat | Public content |
| Status page | **BUY** | Must be independent of our infrastructure — that is the entire point. | Flat | None |
| E-signature for contracts | **BUY** `[FUTURE]` | Legal-grade signing is a regulated specialism. | Per envelope | Contract documents |
| Tender/government portal integration | **NEITHER** — manual/assisted | Canon §0: do not invent third-party APIs. Discovery is assisted; submission is human. | — | — |
| Payroll statutory filing | **NEITHER** — export only | §20: we produce registers and export files; we do not file, and we do not assert what any authority requires. | — | — |
| CI/CD, IaC, secrets | **BUY** managed | Commodity, security-critical, well-served. | Low | Secrets — the crown jewels; scoped and rotated |

### 57.6 Architecture decision records

The fifteen decisions that most constrain everything else. Status values: **Accepted** (decided and in force), **Accepted (provisional)** (decided, with a named re-evaluation trigger), **Proposed** (recommended here, awaiting sign-off).

| ADR | Context | Decision | Status | Consequences |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ADR-01** Modular monolith | A 5-person team, 5 web properties, 4 apps, one desktop app, and a domain with heavy cross-module transactions (roster ↔ attendance ↔ payroll ↔ invoice). | One deployable `api` with enforced internal module boundaries; separate processes only for ingest, real-time and workers. | **Accepted** (canon §4) | + One transaction, one deploy, one debug session. − One blast radius; module discipline must be enforced by tooling or it decays. Extraction later is enabled by the three-pool split (§57.2.2) and the outbox. |
| **ADR-02** Shared-schema multi-tenancy with RLS | Hundreds of agency tenants of wildly different size, plus `SURAKSHA-HQ`. | `tenant_id` on every tenant row + RLS + application context + an isolation test suite. Database-per-tenant only for named Enterprise cases. | **Accepted** (§32.1.1) | + Cheap, simple, one migration path. − A single isolation bug is a cross-tenant breach; hence the suite is a permanent release blocker. Noisy-neighbour risk handled by per-tenant limits. |
| **ADR-03** Postgres as the single source of truth | Ledger, roster and compliance data are integrity-critical and interrelated. | One Postgres cluster; PostGIS in-engine; partitions for time-series; one replica for reports. No second OLTP store. | **Accepted** (§32.0.1) | + Transactional integrity everywhere; one backup chain. − Single-writer ceiling; storage growth from `location`/`audit_log` is the cost driver, making retention a financial control. |
| **ADR-04** Separate ingest path | GPS pings must never contend with invoices, and a slow primary must never stall a guard's app. | Pings go `/ingest` → Redis Stream → consumer → partitioned store, bypassing the business modules entirely. | **Accepted** (§34.3) | + Guard app stays fast under any OLTP load; ping loss is survivable by design. − A second write path to reason about; positions are eventually consistent with the operator board. |
| **ADR-05** Offline-first for the Guard App only | Guards work in basements, industrial estates and 2G shadows; every other user has a desk. | Durable encrypted local queue + idempotency keys + server-steered config for the Guard App; all other clients assume connectivity. | **Accepted** (canon §4) | + Field reliability without building sync everywhere. − Genuine ambiguity between "offline" and "absent" (§57.4.9); resolved socially, not technically. |
| **ADR-06** Guard App native Android; other apps React Native | Battery budget, exact alarms, OEM process killers, SOS cold start, app size on full 32 GB phones. | Kotlin + Compose for the Guard App; RN for Customer/Agency/Admin; iOS Guard App deferred. | **Proposed** (`D-600`; modifies the working default in D-125) | + Fewest layers under the safety-critical path. − An Android-specific hire; duplicated client-side concerns for one app; no iOS Guard App at launch. |
| **ADR-07** Tauri for the desktop app | Same account/data/modules as `ap.`, plus OS notifications, file dialogs and signed installers on three OSes. | Tauri v2 wrapping the AP web bundle. | **Accepted (provisional)** — revisit on Linux webview defects | + ~10× smaller download, far lower memory. − Three webview engines to test; a small Rust surface; a minimum-OS requirement must be enforced. |
| **ADR-08** Build identity, buy delivery | Cross-tenant identity, device binding, scope resolution and impersonation are the load-bearing parts; hosted IdPs price per MAU and guards are MAU. | Build the identity service on audited libraries; buy OTP delivery; buy enterprise SSO later. | **Accepted** (canon §4 fixes the behaviour) | + No per-MAU cost curve, no identity-migration trap, full control of custom flows. − We own authentication security permanently; mandatory pentest scope and two-reviewer rule on that module. |
| **ADR-09** Redis for delivery, Postgres for truth | Needed queues, streams, cache, locks and pub/sub without adding a broker to a small team's on-call. | Redis Streams + transactional outbox; Kafka deferred behind named triggers. | **Accepted (provisional)** (§34.4, §34.7.2) | + Zero incremental infrastructure; adequate to ~100× current volume. − Weaker durability and bounded replay; a queue-interface abstraction must be maintained so the eventual swap is an adapter. |
| **ADR-10** Transport per use case, not one transport | Consoles, guard phones and client portals have incompatible constraints. | WebSocket for consoles; push for guards; 60 s polling for client live views. | **Accepted** (§34.2) | + Each client gets the cheapest adequate mechanism; guard battery preserved. − Three code paths and three failure modes; polling means client views lag by up to a minute, which must be stated in the UI. |
| **ADR-11** AI proposes, humans dispose | Canon §1.7 prohibits autonomous action on money, permissions, employment and compliance. | Permission pre-check before retrieval; four action classes enforced in code; AI executes only through the same services with the same principal. | **Accepted** (§25, §41) | + AI cannot become a privilege-escalation path; every action is auditable and attributable. − Slower AI feature delivery; some genuinely useful automations stay in Approval-required. |
| **ADR-12** Compliance and jurisdiction rules as data | Canon §0: never encode legal conclusions; PSARA licensing is state- and district-scoped and changes. | Rule sets, thresholds, document requirements and statutory components are configuration with effective dates, never code. | **Accepted** | + A rule change is a data change reviewed by Compliance, not a release. − A configuration engine is real work and needs its own versioning, testing and audit. |
| **ADR-13** Money as integer paise with a double-sided ledger | Canon §4; financial records can never be silently modified (BR-003). | `Money` value type, integer paise, double-entry ledger, soft delete, append-only audit; corrections are reversing entries. | **Accepted** (§35) | + Financial disputes are answerable from the ledger alone. − No convenient "just fix the row" path; every correction is a documented event, which is the point. |
| **ADR-14** One cloud, Indian region, managed containers — not Kubernetes | Data residency for guard identity/biometric/location data; a team that must operate almost nothing. | Single cloud, Indian primary region, managed container runtime, managed Postgres/Redis/storage; multi-region only on contractual trigger. | **Accepted (provisional)** (`D-601`) | + Small operational surface; defensible privacy posture; low latency. − The document's largest lock-in; mitigated by containers + open-source-equivalent services + Terraform. |
| **ADR-15** Curated analytics before self-serve BI | One number, one definition (SUR-ANL-004); an invoice and a dashboard must never disagree. | Product metrics from Postgres read models with a metric registry; PostHog for behaviour; warehouse deferred to §32.6.5 triggers. | **Accepted** (§42) | + Numbers are trustworthy and permission-scoped. − Slower to answer novel ad-hoc questions; analysts will feel constrained until the warehouse arrives. |

### 57.7 Known weaknesses of this architecture

Written plainly, because an architecture document that claims no weaknesses is not an architecture document. These are the eight places this design will hurt as scale grows, in rough order of when the pain arrives.

| # | Weakness | Why it happens | Early symptom | Planned response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **W-1** | **The single Postgres primary is the whole system's ceiling.** Writes from `location`, `audit_log`, attendance and the outbox all land on one instance. | ADR-03 chose integrity and simplicity over write scale, deliberately. | Write IOPS saturation; replication lag spikes at month-end; vacuum pressure on the largest partitions; p95 write latency creeping past 100 ms. | Ordered and pre-decided: (1) instance size up; (2) enforce partition pruning and retention; (3) move `location` to its own instance (§34.7.2); (4) move `audit_log` out; (5) PgBouncer and connection discipline; (6) only then consider sharding or a cell topology. Each step has a trigger metric; none is taken on anticipation (SUR-RT-014). |
| **W-2** | **The modular monolith will erode.** Module boundaries enforced only by review always decay; in eighteen months some module will import another's internals and the "extract a service" option quietly disappears. | Human nature plus deadline pressure. | Import-graph cycles; a payroll change breaking an attendance test; deploy fear. | Enforce boundaries in tooling from week one: per-module public interfaces, an import-linter in CI that fails on cross-module internal imports, an architecture-fitness test that asserts the allowed dependency graph, and a quarterly review of the graph. Treat a boundary violation as a build failure, not a comment. |
| **W-3** | **Offline-first creates a permanent truth gap.** The board can be confidently wrong for hours (§57.4.9). As the fleet grows, "no signal" volume grows linearly, and operators will learn to ignore the category. | Physics of field connectivity, not a bug. | Rising ratio of `device_no_signal` to `confirmed_absent`; operators bulk-acknowledging alerts; supervisors distrusting the board. | Keep the two states visually and semantically distinct forever; track the ratio as an operational KPI; make supervisor confirmation a first-class one-tap action; measure alert-acknowledgement quality, not just count; and consider SMS-based check-in fallback for chronically dark sites `[FUTURE]`. |
| **W-4** | **Redis is load-bearing for delivery, and it is our least durable component.** Ingest, notifications, webhooks, jobs, rate limits and the token deny-list all depend on it. A Redis failure degrades far more than a cache should. | ADR-09 traded durability for simplicity and cost. | Memory pressure; stream backlog growth; a failover that drops in-flight stream entries. | The outbox already protects correctness. Additionally: bound every stream, alert on backlog and on consumer liveness, treat the token deny-list as fail-closed (if Redis is unavailable, shorten token acceptance rather than skipping revocation checks), and pre-write the runbook for "Redis lost" so the response is rehearsed, not improvised. Move notifications to a durable queue when a single loss becomes commercially unacceptable. |
| **W-5** | **The permission model is deep and will get deeper, and its evaluation is on every request.** §31's matrix crossed with tenant → branch → site scope, entitlements, and temporal conditions is a lot of logic in a hot path. | Genuine domain complexity; four audience families with legitimate different needs. | Permission evaluation appearing in latency profiles; a growing set of special cases; a bug that grants or denies wrongly in an edge case. | Keep the evaluator pure and cacheable (keyed by `permission_version`); make the matrix data-driven and testable in isolation; maintain the exhaustive route-permission test; and resist per-customer permission special cases — new needs become new *roles* or new *scopes*, never new conditions in the evaluator. |
| **W-6** | **Third-party concentration on the notification path.** DLT template approval, WhatsApp category policy and aggregator throughput are outside our control and sit on the T0 escalation path. | Regulatory and platform-policy reality in India. | Template rejections; delivery-rate dips by operator; WhatsApp category reclassification; a mass-alert throttle. | Two SMS aggregators from day one with priority routing (§36); canonical templates stored first-party with provider IDs mapped; delivery-rate monitoring per provider per operator with automatic failover; rate-shaping for mass events; and an explicitly designed "SMS-only degraded mode" that is tested, not assumed. |
| **W-7** | **Cost per guard is not yet proven, and three lines can run away.** SMS/OTP volume, map API loads and AI (especially voice/ASR) all scale with usage in ways that are only loosely coupled to revenue — a ₹5,000/month Starter tenant with 300 guards can plausibly cost more to serve than it pays. | Consumption-priced dependencies under a flat-rate SaaS plan (canon §1.4 fixes the prices). | Cost-per-guard-per-month rising month over month; a tenant appearing in the top decile of AI or SMS spend. | Meter everything per tenant from day one (§59.12); set plan-level quotas for AI and voice (D-003); WhatsApp/passkeys to displace SMS OTP; enforce the map caching rules; publish a monthly unit-economics review; and, if a tenant is structurally unprofitable, treat it as a pricing decision to escalate rather than an engineering problem to absorb. |
| **W-8** | **The real-time gateway is our only stateful, sticky, self-operated component — and it sits on the T0 console path.** Deploys drop connections; a bad release is immediately visible to operators; scaling is memory-bound and less elastic than the stateless tiers. | We chose to own the SOS path rather than rent it (ADR-10). | Reconnect storms after deploy; gateway CPU/memory creep; operators reporting a stale board. | Connection draining with staggered `reconnect_after` (§34.2.3); the mandatory 10-second polling fallback (SUR-RT-007) exercised by a scheduled chaos test, not just specified; a synthetic SOS probe running end-to-end continuously (§58, §59); and isolation of the SOS channel from all other traffic before the gateway is ever scaled for volume. |

**Two honest non-weaknesses worth stating.** First, the absence of microservices is not a weakness at this stage and should not be treated as technical debt — it is a correct decision that has a documented exit. Second, the absence of Kafka, a warehouse, a search engine and Kubernetes is not under-engineering; each has a named trigger, and building them early would consume the team's entire capacity for a year.

**And one thing genuinely not yet decided:** the payout rail (D-243) is a hole in the architecture, not just in the commercials. Guard salary disbursement and agency settlement are core to the product's promise (payment timeliness is the single strongest guard-retention lever, §59.8), and the reconciliation design, failure handling and treasury operations all depend on which rail is chosen. This must be settled before payroll disbursement is built, and it is called out again in §58 as a launch-scope question.

#### 57.8.3 What changes between them, and what must not

| Dimension | Day one | Year three | Trigger to move |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compute orchestration | Managed containers | Same, or Kubernetes if the container count and team justify it | >20 distinct services **and** a platform engineer exists |
| API tier | 3 pools, same image | Autoscaled pools; `api-enterprise` fully isolated | Enterprise API volume affecting console latency |
| Database | 1 primary + standby + 1 replica | OLTP cluster + separate ingest cluster + N replicas | §34.7.2 write triggers |
| Streaming | Redis Streams | Kafka/Redpanda for the topics that need durability/replay | §34.7.2 (>2,000 events/s, >7-day replay, >6 consumer groups) |
| Analytics | Read models + replica | Warehouse + self-serve BI | §32.6.5 |
| Search | Postgres FTS | Dedicated engine for the document/OCR corpus | §57.3.9 |
| Real-time | 2 gateway instances | Autoscaled, topic-sharded, SOS channel physically isolated | >20,000 concurrent sockets or any SOS latency incident |
| Regions | 1 region, 2 AZs | Primary + warm standby region with a documented RPO/RTO | A contractual DR requirement (§49) |
| Tenancy | Shared schema + RLS | Same, plus dedicated instances for named Enterprise tenants | §32.1.1.4 |
| SOS path | Shares infrastructure, dedicated queue (`worker-critical`) | Physically isolated cell: own compute, own DB pool, own provider account, own deploy lane | **One** incident where SOS latency was harmed by unrelated load |
| **Must not change** | Postgres as truth · integer-paise double-entry ledger · one permission evaluator · one identity · append-only audit · tenant_id + RLS · AI never autonomous on the canon §1.7 list · location evaluation first-party · offline-first only for the Guard App | Identical | These are invariants; changing one is a new architecture, not an evolution |

## 58. Launch Readiness Checklist

### 58.0 How to use this section

This is the document that stands between a system that demonstrates well and a system that can carry a real client's real guards on a real night. It exists because launch decisions are made under commercial pressure, and the only defence against that pressure is a list written before the pressure arrived.

**Scope of "launch".** §51.10 defines the minimum viable launch as *one client, one site, one to three posts, four to eight verified guards, two shifts a day, one serviceable city, one calendar month* — and recommends a **Phase 1 soft launch** with the **Phase 2 exit as the marketing launch**. This checklist is written for the *soft launch*, because that is the first moment a real guard is deployed under this platform and every safety, legal and financial obligation becomes live. A shortened re-run of the same checklist gates the marketing launch, with the additional rows marked `[MKT]`. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-603]` — confirm the two-gate model, because a single-gate launch changes the blocking set materially.

**Row identifiers.** Rows are labelled `LR-nnn`. These are checklist row labels, **not** requirement IDs under canon §2 — the underlying requirements live in the owning sections and are cross-referenced.

**The five columns.**

| Column | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Item** | One verifiable thing. If it cannot be shown to a sceptical outsider in under five minutes, it is written wrong and must be split. |
| **Owner role** | The single role accountable for producing the evidence. Canon §3 role names where one applies; where the platform role vocabulary has no engineering equivalent, `CTO` (Co-founder, per canon §1) is used. One owner, never two. |
| **Evidence required** | An **artefact**, never an assertion. A screenshot, a signed document, a test run ID, a provider dashboard export, a ticket link, a log query result. "Confirmed by the team" is not evidence. |
| **Blocking?** | `HARD` — vetoes launch, no waiver possible. `SOFT` — launch may proceed only with a dated, named waiver recorded in the launch log with an owner and a close-by date. `INFO` — tracked, not gating. |
| **Verified by** | A **different** person from the owner. Self-verification is not verification. Where the verifier is external (counsel, pentester, auditor), that is stated. |

**Two standing rules.**

1. **Evidence expires.** Every `HARD` row's evidence must be dated within 14 days of the go-live date, except pentest reports (60 days) and legal reviews (90 days). Stale evidence is treated as absent.
2. **A waiver is a debt.** Every `SOFT` waiver enters the launch log with an owner and a close-by date, is reviewed at the first weekly leadership meeting after launch (§59.1), and is reported until closed. A waiver with no close date is refused.

### 58.8 Fabricated content remediation — the hard blocker

This is the single most important row set in §58. Canon §1.8 records that the live website currently carries fabricated team members, clients, testimonials, tenders, awards, statistics and a placeholder phone number. **Launching a real security business on a website that misrepresents its track record is not a marketing problem. It is a misrepresentation exposure, a due-diligence failure, and an existential brand risk for a company whose entire proposition is "TRUSTED. VERIFIED. ALWAYS."**

**Standing rule: no `SOFT` waiver is available anywhere in §58.8.** Commercial pressure, a demo deadline, an investor meeting and a client's launch date are all explicitly insufficient reasons. This is the veto that §58.19 makes non-negotiable.

#### 58.8.1 Remediation matrix

| Ref | Problem (canon §1.8) | Required end state | Evidence required | Owner role | Verified by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LR-064 (P1) | Fake team names | Only real people appear: Suhail Ali (Co-founder & CEO), Yash (Co-founder & CTO), Ajay (Co-founder & COO), RS Meena (Chief Strategic Advisor, Retd. DIG Rajasthan). Every other profile removed, not renamed. Each named person has given written consent to their bio, photo and title | Consent email per person + live page screenshot + a content-DB query returning zero legacy profile rows | Marketing | Founder/Management |
| LR-065 (P2) | Fake clients and testimonials (Apollo, Reliance, DLF, Sunburn) | Zero client logos or testimonials on any surface unless backed by a **signed written permission** from that client naming the exact usage. Until real permissions exist, the section is removed — not replaced with "trusted by leading brands" | Permission letters on file for every logo/quote displayed; or a screenshot showing the section absent. Plus a full-site grep for each fabricated brand name returning zero hits | Marketing | External counsel |
| LR-066 (P3) | Fake tenders (Delhi Metro ₹2.4 Cr, Infosys, Indian Oil, SBI) | Removed entirely. If a tender-discovery capability is shown, it displays **only** genuinely sourced listings, with the source attributed and the sourcing method described honestly (§13, §37) | Zero-hit grep for each named entity across content DB, static assets, screenshots and marketing collateral + a screenshot of the replacement state | Marketing | Founder/Management |
| LR-067 (P4) | Fake awards and press | Removed. Any award or press mention retained must link to a verifiable public source | Link-check report showing every remaining claim resolves to a live third-party source | Marketing | External counsel |
| LR-068 (P5) | Contradictory statistics (1,200+ vs 40,000+ vs 452 guards; 8 cities vs 26 states) | One number, one source of truth. Every public statistic is generated from a platform query with a named metric definition (§42), a stated as-of date, and a refresh owner. Hand-typed statistics are prohibited | The metric definition + the query + a screenshot showing the rendered figure with its as-of date; plus a site-wide inventory proving no hard-coded numbers remain | CTO | Auditor |
| LR-069 (P6) | Placeholder phone +91 90000 00000 | A real, monitored, 24/7-answered number published, tested by an outside caller at 02:00 local time on a weekday and on a Sunday | Two call logs with timestamps and the answering person's name; plus a zero-hit grep for the placeholder string | COO / National Operations | Founder/Management |
| LR-070 (P7) | Template legal pages | Covered by LR-060; repeated here so the P-series is closed in one place | Counsel review letter | Compliance | External counsel |

#### 58.8.2 Evidence standard for this subsection

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Mechanical proof, not visual proof | A page can be edited and a screenshot can be old. Every removal row requires a **string search across the entire estate** — content database, static site, CMS drafts, PDFs, sales decks, PPT collateral, the Trinetra marketplace copy, app-store listings, social profiles, and any cached CDN object — returning zero hits, with the search command and its output attached. |
| Third-party surfaces | Fabricated claims may already exist outside our control: directory listings, aggregator sites, an old Google Business profile, screenshots on partner sites. Owner must produce a takedown or correction request log for each discovered instance. `[ASSUMPTION: A-603]` — that all such surfaces can be enumerated within the launch window; where they cannot, the residual list is disclosed to Founder/Management before go-live. |
| Prevention, not just cleanup | A CI content check must fail the build if any string on the prohibited list reappears, and a new-claim review step must exist in the marketing publishing workflow. Cleanup without prevention is a repeat incident waiting to happen. |
| Correction posture | `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-611]` — whether to publish a short, dignified correction notice ("our earlier site included illustrative placeholder content; this site now shows only verified information") or to remediate silently. Recommended default: silent remediation plus honest answers if asked, with a prepared holding statement; a proactive notice draws attention to the problem without a proportionate benefit. Counsel should be asked whether any disclosure obligation applies before choosing. |
| Sales collateral parity | Every deck, one-pager, proposal template and email signature in circulation must be re-issued from the cleaned content set, and the old versions withdrawn from the shared drive. A cleaned website with a dirty proposal deck is not remediated. |

#### 58.8.3 The claim register

`[RECOMMENDED]` Establish, before launch, a permanent **public-claim register**: every factual claim made on any public surface, with its source, its owner, its verification date and its next review date. Claims without a live source are removed at review. This is the mechanism that makes P1–P7 a one-time event rather than a recurring one, and it is the artefact an acquirer or a regulator will ask to see. Ownership: Marketing, reviewed quarterly by Compliance (§59.1).
