---

### 59.17 The first 90 days after launch

The purpose of this plan is to convert a launch into an operation before the launch adrenaline runs out.

#### 59.17.1 Days 1–7 — hypercare

| Focus | Actions |
|---|---|
| Presence | Someone from Suraksha physically at the launch site for the first three nights, including a full night shift. Not to supervise the guard — to see what the software does at 03:00 |
| Cadence | Twice-daily standups (09:15 and 21:00), founders on both; engineering on elevated alert; no non-emergency deploys for 72 hours |
| Measurement | Every SOS, wake check and attendance event manually reconciled against what actually happened, daily, for seven days. This is the calibration of the entire evidence chain |
| Guard contact | Every guard in the launch cohort spoken to individually by day 3, in their language, about the app specifically |
| Client contact | Daily check-in call with the launch client for the first week |
| Exit criterion | Zero unexplained discrepancies between platform records and observed reality for two consecutive days |

#### 59.17.2 Days 8–30 — stabilise

| Focus | Actions |
|---|---|
| Defects | Burn down every S1/S2 found in week one; publish the known-issues list to the client honestly |
| Waivers | Close every `SOFT` waiver from §58; any that cannot close gets a founder decision, not a quiet extension |
| Alert tuning | Reduce pages per on-call week to ≤3; delete or downgrade every alert that fired without requiring action |
| Runbooks | Write the runbook for everything that surprised anyone in week one — the surprise list is the syllabus |
| Rhythm | Move from twice-daily to the §59.1 cadence; hold the first real weekly quality review and the first monthly close |
| Second site | Only after the first site is boring. Boring is the acceptance criterion |
| Workforce | First 30-day attrition read; first grievance-channel test (a real guard raising a real issue and getting a real answer) |

#### 59.17.3 Days 31–60 — prove repeatability

| Focus | Actions |
|---|---|
| Scale the pattern | Second and third sites, ideally with a different service lane and a different client type, to find what was accidentally site-specific |
| First full financial cycle | Complete monthly close: invoice, collect, run payroll, disburse, reconcile, and compare against the §52 model with the variance explained line by line |
| Agency tenant | Onboard the first paying agency tenant through §59.6, all the way to M5, and instrument every point of friction |
| Compliance dry run | Run the audit-readiness pack as if an inspection were happening; time it |
| DR | Execute the first post-launch restore drill against production-shaped data (§49.5) |
| Support | Publish the help centre gaps found in the first 60 days; measure ticket deflection |

#### 59.17.4 Days 61–90 — institutionalise

| Focus | Actions |
|---|---|
| Rota | Third engineer on the on-call rota; founders removed from the routine escalation path (D-605 resolved) |
| Metrics | First full quarterly review of the §59.15 set with real trend data; re-baseline every assumption that was a guess at launch (A-606, A-607, and the §52 model inputs) |
| Roadmap | First post-launch roadmap re-plan driven by real feedback rather than pre-launch belief |
| Security | First quarterly security review, including an access review and a retest of anything waived at launch |
| Honest retrospective | A written 90-day retrospective covering what the PRD got wrong. The specific question to answer: which assumptions in this document did the first 90 days disprove, and what changes as a result |
| Decision | Formal go/no-go on the §51 Phase 2 marketing launch, using the shortened §58 checklist |

**The 90-day exit criterion.** The operation runs for one full week without founder intervention in any routine process: no founder approving a roster, answering a support ticket, chasing a verification, or being paged at night. If that week cannot be produced by day 90, the constraint is not the software — it is the operating model, and scaling on top of it will multiply the problem rather than dilute it.

---

## 60. Future Roadmap

### 60.0 How to read this section

Everything in §60 is marked `[FUTURE]`. None of it is in scope for the phases in §51, none of it is costed in §52, and none of it should appear in a sales conversation as a commitment. This section exists for a specific reason: a platform that touches guards, sites, clients, compliance and money will be *asked* for all of these things, repeatedly, by people willing to pay. Without a written position, each request gets answered by whoever is in the room, and the architecture drifts toward whichever customer shouted loudest.

Each item is presented as:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Strategic rationale** | Why this is a real opportunity for *this* company, not just an adjacent product that exists |
| **Trigger** | The observable condition that makes it worth doing. Before the trigger, the answer is "not yet" — and that is a complete answer |
| **Dependencies** | What must exist first, in this platform or in the world |
| **Risk** | What goes wrong if we do it, or do it early |
| **Stance** | The recommended posture today |

Item labels are `F-nn`; these are not canon §2 requirement IDs.

**One governing rule for all of §60.** Nothing here may weaken the invariants named at the end of §57.8.3 — Postgres as truth, the integer-paise double-entry ledger, one permission evaluator, one identity, append-only audit, `tenant_id` plus RLS, AI never autonomous on the canon §1.7 list, first-party location evaluation, offline-first only for the Guard App. A future capability that requires breaking one of these is not a feature; it is a different product, and it needs its own architecture decision.

---

### 60.1 F-01 [FUTURE] Deeper B2G capability and real government integration

§13 already specifies the B2G requirements the platform supports today, and §37 is explicit that government portal APIs are not to be invented. The future item is what becomes possible **if** machine-readable interfaces appear: automated tender discovery from an official source rather than assisted scraping and manual curation; licence status verification against an authoritative register instead of document review; e-invoicing and payment-status integration with government buyers; automated EMD and bid-document workflows.

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Government guarding contracts are large, long, and renew. The barrier is not capability but bid administration — compliance evidence, documentation packs, deadline management — which is exactly what a compliance-native platform is good at. If we can make a mid-sized agency bid-ready in a day, that is a durable advantage in a market where most agencies bid on paper. |
| Trigger | (a) A stable, documented, machine-readable interface exists from an authoritative source, **or** (b) ≥5 Professional/Enterprise tenants derive material revenue from tenders discovered through the platform, justifying investment in the assisted path even without APIs. |
| Dependencies | §13 B2G module; §40 compliance engine as the evidence source; §37 integration abstraction so a portal can be swapped without rework; a human curation function that does not scale linearly with listings. |
| Risk | Building against an undocumented or unstable interface creates a maintenance burden that silently consumes a whole engineer. Government procurement also carries integrity risk: any feature that looks like it optimises bid outcomes through means other than genuine capability is a hard no. |
| Stance | Keep the assisted/manual path as the product (canon §0: do not invent APIs). Maintain an integration adapter shape so that a real interface can be plugged in. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-602]` — whether B2G becomes a dedicated business line with its own compliance staffing, or remains a feature of the agency SaaS. |

---

### 60.2 F-02 [FUTURE] Body-worn cameras and video

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Video is the one evidence type the platform cannot currently produce. For incident disputes, client complaints about guard conduct, and guard protection against false allegations, video resolves arguments that GPS and timestamps cannot. It is also the single most requested premium add-on in comparable markets, and it changes the contract value per site materially. |
| Trigger | ≥3 enterprise clients contractually requesting it with a willingness to fund hardware, **and** a storage/retention cost model that survives §52 scrutiny at the target site count. |
| Dependencies | Object storage tiering and lifecycle (§57.3.10); a media pipeline that can handle upload from poor networks; §39 privacy framework extended to continuous recording; consent from guards *and* notice to third parties captured on camera; chain-of-custody controls for anything used as evidence; hardware supply and device management. |
| Risk | Three distinct and serious ones. **Cost:** video storage at retention periods clients ask for is an order of magnitude above every other data class, and it grows with sites, not with users. **Privacy:** continuous recording of a workplace captures bystanders, client staff and the guard's own private moments; the §39.5 guard-privacy boundary becomes much harder to hold. **Evidentiary:** the moment video is used in a dispute, integrity, retention and access become legal questions, and a gap in the footage becomes an accusation. |
| Stance | Do not build the hardware. If pursued, integrate a device vendor and own only the evidence chain, the retention policy and the access control. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-612]` — build / partner / decline, decided before any client commitment. `[ASSUMPTION: A-608]` — that the per-site cost curve for camera hardware and storage falls enough to be commercially viable in this price band; this must be re-tested, not assumed. |

---

### 60.3 F-03 [FUTURE] Vehicle and patrol-fleet telematics

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Mobile patrol and cash-in-transit are adjacent services many agencies already run on spreadsheets and phone calls. The platform already models routes, checkpoints, geofences and time windows; extending them from a walking guard to a patrol vehicle is a small conceptual step with a large commercial one, because vehicle-based services carry higher contract values. |
| Trigger | ≥10 tenants operating patrol vehicles ask for route and fuel visibility, **or** Suraksha's own operation runs ≥5 patrol vehicles. |
| Dependencies | The §34 ingest path (already built for high-frequency location); a device abstraction so an OBD/GPS tracker is just another signal source; route-plan and deviation logic on top of the existing geofence engine; fuel and maintenance records in the asset module. |
| Risk | Hardware support becomes a support burden that the team is not staffed for — trackers fail, get unplugged, and are disputed. Also a scope-creep risk: fleet management is a full product category with mature incumbents, and half-building it satisfies nobody. |
| Stance | Integrate rather than manufacture. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-606]` — whether to certify a small set of third-party trackers or to accept any device that can post to the ingest endpoint. Recommended: certify a short list; an open endpoint creates a data-quality problem that lands in operations. |

---

### 60.4 F-04 [FUTURE] Alarm monitoring and electronic-surveillance convergence

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | The Command Center (§24) is already a 24/7 monitored response desk. The distance between "a wake check was missed" and "an alarm panel fired at gate 3" is smaller than it looks — both are events requiring triage, escalation and a dispatched human. Converging manned guarding with electronic monitoring is the dominant consolidation pattern in mature security markets, and it makes each site stickier because the client's alarm system and their guards are managed on one desk. |
| Trigger | The Command Center has demonstrated sustained sub-target response times at meaningful volume for ≥2 quarters, **and** ≥5 clients ask for their existing alarm systems to be monitored by us. |
| Dependencies | A hardened, physically-isolated alert path (§57.8.3 names this as the year-three SOS cell); integrations with alarm receiver protocols; a false-alarm management process, because false alarms will outnumber real ones by orders of magnitude; possible additional licensing under the configured jurisdiction rules. |
| Risk | The Command Center's attention is a finite, safety-critical resource. Adding a high-volume, high-false-positive event stream to the same desk that handles guard SOS is the fastest way to degrade SOS response — the exact failure the whole platform exists to prevent. Any convergence must be on a separate queue with separate staffing, or not at all. |
| Stance | Attractive and dangerous. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-617]` — build, partner, or acquire. Recommended: partner first with an established monitoring provider to learn the operational shape before owning it, and never share a queue with SOS. |

---

### 60.5 F-05 [FUTURE] Guard training and certification as a product

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Training is already an entity in the canon vocabulary and a compliance input (§40). Turning it into a product does three things at once: it improves the quality of the supply we deploy, it creates a differentiated guard tier that clients will pay more for, and it gives guards a reason to stay with a platform rather than an employer — a genuine retention lever in a workforce where attrition is the dominant operational cost. |
| Trigger | ≥1,000 guards on the platform (a content investment needs an audience), **and** either a client willing to pay a premium for certified guards or a measurable attrition difference between trained and untrained cohorts. |
| Dependencies | Mobile-first, low-bandwidth, in-language content delivered in the Guard App; assessment that works for low-literacy users (voice and video over text); the certification record as a first-class compliance object with an expiry and a renewal ladder; alignment with whatever the configured jurisdiction rules require for training. |
| Risk | Content production is a different business with a different cost structure and a different team. Producing 19 languages of video content is not a side project. There is also a credibility risk: a certificate that means nothing devalues the brand more than having no certificate. |
| Stance | Start by *recording and verifying* training that already happens elsewhere, which costs almost nothing and immediately improves compliance evidence. Produce original content only after the trigger, and consider partnering with an accredited training provider rather than becoming one. |

---

### 60.6 F-06 [FUTURE] Guard benefits, insurance and credit — with a strong caution

This item carries the heaviest ethical weight in §60 and is written accordingly.

**Benefits and insurance** — accident and life cover, health cover, assistance with statutory scheme enrolment — are unambiguously good for the workforce and are a real retention lever. They are also comparatively simple: the platform already knows who is deployed, where, and for how long, which is exactly what an insurer needs to price a group policy.

**Credit is a different thing entirely, and the caution is deliberate and strong.** A platform that knows a worker's income, their employer, their attendance and their bank account, and that also controls their wage disbursement, is in an extraordinarily powerful position relative to a low-wage borrower. Salary advances and small-ticket credit are genuinely useful to people who face a medical bill before payday — and they are also the mechanism by which workers become indebted to the entity that employs them. The failure modes are well documented in comparable markets: advances that roll over, effective interest rates that are far above the headline, deductions at source that leave a worker with nothing, and an employment relationship that becomes a debt relationship.

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Benefits: retention, differentiation, and a genuine improvement in workers' lives. Credit: a revenue line and a retention lock — the second of which is precisely the reason to be suspicious of it. |
| Trigger | Benefits: ≥2,000 guards, enough scale for a group policy to price sensibly. Credit: **no volume trigger is sufficient on its own.** The trigger is a completed ethical and regulatory review plus a governance structure, not a headcount. |
| Dependencies | Verified identity and employment records; reliable payout rails (§35); an insurance or lending partner who is regulated for the purpose; guard-facing disclosure in-language that a low-literacy user actually understands. |
| Risk | Benefits: mis-selling, claim-servicing burden falling on our support team, and reputational damage if a claim is denied. Credit: worker indebtedness, coercion (real or perceived) around deductions, regulatory exposure, and permanent brand damage to a company whose promise is "TRUSTED". A single well-reported story about guards trapped in debt to their own platform would be worse than any outage in this document. |
| Stance | **Pursue insurance and benefits; treat credit as a decision requiring the highest bar.** `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-614]` — whether Suraksha ever facilitates lending to guards at all. If it is ever pursued, four conditions are recommended as absolute preconditions: a regulated partner bearing the credit risk (never Suraksha's balance sheet), a hard cap on total deductions as a share of net wage, no automatic deduction at source without a separate revocable consent, and no linkage whatsoever between credit uptake and shift allocation or employment. If those four cannot be guaranteed, the answer is no. `[ASSUMPTION: A-609]` — that a regulated partner will accept these constraints; if not, that itself is the answer. |

---

### 60.7 F-07 [FUTURE] Guard career and skills graph

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Today a guard's history is scattered across employers and evaporates when they change agency. A portable record — verified identity, verified documents, shifts worked, sites served, incidents handled well, training completed, supervisor ratings — turns a commodity worker into a professional with a track record. That is good for the guard (better posts, better pay), good for clients (evidence-based selection), and creates the strongest possible network effect for the platform, because the record follows the person across agencies. |
| Trigger | ≥10,000 guards with ≥6 months of history each, and ≥3 agencies willing to hire on the basis of another agency's record. |
| Dependencies | Cross-tenant data sharing that does not breach §39 or the tenant isolation invariant — this is the hard part, and it requires explicit guard consent as the legal and ethical basis, with the guard controlling what is shared and with whom. Identity assurance strong enough that a record cannot be claimed by the wrong person. |
| Risk | A permanent, portable performance record about a low-wage worker is a surveillance artefact as much as a career asset. A single unfair rating, a disputed incident, or a supervisor's grudge could follow someone across the industry. Any such graph needs: guard visibility of everything in it, a dispute and correction path, time-decay on negative entries, and a prohibition on using it for anything other than what the guard consented to. Without those, this becomes a blacklist. |
| Stance | Design guard-controlled from the first line of code. The guard owns the record and grants access; agencies never see it by default. |

---

### 60.8 F-08 [FUTURE] Cross-agency mutual aid networks

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Every agency has the same problem on the same days: a guard does not turn up, and a post is uncovered in two hours. Individually they solve it by phoning friends. A structured mutual-aid network — agency A covers agency B's post for a shift, at an agreed rate, with the compliance and payment mechanics handled — turns an informal favour economy into a marketplace transaction. Trinetra (§19) is already the substrate for this. |
| Trigger | ≥50 agency tenants in the same city, with measurable unfilled-post volume that the network could absorb. |
| Dependencies | Marketplace and settlement (§19, §35); compliance verification that works across tenants (whose licence covers this deployment? whose insurance? who is the employer of record for that shift?); a trust and rating layer; rapid dispute resolution. |
| Risk | The employer-of-record and licence-coverage questions are genuinely hard and are legal questions we may not state conclusions about (canon §0) — they must be handled as configured jurisdiction rules and reviewed by counsel per market. There is also an adverse-selection risk: agencies will offer their least-wanted shifts and their least-reliable guards, and the network's quality collapses unless the rating layer has teeth. |
| Stance | High strategic value, high complexity. Prototype in one city with a small, hand-picked set of agencies before generalising. |

---

### 60.9 F-09 [FUTURE] International expansion to comparable regulated markets

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | The architecture is already multi-jurisdiction by construction (§40.8): licence geography is a first-class object, compliance rules are configuration rather than code, and money is stored as integer minor units. Markets with a similar shape — a licensed private-security regime, a large low-to-mid-wage guard workforce, fragmented agencies, and smartphone penetration — could reuse most of the platform. The Gulf, South-East Asia and parts of Africa are the usual candidates. |
| Trigger | The domestic operation is genuinely repeatable — the §59.17.4 exit criterion met at multiple cities — **and** an in-market partner exists who owns local licensing and operations. Never expansion by remote control. |
| Dependencies | Localisation beyond translation (right-to-left where relevant, local number/date/address formats, local payment rails, local identity documents); data residency per market, which may force a second regional deployment (§57.8); local compliance rule sets authored by local counsel; a support model in local time zones. |
| Risk | Expansion is the classic premature-scaling failure: it consumes the founding team's attention at exactly the moment the domestic operation needs it most. It also multiplies the compliance surface, and a compliance failure in a new market can jeopardise the licence position in the home market. |
| Stance | Not before the domestic business is boring. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-616]` — the first market, chosen on regulatory similarity and partner availability, not on market-size decks. |

---

### 60.10 F-10 [FUTURE] API and partner ecosystem, and an app marketplace

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | The Enterprise plan already promises an enterprise API (canon §1.4). Turning that into an ecosystem — documented public API, sandbox, webhooks, OAuth app registration, a directory of partner integrations (accounting, HRMS, access control, visitor systems, facility management) — moves the platform from a product to infrastructure, and lets other people build the long tail of integrations we will never prioritise. |
| Trigger | ≥10 Enterprise tenants with custom integrations already built by hand, **or** ≥3 unsolicited requests to build on top of the platform. Both are signals that the demand is real rather than aspirational. |
| Dependencies | API versioning and stability guarantees (§33) — an ecosystem cannot be built on an API we still change weekly; a scoped OAuth model layered on the one permission evaluator (§57.4), so a third-party app can never exceed the granting user's permissions; per-app rate limits and metering; a security review process for listed apps; the isolated `api-enterprise` pool from §57.2.2. |
| Risk | A public API is a permanent compatibility commitment and a materially larger attack surface, particularly around tenant isolation — a third-party app with a token is the most likely future vector for a cross-tenant leak. An app marketplace also creates a review and liability burden nobody budgets for. |
| Stance | Sequence it: stable versioned API → webhooks → sandbox and docs → OAuth apps → curated directory → open marketplace. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-618]` — curated (we review and approve every listed app) versus open. Recommended: curated indefinitely, given the sensitivity of the data. |

---

### 60.11 F-11 [FUTURE] Predictive site and area risk intelligence

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | The platform will accumulate the richest operational dataset in Indian private security: incidents by type, location and time; patrol and attendance patterns; SOS events; site characteristics. That supports genuinely useful products — risk scoring for a prospective site (which drives accurate pricing), staffing recommendations by time of day, early warning where incident patterns are shifting, and evidence-based conversations with clients about what their site actually needs. |
| Trigger | ≥2 years of incident data at sufficient density in at least one city. Below that density, any "prediction" is noise dressed as insight. |
| Dependencies | Data quality operations (§59.10) — this is the dependency that actually decides whether it works; the analytics warehouse (§32.6.5, §57.8); §41 AI governance for model evaluation, drift monitoring and explainability. |
| Risk | Three, all serious. **Spurious confidence:** a risk score presented to a client as fact when it is a weak correlation. **Feedback loops:** sites we score as high-risk get more patrols, which generate more recorded incidents, which raise the score. **Discrimination:** area-level risk scoring can encode socio-economic and communal bias and produce outcomes that are indefensible — for example, systematically pricing certain neighbourhoods higher or refusing service. §41.6 fairness obligations apply in full. |
| Stance | Build the descriptive analytics first — "here is what actually happened at sites like yours" is valuable, honest, and carries none of the predictive risk. Move to prediction only with an explainability requirement, a documented fairness evaluation, and human review before any score affects pricing or service availability. |

---

### 60.12 F-12 [FUTURE] Drone and IoT sensor integration

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Large industrial sites, warehouses and construction projects have perimeters that are expensive to patrol on foot. Sensors (door contacts, motion, gate barriers, temperature, environmental) and, in some jurisdictions, drone-assisted perimeter patrol, reduce the headcount needed for the same coverage. Architecturally these are just additional signal sources into the ingest path built for GPS. |
| Trigger | ≥3 industrial clients requesting sensor-linked monitoring, with contract value that justifies the integration and support cost. |
| Dependencies | The generic signal-ingest abstraction (§34.3, §57); a device registry and health monitoring — an offline sensor that nobody notices is worse than no sensor; alert-triage logic that does not swamp the Command Center (see F-04's warning); for drones, a regulatory review under the configured jurisdiction rules, plus trained operators. |
| Risk | Device fleet management is an operational burden the team will underestimate. Drones carry a heavier regulatory and safety load than anything else in this document, plus privacy exposure from aerial imagery over neighbouring property. Sensor false positives degrade the response desk exactly as alarm monitoring does. |
| Stance | Sensors: plausible, incremental, and a natural extension of the ingest path. Drones: treat as a separate business decision with its own regulatory review, not as a platform feature. |

---

### 60.13 F-13 [FUTURE] Facial recognition — a high-bar decision, not a feature

The platform already uses face capture for guard enrolment and attendance verification against the guard's *own* enrolled template, with consent, under §39. That is 1:1 verification of a consenting worker, and it is in scope today. **Facial recognition in the sense meant here — 1:N identification of people who have not consented, watchlist matching, visitor identification, or recognising individuals across sites — is a categorically different capability, and this document recommends treating it as a decision at board level rather than a feature request in a backlog.**

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale (stated fairly) | Clients will ask. Visitor management, banned-person alerts at retail and event sites, and unauthorised-access detection are genuine security use cases, and competitors will offer them. Declining has a commercial cost, and it is honest to say so. |
| Trigger | **No commercial trigger is sufficient.** The only condition under which this should be considered is: a settled legal basis under the configured jurisdiction rules, reviewed by counsel; a documented, tested accuracy and demographic-bias evaluation on a population representative of where it would be deployed; an operational model where a match is a *prompt for a human to look*, never an automatic action; and a public position we are willing to defend by name. |
| Dependencies | §41 AI governance in full; §39 privacy with a lawful basis for non-consenting data subjects; notice at the point of capture; retention limits measured in hours, not months; an audit trail of every match and every human decision. |
| Risk | The highest in this section. Demographic accuracy disparities are well documented and would fall hardest on exactly the populations most likely to be misidentified at a gate. A false match at a security checkpoint is not a bad recommendation — it is a person being detained. The reputational, regulatory and human cost of getting this wrong is unbounded, and the regulatory trajectory is uncertain and tightening in most comparable jurisdictions. `[ASSUMPTION: A-610]` — that the regulatory position will continue to tighten rather than relax; if that assumption is wrong the calculus changes, but not the ethics. |
| Stance | **Recommended default: decline.** Offer the consented 1:1 guard-verification capability that already exists, and decline 1:N identification of non-consenting individuals. `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-613]` — whether this capability is permitted in the product at all. If the answer is ever yes, it should be a written, named, board-level decision with the evaluation evidence attached — not an integration a client procured. |

---

### 60.14 F-14 [FUTURE] Platform data products

| Field | Position |
|---|---|
| Strategic rationale | Aggregate, anonymised insight has genuine value to parties who cannot obtain it elsewhere: wage and attrition benchmarks by city and role for agencies; incident-pattern reporting for insurers and industry bodies; sector reports that establish Suraksha as the authority on how Indian private security actually operates. §42.7 already contemplates cross-tenant benchmarking within the product. |
| Trigger | ≥100 tenants and ≥50,000 guards — below which "aggregate" is not aggregate enough to be either statistically meaningful or safely anonymous. |
| Dependencies | §39 privacy constraints as the binding limit, not as a compliance checkbox: a documented anonymisation method, k-anonymity thresholds with a minimum cohort size, suppression of small cells, and a re-identification risk assessment before any external release. Tenant-facing transparency about what is aggregated and a genuine opt-out. Contractual clarity in the tenant agreement, agreed in advance rather than retro-fitted. |
| Risk | Two failure modes. **Re-identification:** in a market where one agency dominates a city, "aggregate city data" is that agency's data. **Trust:** the moment tenants believe their operational data is being sold, the SaaS proposition is damaged in a market where agencies talk to each other. Guard-level data — location, biometrics, personal identifiers — must never be part of any data product in any form, aggregated or otherwise. |
| Stance | Start inside the product: give tenants benchmarks about themselves versus an anonymised peer set, which is valuable and low-risk. External commercialisation only after `[DECISION REQUIRED: D-615]` — whether anonymised platform data may be commercialised at all, with the tenant agreement, the anonymisation standard and the opt-out settled first. |

---

### 60.15 Sequencing

The items above are not equally distant, and doing them in the wrong order wastes the platform's structural advantages. This is the recommended ordering, expressed as horizons rather than dates, since dates for `[FUTURE]` items are fiction.

| Horizon | Items | What makes them first |
|---|---|---|
| **H1 — natural extensions** (reuse what exists, small new surface) | F-05 training record-keeping · F-11 descriptive site analytics · F-14 in-product benchmarks · F-10 stable versioned API and webhooks | Each is a thin layer over data and infrastructure that already exists, with contained risk and immediate tenant value |
| **H2 — adjacent capability** (new integrations, new operations) | F-03 telematics · F-12 sensors · F-06 insurance and benefits · F-08 mutual aid pilot | Each needs a new external dependency or a new operational process, but no new invariant |
| **H3 — new businesses** (different cost structure, different team) | F-02 body-worn video · F-04 alarm monitoring convergence · F-07 career graph · F-01 deeper B2G · F-10 open marketplace | Each is effectively a second business with its own economics, staffing and risk profile |
| **H4 — high-bar or deferred indefinitely** | F-09 international · F-13 facial recognition · F-06 credit · F-12 drones | Each requires either a settled regulatory position or a domestic operation that runs without founder attention — and two of them may correctly never happen |

---

### 60.16 What would make us wrong

Three strategic assumptions carry this plan. If any of them is false, parts of this document are not merely wrong in detail — they are wrong in kind. Each is stated with the early indicators that would tell us, well before the financial statements do.

#### 60.16.1 Assumption 1 — agencies will adopt software at all

Everything in canon §1.4, §19, §20 and §52's second revenue engine assumes that a meaningful share of India's ~35,000 licensed agencies (A-001) will pay ₹5,000–₹10,000 a month for operational software and will actually change how they work. The counter-case is serious: this is a low-margin, relationship-driven, paper-and-WhatsApp industry where the buyer is often the owner, the workforce is transient, and the current process — however inefficient — works well enough that switching costs feel larger than the benefit. If agencies buy the software and never reach activation milestone M5 (§59.6.1), we have built a SaaS business with SaaS costs and services-business retention.

| Early indicator | What it would tell us | Watch from |
|---|---|---|
| M5 (80% of shifts with platform attendance by day 14) conversion below 50% across the first 20 tenants | The product is being bought and not used — churn is already decided | Month 2 of SaaS availability |
| Median weekly active users per tenant stuck at 1 (the owner) | No operational adoption; it is a dashboard, not a system of record | Month 3 |
| Renewal conversations dominated by price rather than by feature requests | We are a cost line, not a dependency | First renewal cohort |
| Support tickets that are all onboarding and none operational | Nobody has got far enough in to have real problems | Continuous |
| **If false** | The SaaS engine is repositioned: sell the marketplace and the deployment service, not the ERP. The Agency Portal becomes the operational tool for *our* supply network rather than a standalone product, and §52's Engine B economics are rebuilt around take-rate rather than subscription. The architecture survives — the multi-tenancy is exactly what a supply network needs — but the pricing, the sales motion and the roadmap change substantially. | |

#### 60.16.2 Assumption 2 — clients will pay a premium for verifiable delivery

The entire product thesis — GPS attendance, wake checks, patrol evidence, live tracking, an audited compliance chain — assumes that buyers of guarding services will pay more for *proof* that the service was delivered. The counter-case is that guarding is procured on price by facility managers whose incentive is to hit a budget line, that the evidence is used once during onboarding and never looked at again, and that our cost base is therefore higher than competitors who send a guard and a paper register.

| Early indicator | What it would tell us | Watch from |
|---|---|---|
| Win/loss analysis where price is the stated reason in >60% of losses and evidence is never cited as a reason to win | The premium does not exist in this buyer's mind | First 20 competitive deals |
| Client portal engagement collapsing after month 1 (logins, live-view sessions, report downloads) | The evidence is bought once and never consumed | Month 2 of each client |
| Renewal negotiations that discount to match a non-technical competitor | The differentiation is not defensible at contract time | First renewal cohort |
| Clients declining patrol/wake-check modules to reduce price | They are optional in the buyer's mind, not core | Continuous |
| **If false** | The premium positioning collapses into a cost-efficiency argument: the platform must then justify itself by lowering *our* cost to deliver (fewer supervisors per site, lower attrition, faster replacement, less admin) rather than by raising price. That is a viable business, but it makes operational efficiency the north star instead of evidence quality, and it changes which parts of §51's roadmap matter most. | |

#### 60.16.3 Assumption 3 — guards will use the app reliably, on their own phones

Offline-first, GPS attendance, wake checks and SOS all assume that a low-wage guard, on a low-end Android phone they paid for, with a data pack they paid for, will install the app, keep it installed, keep it permitted, keep it excluded from battery optimisation, and use it on every shift. §57.3.3 argues the mobile stack decision precisely on this basis. The counter-case is uninstalls after a battery complaint, phones shared or sold, permissions revoked by an OEM cleanup tool, guards who resent being tracked, and supervisors who quietly go back to a paper register because it is faster.

| Early indicator | What it would tell us | Watch from |
|---|---|---|
| Daily active guards ÷ guards on duty below 90% in the launch cohort | The app is not the system of record; the paper register still is | Week 1 |
| Uninstall or permission-revocation rate above 5% per month | Battery, data cost or trust is driving guards off the platform | Month 1 |
| Rising share of attendance recorded by supervisor override rather than by guard check-in | The workaround has become the process | Week 2 |
| Wake-check acknowledgement latency drifting upward, or acknowledgements clustering suspiciously | The mechanism is being gamed, which is worse than it not existing | Month 1 |
| Guard grievances or exit interviews citing surveillance | The consent (§39.5) is nominal, not real, and there is an ethical problem as well as a product one | Continuous |
| **If false** | The response is layered, and each layer costs money. First: company-provided devices for a subset of posts, which changes the §52 cost stack materially. Second: site-based capture — a fixed device or NFC/QR checkpoint at the post rather than in the guard's pocket — which changes the data model's assumption that the guard's phone is the sensor. Third, and most consequential: if guards will not carry a tracked device at all, the SOS and wake-check propositions require dedicated hardware, and the product becomes a hardware-and-service business rather than a software one. This is the assumption whose failure would change the architecture most, which is why §57.3.3 argues it at length and why §59.17.1 puts a person on a night shift in week one to watch it happen. | |

#### 60.16.4 The habit this section is asking for

None of the three is settled by argument; each is settled by looking. The commitment worth making is procedural rather than analytical: these nine indicator sets are reviewed by name at the quarterly leadership meeting (§59.1) alongside the metric set, and each one has a pre-agreed threshold at which the response is triggered rather than debated. A strategy document is only useful if it has written down, in advance, what would change its mind.
